By the Tiantai śramaṇa Fazhao.
The Profound Meaning of the Mysterious (2):

The Profound Meaning of the Secret Teaching (1) (7). The meaning of "secret and indeterminate" is not as [some claim]. For the Tathāgata has attained the supreme mastery over all dharmas; if it were [otherwise], his wisdom...
Whether in terms of capacity, time, or place, the three mysteries and four gates are without obstruction or hindrance. At this seat, the Sudden is taught;

in the ten directions, the Gradual and the Indeterminate are taught. Those in the ten directions do not hear what is taught at this seat of the Sudden, nor does this seat hear what is taught in the ten directions.
Or, while the ten directions teach the Sudden and the Indeterminate, this seat teaches the Gradual; each is unaware of or hears nothing from the other. This is what is revealed here.
That is the esoteric; or for one person, he may teach the sudden, or for many people, he may teach the gradual; or he may teach the indeterminate.
Or for one person, he may teach the gradual, while for many people, he may teach the sudden, each being unaware of the other, thus manifesting the exoteric and the esoteric to one another.

Or in one seat, while remaining silent, he may speak throughout the ten directions; or while the ten directions remain silent, he may speak in one seat; or both may remain silent, or both may speak, each being unaware of the other.
Know that these mutually manifest the exoteric and the esoteric.

Regarding the commentary (Jian, Vol. 1, Section 22) on "whether it be wisdom or capacity": "Wisdom" refers to the skillful stratagems of the Great Sage; "capacity" refers to the differing stages [of practitioners].
Without selecting for time or place, the secrets of body, speech, and mind—regardless of which of the four gates they follow—are unimpeded and sovereign, responding appropriately to the moment.

All these assemblies are established without fail. Regarding the detailed explanation of their characteristics, I shall provisionally rely upon three dharmas to manifest those characteristics. Why is this?

Because when these three dharmas are contrasted with the secret [teaching], the four teachings of the transformational ritual (hua-yi) become complete in both text and meaning, spontaneously encompassing the four [vehicles] such as the Tripitaka.

Within this, there are further two parts: first, an explanation based on the characteristics of the three types of preaching; second, an explanation based on the characteristics of preaching and silence.
Regarding the first three [statements], the middle two are explained first by way of mutual relation across the ten directions, and then alternatively by way of many people within a single direction.
Since it is so for one direction, it is likewise for all ten directions. In each of these two passages, there is first a formal explanation, followed by a conclusion beginning with "each and every.
Within the section concerning the mutual relation between speaking and silence, the two meanings of both the ten directions and the people should also be fully present.

Regarding the passage stating that "those who are not in mutual relation with others" is abbreviated, it is because both are silent or both are speaking; logically, this should be as previously explained.

By analogy, when the first three dharmas are in mutual relation, one should likewise say "both sudden and gradual," "both indeterminate," and so forth. Since the text omits these, they are also abbreviated.
Now, if it is said that being "both silent and speaking while mutually unknown" constitutes "secrecy" (*mimi*), what prevents "both sudden and gradual" from being the same?

"Mutually unaware of one another" is also a binding [classification] for each case below. Regarding "mutually unaware of one another," although the preceding text merely says "in this" or "in that," it should also be explained as mutual;

by citing one instance as an illustration, one can verify that the "indeterminate" and the "esoteric" are distinguished solely by whether there is mutual awareness or mutual unawareness. Here, the "manifest" [teaching] also extends its meaning to the others.

The seventh [category] is "secret" because these seven do not emerge from it; therefore, as the preceding text states, since there are "revealed gradual and sudden" and "revealed indeterminate," all seven are intended to be revealed.

Question (17): If the Mahāyāna of the *Avataṃsaka* and the Hinayāna of the Deer Park are eternally separated, why is it that as soon as the Vaipulya is preached, those in the same assembly hear it together?

Answer: If one considers its secret, horizontal manifestation, there is no time when it is not all-pervasive; however, if one discusses its vertical progression in relation to the horizontal, then its concealment or manifestation depends upon the capacity of the sentient beings.
The divination slip states: "As for the five flavors, they constitute a single path of vertical progression; in every flavor, the aspects of 'half' and 'full' mutually complete one another.

This means that while the Southern masters exclusively employ the five flavors and the Northern masters exclusively employ the half-and-full, if one employs them according to the mutual completion of the five flavors and the half-and-full, then in the *Avataṃsaka* there is only the full and no half, whereas in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the half is discarded to clarify the full. It is not so.
The five flavors each have their own partial and complete aspects. Furthermore, it is said that it was only upon reaching the Deer Park that the Exoteric and Esoteric were distinguished;

this describes how those of the Lesser Vehicle and the initial stages of the Human and Heavenly vehicles did not pass through the *Avataṃsaka*, and thus the story of Trapusa still belongs to the Exoteric, with the distinction between Exoteric and Esoteric only occurring at the Deer Park.
Regarding the "Secret" (in *Wenju* 1 and 5): it is hidden and not transmitted.

Regarding the "Profound Record" (in *Miaoji* 1 and 17): that which is secret and not transmitted is because from the time after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa until now, it has not been the subject of exposition;

it is something that even Ānanda was unable to receive, so how could it be within the measure of those who propagate the teachings? Furthermore, it is not that Ānanda did not transmit secrets; rather, there are secrets conveyed according to the capacities of sentient beings.
Because it is not something transmitted by ear, that which is employed in the esoteric is entirely manifest teaching; therefore, transmitting the esoteric is merely termed transmitting the manifest.
*Miaoxuan* (6.18): Since the esoteric is hidden and not widely circulated in the world, this is set aside and not discussed.
The seventh and tenth sections on the "Secret" (mi) are kept hidden as the Great Sage responds to the capacities of beings; for now, they shall be set aside and not discussed.

If one were to explain them, they would merely be called the "Oral Secret" (kōmitsu) in responding to the four types of karmic conditions. That these various instances are mutually unknown to one another is precisely their intended meaning.
Although the manifest and the secret differ, the teaching does not transcend these four; therefore, they are not further discussed here.
Regarding *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (1–8): The Teaching is the speech of the Sage directed toward those below. The Sage is able to manifest both the exoteric and the esoteric;
when ordinary people proclaim it, they can only transmit the exoteric and cannot transmit the esoteric. Why is it that listeners are able to form contemplations?

Or, why is it that those who have attained the stage of the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*)—being able to pervade the three thousandfold world-system with a single wondrous sound and reaching everywhere at will—are able to transmit it?

Regarding the "Esoteric Teaching" (*Bijiao*): In the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*), fascicle 1, part 1 (33), it is stated that [the discussion] strictly concerns the Master of Transformation (*huazhu*) in terms of whether he attains or does not attain the esoteric; this specifically refers to a Sage, for whom the Sage can provide dual benefit.

Since the present discussion concerns an ordinary teacher (*fanshi*), the esoteric aspect is omitted. Therefore, for one who cultivates contemplation, there is no sense of esoteric benefit; hence it says, "for the listener."

For what reason? During the sequence of contemplation, one may occasionally attain a lower level of meaning and be established in the stage of attainment; although such a person remains an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), there are many types of ordinary teachers.
Those at the fifth grade and below are still said to be "not yet having attained" the stage of the purity of the six faculties (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*).

Although they lack the benefit of the three wheels of the secret oral transmission, they are able to transmit the wondrous sound throughout the great trichiliocosm. Because this differs from the transformative power of a Buddha, it is said that those who receive the teaching are able to transmit it.
Nevertheless, there is no hidden benefit.
The *Miaoxuan* (10/15), citing the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, states: "When I first attained Buddhahood, bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges came to inquire about this meaning;
they were no different from you. All such meanings and categories found in various Mahāyāna sūtras are termed the characteristics of the Sudden Teaching (*dunjiao*).
Divination Stick (10) (18): Those who first attained the Way merely borrowed the aid of the secret [teachings] to enter this;
it clarifies that even the initial attainment at the Deer Park has the meaning of the sudden, let alone the various other sūtras.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, fascicle ten (twenty-three), states: "I sat at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree and first attained perfect awakening...
(and so forth). This passage connects back to what preceded it.

Zhi Guan (9) (28): Furthermore, I have said that when the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions first asked about this meaning immediately after my attainment of the Way, there was a secret teaching concerning the twelve links of dependent origination within the context of Nirvana.

*Fuxing* (Vol. 9, Part 2; 14): Furthermore, the passage below cites evidence from the secret teachings (*guhyaka-śāsana*) [and so forth]. Thus we know that even at the very beginning of the gradual teaching, there were bodhisattvas who secretly heard this meaning.

Commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (4) (10). Regarding the old interpretation that those who sat at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) also once asked [questions], some say these were questions from within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, yet the translation of the text was incomplete and the passages have not yet arrived.
Others say they are texts from the "partial" or "indeterminate" teachings, which likewise have not arrived.

Still others say they belong to the "secret teachings" and are not included within the "revealed" category; however, all such views are incorrect. Herein it is clarified that the "site of enlightenment" refers precisely to...
The second fascicle of the *Yuanchu yuanman shizuo feifangbian daochang* (The Original Beginning, Perfectly Complete, Initial Seating, Non-Expedient Path) states:

"I have long since, throughout immeasurable kalpas, already attained Buddhahood; it is just as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where it is said that since my attainment of Buddhahood, an extremely long time has passed.
This directly addresses past inquiries, which are no different from those of today; it is not merely for the sake of a single transformation.

The Profound and Mysterious Meaning of the Twelve Divisions of Scripture (1–17). Furthermore, within each individual teaching, there are likewise twelve divisions of scripture, each arising through the application of *siddhānta*.
If one seeks to hear the various phenomena accomplished by the tenfold dependent origination, or the true causes and conditions regarding worldly affairs, [one should rely on the *Sūtra* division].
When the Tathāgata speaks directly of the dharmas of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases—whether provisional or real—this is called *sūtra*.
When he uses four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, or ten lines of verse to reiterate matters concerning the world, the aggregates, the sense bases, and so forth, this is called *geya*.
When he directly records future events for sentient beings, even up to the prediction that a pigeon or a sparrow shall attain Buddhahood, this is called *vyākaraṇa*.
The exposition of matters such as the world, the aggregates (skandhas), and the bases (āyatanas) through prose or isolated verses is called *gāthā*.
When one speaks of worldly matters spontaneously without anyone having asked, it is called *udāna*.
When prohibitions are established based on unwholesome events in the world, it is called *nidāna*. When worldly matters are explained by means of similes, it is called *avadāna*.
That which describes events from former worlds is called Itivṛttaka; that which describes events of past births is called Jātaka;
that which describes the vast occurrences of the world is called Vaipulya; that which describes unprecedented events of the world is called Adbhutadharma;
and that which consists of inquiries and refutations concerning the world is [the Praśnavyākaraṇa].
This is called *upadeśa*. These twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) arise from the perspective of the world-standpoint (*loka-siddhānta*) in order to gladden sentient beings.
(6) (15) Now, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the titles are designated as follows: first, *sūtra*, which is translated here as "Dharma-source" (*dharmamūla*).

The Scripture on the Revelation of Expedient Means (Chapter on the Collective [Teachings] of All Buddhas, Chapter on Expedient Means): Śāriputra, the underlying intent of the Buddhas’ preaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate is difficult to understand. Why is this?
It is because I have expounded it through immeasurable and innumerable expedient means, by means of various causes, conditions, parables, and modes of expression.

Regarding the various dharmas, the commentary (4) [states]: From "preaching according to what is appropriate" onwards is the opening of the provisional means (*upāya*). (And so forth. First, it clarifies that the Buddha-way is taught as a provisional means according to the three types of capacities;
therefore, it says "according to what is appropriate. However, while the Buddha’s intention lies in the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*), sentient beings are unable to understand it.
Therefore, it is said that the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) is difficult to understand.
[Section 4] (32) First, explaining that the Buddha-way is most difficult to know refers to the intent behind the bestowal of provisional means (*upāya*).

Since the name "bestowal" does not appear in the various teachings, and because one now wishes to clarify the opening [of the truth], one first describes that which is opened—namely, that which is bestowed. Therefore, this is the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text).
One should know that when the intent of "establishing the provisional" lies in the real, it means opening the provisional to reveal the real;
when the intent of "opening the provisional to reveal the real" lies in the provisional, it means concealing the real within the provisional. Thus, there is nothing outside of the real.

Whether concealed or revealed, the benefit for sentient beings resides in the fundamental source, which has never increased or decreased. Therefore, prior to its being opened, it was not merely that [the real] was not spoken of.
Since the name "revealing the reality" contains no words for "provisionally employing expedients," when one speaks of words that are "suitable for expedients," it must necessarily reveal the reality.
(4) (16) Regarding the phrase "by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful means": this clarifies the opening of the expedients; these dharmas are all for the sake of the One.
Because it is the Buddha-vehicle (buddhayāna), it clarifies the reality (*tattva*).

Regarding the commentary on fascicle five (and eight): although the "Chapter on the Three Times" states that clarifying reality means "this dharma," and the "Chapter on Śākyamuni" uses these two characters [to mean] that both the provisional and the real are pointed out as being real, it is therefore called "clarifying reality.
Why? Because in the past, when the provisional was bestowed, there was not even yet the name "provisional."
How much more so, since the real exists; now that the provisional is revealed, the provisional is itself the real. Therefore it is said, "All these dharmas are for the Buddha-vehicle.
Thus we know that the description of the bestowal of the provisional is intended to reveal the real.
[Sūtra] (Expedient Means Chapter): "The Dharma attained by all Buddhas is taught to sentient beings through immeasurable powers of expedient means...
[etc. [Commentary] (4) (22): "The Dharma attained by all Buddhas" refers to the various provisional dharmas attained through the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanāmārga*).

[Sub-commentary] (5) (14): "Various provisional dharmas attained through the cultivation of the path" refers precisely to the provisional dharmas realized when the causes for one's own practice have reached fulfillment.
When one speaks of the "power of self-benefit" (svārtha-vaśitā), this very dharma-body cannot be described [in its ultimate nature];

yet, for the sake of sentient beings, it is explained through skillful means (*upāya*) as the "power of benefiting others" (*parārtha-vaśitā*), and so forth. Thus, we know that the single phrase "opening the provisional" (*kaikuan*) established here actually possesses two meanings:

first, it surpasses what was previously bestowed; second, it reveals the reality (*bhūtārtha*) which was not pointed out by the former [teachings]. That which is opened has no [independent] existence.
By explaining the ultimate reality (*bhūta-artha*), it points to the provisional; this is known as the provisional, which is not the final goal.

Once the ultimate has been revealed, the provisional is entirely the ultimate. (1) (22) Ninth, "Opening the Provisional to Reveal the Ultimate": Among all dharmas, there is none that is not wondrous. A single form and a single fragrance are nothing other than the Middle Way.
Yet, because sentient beings' deluded minds obstruct the wondrous, the Great Compassion accords with their capacities and does not contend with the world.

Therefore, it clarifies that the provisional and the real are not the same (and so forth). Now, opening the gate of skillful means and revealing the mark of reality, [the Buddha] speaks only of the one great cause and condition for a single purpose:
he teaches the unsurpassed path, opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and enables all to enter the ultimate reality.
The destruction of the conjured city is the resolution of the coarse; the arrival at the treasure site is the entry into the subtle.

Divination Stick (2)(9): First, a general clarification of the fundamental reality of all phenomena; second, "Next, through great compassion," etc., explaining the provisional application of means; third, "Now, by opening [the provisional]," etc., revealing the ultimate reality. Regarding the first section:

since the Dharma is fundamentally wondrous, its appearance as coarse is due to the mental dispositions of sentient beings; therefore, one knows that by merely opening [the provisional], the mental and emotional conditions naturally return to their original state (and so forth).

Within the actual opening [of the provisional], there are again two parts: first, a general opening based on the Dharma to clarify the original intent behind the application of transformative teachings; second...

Having eliminated the subordinate reliance on the Two Vehicles, it is difficult to explain; yet by clarifying the aspect of opening, it is shown that the coarse is itself the subtle, and the provisional city of transformation is itself the treasure abode.

now, the two conceivable [aspects] are merged back into the two inconceivable [aspects]. The two inconceivable [aspects]...
Pure and singular *amṛta* (the supreme essence).
[Verse] (3) (22). If one relies on the text of the present sutra, such a matter has never been spoken to others.
[Commentary] (4) (7). Regarding the phrase "never spoken," this refers generally to the teaching and so forth; it means that previously, when discussed individually, it had not yet been revealed.
Regarding the principle of practice, it was either previously encountered or already established; however, as for the "opening" (kai) of persons, this was not present in the previous teaching.

Because the categories [of the current teaching] are established based on what was absent in the previous teaching, we know that it is not the same substance. Without the skillful means (upāya), there would be no basis for applying the opening and so forth. (This clarifies the principle by which opening is possible.)

Regarding the six phrases (19): the "Recorded" (7) [section] states that taking across the sections constitutes sameness, while remaining within the respective divisions constitutes difference. Thus, sameness refers to the same substance, and difference refers to different substances.

Difference concerns the provisional application of skillful means (*upāya*), while sameness concerns the revelation of the ultimate truth. It is like a single official or citizen who, by their nature, belongs to two jurisdictions (revealing what was already known as the same).

*Śikṣānanda’s Commentary on the Śraddhābhiṣamaya*, Part 6 (28); *Fuxing*, Part 6, Lower (13): At the summit of the true Dharma-realm, he opens the topknot of expedient means that is of one essence with reality, revealing the bright pearl of the true mark (spoken from the perspective of the response).

[Divination Stick (6), End] Regarding the opening of the aforementioned various coarse [manifestations], one must also, in accordance with the Path of Teaching (*jiaodao*), open the Buddha’s manifestations of the two teachings.
Master Beifeng said: "One must know that the opening of the provisional is precisely for the sake of the sentient beings' capacities and emotions (*jinqing*).

If one discusses the Buddha's own intent, there is nothing that is not of the same essence (*tongti*). However, the current opening and manifestation is not for the sake of the Buddha's intent, but precisely for the sake of the sentient beings' capacities and emotions. This is truly because..."
Within the Tathāgatagarbha, the provisional and the real are inherently complete; the provisional and the real share a single essence, and that essence is fundamentally perfect and wondrous.

However, because sentient beings fail to understand this due to their capacities and conditions, the Tathāgata employs skillful means to accord with those capacities, establishing provisional teachings for the sake of the ultimate.

Thus, the *Zang* (Treasury) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings exclusively expound the partial truth (*ekāṃśika-satya*), while the *Bie* (Distinct) teaching involves the gradual severance of the nine grades [of afflictions]. Sentient beings, however, cling to these [provisional teachings].

That which can lead toward reality but cannot yet be reality itself is called "partial" and "coarse"; it refers to provisional teachings that possess a different substance [from the ultimate]. When the assembly at the Lotus Sūtra gathering reached maturity, the time required for the opening [of the truth] arrived;
he pointed out that what they clung to as "self" was merely a provisional teaching of skillful means (*upāya*) taught as if it were real.

By bestowing the provisional, it is realized that the provisional is itself the real; thus one comes to know that the coarse is itself the subtle, and difference is itself identity. As the *Xuan* (Mysterious Commentary) says: "The primordial source is suchness (*tathatā*)."
[This refers to] the *ālayavijñāna* and so forth.

The *Zhinan* (Guide) states: "The *Zhenglun* (Treatise on Correctness) takes the distinct entities as that which is opened [and revealed]. One must know that within the Secret Treasury (*guhyagarbha*), the provisional and the real are one in essence.

Sentient beings, failing to understand this, give rise to false conceptualizations and consequently produce craving and attachment. The followers of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) drift through the five paths of rebirth."

The Buddha causes beings to return to their original nature; he cannot avoid employing provisional means (*upāya*) to mature their capacities and conditions, ultimately leading them to realize the ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*).

Thus, the *Xuánwén* (Profound Meaning) explains three stages: first, clarifying that all dharmas are fundamentally real; second, the great compassion of employing provisional means; and third, opening up those provisional means to reveal the ultimate reality. To investigate the "opening" (*kāi*) of these distinct entities:

because provisional means were previously employed in accordance with their capacities, the Master of Records (Zhiyi) stated: "If there were no prior distinction, what would there be to discuss as identity?"
There is indeed a profound reason for this.

The *Caolu* (Record of Grass) states: "In examining and discussing the True Lineage of the *Lotus Sūtra*, once the provisional teachings have been opened, that which is inherently subtle is the Buddha’s own earnest praise of the three cycles of the expedient means (*upāya*) as the true essence [of the teaching]... [It continues: "I do not know what the original sūtra intends regarding the aforementioned point."
This scripture explains the opening of the gate of skillful means (*upāya-mukha*), referring to the Buddha’s use of skillful power to manifest the teachings of the Three Vehicles;

this constitutes the brief exposition of the main text. Regarding the term "Śrāvaka" (Voice-hearer), it refers to those who have recently exhausted their afflictions through the merit derived from this sutra.

As for the title of the chapter, "The Wonderful Dharma" (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*), both the secret and the marvelous, as well as the provisional and the ultimate, are already wondrous; fundamentally, there is no contradiction between them. As soon as—

If "penetrating" (*she*) refers to the ultimate reality (*shishi*), it is not the opening of the provisional; if one were to judge this according to the theory that the provisional and the real are of different substances (*yiti*), the meaning of the text would be that after the Buddha has praised the provisional, he then opens [the truth].
But how much more so when it is the opening of the wondrous provisional of the same substance (*tongti*)? For how could the Buddha’s power of skillful means (*upāya*) be of a different substance?
To resolve doubts regarding the nature of the Dharma-body and to assist in the opening of the internal provisional within the same substance, I shall now evaluate this from four perspectives. First.

First, you do not understand the intent behind the transformation; if we discuss the Buddha’s intention, there is fundamentally no identity or difference, yet it is only because the emotions of sentient beings obstruct the Sublime that [the distinction arises].
Now, if the provisional is revealed, how could this be revealing the Buddha’s intention? Second, you do not distinguish between self and other:

furthermore, when the provisional is now revealed, is it for the sake of transforming others or for one's own practice? If it is for transforming others, is it not then a case of difference? Thus, the *Wenju* (Volume 3, Section 20, Part 3) states:
Whether the teachings be general or specific, their respective divisions are all the provisional and real of "transforming others" (化他);

whether the teachings be general or specific, their respective divisions are all the provisional and real of "self-cultivation" (自行). These three aspects of transforming others are all termed "provisional," while self-cultivation is all termed "real.
(Text) One should reflect upon this passage where the Great Master judges the provisional and the real; it is not recognized by those of today or the past.
That which is opened belongs to the past and is termed "different substance" (yiti), while the present sutra that opens it is termed "identical substance" (tongti). Thus, Master Xuán says:

"Opening the differences of the past to reveal the identity of the present. This correctly means opening the different to achieve the identical; why then take the "different substance" of what is grasped as the "identical substance" that performs the opening?
Fourth, if one does not recognize the capacity of the sentient beings' minds—if it were the identical that was being opened—where would one find the capacity of their minds to know this?
If they are identical, why is it that in the *Anantārthasūtra* [the Buddha] provides a brief opening and refutation as a skillful means (*upāya*) to shake attachments and give rise to doubt?

If they are identical according to the five Buddhas, then this is precisely an opening of difference to establish identity; how can you simply say they are "of the same substance" (*samāna-svabhāva*)?

The Profound and Mysterious Meaning of the Common and Distinct Aspects of the Three Sutras (2) (24). The title *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* distinguishes it from other scriptures; its designation as a "sūtra" makes it common to them.

These two names are established based on three general principles: namely, that teaching, practice, and principle are contingent upon conditions—thus they are distinct—and that they are contingent upon the speaker—thus they are common.

The teaching is "universal" because it accords with that which is realized; the practice is "distinct" because it accords with that which is realized; the practice is "universal" because it accords with the principle; and the name is "universal" because it accords with the principle.

Regarding the first passage of the commentary (fascicle 2, section 11): although this current sutra is contrasted here with other texts, there is no lack of both universality and distinction, provided it is "wondrous."
The name and meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* differ from those of other sūtras; while the single character "sūtra" (經) is the same in name as in other texts, its meaning differs.
Here, we speak of it as "common" (*tong*) because we follow the commonality of the name. As for the intention behind establishing this name:
for what reason was the title of this sūtra established? Since the name encompasses the entire work, and the purport of the work does not exceed three [aspects], the name is thus comprehensive.

The three meanings of "distinct" (*bie*) and "not distinct" (*bu tong*) also follow their names in being both general (*tong*) and specific (*bie*). In explaining these three meanings, the coarse and subtle are distinguished;

teaching (*jiao*), practice (*xing*), and principle (*li*) differ, while the general and specific follow divergent tracks (and so forth). Among all the names in the holy teachings of a single lifetime, there are none that do not possess these three—teaching, practice, and principle.
There is nothing that does not accord with the general through the specific, and nothing that does not respond to the specific through the general.

Because these three categories comprehensively encompass all Buddha-dharmas, they are distinguished as follows: "Teaching" refers to the correspondence between the capacity of the recipient and the response of the teacher; "Practice" refers to the correspondence between cause and effect;

and "Principle" refers to the correspondence between name and reality, which is also the correspondence between phenomena and principle. If these three pairs were not established to provide both a general and specific framework, they would be set forth in vain.
Xuan (2) (24): Now, what is called the *Sūtra of the Sublime Dharma* is the general and specific name for the Teaching;
granting the sons and others a single great vehicle is the precious vehicle that leads directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), which is the general and specific [name] for the practice.

It is also called the "True Reality" (*bhūtatathatā*), the "Buddha’s Knowledge and Vision," the "Great Vehicle's Family Heritage," the "Single Ground," the "Actual Matter," the "Jewel at the Place of Treasure," and "Equal Greatness."
"Wisdom and so forth" (*hui deng*) refers to the general and specific aspects of the principle.

Regarding the commentary (Jian, 2.12): "Now, 'and so forth' (*deng*) is used because the *Miaofa* (Wondrous Dharma) is distinct from other sutras; yet the sutra itself is the general [category], as it is the common name for all sutras.
Thus we know that this sutra’s general and specific [titles] begin with 'Thus' (*ru shi*) and end with '...thus did I hear' (*wo wen ru shi*), and everything therein is none other than the Buddha."

It is taught that both are the wondrous Dharma; from beginning to end, they are all distinct yet concurrent. Within this teaching, the "concurrent" (tong) and "distinct" (bie) aspects expound upon practice and principle through their respective concurrent and distinct modes.
Thus, one knows that the fundamental and the manifested (ben and ji) are nothing other than cause and effect, as well as name and reality.

Since it would be impossible to cite every instance, I shall briefly indicate the general direction by roughly citing analogies to demonstrate the concurrent and distinct aspects of practice, as well as the skillful means therein.

Regarding the "identity of reality" (*tathatā*) and so forth as the principle that encompasses both the particular and the universal within the parable: the fact that the sons' causes for practice differ is the "particularity of practice" (*caryā-bheda*);

the equal bestowing of the great chariots leading directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) is the "universality of practice. The great chariot is the vehicle that conveys one universally toward the principle;
the site of enlightenment is the reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) to which one accords. Even the names such as "Great Wisdom" (*mahāprajñā*) are particulars among names, each being distinct.
The names all accord with principle, and that which accords with principle is precisely what penetrates this; this is the current principle of the distinction between the general and the specific.

(Part 1 of the *Miaozong*) Other commentators’ explanations of the sutra title all take the character "sutra" (*jing*) as the teaching that expresses (*neng-quan*), while they treat the remaining characters as the meanings expressed (*suo-quan*).

To divide them in this way is a grave violation of the Buddha’s intent. Furthermore, since the person, the dharma, and the analogy are all merely names, how [could one single character alone represent the teaching]?
How can that which is not a designator (*vācaka*) be exclusively attached to the designated meaning? The word "sūtra" cannot be exclusively attached to the teaching (*deśanā*).
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "The treasury of the *Dharmaparyāya* is profound, solid, remote, and deep; no one is able to reach it. It further says:

"Being protected by the Buddhas, planting the roots of all virtues, entering the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and giving rise to the mind that seeks to save all sentient beings, one accomplishes the four [immeasurables]."
The Dharma necessarily involves obtaining this sutra; the commentaries explain these four stages—opening, showing, awakening, and entering—as the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*).
To realize the principle is called "obtaining the sutra. Are these two not, therefore, taking the principle as the sutra?

The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states that the Buddhas of the ten directions constantly keep this sutra in mind; how could it mean that the Buddhas merely keep the teaching in mind? Such examples are numerous and cannot be fully enumerated.

Because [the preceding] has been fully cited, we know that various masters have severely erred in their interpretation of the titles of the various sutras by treating the designator (*nāman*) and the designated (*artha*) as separate.
The present school, however, employs both the general (*pāribhāṣika*) and specific (*viśeṣa*) interpretations of the title so as to avoid such error (and so forth).

In our current explanation, both the general and specific names of the various sutras are equally the designators and equally the designated. This is because each—whether general or specific—individually possesses the aspects of teaching (*śāsana*), practice (*pratipatti*), and principle (*adhigama*).
Therefore, do not say that these two names exist only at the level of the teaching; one must know that the general and the specific possess their own names for teaching, practice, and principle.
For example, in a specific title, "The Buddha Speaks" refers to the teaching, "Contemplation" refers to the practice, and "Immeasurable Life Buddha" refers to the principle.

Are these not the specific teaching, specific practice, and specific principle? When these three specific aspects are contrasted with the word "sūtra" (the scripture), they constitute the general teaching and the general [principle].

Regarding the passage "The practice penetrates the principle" (and so forth), the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) judges the penetration of practice as being both general and specific based on cause and effect;

one must understand its underlying intent. It does not mean that the practice only becomes general upon reaching the fruit. To know this intent: when each cultivates their own cause, it is termed "specific practice";

when these specific practices converge toward a single fruit, that very specificity is itself the general. This is precisely what is meant by "the general is discussed from the perspective of specific times" and "the specific is discussed from the perspective of general times. How could this be...?

The practice alone is thus, and the principle of the teaching is likewise. Just as the response to capacities corresponds to the teaching—whether general or specific—the Buddha preaches the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each obtain understanding according to their kind.
While each obtains understanding, the capacities are distinct; while it is a single voice, the response is universal.

This individualized understanding does not depart from the single voice, nor does the single voice obstruct individualized understanding. As stated in the *Xuan* (Profound Commentary) on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*: "Regarding the expressive text..."
Characters constitute the teaching and principle because they are capable of expressing [the meaning]; their differentiation as teachings is precisely the four *siddhāntas*.
Each *siddhānta* employs characters, and each character does not depart from the *siddhāntas*.

Just as names and realities are paired with principles—whether general or specific—multiple names do not depart from the single reality, and the single reality does not preclude multiple names; thus, the three [aspects] are both general and specific.
All are simultaneous and of the same category; regarding the melodic tones of the pipes within the music, they are "general" in terms of sound and "specific" in terms of the musical pieces.
These two functions—general and specific—do not obstruct one another. (Again, eleven pages) Within each and every sutra title during the five periods, both the general and the specific are present.
If one does not employ this method of judging through teaching, practice, and principle, then merely distinguishing between the general and the specific is entirely without foundation. However...
Infinite practices converge upon the One; the four teachings and four gates equally expound the single principle.

If one is exclusively devoted to the Vaipulya [Mahāyāna] sutras yet remains unable to hear this, it is because they have prematurely grasped the intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and are speaking across the stages [of the teaching].

If one explains various sutras after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa without relying on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, how could one ever exhaustively comprehend the entirety of the Buddha’s transformation? (And so forth. It is intended to cause the practitioner to realize this very [principle]...
The title states that by explaining the teaching, one can give rise to contemplative practice and perceive the principle of the True Buddha.
Regarding the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary), the phrase "the great carriage" refers to what is mounted; the two characters "principle" (*li*) and "teaching" (*jiao*) below should be deleted.

Someone may ask: "Various texts clarify both principle and teaching, as well as person and practice; why is one now missing? I reply: Teaching, practice, and principle—these three are used to explain the title of the sutra. Furthermore...

This treatise discusses the Dharma and not the person. If one seeks the teaching through its meaning, since practice already involves the correspondence between stimulus and response (induction) and cause and effect, it follows logically that there must also be [the other categories].
Furthermore, it is asked: "In various scriptures, the teachings on wisdom, severance, stages, practice, and the causes and effects of the fruits are all explained;

why are these five now omitted? It is said in reply: Wisdom, severance, stages, and the causes and effects of the fruits are all subsumed within "practice" (xing), and therefore they are not explained separately. Furthermore—

Question: Do the three sutras, when combined with their general and specific aspects, constitute five chapters? Answer: Their wording differs but their meaning is the same. What are these? "Teaching" (*jiao*) refers to the first and last chapters;
"Principle" (*li*) refers to the essence of the sutra; and "Practice" (*xing*) refers to its purpose and function. The forward progression of practice is called the "purpose" (*zong*);

the subduing and severing [of afflictions] through practice is called the "function" (*yong*). Therefore, the Great Master said: "The manifestation of the essence is the Principle; the purpose and function are Practice."

Section on the Subtle and Profound [Teachings] Within Their Own Divisions (1) (24). Question: Since the teachers are different and their established teachings are also distinct, how can it be said that the golden mouth and Brahma-sounds constitute a "universal teaching"?
Answer: There are two meanings here: first, within their own divisions; second, across the divisions. Regarding "within their own divisions," it is as follows:

The Buddha of the Tripitaka responds to various conditions by teaching various doctrines; because the conditions differ, the teachings are distinct, yet because the principal subject is one, the teachings are universal.

Based on these teachings, there are practices that can accord with the object of accord, which are given various names according to their principles. Yet the principle itself has no variety. (And so forth.

This refers to the teaching where the principles of body and speech are explained as being equal in their divisions; one must not interpret this otherwise regarding the categories of the Shared, Distinct, and Perfect [vehicles].

The same applies to the respective divisions of teaching, practice, and principle; while this meaning is easy to understand, the underlying principle is difficult to reconcile (and so forth). Second, regarding "spanning the sections":
where else would there be four distinct teaching masters, each with their own body and their own speech?

It is merely that they conceal their bodies adorned with immeasurable merits and manifest as those sixteen feet tall with purple-golden radiance (and so forth). If one were to open up the square [of the mandala]...
The provisional gate reveals the true reality: the body as it is is the perfect and eternal body; the Dharma as it is is the perfect Dharma;
practice as it is and principle as they are are all identical to reality. Thus, this universal teaching is that of a single sound, yet it possesses the distinctions of Great and Small vehicles.

The capacity to accord with it may be long or short, but that which is accorded with is only the One Ultimate. Though there are various names, they name the One; though there are various ultimates, they are the One Ultimate.

In conclusion, regarding the various names [of the teachings], if one were to formulate a discourse such as this— wherein the principles of practice (*caryā*) and realization (*yukti*) are both general and specific—
the characteristics would be difficult to understand, whereas the underlying principles would be easy to clarify (and so forth).

[In the second fascicle, section twelve,] among the questions, the reason for inquiring only about the teaching (*śāsana*) is that the teaching, practice, and realization are mutually interpenetrating.
Since we are currently abiding in the first [period], we follow the teachings of that period; as for the remaining two types, they are revealed through their own respective teachings.

The two interpretations—extensive and abbreviated—are generally applicable to all teachings; therefore, they are collectively designated as "one Buddha" in a general sense. Now, however, when distinguished, they constitute four different Buddhas.

Because each Buddha possesses its own various gates and distinct teachings, it is said that the "teachers of the doctrine differ" and their "establishment of the teaching also differs. Why is this so?

Regarding the objection raised below based on the previous general principle, the meaning of the current response concerning the four specific [teachings] should be understood as encompassing both the "within-the-stage" (*dang-fen*) and "crossing the stages" (*kua-jie*) meanings.
These two meanings are no different from the two excellences of "relative" (*dai*) and "absolute" (*jue*). Furthermore, the previous two interpretations also possess these two meanings:

if one relies on the employment of skillful means (*shiquan*), it corresponds to the "within-the-stage" meaning; if one refers to the Buddha’s intention, it corresponds to the "crossing the stages" meaning.
Although "integrity" (*jieyi*) possesses two meanings, one does not discuss their specific intent;

yet, to provide a general explanation based on this [single] meaning without discerning between these two paths, the intent remains seemingly accessible but not yet clearly revealed. For this reason, it is necessary to answer by distinguishing between the two meanings.
While each part may be universally applicable throughout a single era, in the present context they become mutually dependent (*xiangdai*). The transcendence of these stages lies solely in...

Now, the Buddha’s intention in this sutra does not apply solely to the present [period] (and so forth). Next, regarding the section on "concealment" (*zhi yin*), it clarifies the meaning of the "present division" (*dang fen*).

The reason for establishing the "present division" is that, having completed the provisional application of means (*shiquan*), the provisional and the real are set in contrast; thus, there are four masters, each of whom is distinct. As for clarifying this meaning: there is no separate "present division";

it is simply the concealment of the real and the establishment of the provisional, which is provisionally termed the "present division. This begins from the passage "until the golden radiance" (*jin hui*).
This refers to the manifestation of the divided bodies (as explained at length). If one opens the following section, it correctly clarifies the characteristics of "spanning the sections" (kua-jie).

Third, within the summary of the intent, there are three points of intent; the first states that while the teaching is universally a single sound, there are distinctions between the Great and Small Vehicles.

This present case is the single sound of the Lotus Sūtra that spans the sections, which differs from the single sound of the Small Vehicle restricted to its own specific stage, as is fully detailed in the *Zhi guan*.
Because it is the primary record, according to the *Vibhāṣā*, the Buddha’s single voice consists only of the Three Piṭakas.

By analogy with this principle, both the general and the specific [teachings] should each possess their own "single voice" within their respective domains (*dang-fen*). Within the meaning of these respective domains, four types of teaching masters are distinguished, each having their own specific discourse and the principles and essence they practice;

thus, the meaning is easily understood, and there are no various kinds of principles. Why, then, does each of the four teachings have its own object of expression (*lakṣya*), and what is that which is expressed?

Because they are distinct, it is logically unsuitable for them to be identical; thus it is said that they are difficult to harmonize. Within the meaning of "spanning the sections," the four teachings are not differentiated as each separately explicating the principle;

thus it is said that they are easy to clarify. The causes and effects taught in the various sutras are each distinct; now, transcending those distinct meanings, we discuss only the single principle, and therefore its characteristics are difficult to understand.
If the two meanings mutually support one another, then both the principle and the characteristics are easy to comprehend. If the two meanings...

When separated by temporal distance, both meanings are difficult to clarify; therefore, the two meanings must mutually support one another to be established within their respective contexts (*dang-fen*).

Thus, from the perspective of the "mutual reliance" (*xiang-dai*) meaning, it is established within its own section; from the perspective of the "opening of the provisional" (*kai-quan*) meaning, it is established across sections.

Furthermore, regarding the "respective context" meaning found in the Vaipulya, Prajñāpāramitā, and Avataṃsaka sūtras, these still constitute the bestowal of the provisional; however, when they reach the "respective context" meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, [the true is revealed].

Once the provisional and the real have been determined, the provisional is immediately discarded; once discarded, it is immediately opened up. This opening and discarding are mutually identical and cannot occur at different times.

(6) (73) If one transcends the sections, all the dharma-gates of the teachings arise from the Perfect [Teaching]. If one remains within their respective divisions, each possesses its own immeasurable dharma-gates arising as the Buddha-fruit of that specific teaching.
*Wenju* (5.3): "Transforming" refers to the Buddha’s method of transforming others within his own mind; entering into the minds of others is called "turning the wheel of the Dharma.
*Miaole* (5.32): Regarding "the Buddha’s transformation," there are two meanings. If one considers it across the sections, it applies universally to the four Tathāgatas.

All dharmas are fully present, responding to whatever is struck [by the capacity of the listener]. Whatever is spoken is none other than a transformation for others; it is not a discourse on what one has personally realized for oneself.
If one takes the Perfect [Teaching] as "self" in contrast to the three other teachings, this is also termed "other" from the perspective of the Dharma;

however, here we follow the gradual approach and speak from the standpoint of the initial stage. Since this refers to what the Buddha internally realized, it is said that he realized it within his own mind. Because the provisional Dharma benefits sentient beings, it is termed "other."

Question: Regarding the "spanning of the sections" (*kuajie*), why does the *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) commentary state that if one considers the spanning of the sections, it applies to all four Tathāgatas?

It says: "Prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, the four teachings were each taught differently according to the capacities of beings; now, speaking in terms of the 'opening of the provisional' (*kaiquan*), there is only the single Perfect Buddha.
One should look at the word "applies" (*tong*) here. Therefore, the *Biexing Xuanyi Ji* (Record of the Profound Meaning of the Separate Practice) by Siming states: "In terms of... [text continues].
The *Kuajie lun* (Treatise on Transcending Sections) states that the One Perfect Buddha, responding to four types of capacities, preached four kinds of teachings.

Regarding the three dharmas—universal and specific—the *Miaoxuan* (2) (1) records that Master Nanyue cited three kinds, namely: the dharma of sentient beings, the dharma of the Buddha, and the dharma of the mind (*yuxun*). Now...
Based on these three dharmas, there is a further detailed analysis: if one broadly analyzes the dharmas of sentient beings, this generally encompasses all causes and effects as well as all dharmas;
if one broadly analyzes the dharmas of the Buddha, this is based on the fruit; if one broadly analyzes the dharmas of the mind, this is based on the cause.
Divination Stick (2) (20): Next, it clarifies how the Great Master, following the intent of Nanyue, further elaborates and distinguishes [the teachings] (etc.). It says:

"If one were to broadly discuss the phenomena of sentient beings, generally speaking, this would encompass all causes and effects as well as all dharmas. Now, because the meaning of "sentient beings" is pervasive, it is said to be a "general discussion.
However, because the meaning of such a general discussion is not ultimate, it is called "generally speaking" (*yiwǎng*). Although it is "generally speaking,"...

If one considers both directions, these two are restricted and do not extend to the Buddha or to the stage of the cause alone; as for the Buddha-dharma and the mind-dharma, they are not said to be "one-way.
This is because the Buddha-dharma is definitively situated in the fruit, while the mind-dharma is definitively situated in the cause. For this reason, these three dharmas receive distinct names.

Why is this so? Just as the Buddha-dharma and mind-dharma within the bodies of sentient beings still encompass both cause and fruit, how much more so must this be the case for sentient beings themselves?

The name "pervasion" (tong) signifies that it pervades both the ordinary and the sagely. Even the mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) of sentient beings within the Buddha’s body are definitively contained within the mental phenomena of the fruition (*phala*).
Thus, the Buddha-dharmas and the sentient-being dharmas—these two exist in the causal stage (*hetu*). If this is so, why does the Sūtra state that the three are without distinction?

The answer is: the principle-nature (*li-ti*) has no difference; the difference pertains to their functional activity (*shi-yong*). This meaning is explained in detail, as fully set forth in the "Ten Dharmas" section of the *Mohe Zhiguan*.
In the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, it is stated that this refers to both mental phenomena (*cittadharma*) and sentient beings (*sattvadharma*).

Furthermore, that Buddha-dharmadhātu encompasses both the cause and the fruit, rather than being restricted solely to the fruit; for that text elucidates the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) by way of the fruit.

Essential Points (Part One) (5): One should know that mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) are distinguished according to delusion and according to phenomena. Thus, the *Shiqian* states: "The phenomena of sentient beings (*sattva-dharma*), in one sense, encompass both cause and fruit;
in another sense, they are restricted solely to the cause. The phenomena of the Buddha (*buddha-dharma*) are fixed in the fruit; the phenomena of the mind (*citta-dharma*) are fixed in the cause.

If one divides them according to delusion and awakening, the Buddha belongs exclusively to awakening, while both [sentient beings and the mind] reside in delusion. Furthermore, within delusion, there are sentient beings...

Since those belonging to others pertain to all [beings], while mental factors belong to oneself, one specifically points to one's own mind (and so forth). Only when each of these three factors possesses both the phenomenal aspect (*vastu*) and the principle aspect (*tattva*), and constructs them accordingly, will there be no distinction.
*Zhiguan* (5) (10); *Fuxing* (5b) (1); *Miaole* (4) (15); *Xuyiji Xia* (4).
The three dharmas receive their names individually. Regarding the "dharmas of sentient beings," if interpreted as two [categories], they are restricted and do not extend to the Buddha;
this is distinguished in contrast to the Buddha. As for "and" (*ca*) being used in contrast to the mind, some say it refers exclusively to the causal stage;
others say that "and" is a scribal error. Still others say that since both the dharmas of sentient beings and the dharmas of the mind exist in the causal stage, the word "and" is employed.
The nature of the Dharma-realm is all-pervasive and nowhere absent;
it is not absent from the Buddha, but resides in sentient beings, and if not in sentient beings, it resides in the mind. Because these three are thus non-differentiated, it is called "wondrous."

By the Tiantai Śramaṇa Fǎzhào.
The *Miaoxuan* (3), citing the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (20) (5), states: "Ignorance and craving—between these two is precisely the Middle Way. Thus it is said.
The Middle Way can shatter all of birth and death. *Miaoxuan* (2.15):

Regarding the two branches of the twelve links of dependent origination, those two belonging to the past stop the view of permanence; those two belonging to the future stop the view of annihilationism;
and the present reveals the Middle Way. By inferring the three causes of the present, one explains the two fruits of the future. By inferring...

The five fruits of the present are explained as being derived from two causes of the past; thus it is said that all three time periods possess the twelve links, for the purpose of inferring cause and effect.

The *Shi* (Commentary), fascicle 3, states: "The Middle Way is simply the avoidance of the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism," and so forth. Next, regarding the inference within the three time periods, it says: "The three time periods..."

That each possesses twelve [links] is established by inferring the effect from the cause, as explained here. Although the three time periods are all termed "cause and effect," the number of links differs;
this is detailed in the *Abhidharmakośa*, which states that the result is abbreviated and the cause is abbreviated, with the middle [period] allowing one to infer the other two.
As noted in the third fascicle of the *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation), since the present constitutes twelve links in relation to the past and future, it should be understood accordingly.

Since the past and future also each have their own past and future when viewed in relation to one another, there would be twelve for each; however, for the time being, we follow the present perspective, and thus there are only twelve.
*Fuxing* (Vol. 3, Part 2): The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Three afflictions, two karmas, and seven entities are also called 'fruits. This is a brief enumeration of fruits and..."

From the brief explanation of the causal conditions, one may infer that two [categories] arise from afflictions: namely, afflictions and karma; from karma, things arise; and from things, both things and afflictions arise.
This is the principle of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*). Regarding the first four lines, because they briefly encompass the extensive, the treatise states:
"One should know that although dependent origination has twelve links, its nature consists of two or three. 'Three' refers to afflictions, karma, and things; 'two' refers to cause and effect."

Within this, there are further two parts: first, the two initial lines correctly clarify the mutual inclusion; second, the two subsequent lines resolve potential objections. The objection asks: "Why is the past and future treated briefly while the present is explained extensively?
The response states: "Because by means of the middle [the present], one can infer the past and future; since the present is termed the 'middle,' it is therefore explained in detail.

Next, from afflictions arise afflictions, meaning that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) gives rise to grasping (*upādāna*). From afflictions arises karma, meaning that grasping (*upādāna*) gives rise to becoming (*bhava*), as well as ignorance (*avidyā*).
It is said that "the arising of clarity [is] from formations; the arising of things [is] from karma" means that consciousness arises from formations, and birth arises from becoming.

It is said that "the arising of things and afflictions [is] from things" means that things arise from things—that is, name-and-form arises from consciousness, up to feeling arising from birth—and afflictions arise from things—that is, craving arises from feeling.
Section on Light (Middle) (25): Although the two vehicles are alike in their contemplation, there is a difference in how they contemplate the dharmas.

The Śrāvaka contemplates all fruits collectively as the single Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), and contemplates all afflictions and karma collectively as the single Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).

Furthermore, since both suffering and origination pertain entirely to the present, this is called the "contemplation of general characteristics" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). The Pratyekabuddha, however, contemplates suffering as sevenfold in the present.

Regarding the five future [factors] and two observations combined as five, and the three distinct observations of the past and present, because suffering and its origin are separately analyzed across the three periods of time,
this is called the "distinct-characteristic observation" of the pratyekabuddha.

Commentary (4) (16): First, regarding the Śrāvakas, if one considers their causal conditions, the seven branches are collectively treated as one suffering (*duḥkha*), and the five branches are collectively treated as one origination (*samudaya*).
Furthermore, without distinguishing between past and future, both suffering and origination are taken as being entirely present, because their faculties are dull;

thus, the characteristics of the dharmas are summarized and abbreviated. Second, regarding the Pratyekabuddhas, they open up the general categories of the Śrāvakas into specific characteristics, taking the present as the basis.
The five [factors]—consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling—are the two future [links].
The two past [links]—ignorance and formations—are the specific characteristics of suffering. The three present [links]—craving, grasping, and becoming—are the specific characteristics of origination.

Furthermore, because the three periods of time are opened up rather than being restricted to the present alone, it is said that the results and causes are abbreviated; this can be understood through the middle [period].

In comparison with these two [stages], all three time periods (the *tri-kāla*) each possess twelve [factors]. Because merit (*puṇya*) serves as the support for wisdom (*jñāna*), one is able to observe them individually.

Regarding the "Phrases on Light" (Section 30), the three time periods are as follows: the two causes of the past refute the view of a permanent self (*ātman*); the five fruits of the present refute the view of a substantial self (*pudgala*);
and the three causes of the present and the two fruits of the future refute the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). This is the conventional path.

The Application: (4) [Section] Twenty-three. First, refuting the permanence of the self (*ātman*) by means of the three periods of time: because that which has passed in the past has already ceased, it is not permanent.

Second, refuting the self of the person (*pudgala-ātman*) by means of the present: because all five fruits are merely a combination of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), there is no self. Third, [refuting the self] by means of the future...

Regarding the refutation of the self (*ātman*): because there is a fruit in the future, it is not a total annihilation. All who speak of the "self" are outsiders who cling to the body as being either annihilated or eternal;
since this doctrine of the three times is commonly transmitted by the world, it is said to be what is used in ordinary discourse.
The twelve links of dependent origination do not transcend the three periods of time, as each possesses its own cause and effect.
Although there are slight differences in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) regarding the citation from the *Abhidharmakośa*, the meaning is already fully established therein; thus, Master Jingxi said:

"The principle of dependent origination is the root of the Buddha-dharma, the beginning of turning away from the heterodox and toward the orthodox, and the source for entering the Path and practicing contemplation. Therefore, those who study the Buddha-dharma..."
One must not be entirely deluded.

(2) The Profound and Mysterious Sevenfold Two Truths (24). Regarding what are called the sevenfold two truths: first, that which exists substantially is conventional; that which exists substantially is [the ultimate].

1. Cessation (*nirodha*) as the ultimate truth; 2. that which exists as an illusion (*māyopama-bhāva*) as the conventional truth, and the emptiness of that illusory existence as the ultimate truth; 3.
that which exists as an illusion as the conventional truth, and the coexistence of the emptiness and non-emptiness of that illusory existence as the ultimate truth; 4.

that which exists as an illusion as the conventional truth, and the fact that illusory existence is itself both empty and non-empty—with all phenomena tending toward this emptiness and non-emptiness—as the ultimate truth; 5. illusory existence and the fact that illusory existence is itself empty are both... [the ultimate truth].

Sixth: that which is called "conventional" is neither existent nor empty; this is the "ultimate. Furthermore, illusory existence and the fact that illusory existence is itself emptiness are both termed "conventional";
that all phenomena tend toward being neither existent nor empty is the "ultimate. Seventh: illusory existence and the fact that illusory existence is itself emptiness are both termed "conventional";
that all phenomena tend toward existence, tend toward emptiness, and tend toward being neither existent nor empty is the [ultimate].
True. The *Shiqian* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), fascicle 3, section 17, and so forth;

and the *Niepan Shu* (Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra), fascicle 9, section 9, state: "Now, the Great Master Mingzhi [Zhiyi] has seven [interpretations of] the Two Truths; although their names differ, their meaning is [the same]."

One may synthesize these into seven categories: (1) the conventional; (2) the two types of non-arising; (3) the mundane and the re-actualized true; (4) the mundane and the meditative within; (5) the re-actualized mundane and the meditative within;

(6) the re-actualized mundane and the re-actualized within; and (7) the perfection of the two truths. One should know that while the names and characteristics differ slightly from those in the *Fahua Xuanyi*, their underlying meaning must be identical. Those who read this should understand this point.
*Zhiguī Chāo*, Volumes 11–20: Because the Middle Way of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) lies outside of biased emptiness, it receives the name "double truth" (*fuzhen*);

because the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) realizes that the extremes are themselves the middle, it is called "meditative" (*chan*). If the *Fahua Xuán* states that both types of "double reception" in the Shared Teaching are termed "double truth," this is merely a general classification;
a detailed analysis is as presented in the current text.
*Miaoxuan*: The *Zang* (Treasury) [teaches] birth-and-death and nirvana; the *Tong* (Common) [teaches] non-arising; the *Bie* (Distinct) [teaches] the connection to the common;
the *Zhijian* (Sub-commentary) is precisely that which contains the Middle Truth; and the *Chansu Fuzhen* (The Profound and Ordinary Reveal the True) [is likewise].

The Perfect [Teaching] connects with the Separate: its commentaries (*śāstra*) likewise contain both truths (*satya*). In the case of "Zen for the laity" and "Zen within the Middle," they are separate.
The commentaries on the Separate involve a double mundane truth and a single middle truth; the commentaries on the Perfect involve a double mundane truth and a single middle truth;
and the Perfect connects with the Separate: its commentaries likewise involve a double mundane truth and a single middle truth, as well as a double mundane truth and a double middle truth.

The *Yuanqi* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning): "The two truths of the Perfect [Teaching]—both conventional and both middle—are explained through the three dharmas as the source of the wondrous mystery (2) (24).
Regarding the two truths of 'illusion' as empty or non-empty: the conventional is no different from the previous [teachings], while the true consists of three."
The categories are not one; according to the conventional, there are three, and according to the real, they constitute the three types of the two truths. What are their characteristics?

As clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, regarding that which is neither out-flowing (*āsava*) nor non-out-flowing: the first person says it is "non-out-flowing" because it is not the conventional, and "not non-out-flowing" because it dispels attachment. Why is this?

Because practitioners may give rise to attachment toward the non-out-flowing, just as they might give rise to latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) by taking cessation as an object; thus, one destroys that mind of attachment and returns [to the truth].

Entering the outflow-free (anāsrava) constitutes one set of the two truths. Next, when a person hears that it is neither outflowing nor outflow-free, they understand this as being distinct from the two extremes and as manifesting the Middle Principle;
since this Middle Principle is the Truth, this is another set of the two truths.

Furthermore, when a person hears that it is neither with-outflows nor outflow-free, they immediately know that this "double negation" (ubhayābhāva) directly manifests the Middle Way. The power and function of this Middle Way Dharma-realm are vast.
The Great [Vehicle] is equal to empty space; that all dharmas tend toward being neither outflowing (*sāsrava*) nor non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) is yet another aspect of the two truths.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "Śrāvakas see only emptiness and do not see non-emptiness; the wise see both emptiness and non-emptiness. This is precisely that meaning.
The followers of the Two Vehicles are said to be attached to this emptiness; therefore, [the Buddha] refutes their attachment to emptiness. Thus it is said.
Regarding the statement "not empty": if one is attached to emptiness, then upon its refutation, one merely perceives emptiness and fails to perceive non-emptiness.
For those who benefit others, it is said that "non-empty" refers to wondrous existence; thus they speak of non-emptiness.

When those who benefit others hear of non-emptiness, they take it to mean the *tathāgatagarbha*, wherein all phenomena converge within the *tathāgatagarbha*. Returning to the categories of empty and non-empty, there are thus three kinds of two truths. Furthermore:
Regarding the threefold distinctions revealed by the principle that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) tend toward that which is neither outflowing (*āsrava*) nor non-outflowing:

first, when a person hears that all phenomena tend toward that which is neither outflowing nor non-outflowing, they understand that all phenomena do not depart from emptiness (*śūnyatā*), yet they circulate throughout the ten directions of the world-system, remaining as they were in their original locations, like a water jar.
Furthermore, another person, upon hearing "tending toward," understands that the principle herein requires that all practices (*sarvacaryā*) must come and proceed toward its manifestation.
Furthermore, when a person hears that all destinies (*gati*) are neither outflows (*āsrava*) nor non-outflows, yet are endowed with all phenomena (*sarvadharma*),

it is for this reason that one conventional truth is said to revolve according to three levels of ultimate truth: either in relation to a single ultimate truth, or in relation to a composite ultimate truth, or in relation to the inconceivable ultimate truth.

Stanza (3) (19): Next, regarding the explanation of the meaning of "reception" (*jieti*), this refers to entering the Truth while remaining within the Middle. This section consists of three parts: first, a single dharma is presented as a heading;

second, from "the conventional" (*su*) downward, the matter is briefly indicated by means of three dharmas; third, from "their characteristics" (*qixiang*) downward, the mutual correspondence of these characteristics is analyzed by correlating them with the three dharmas.
Since the out-flowing (*āsrava*) and non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*) are fundamentally universal dharmas (*sāmānyadharma*), the pair is established in order to fulfill the meaning of reception.
That which is neither empty nor non-empty is fundamentally a distinct dharma; that all dharmas tend toward [the ultimate] is fundamentally a perfect dharma.
Regarding each individual dharma, there are three types of people who understand it differently; this is truly because their capacities are awakened differently, and thus what they hear differs.

Furthermore, because the roots of Bodhisattvas in the Shared Teaching (tongjiao) are either sharp or dull and their cultivation is awakened differently, those with dull faculties remain equal to the Two Vehicles until the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

It is precisely because those who have already been received into the Middle Way through the [Sudden] Teaching are now being received into the [Perfect] Assembly that they both observe the conventional world as illusory existence and realize the Truth;
yet, because their capacities differ, the distinct and perfect faculties are aroused, while those of dull capacity remain fixed in emptiness—thus the three distinctions are established.

Therefore, the explanations for the latter two types of reception must be contrasted with the "Common" and "Dull" capacities to collectively form three types of people who hear differently despite hearing the same thing; hence, this is discussed in terms of "outflows" (āsrava).
This is shown to clarify the source of understanding; if one grasps this intent, one will attain unimpeded mastery over all phenomena (and so forth).
Regarding the initial passage, although all three individuals employ the name "double negation" (*ubhayābhāva*), their comprehension is not equal.

This section is divided into three parts: first, establishing [the position] based on the teachings; second, clarifying the mode of practice for the first person and below; third, providing a further explanation of why it is not non-outflow (*anāsrava*).

Those who have abandoned attachment are untainted and unattached; however, because practitioners still take such [states] as objects with an attached mind, this [teaching] now breaks that attached mind.
Therefore, it is called "not" (non-), and thus it is said to be "not untainted. This is like citing an example from below to explain and establish the original position:

the True Truth is free from attachment and is called "not," yet it returns to the state of being untainted. This is the view of the first type of person. Furthermore, it also applies to those of dull faculties. Second, again...

The "person" refers to the two types of those with sharp faculties; the person of the Perfect Teaching is also called "neither of the two," because they incorporate the provisional means of the Shared Teaching—this is why it is so.
Next, by citing the analogy of emptiness and non-emptiness from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, the distinction between the tainted and the untainted can be understood through reflection.

Regarding the statement that the three types of people hear of the "tending toward" (yiqù): as for the first type, they say that all dharmas do not depart from the meaning of emptiness, because all dharmas tend toward emptiness.
The illustrative example states: "As with a vase, so with all things; 'as' (tathatā) is emptiness.

Since the emptiness of the vase is not different from the emptiness of the ten directions, the emptiness of the ten directions all tends toward the emptiness of the vase; this is the "person who penetrates" (the universal).

Next, when another person hears of this "tending toward," they understand that although this is merely the Middle Way, one must cultivate all practices prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) in order to approach and subsequently give rise to the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
The principle of the Way is precisely the differentiation of persons. When the third person hears it, they fully comprehend all [aspects], which is termed "the destination" (*gati*).
Furthermore, in the section on the synthesis, it says "either the counterpart": the three truths are the counterparts, while the one conventional truth is that which is countered.
The Great Master Tiantai’s *Xuanwen Sanfa* (Explanation of the Three Dharmas), in its section on "Resolving the Source," provides a structural outline and states:

"Leakage and non-leakage are fundamentally universal dharmas; in order to establish the meaning of 'reception' [of the teaching], the 'double negation' (*ubhaya-apratiṣedha*) is established. Furthermore, the section for the formal explanation states: "First, establishing this based on the Teaching.
From this, it is known that the "double negation" was indeed established by the Great Master himself.

*Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra*, Volume One (translated by Paramārtha; contained in the "Ye" [曰] case). The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten superior characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) such that their teachings are incomparable and surpass all other doctrines.

These ten superior characteristics are: first, the superior characteristic of the basis of what is to be known (*jñeya-āśraya-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*); second, the superior characteristic of what is to be known (*jñeya-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
