In the sixth chapter of the *Miaoxuan*, regarding the sixfold classification of fundamental and trace, only the single category of essence and function (tǐyòng) cites the fundamental text as proof;
the remaining five are all from the text concerning the traces. Yet, the *Shiqian* states that "the first three cite the traces and the latter three cite the fundamental. This is likely because...

The Master of the Commentary (Jizhu) points out that the profound intent of the Sūtra’s reality and expediency is already present here; he simply takes the text concerning the "traces" (*jì*) as the "original" (*běn*).

Therefore, he says: "Now that the provisional has been explained, the original is now presented; this alone is the true teaching. If so, why did the first three [sections] not point to the traces as being the original? It is said:
Since the first three are universal, they merely use the traces as an analogy for the original. As for the latter three, they are within the universal.

Furthermore, because they are distinct, it is necessary to point to the "trace" (*ji*) as the basis; one may observe both the general and specific characters in this regard, as there are many such examples in the *Wenju* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra).

For instance, in the first volume, section three, which clarifies the unity of the fundamental and the trace: first, the *Shouliang-pin* (Life Span Chapter) quotes: "Since my attaining Buddhahood, it has been exceedingly long ago";
and furthermore, the *Fangbian-pin* (Expedient Means Chapter) says: "I originally established vows to cause all sentient beings to likewise [attain enlightenment]."
Regarding the attainment of this path, the "Chapter on the Five Hundred Predictions" states: "Internally they conceal the practice of a bodhisattva, while externally they manifest as śrāvakas.
(1) (11) First, the main text is cited; second, the "trace" text is cited below [the section on] "expedient means," because within the trace-text the fundamental intent is secretly revealed.
If it were explained openly, it would be the "fundamental-trace" relationship within the trace-text, as clarified in the subsequent passage.

Furthermore, the *Myōryaku* (Vol. 3, p. 39) has already cited this extensively. Now, among these eight [sections], the first seven belong to the Gate of Traces (*jimon*), while the eighth belongs to the Gate of the Origin (*honmon*).

Although the Origin has not yet been reached, because the principle of provisional and real (*kenjitsu*) is omnipresent, the following text states: "This is my skillful means (*upāya*); all Buddhas are likewise.
Thus, the name "skillful means" applies to both the Origin and the Traces. Since this has already been explained in the *Gen* (the *Hokke Genki*), it is not the same [as the current discussion].

Regarding the interpretation of the text: some say that the first three [passages] are texts concerning the descent of the fundamental into the manifested, while the latter three are texts on revealing the fundamental by manifesting the trace;
hence it is said, "three citations of the trace-texts. Others say that the profound discourse on the great purport does not distinguish between the difference of fundamental and trace.

Still others say that although the text belongs to the *Honmon* (the Gate of the Fundamental), its wording happens to temporarily coincide with the wording of the *Jimon* (the Gate of the Trace). Therefore...
Some say that the text of Jingxi contains an error; others say that the first three [causes] are the trace (迹) while the latter three are the source (本);
still others say that because the distinct [teaching] contains the meaning of the source, it is said that "three" refers to the original text.

The Profound Mystery of Determining the Fundamental and the Traces (7–9): If the Sahā world were turned into ink and one drop were placed for every thousand worlds to the east, and if these drops and non-drops were all wiped away to become dust,
with each particle of dust representing one kalpa— and even exceeding this by hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of kalpas— [it would still not reach the end of the Buddha’s life].
Maitreya, as the Regent, even with the provisional wisdom that issues from the ultimate, cannot know the worlds by direct enumeration, let alone count their atoms;
how then could he exhaustively reach them? This is merely a skillful metaphor of the Tathāgata to manifest their long-lasting nature;
how much more so when using worldly wisdom and its clever calculations? As the text says: "With my Buddha-eye, I observe that distant past as if it were today."
Only the Buddha can know that such a vast duration of time consists entirely of provisional causes (*traces*) and not fundamental causes.
In the second fascicle of the *Shiqian* (Exegesis on the Profound Meaning), it says: "If the Sahā world were turned into ink, would it ever be exhausted?

This citation refers to the text from the "City of Illusion" chapter in the *Trace Gate* (*Jimen*), and it is inappropriate to cite the words regarding Maitreya and others; for the statement that "Maitreya does not know" appears in the *Fundamental Gate* (*Benmen*).

Alternatively, one might borrow the text from the *Benji* (Original Record) to serve as an analogy here: even the power of wisdom of a Bodhisattva in his final birth (*sāmantaka*) cannot know the number of "dust-motes" within the three thousandfold world system.
If one were to strictly employ the text from the *Ji* (Trace Record), then the twenty-five characters concerning Maitreya and others would have to be excluded;

however, this interpretation accords with the Master’s [Zhiyi’s] words, who feared there might be a separate underlying meaning. Nevertheless, although the phrasing of Maitreya’s words is cited here...
This differs slightly from the text of the Fundamental Gate (Honmon), which merely states: "We dwell on the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika), yet we do not comprehend this matter.

In the present passage, it is said that one does not know the number of worlds using the wisdom of emerging into the conventional (nishyanda-prajñā); how much less could one know the number of their atoms?
If one were to know the number of atoms, one would simply have to employ the wisdom of emerging into the conventional. Therefore, the preceding text should be applied here.

The Great Master, having finished citing the sutra, concludes by stating that only a Buddha can know such a vast duration; thus, from Maitreya, who holds the position of the successor, downward, none can know it.
This is merely an explanation based on the underlying intent, and does not mean that he is borrowing the concepts of "original" and "traced."
As for the text, it was simply because the Master [Zhiyi] viewed it as a text concerning the provisional and the real (honjaku);

furthermore, Shintei’s interpretation—that Maitreya of the Real Gate does not know the realms of kalpas as numerous as motes of dust and thus cannot look down upon a single mote—is incorrect, as that still treats him as one who remains within the provisional.

4. The Miraculous and Profound Account of the Four Buddha Footprints (7–11) Some say that in the past, as a young brahmin (*maṇava*), he encountered the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. He offered five flowers as an oblation and covered the mud with his own hair.

Leaping into the air, he attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). The Buddha bestowed upon him the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), naming him Śākyamuni. This is recorded in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
It is also said that the meaning of attaining the prediction of enlightenment within the city of *Avataṃsaka* is identical to this;

since both accounts speak of severing delusions, it is known that these describe the characteristics of the Buddha’s practice during his causal stage. Some say that in the past, as the Brahmin Ratnasāgara, he performed great *vīrya* (diligence) under the Buddha Ratnagarbha of the kingdom of Saṃtāna, where the Buddhas of the ten directions sent flowers as offerings. Since he was also the father of the Buddha Ratnagarbha, and furthermore—
Because the teacher of Amitābha praised his meritorious virtues as being inconceivable, we know that this refers to the characteristics of the causal practices of the Separate and Perfect [Vehicles].

As for the passage in the *Shiqian* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), fascicle 8, section 3, regarding his former life as a Māṇava: the details are exactly as described in the *Ruiying Jing* (Sūtra of Auspicious Responses), concerning how he received the prediction from Dīpaṃkara and attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Thus we know that he is a Universal Buddha. Formerly, when he was the Brahmā-śrāvaka Ratnasāgara, it was exactly as described in the second fascicle of the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*:
there was a bodhisattva named Śāntamati who asked the Buddha, "The worlds of other Buddhas are pure;
why does the present World-Honored One dwell in these five turbidities and preach the Three Vehicles? The Buddha said, "Whether a land is pure or impure is due to one's original vow. As for me..."
In the past, during incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, this Buddha-world was named Santirana; the kalpa was named Susthitacakra;
and the Wheel-Turning King was named Araṇemin. Within the four continents, there was a minister named Ratnasāgara, born of the Brahmin caste and skilled in the interpretation of signs.
At that time, he gave birth to a son endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, whom the devas [prophesied].
He constantly came to make offerings, for which reason [the Buddha] gave him the name Ratnagarbha. Later, he left the household life and attained the Way, also being named Ratnagarbha.
Having turned the Wheel of Dharma and delivered sentient beings, he traveled next to a village to preach the Dharma for a holy king.

After the king invited him to enter the retreat season (*varṣā*), the king’s seven treasures also personally extended their offerings. The king had a thousand sons, each of whom also made offerings for three months.

The manner of his nurturing was as described in the sutra: after a full two hundred and fifty years had passed, Ratnasāgara came to where the Buddha was and received the prediction that he would become a buddha.
At that time, all the sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the atoms of the ten directions who had previously been converted by Ratnasāgara attained the Way simultaneously.
Subsequently, Ratnasāgara exhorted the wheel-turning king to resolve his mind on enlightenment, then exhorted the prince to resolve his mind on enlightenment, and finally caused [the ministers] to...
The eight classes of devas and others resolved their minds [on enlightenment], and even throughout the three thousandfold world system, all gave rise to the bodhicitta.
Subsequently, within the realms of animals and hell-beings, he manifested the body of a Buddha before each and every being, causing them to be freed from suffering.
For seven years, among humans, devas, and the eight classes of beings, those without desire all offered worship; furthermore, this was the teacher of Amitābha.
In that "Chapter on Bestowing Prophecies," that Buddha first entered samādhi and manifested the pure lands of the ten directions, gathering all the bodhisattvas.
He first bestowed the prophecy upon Ratnasāgara, next upon Amitābha, and then upon the crown prince of the Wheel-Turning King, saying:
"Observe the realms of humans, devas, and the three evil paths; give rise to great compassion, sever all suffering and affliction, and cause them to abide in peace and happiness. Now, you should..."

I name you Avalokiteśvara; from the crown prince of the Universal Monarch down to all devas and worldlings, there is none who has not been encouraged by this brahmin to resolve his mind on enlightenment; therefore, he is the teacher of them all.

The *Xuanqian* (Profound Commentary) on the *Ruiying Jing* (Sūtra of Auspicious Responses) takes the aspect of severing delusions as evidence that [the Bodhisattva] has attained the stage of a *pratyekabuddha*.

However, the *Sijiao Yi* (Outline of the Four Teachings), citing the account of spreading one’s hair to cover the mud, identifies this as the second *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* of the Tripitaka (Śrāvaka) vehicle, because at that stage one has not yet attained the "endurance" (*kṣānti*).

Within the causal stages of the Distinct and Complete Teachings, speaking in terms of father and son, Bao Hai is the father of Bao Cang Fo; this is based on the relationship between teacher and disciple.

Regarding the statement that "Ratnagarbha was the teacher who bestowed the prediction upon Ratnasāgara," the text of the "Chapter on Bestowing Predictions" first bestows the prediction upon Ratnasāgara and subsequently bestows the prediction upon Amitābha.
Thus, Ratnagarbha is the teacher who bestowed the prediction upon Amitābha, while Ratnasāgara is the teacher who exhorted Amitābha to resolve his mind [on enlightenment];
it does not mean that Ratnasāgara bestowed the prediction upon Amitābha. The *Shu-ki* (Commentary) states: "Ratnasāgara, next..."

Regarding the two characters "Duobao" (Prabhūtaratna) and "Hai" (Sāgara) in the prophecy of Amitābha, I consulted the *Ruiying jing* and the *Beihuajing* within the ancient collections of the Great Compassionate One and the Holy Water, and found their explanation to be as follows.

The Profound and Mysterious Attainment of Enlightenment by the Four Buddhas (7) (12): Some say that beneath the Bodhi tree, upon a seat of grass, the thirty-four moments of mind sever both the delusions of views and the delusions of thought (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava* and *bhāvanā-āsrava*)—this is the characteristic of the fruit of Buddhahood according to the Tripiṭaka [teaching].
Others say that beneath the Bodhi tree, with celestial robes as a seat—this is... [the characteristic of the fruit of Buddhahood according to the Shared Teaching].

This refers to the common characteristics of the attainment of the Buddha-fruit. Some say that the seat at the site of tranquil extinction (śītinā-vimokṣa-maṇḍala) consists of flowers made of the seven treasures (*sapta-ratna*);
this refers to the distinct characteristics of the attainment of the Buddha-fruit. Others say that the site of tranquil extinction takes empty space as its seat;
this refers to the perfect characteristics of the attainment of the Buddha-fruit.
*Record of the Western Regions* (Section on the Conversion of Words, Volume Eight): In the exact center of the enclosure of the Bodhi tree is the Vajrāsana.

It was formed at the beginning of the present Bhadrakalpa and arose simultaneously with the great earth. Situated at the very center of the trichiliocosm, it reaches down to the Golden Wheel (*kāñcanamaṇḍala*) and extends upward to the surface of the earth.
Composed of diamond (*vajra*), it measures over a hundred paces in circumference. The thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa sit upon it and enter the state of *samādhi*.
Because it is firm and stable, it is called the Vajrāsana (Diamond Seat). ... As for the Bodhi tree, it is the Pippala tree.

... Regarding the passage [1.8] stating that one who manifests the special marks of excellence (*vyañjana-lakṣaṇa*) and sits upon a lotus pedestal to receive the office of Buddhahood is a distinct Buddha in his own right: *Note: This translation reflects the technical terminology of Chinese Buddhist scholastic commentaries, specifically addressing the distinction between the universal Buddha-nature and the manifestation of specific Buddhas.*
"Awakening oneself and awakening others.
Regarding "Miaole" (1.24), it is also said that all Buddhas of the three periods of time attain the Unsurpassed Way at the Akaniṣṭha Heaven,
and this refers to the distinct characteristics of individual Buddhas (and so forth).

The predecessors have said that there is but a single Vajra Seat; it is only that the visions of the four types of disciples who attained enlightenment there differ, while those who explain this are muddled regarding the characteristics of the turning of the Dharma wheel and thus find it difficult to understand where the Buddha attained enlightenment. Alas! Some may ask:
"Why is it said that he attained the Unsurpassed Way on the Ultimate Heaven (Akaniṣṭha)? This is merely a provisional teaching of the gate of instruction.
Some say that this heaven is at the summit of the ten heavens of the six desire realms and four dhyāna realms, signifying that the Buddha dwells above the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, it accords with the shape of that heaven’s crown; he attained enlightenment while wearing a crown.

Moreover, regarding the characteristics of the land of true recompense, those transformed through the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-yāna*) are exclusively bodhisattvas, all adorned with various jeweled crowns.
The Quiescent Light has characteristics and is wondrously profound (7) (13). Some say that the dwelling place of the Buddha, named Constant Quiescent Light, is the Ultimate Land (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*).
The principle of Quiescent Light is universal, like a mirror or a vessel; the various lands are distinct from one another, like reflections or food.
The *Shiqian* (8.5) states that regarding the "Eternally Quiescent Light Land" (*nitya-prabhāsvara-kṣetra*), there are two parts: first, the heading, and second, the explanation.

As in the "Original Gate" (*mūla-parivarta*), where the bodhisattvas who emerged from the earth dwell in the space below and, after emerging from the earth, also proceed to the empty space of the Seven-Jeweled Wondrous Stupa;
both these spaces are the Quiescent Light. Regarding the statement that "the principle of Quiescent Light is pervasive, like a mirror or a vessel," it is, for example, as follows:
The various devas eat together from precious vessels, as recorded in the third note of the *Zhiguan* (Mohe Zhiguan).

The *Shiqian* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), fascicle 7, states: "Externally, it means that by relying upon those [beings'] physical and mental bases (*āśraya*), one realizes that they are immediately emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle Way.

Because this immediate emptiness, provisional existence, and Middle Way are wondrous, the substance of form and mind is transcended, becoming solely the single true nature. Yet, within this absence of emptiness, provisional existence, or the Middle Way, form and mind remain vividly present, opening up into a state of total identity."

In true purity, there are no longer sentient beings nor the distinctions of the seven stages of expedient means; one does not perceive differences between pure and defiled lands, yet the Indra’s net of the dependent and primary realms remains ever resplendent.

The *Miaole* (Vol. 10, 11) states that only the Perfect [Vehicle] is contemplation: the three thousand realms in a single thought-moment, wherein the three truths are fully present—this is the One Mind.

All minds are one body; all bodies are one land; all lands are observed in a single moment of thought—whether it be mind, body, or land, or whether it be emptiness, the provisional, or the middle—there is no longer any sequence of before or after.

Therefore, when contemplation is perfected, a single mind perceives all minds, a single body perceives all bodies, and a single land perceives all lands, because they manifest within the bodies of the Buddhas of the ten directions. Thus it is said.
Within the constant tranquil light of one’s own mind, one universally perceives all bodies and lands throughout the ten directions.

*The Profound Meaning of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, Fascicle 5 (9): "If the liberation of inconceivable [wisdom] has no substance of form or mind, yet if the inconceivable [liberation] does have a substance of form and mind."

Vimalakīrti Sūtra Commentary (3) (11): The first three [stages] are provisional, while the last one is real. When delusions regarding phenomena and principle are eliminated, the primary retribution immediately attains the fruit of Buddhahood, and the secondary retribution becomes the eternally quiescent light of ultimate purity.
*Myōshū* (The Wondrous School), Part One (3). Question: Since the three lower pure lands all possess characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it is possible to discuss matters such as gold and jewels.
However, the Pure Land of *Sambhogakāya* (the Land of Peace and Light) is entirely devoid of characteristics; how can one speak of gold, jewels, lotus ponds, and jade trees therein? Answer:

When the sutras and śāstras state that the *Sambhogakāya* Land is without characteristics, they mean that it has completely exhausted all defiled and obstructive characteristics (*saṃkleśa-vighna-lakṣaṇa*). It is not like [the absence of characteristics in] empty space.
Space contains not a single thing; it is because the three delusions are ultimately pure that the environment and its inhabitants, as well as form and mind, are ultimately manifest.
Thus, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra says: "By the cessation of this [conditioned] form, one attains eternal form; feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness are likewise so.

The *Renwang jing* calls these the "five aggregates of dharma-nature," and they are also referred to in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* as the "eternality of worldly phenomena" and in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
That form and fragrance are none other than the Middle Way is what is called the ultimate Land of Bliss, the ultimate land of gold and jewels, the ultimate lotus pond, and the ultimate jade tree.
Furthermore, this is because it exhausts the abandonment of the defiled to fully attain the pure, reaching the very source;

thus, realms such as the "domain of suffering" are judged to belong to the three obstacles, while the gold and jewels of the Land of Bliss constitute the Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*). If, however, one proceeds from the perspective of the equality of the pure and the defiled...
As for Tan, he takes the mud and sand of the ultimate realm of suffering to be the *sukhāvatī* (Land of Peaceful Light). These two views merely accord with the *siddhānta* (the established tenet);

there is nothing in them that is not perfectly complete. If one asks whether the Buddha’s unsurpassed retribution is the principle within the phenomenon—such as gold—and the ultimate *sukhāvatī* is the principle within the phenomenon, how could there be gold and so forth? If they are identical in having both phenomenon and principle, then...

Question: How are the two lands distinguished in meaning? Answer: The Buddha’s unsurpassed *vipākaphala* (fruition) is ultimate *ārambha-avabodha* (initial awakening), and its superior-grade quiescent light is ultimate *mūla-avabodha* (original awakening).
Since both the initial and original awakenings have reached their ultimate limit, how could they be divided into two distinct entities?

One should know that although the two lands are distinguished in terms of phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*), they are in reality neither existent nor non-existent. How could the true, excellent, and wondrous existence not be the principle? This is the secret treasury.

How could the principle be the same as that of the "Small Emptiness"? Therefore, these two names—principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*)—refer to a single essence. Because it is the restoration to the original source, it is called the "Unsurpassed Reward Phenomena" (*shibao shi*);
because it is the restoration to the original source, it is called the "Supreme Quiescent Light Principle" (*shang jiguang li*). Thus, the *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) states:

"The four virtues attained through cultivation and the four virtues inherent from the beginning are equal in their two meanings; only then do they constitute the characteristics of the body and land of Vairocana. How much more so in the case of the Pure Name (*Jingming*)!
The Commentary clarifies that the *Sukhāvatī* (Ultimate Reality) is the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive environment) of the Buddha;

therefore, we know that those who insist that the *vipākabhūmi* (retribution land) must possess gold, jewels, and so forth, while the *sukhāvatī* must lack them, are deluded regarding the terminology and entirely ignorant of its meaning.

The Sublime Doctrine (Part 7): First, establishing the name by defining its essence. The previous three [realms] are established according to phenomena; thus, their names for the lands are derived from the causes and effects of human cultivation and severance.
This land, however, belongs to the principle (*li*); therefore, it is named after the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) of its fundamental essence.
Commentary on the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra* (Part II) (17): The essence of the Dharma-nature of the Mahāyāna is fundamentally eternal; it is the source of all form and mind. Why is this?
The Small Vehicle [teaches] that form and mind exist because of the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); therefore, when the bondage is severed, their fruit is eternally extinguished.

The Great Vehicle teaches that form and mind arise from delusions and are subject to birth and extinction, yet they do not exist by virtue of those delusions; their essence is the Dharma-nature. If views and thoughts are exhausted...
When ignorance is entirely present, the true reality of the dharma-nature—the physical and mental faculties—appears as the conventional arising and ceasing of ignorance;

yet, when the aspect of ignorance is partially broken through and the aspect of original nature is revealed, this is the meaning of the Middle Way wherein the dharma-nature of the physical and mental faculties manifests as the true recompense, while ignorance is ultimately exhausted.
Thus, the physical and mental faculties of the original nature are eternally abiding, free from the marks of arising and ceasing, and constitute the eternal, quiescent light.
The essence of the dharma-nature is eternally abiding and unchanging; being quiescent yet constantly illuminating, it is called the "Quiescent Light" (*jigō*).
It is the dwelling place of all Buddhas and the original nature of all sentient beings; it is the ultimate source for the transmission of the Buddha-dharma throughout the world.

This is precisely where the profundity of what Tiantai expounds lies. Therefore, the *Miaozong chao* (Excerpts on the Profound Source) states that the Quiescent Light possesses form (*sō*). However, this...

The essence of the Dharma-nature of the Quiescent Light (Jikō) fully encompasses both the environment and its inhabitants, as well as form and mind; every characteristic is distinct and vivid, and every phenomenon is identical to the nature itself.
How could this be the same as the "true emptiness" (shinkū) of the Lesser Vehicle, which is a mere empty void, devoid of substance, and characterized only by silent stillness?

Because the Venerable Hōzō attained the wondrous realization that the Quiescent Light is replete with all characteristics, he understood the dharma-gates as they were judged within our own school. Thus, it is called [the teaching of] the Name.
In principle, there is no interval between high and low, nor between self and other; there is nothing that is not the nature inherently possessed.

If one speaks of the single nature, it is said that although the nature is one, it lacks a fixed "oneness" as a nature; therefore, the three thousand phenomena of form and mind appear distinct in every aspect.
Is this not because reaching the source reveals that the single nature is fully endowed with both self and other? Thus, regarding the two types of creation, it is said that the principle...

Since each of the two—the phenomenal and the noumenal—possesses the three thousand [realms], is it not that reaching the root depends entirely upon the inherent nature (li-jù) for there to be phenomenal function?
Therefore, when speaking of the three bodies, it is said: "It is simply that there is no attachment to emotions or the hindrance of defilement;

it is not that the subtle and wondrous bodies inherently possessed by nature are absent. Is this not reaching the essence—that the equal Dharma-body also possesses the three virtues? Hence, the four [bodies] are spoken of.
The *Dichijing* says: "When ignorance is exhausted, one returns to the original nature; the constant abiding of form and mind is the eternal tranquil light.
Is this not because one realizes that the two retributions—the environment and its inhabitants—reside within a single thought? Regarding the five abodes (*pañca-vāsa*), it is said:

"The five abodes, along with their active and habitual tendencies, are together in a single thought; taking delusion as the contemplation. Is this not because one realizes that the poisonous nature of phenomena is identical to the Dharma-nature? Thus, it speaks of the six [perfections].
It is said that one should know that the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjia) clarifies the principle that the three thousand [realms] are already complete;
for is it not the case that the realization of Vairocana’s body and land does not exceed a single thought-moment of an ordinary person?

By this analogy, one will thoroughly penetrate all the various names and meanings—such as teaching and contemplation, essence and function, cultivation and nature—as well as the various dharma-gates of this One Vehicle. Let us set this matter aside for now.

However, since even the partial teachings of the Three Vehicles still possess that which is realized, how could the realization of those of the Perfect Teaching involve destroying the substance of phenomena to become empty, quiescent, and signless?
If you say that the principle of the Perfect Teaching is signless because its nature of wisdom differs from mere emptiness, I now ask:
is this nature of wisdom not simply the nature of cognitive awareness? When has a Bodhisattva of the Separate Teaching ever lacked it?
Does the Buddha-nature of the "Dunzhong" (But-Middle) possess awareness? It is precisely because the Dunzhong does not encompass all phenomena that it differs from the Perfect Principle (*yuanli*).
Students should know that the text of the *Miaozong* contains two meanings: first, it clarifies the abandonment of defilement to its ultimate limit and the grasping of purity to its source;
it takes the mud and sand of the realm of suffering as the three lands, and the gold and jewels of the blissful land as the Land of Tranquil Light (*jiguang*).

Is it not the meaning of "separation" (li)? Next, regarding the equality of purity and impurity, where the realm of suffering, the mud, and the sand are entirely the Land of Peaceful Light (Jiguo)—is this not the meaning of "identity" (ji)?

Thus, there are characteristics of both identity and separation. Now, seeking more subtly, within the very meaning of identity—the equality of purity and impurity—there is already the meaning of separation.
This is because that which is seen by those of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanren) is threefold: [the pure, the impure, and their equality].
The obstruction of the defiled realm is entirely the aspect of the *sukhāvatī* (Pure Land of Peaceful Light), yet it appears as a realm of obstruction to those of partial understanding.

Is this not because within the Middle Way itself there is the meaning of transcendence? Someone asks: "Among the three truths, to which truth does the *sukhāvatī* with its phenomenal aspects described here belong?
I reply: "The essence of *sukhāvatī* is the wondrous principle of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*). The principle of true reality is the three truths."

Jiuzú (具足) further asks: regarding the statement in the *Miaole* (妙樂) that "in the Land of Constant Quiescent Light (*nitya-praśānta-ābhāsvara-kṣetra*), beauty and ugliness are both extinguished," and the *Lüji* (略記) [Volume Shang zhi shang san] stating, "Because the Quiescent Light is without marks (*animitta*), the three [realms] are all obliterated," and furthermore, "In the Quiescent Light, the substance of form is eternally quiescent"—how are these passages to be understood?
Answer: The mark of the wondrous essence of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) of the Quiescent Light is precisely the profound stillness of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The marks of beauty and ugliness are the marks of extinction; the mark of extinction is the mark of non-marking.
Such a mark is called the mark of *Sukhāvatī* (the Land of Peaceful Light), the true, good, and wondrously existent, the subtle and wondrous mark. The *Zabian* says:

The *Fuxing* commentary states that the land of eternal peaceful light (*nitya-śānta-prabhā*) and the pure *dharmakāya* have nothing that can adorn them and nothing that is adorned; yet, for the sake of sentient beings...

Because the three lands are taken up, one knows that the Land of Peaceful Light (Sukhāvatī) has neither the characteristic of being defiled or obstructed, nor the characteristic of the environment (receptacle world) or its inhabitants (sentient beings).
Critique: This teaching holds that the Land of Peaceful Light and the Dharmakāya are both gates of essential nature (*dharmatā*).

Because every phenomenon accords with this nature, there is neither that which adorns nor that which is adorned; it does not mean, however, that they lack characteristics. Thus, we know that Zhiyi (the Fourth Ming) profoundly mastered both the words and their meaning.
Second is the wondrous awakening to the essence of the Dharma; third is the thorough penetration of the gates of meaning. Pure Awakening (Jingjue) reverses this. Furthermore, the *Zapi* states:

"The *Miaole* clarifies that the three bodies have both the meanings of preaching and not preaching the Dharma: the Dharma-body is definitively non-preaching; the Reward-body encompasses both meanings;

and the Response and Transformation bodies are definitively preaching. If they are mutually identical, then all preach and all do not preach. That which was previously called the "Dharma-body" refers to this.

"In the *Jigguang* (Peaceful Light) realm, there is certainly no body associated with [discursive] correspondence; in all other lands, there are certainly marks and characteristics. This is likely based on this principle. The critique states:
The intent of the text is to refute the claim that the Dharma-body preaches the Dharma in the newly translated *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Since preaching the Dharma is necessarily an application of the Dharma-body for the sake of those to be converted (*vineya*), how could the Dharma-body itself—which is the Dharma-substance—possess the capacity to preach? Therefore, it is said: "The Dharma-nature is certainly without speech. Now...

How can one take the nature of the inherent presence within the tranquil light (jìguāng) as revealed by Zìmíng as an analogy for this, and thereby seek to claim that what is inherently present is severed and non-existent?
The *Zábiān* further states: "The *Jìngmíng shū* says: 'The land has both the phenomenal and the principle;

the phenomenal is the domain of the response-body (sànyīn), while the principle is the realm illumined by ultimate wisdom. Since wisdom and principle are empty and quiescent, fundamentally there is no distinction between the object and the wisdom.'"
How could there be a distinction between the agent and the object? It is merely that, in order to respond to sentient beings according to their capacities, one speaks of the True and the Responsive;

thus, the phenomena and the principle are clarified. The critique states: This refers to the essence of the nature of equality, which is realized through one's own practice and is fundamentally beyond verbal expression, wherein the four lands are all extinguished.
However, when responding to capacities, one speaks of the existence of the four lands; yet it is not that the Land of Tranquil Light (Jiguang) definitively lacks the other three lands.
The wisdom that is like clouds is fundamentally quiescent and void; it originally lacks any distinction between object and wisdom, thereby transcending the Pure Light (寂光).
How could there be any differentiation between subject and object? It transcends the three lands. Whether partial or complete, provisional or real—[all are subsumed therein].

*Miaoxuan* (7) (20). Question: Among the intermediate [teachings], there are both the partial (*bian*) and the perfect (*yuan*), as well as the provisional (*quan*) and the real (*shi*). If they are all equally termed "provisional," should they also be equally termed "partial"?

Answer: From the perspective of the general meaning (*tongyi*), this is so; however, from the perspective of the specific meaning (*biyi*), it is not. The distinction between the partial and the perfect concerns the Dharma (*fa*);

since the nature of the Dharma is already fixed, the partial is not the perfect, and the perfect is not the partial. The distinction between the provisional and the real concerns the teaching (*jiao*); within the traces (*ji*), these are established as being equally [provisional].
Because they are provisional, one speaks of them as provisional from the perspective of the provisional.

Regarding the intent of the questions in the *Shiqian* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), volumes 8 and 10: after the original manifestation (*benxing*) has been established, during the intervening period of manifesting traces (*chijie*), both the partial and the complete, as well as the provisional and the real, are equally termed "provisional.
This is because they are all manifestations; therefore, they are all provisional. Since the provisional is the partial, they may all be designated as such.

Regarding the second response concerning the distinct meanings of "partial" (*pian*): this does not apply to the Dharma. Since the Dharma is already established as being either "fundamental" (*ben*) or "tracied" (*ji*), it is fixed as either partial or perfect (*yuan*).
The teaching is not like this: when it is fundamental, both the provisional (*quan*) and the real (*shi*) are fundamentally fundamental, and thus they are real;
when it is tracied, both the provisional and the real are tracied, and thus they are called provisional.

*Wenju*, fascicle 9 (4): "Furthermore, 'not being arrogant' means not relying on the Perfect [teaching] to despise the Partial, nor regarding the Real as important while treating the Provisional as light.
*Miaole*, fascicle 9 (11): 'Not relying on the Perfect' means that even the Buddha still employed various skillful means and other profound dharmas to assist the True Path;

how much more so for later students who must follow the teachings—how could they stubbornly oppose them? Even if one’s practice of the Real is still slight, one must not despise the partial and small [teachings]; one must accord with them."

The Buddha’s intention was to protect and guide sentient beings according to their capacities. When asked about the distinction between the partial and the perfect, or the provisional and the real, what was the answer?

Generally speaking, there is no difference; however, when discussed specifically, there are slight variations. "Partial" and "perfect" are categorized according to the teachings (*jiao*), while "provisional" and "real" are categorized according to the Dharma (*fa*). The Dharma refers to that which is expounded beneath the teachings, encompassing both principle (*li*) and wisdom (*zhi*), as well as practice (*xing*) and so forth.
The *Miaoxuan* states: "The categories of 'partial' (*bian*) and 'complete' (*yuan*) are applied to the Dharma, while 'provisional' (*quan*) and 'real' (*shi*) are applied to the teaching.

The *Miaole* states: "The categories of 'partial' and 'complete' are applied to the teaching, while 'provisional' and 'real' are applied to the Dharma; the sequence of their arising each has its own reason. Now, the *Miaoxuan* treats 'partial' and 'complete,' as well as 'provisional' and 'real,' by collectively designating them as 'provisional' when contrasted with the 'partial.
Consequently, there are both general and specific responses. Why does the specific meaning not serve as a precedent [for the other]?

Regarding "partial" (*pian*) and "perfect" (*yuan*): if defined in terms of the Dharma, they are fixed as provisional (*quan*) and real (*shi*); if defined in terms of the teaching (*jiao*), this is not the case. Thus, one should know that they cannot be universally termed "partial.

Since the *Wenju* (Text) states that one does not rely on the perfect to disparage the partial, and further states that the real is valued while the provisional is slighted, the Master of the Commentary (*Jizhu*) raises this question.
There are both general and specific answers; specifically, there is a slight difference between "small" (*xiao*) and "partial/perfect" (*pian/yuan*).

Because there are differences between the provisional and the real regarding the teaching that expresses [the truth], and because there are distinctions between the phenomena expressed and their capacities, it is said that they differ slightly.

Thus, one knows that the meaning and intent of these two passages are fundamentally distinct. It is an error for Cao’an to claim that the text in the *Miaole* is mistaken and that the *Xuanyu* should be taken as correct;
he has missed the point.
*Sanbudui Miaoxuan* (7) (22):
In the *Avataṃsaka*, the stage of *avaivartika* is explained primarily through the enumeration of phenomena (*vastu-saṃkhyā*).
*Shiqian* (8) (12): Regarding the statement that the *Avataṃsaka* explains *avaivartika* primarily through the enumeration of phenomena, etc., furthermore:
The levels of the stage of non-retrogression differ in their height. If one is at the stage of non-retrogression prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*), one merely hears the enumeration of phenomena;
because one knows that phenomena are themselves the principle, one opens up the provisional to reveal the real and enters the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).

At the stage of non-retrogression in mindfulness, one is able to realize that these very provisional teachings are the true aspect (*dharmatā*). How could one seek the true aspect apart from this? It is said to be the "first stage" in contrast to those who have not yet reached it (*avaivartika*).
Regarding the phrases (2) and (12): "Non-retrogression" (*avaivartika*) should be analyzed according to four types—stage, practice, and mindfulness.
Not being born in the three evil realms is non-retrogression of stage; not being born in borderlands, having all faculties intact, and not receiving a female body is non-retrogression of practice;
constantly knowing past lives is non-retrogression of mindfulness. One who possesses these is said to have attained the stage of *avaivartika*.

This is the meaning of the Tripitaka. If, prior to the sixth mind, the Bodhisattva Light-Fur has not yet established the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), his position remains subject to regression.

From the seventh mind upward, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) through the sixth stage, he does not regress; this is termed "non-regression in rank" for those who are still ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) or followers of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

Although their active afflictions (*kleśa*) may already be exhausted, they have not yet been able to universally cultivate the myriad practices; thus, their practice still regresses until the seventh [stage].

Regarding the stage of "Non-retrogression in Practice" (*caryā-apratyudāvartana*): because one still gives rise to thoughts of the Two Vehicles despite being on this ground, there is "retrogression of thought.

Upon reaching the eighth ground, where contemplation and practice flow together into the stream of the Dharma, it is called "non-retrogression of thought. This is termed the stage of *avaivartika*. This, however, is merely the meaning of the ten grounds common to the Three Vehicles.
The Master Di (Dharmatrāta) said: "The ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) constitute non-retrogression through realization; the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) constitute non-retrogression through position."
The non-retrogression of the ten *pariṇāmanā* (dedications) constitutes the non-retrogression of practice; the ten stages (*bhūmi*) constitute the non-retrogression of mindfulness.

This is the meaning of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*), which does not accord with this sutra and is therefore not employed here. The *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (or *Śrī-mālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*) states that in the first stage, the three contemplations manifest before one, the mind is quiescent at every moment, and one naturally flows [into the path].
This too is the non-retrogression of the Separate Teaching and is likewise not employed here. As for what is clarified in the *Avataṃsaka* regarding the beginning...

Abiding in the attainment of the Tathāgata’s single body as infinite bodies, one possesses the three non-regressions; this is the non-regression of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), which is the One True Reality (yishishi).
Now, this is used to judge the stages [of practice].
Regarding *Miaole* (2) (21): One who possesses these [qualities] is called an *avaivartika*. *A* means "non-" and *vaivartika* means "retrogression.

Because one attains the three types of non-retrogression (*tri-avaivartika*) prematurely during the third *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, and because one attains all three meanings simultaneously upon being freed from the five obstacles, this refers to the third *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* extending through to the hundred kalpas;
it encompasses all three types of non-retrogression. Upon reaching this stage, it is termed "superior patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*). Thus it is said.

Next, regarding the "six minds" induced by the stages of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*): since there are no distinct stages to discuss prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) of the Shared Teaching, one borrows the names of the stages from the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*) to designate its own stages;
this refers specifically to entering the stage of Dry Wisdom (*ganhui*) from the seventh level of faith (*xin*) upward in the Distinct Teaching.

Therefore, it is said that from the first ground up to the sixth ground, one is designated as having attained "non-retrogression of position. Alternatively, it may refer to the seven sages (*qixian*) provisionally established prior to the grounds, specifically the stage of Patience (*ren*).

Regarding the stage as the sixth mind, although it is called the "stage of patience" (kṣānti-bhūmi) within the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), it is termed "non-retrogression in position" (avivarta-sthāna);

yet, when compared to the Bodhisattva vehicle, it is still termed "retrogression. Next, because the *Dichilun* masters are permitted [to hold this view] within the Separate Teaching (Bianjiao), it is not refuted here [and so forth].

As for the Perfect Teaching (Yuanwei), which possesses the three types of non-retrogression: if one first explains them by borrowing the sequence of the non-sequence (buzhi), then the seventh faith is termed "non-retrogression in position."
That which is beyond the eight stages of faith is called "non-retrogression of practice"; that which is from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward is called "non-retrogression of mindfulness.
Now, because one already possesses the three virtues from the first stage onward, they are termed the "three non-retrogressions," and thus it is said that they are "complete.

Prajñā is the stage, for it is free from the two deaths; Vimukti is the practice, for all activities are complete; and Dharmakāya is called "mindfulness," for it realizes the true object. (And so forth.)
*Jingming shu* (5) (34): Each of the four teachings has three stages of position, practice, and mindfulness.

If we speak of the bodhisattvas of the *Tripiṭaka* [teaching], those who have attained the "three non-retrogressions" enter the stages of *ūṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, and *kṣānti* after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* of practicing the path; this constitutes the stage of non-retrogression.

If calculated numerically, the three grades of the dharma of *kṣānti* are divided into the three non-retrogressions. According to the *Píngchéng lùn* (*Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*), these are established as positions based on the four foundations of mindfulness.

Non-retrogression through the stages of *uṣmagata* (warmth) and *mūrdhan* (summit) constitutes non-retrogression in practice; through the stage of *kṣānti* (patience), it constitutes non-retrogression in mindfulness.

If referring to the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-śāsana*), from the stage of nature (*gotra-bhūmi*) up to the Arhat’s sixth stage, their merit is equal, and they all possess non-retrogression in position. At the stage of the Pratyekabuddha and the seventh stage, their merit is equal;

when the Bodhisattva cultivates skillful means, this is called non-retrogression in practice. For the Bodhisattva of the eighth stage, where the path and contemplation flow as a dual stream, it is termed non-retrogression in mindfulness.
Regarding non-retrogression: at the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), one is equal to the *pratyekabuddhas*; it is only from the ninth stage onward that this constitutes "non-retrogression in thought.

As for the Separate Teaching (*bye-jo*), the Ten Abidings (*daśavihāra*) constitute non-retrogression in position; the Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*) and Ten Transferences (*daśaparikrama*) constitute non-retrogression in practice; and upon reaching the stages (*bhūmi*), when the three contemplations manifest before one, this is non-retrogression in thought.
As for the Perfect Teaching (*en-kyo*), from the initial mind of the Ten Faiths (*daśaśraddhā*) up to the middle of the Ten Abidings, one attains non-retrogression in position.
To practice non-retrogression, one ascends to the first dwelling of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), whereupon one attains non-retrogression in mindfulness.

Furthermore, there are three kinds of semblance non-retrogression within the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), and three kinds of partial true non-retrogression from the first dwelling onward. Of these, the former three are provisional while the latter one is real.

Chuiyu (7) (13) Jingxi says: Regarding "entering the stage of *uṣmagata*," one should cite the *Abhidharmakośa*, which states that those in the stage of *uṣmagata* will certainly attain *nirvāṇa* and that those at the peak (*mūrdhan*) never sever their roots of goodness.

As for the statement in the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika-yāna*) regarding the three types of non-retrogression and the equality of merit from the sixth stage onward, this is because it shares commonalities with the Lesser Vehicle;
thus it receives the name "equality. The term "all" indicates that from the stage of the manifest vehicle (*vyakta-yāna*) and the stage of nature (*gotra-bhūmi*) onwards, [the stages] are equal.
"All do not regress" refers to those at the initial stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) and so forth;
this is because the stage of the ten faiths is divided into the distinctions of the initial and middle minds, with the eighth through tenth faiths constituting the central phase.

*The Wonderful Dharma Lotus Flower Sutra*, Fascicle Lower (22). The Commentary cites "Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" and "non-retrogression," explaining that "the path-knowledge of bodhi" and so forth refer to this.
Translating *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* as "Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment," this is the fruit sought by the nature of the practitioner's mind.

Regarding non-retrogression from this stage, there are three levels: first, the level [of non-retrogression] attained by destroying the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*).

Non-retrogression means never losing the supramundane stage, which is the nature of the cultivated seeds (*śikṣamāṇa-gotra*). Subduing and severing the "dust-like sands" of afflictions is called non-retrogression in practice;
this means never losing the bodhisattva’s conduct, which corresponds to the nature of the innate seeds (*prakṛti-gotra*) and the nature of the path-seeds (*mārga-gotra*).
If one breaks through ignorance, it is called non-retrogression in mindfulness; this means never losing the right mindfulness of the Middle Way, which is the nature of the sages (*ārya-gotra*).

Now, the four teachings and the three stages of non-retrogression are all spoken in reference to bodhisattvas and correspond to their respective ranks; this is merely according to the specific application of the text. Someone may ask:
"Why do the two schools—the Madhyamaka and the Yogācāra—differ in their correspondence of stages? I reply:

The *Śāstra on the Number of Calculations* (Saṃkhyā-śāstra) posits that one attains the three non-retrogressions horizontally through the completion of practices over three great aeons (*kalpas*). The *Treatise on the Establishment of Truth* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra) posits that one attains the three non-retrogressions vertically by traversing the stages in accordance with one's merit.

It is non-retrogressive. If so, for what reason does the *Myōraku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary refer only to the stage of "superior patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) when discussing the three types of non-retrogression?
It is because the stages of patience all correspond to the completion of the three great *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas.

In the text of the *Myōraku*, this refers to the stage where the six perfections are already fulfilled; therefore, it corresponds to superior patience. Furthermore, one may ask: regarding the seven worthies of the Tripiṭaka...
If one has not yet severed the afflictions (*kleśa*), how can one attain the three types of non-retrogression, whether horizontal or vertical?

It is said that this is explained in terms of the functional capacity of those with sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*) as they progress; those with dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*) cannot avoid retrogression. Furthermore, it was asked:

"Since one who has passed through the third and fourth stages has already severed the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), why is it that one only attains non-retrogression at the sixth stage? It is said that this is in reference to...
This is explained by employing a general name to encompass specific cases; if one follows the specific teaching, then even in the third and fourth stages there is no regression.
The distinctions for the Separate (Vyākaraṇa) and Perfect (Samantabhadra) vehicles may be understood accordingly. *Dujiaoji*, Scroll Five.
Reading the *Jiaoji* (Records of the Teachings), Volume Six.
Tiantai Śramaṇa Fazhao. *Miaoxuan* (Excellence of the Profound), Part Six.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that the true essence of the teaching in this land is purity within hearing and sound.
The *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* states that the Muni’s aggregates of Dharma number eighty thousand; their essence is either speech or names, which are material phenomena (*rūpa*).
It is subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). *Miaoxuan* (8.5): First, using sound as the sūtra—just as when the Buddha was in the world, he preached with his golden mouth;

because there was only the sound that explained and distinguished [the meaning], and the listener thereby attained the Way, sound is taken as the sūtra. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "That which is heard from a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*)..."
Furthermore, there are two ways of using [the Dharma]: when the Buddha was in the world, one could take sound as the sūtra;

now that the Buddha has passed away, we transmit and uphold it through paper and ink, so we should use written characters as the sūtra. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "One hears the three dharmas from within the sūtra scrolls.

To use the dharma as the sūtra means that by reflecting inwardly, one's mind accords with the dharma; this does not depend on the instruction of others, nor is it merely paper and ink—it is simply the mind’s clear understanding.
Since awakening is the realization that all phenomena are the Dharma, it is said: "Those who cultivate my Dharma realize it through their own self-knowledge" (and so forth).
In this context, only three sense objects are employed; the other three consciousnesses are dull. If the nose smells paper and ink, there is no cognition;
if the body touches a scripture, it cannot understand; and if the tongue tastes the characters, how could it distinguish right from wrong?
*Shiqian* (8) (22): Now, both ancient and modern scholars commonly refer to *dharmas* as "sūtras" because the text follows this predominant interpretation.

Although the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are established separately, the two categories of sound and form must necessarily rely on *dharma* for their communication; if one sees or hears them without mental reflection (*manasikāra*), there is no way for the teaching to correspond with the mind.
*Miaoxuan* (8.5): If other lands also employ all six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), or employ one sense object exclusively—as in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, which says:
"If one gives a single meal to all beings, those who are equal regarding food are also equal regarding the Dharma;

those who are equal regarding the Dharma are also equal regarding food"—this refers to employing exclusively that which is encountered by the faculty of the tongue as the sūtra. Or there are lands where [the teaching] is conveyed by the touch of celestial robes.
Attaining the Way through the body is to take touch as the primary sūtra; attaining the Way by seeing the Buddha’s radiance is to take form as the primary sūtra;
attaining the Way through silent contemplation of the mind is to take the mind as the primary sūtra.

Just as in the Land of Universal Fragrance, where the work of the Buddha is performed through fragrance, fragrance is taken as the primary sūtra; in other lands, the six faculties and consciousnesses are sharp and distinct.

Question: If the sense objects (viṣaya) are the sūtras because the three faculties (indriya) of this land are dull—such that the nose does not reach [the scent] of donkeys, dogs, deer, and so forth—how can one attain penetration regarding odors, tastes, and tangibles?
Is it not the case that while the faculties are sharp, the sense objects are dull, and thus the objects are not the sūtras?
Answer: The six sense objects are the substance of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu); they are inherently the sūtras. It is not only when they are grasped by sharp faculties that they become such.
Sūtra. Fascicle 8 (22). Second, within the section on other lands, there are two parts. First, the general establishment of the statement: "either six or partial.
This means that either a single land possesses all six [perfections], or a single land is partial in one, or two, three, or four; for example, this land is complete in its application of three.
Furthermore, there are cases where [the faculties] are enhanced, whether individually or possessed in pairs; if this is so, what harm is there?
In this land, the root-natures (indriya-gotra) are not equal, and there are also causes such as taste, fragrance, and touch—as is explained comprehensively in the following passage.

Regarding the phrase "words and phrases" (*vyañjana-pada*): "words" (*vyañjana*) refers to written characters, as they constitute the beginning and end of a section; thus it is said that "words are identical to characters," which serve as the basis for the two [subsequent categories].

"Phrases" (*pada*) refers to syntactic units or stops; since their meaning extends through both long and short sequences, it is said that "names (*nāman*) express intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), while phrases (*pada*) express distinctions (*viśeṣa*)."
*Miaole* (1.20): Some do not permit that the sūtras concerning form after cessation merely state that names and phrases belong to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

If one were to entirely reject the sūtras on seeing, then at the very beginning, "hearing" should be changed to "knowing. One should understand that these [perceptions] are first obtained by the eyes and ears, and only subsequently flow into the aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*).
If even a single character or a single sound were not apprehended simultaneously by both the visual and auditory consciousnesses, then it would be called a name (*nāman*).
The phrases and words are all fully established; these harmonious expressions cannot be deceived.
Regarding the "Chapter on Light and Phrases" (Part 2): this refers to categories of meaning. Within this text, the phrasing and categories follow one another, and these sections are termed *varga*.

*Guangming ji* (1–3): The words and phrases herein are all present in the sūtras. That which can express the teaching is collectively termed the "four dharmas," namely: sound (*śabda*), name (*nāman*), phrase (*pada*), and syllable (*vyañjana*). These are of two kinds:
those existing during the Buddha’s lifetime and those after his parinirvāṇa. Regarding the time of the Buddha’s lifetime, there are the eight tones and four analytical knowledges;

among these, the characteristic of the *brahma-voice* is the one that is real. The bodies of names, phrases, and syllables are merely the winding and turning constructions established upon that sound.

These three are established as conventional sounds belonging to the category of form (*rūpa-dharma*). The bodies of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*) belong to the third aggregate (*skandha*), the formations dissociated from thought (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

According to the *Abhidharmapada* (14), the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (17), and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (24), there are differences in how these are established by the two schools, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Regarding the names, phrases, and phonemes, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Names express intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); phrases express distinctions (*viśeṣa*)."
Phrases (*vyañjana*) are the syllables (*akṣara*), which serve as the basis for the two [names and phrases].

If we consider the compilation by the various noble ones after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa—whether on palm leaves in that land [India] or yellow scrolls in this land [China]—the names, phrases, and syllables contained therein are all established based on the phenomena of shape and color.
Here, I have briefly cited these two; when complete, they correspond to the four [bases of name, phrase, syllable, and dharma].

Supplement (Part One) (7): If one follows the name of the scripture scroll, although it is based on form, since that form is a collection of the sounds and teachings of the original scriptures, following the scripture scroll, it is also called "hearing the name."

Regarding the passage from the *Bǎifǎ Chāo* (not yet verified; cited in the *Bùzhù*) [it states]: "The 'body of syllables' (*vyañjana-kāya*) has no intrinsic nature and is provisionally established based on 'letters' (*akṣara*).

If there is no sense of modification or transition, it is merely called a 'letter. If there is modification and transition beyond a single letter, such that it can express distinctions, it is then called a 'phrase' (*pada*), and so forth.
Although the substance of a syllable is itself a letter, it must serve as the basis for the other two [phrases and words]."

That which possesses the sense of modification is designated as a "phrase" (*vyañjana*); that which does not serve as a basis for the other two and lacks the sense of modification is merely called a "syllable" (*akṣara*).

As for the substance of the teaching, it consists of one real and three provisional entities: the one real refers to form (*rūpa*), and the three provisional refer to the sets of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and phrases (*vyañjanakāya*).

This is stated with reference to the period after [the Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa; however, during the time of the Buddha, as well as in that land and this region, for those of sharp and dull faculties respectively, none of the six sense objects were present.
This can be verified by the patriarchal texts regarding the three characteristics of the provisional (prajñapti). Now, let us briefly clarify them:
names (nāman) express intrinsic nature (svabhāva), such as the various natures of the eyes, ears, earth, water, and so forth; phrases (pada) express distinctions (viśeṣa).
"Phrases" (*pada*) refer to such things as "Buddha-eye" or "fleshly eye," which serve to express meaning. "Sentences" (*vyañjana*) are composed of one or many syllables;

without these, there would be no means of expression. Furthermore, they are called "name-bodies" (*nāmakāya*) and so forth, taking "aggregation" as their meaning—just as the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) aggregate to form a body—and names are of various kinds, as are phrases.

Various types of *mon* (phonemes/characters) are all of the nature of aggregation, whether they be single or multiple. Someone may ask: "The *Kiki* (Record) states that *mon* refers to written characters;
yet, the beginning and end of a single fascicle—this 'fascicle-text' (*mon*)—is something perceived by the eye, and thus properly belongs to form (*rūpa*).
Since form is substantial (*dravya*), how does this differ from the statement that 'the *mon* is itself the character (*ji*)'? [The answer is: It is simply one *mon*.
The term "syllable" (vyañjana) signifies that which penetrates both directions. If explained from the perspective of its essence, it is called the "one reality" (eka-tattva);

if one discusses its functional utility based upon that essence, there is transformation and change. Once this syllable has acquired the name of "phoneme" (akṣara), it subsequently serves as the basis for phrases and sentences, thus belonging to the conventional (prajñapti). Furthermore, one asks: how are the "essence itself" and the "basis" distinguished?

It is said that there is one reality and three provisional designations, which constitute the essence itself. As for the basis [of the teaching], it differs between the time when the Buddha was in the world and after his parinirvāṇa.

During the Buddha’s lifetime, the golden words of his oral activity served as the basis. After his passing, before the compilation of the scriptures, the mental recollections of Ānanda served as the basis.
Following the compilation, the palm-leaf manuscripts of that land (India) and the yellow scrolls of this land (China) serve as the basis.

He asked again: "What is the difference between the essence of the teaching (*śāsana-tattva*), the essence of the sūtra (*sūtra-tattva*), and the essence of the Dharma as it is heard (*dharma-śruta-tattva*)?

He replied: "The essence of the teaching belongs to the signifier (*vācaka*); the essence of the sūtra belongs to the signified (*vācya*); and the essence of the Dharma encompasses both the signifier and the signified. He asked again:

"In both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools, the essence of the teaching is established through the conjunction of one reality and three conventionalities. If this is so, then regarding sound and form..."
One may say this: how can it be that while odor, flavor, and touch possess only one real substance each, they are nonetheless threefold as conventional designations (*prajñapti*)?

It is said: they are "real" in relation to the sense faculties, but "conventional" when entering consciousness. Because they are distinguished by their entry into consciousness, all six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) may be described as being threefold through conventional designation.
See the *Fanyi mingyi ji* (Collection of Translated Terms and Meanings).

The *Miaoxuan* (Profound Mystery) on the Seals of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna (8–12). The *Śāstra* states: "If the various sūtras of the Hīnayāna are sealed with the three seals of impermanence, non-self, and nirvāṇa, they are the word of the Buddha;
practicing them leads to the attainment of the Way. If they lack these three Dharma seals, they are the teaching of Māra. Great.
The Mahāyāna sūtras contain but a single Dharma-seal, namely the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), which is called a definitive sūtra (*nītārtha*) capable of attaining the Great Way;
for if it lacks the seal of the true mark, it is the teaching of Māra. Therefore, Śāriputra said: "The World-Honored One speaks of the true path;
Pāpīyan has no such thing. Why? Because the Lesser Vehicle [teaches] that the three great [aspects] and the one small [aspect]—namely, saṃsāra and nirvāṇa—are distinct, and it regards saṃsāra as...
Taking impermanence as the first seal and non-self as the final seal, these two seals are used to seal the teachings on saṃsāra and nirvāṇa;
yet, one employs only the single seal of quiescence. Therefore, the three greatnesses [of the Mahāyāna] hold that saṃsāra is itself nirvāṇa and nirvāṇa is itself saṃsāra—non-dual and non-distinct.
As Vimalakīrti said: "All sentient beings possess the mark of constant quiescence, which is itself great nirvāṇa."
It is further said: "Fundamentally unborn, now there is no extinction. That which is fundamentally unborn is not the mark of impermanence or non-self;
that which now has no extinction is not the mark of a minor nirvana. It is solely the single true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Because it is the true mark, it is called the mark of eternal quiescence, which is Great Nirvāṇa. This employs but a single seal; this great and small seal seals half [of the body].
When the sutras are complete, non-Buddhists cannot corrupt them and celestial Māras cannot destroy them; just as worldly documents are trustworthy when they bear an official seal,
one should know that all sutras must obtain the seal of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) before they can be called definitive Mahāyāna teachings.

*Shiqian* (8) (26): Regarding the passage from "If there is impermanence" up to the "Three Seals of the Dharma," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 20, states: "All dharmas are impermanent; all dharmas are without self; nirvāṇa is quiescent. Question: Why, within [the seal of] quiescence, is only one [dharma] mentioned and not many? Answer: In the first seal, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are discussed; in the second seal, it is stated that "all" [dharmas] are [without self]. Therefore, in the third seal, it is said that "nirvāṇa alone" is quiescent. This is because the three seals are established based on the three types of sentient beings. Specifically, those who delight in the five aggregates are taught that the five aggregates are impermanent; those who delight in the self are taught that all dharmas are without self; and those who delight in the cycle of birth and death are taught that nirvāṇa alone is quiescent. Thus, these three seals are established according to the inclinations of sentient beings. Furthermore, the first two seals are established based on the principle of "existence," while the third seal is established based on the principle of "non-existence. This is because the first two seals are established through the negation of permanence and self, whereas the third seal is established through the negation of the cycle of birth and death. Moreover, the first two seals are established based on the principle of "defilement," while the third seal is established based on the principle of "purity. This is because the first two seals clarify the nature of defilement, whereas the third seal clarifies the nature of purity. Furthermore, the first two seals are established based on the principle of "suffering," while the third seal is established based on the principle of "bliss. This is because the first two seals clarify the nature of suffering, whereas the third seal clarifies the nature of bliss. Finally, the first two seals are established based on the principle of "conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), while the third seal is established based on the principle of "unconditioned phenomena" (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). This is because the first two seals clarify the nature of conditioned phenomena, whereas the third seal clarifies the nature of unconditioned phenomena. For these reasons, only one dharma is mentioned within the seal of quiescence. It is not that other dharmas do not exist; rather, they are not mentioned because they are not relevant to the specific context. This is similar to how, when explaining the four truths, one speaks of "suffering" and "origination" but does not speak of "cessation" and "path" [in that specific context], or when explaining the twelve links of dependent origination, one speaks of "ignorance" and "formations" but does not speak of "consciousness" and so forth [in that specific context]. Therefore, although the Three Seals of the Dharma encompass all dharmas, they are established by focusing on the most essential points. This is why only one dharma is mentioned within the seal of quiescence. Furthermore, the three seals are established based on the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*). Specifically, the seal of impermanence is established based on the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*); the seal of non-self is established based on the gate of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*); and the seal of quiescence is established based on the gate of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*). This is because the gate of emptiness negates the notion of permanence, the gate of signlessness negates the notion of self, and the gate of wishlessness negates the cycle of birth and death. For this reason, the three seals are established based on the three gates of liberation. Moreover, the three seals are established based on the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*). Specifically, the seal of impermanence is established based on conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-prajñā*); the seal of non-self is established based on the wisdom of the path (*mārga-prajñā*); and the seal of quiescence is established based on the wisdom of cessation (*nirodha-prajñā*). This is because conventional wisdom perceives the impermanence of conditioned phenomena, the wisdom of the path perceives the absence of self in all dharmas, and the wisdom of cessation perceives the quiescence of nirvāṇa. For this reason, the three seals are established based on the three types of wisdom. Furthermore, the three seals are established based on the three trainings (*śikṣā*). Specifically, the seal of impermanence is established based on the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*); the seal of non-self is established based on the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*); and the seal of quiescence is established based on the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*). This is because the training in higher ethics leads to the realization of impermanence, the training in higher mind leads to the realization of non-self, and the training in higher wisdom leads to the realization of quiescence. For this reason, the three seals are established based on the three trainings. In summary, although the Three Seals of the Dharma encompass all dharmas, they are established by focusing on the most essential points. This is why only one dharma is mentioned within the seal of quiescence. It is not that other dharmas do not exist; rather, they are not mentioned because they are not relevant to the specific context.
