Regarding the "assembly of Aṅgulimāla" mentioned in the *Śūrangama Sūtra Commentary* (Fascicle 10, Section 12), the beginning of that sūtra states:

"At that time, the World-Honored One was with immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as the fourfold assembly, devas, nāgas, the eight classes of supernatural beings, vighnas, pūtanas, and so forth."
The Moon Deva and the World-Protectors all speak of them as "immeasurable.

If one does not clarify that they specifically pertain to the five periods, one will not perceive the sequence of the transformative rites; if one does not clarify that they pervade all five periods, one will not perceive how [the Buddha] accords with what is appropriate to reach sentient beings.
In the *Miaoxuan*, it is clarified that the *Prajñā*, *Lotus*, and *Nirvāṇa* sūtras all universally encompass the preceding [periods].
Regarding the fact that only the Vaipulya (fangděng) is not clearly defined, what is said? The *Miaoxuan* states: "The Vaipulya teachings of reprimand and censure follow after the Tripiṭaka;

the time they were applied for censure should be before the twelve years [of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*]. Some say: "If one refers to the manifest teaching (*kai-shi*), as in the *Xuanyiwen*, there are none;
if one refers to the secret teaching (*mimi*), as in the *Jingming shu*, there are. There are also those who cite the *Aṅgulimāla-sūtra*.
This sutra was spoken by the Tathāgata six years after his attainment of the Way; it is a revealed teaching of the Vaipulya that was proclaimed universally before [the assembly].
As for the statement in the *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra* that it was spoken six years later, this refers to a secret teaching and is not what was compiled in the present collection.
Indeed, had it been included in the present compilation, there would have been no mention of "six years" within the text. This is because [Zhiyi] of Tiantai observed other texts pointing this out.
I have recently cited the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Mystery) as evidence, using passages such as those concerning Trapusa and Bhallika.

Having read that scripture in connection with this discussion, I found that although it lacks the specific text regarding the "six years," it is precisely the passage cited in the tenth fascicle of the *Xuanqi* (Profound Commentary).
This text is found in the fourth volume of the "Liang" section of the Tripitaka, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra during the Song dynasty.
The Profound Mystery of the Vaipulya Prophecies (10) (23): Regarding the *dhāraṇī*, it says: "Previously, in Rājagṛha, the śrāvakas were given prophecies;
now, once again in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī, the śrāvakas are again given prophecies. Formerly, in Vārāṇasī, the śrāvakas were given [prophecies]..."
Regarding the prediction for Śāriputra, it says: "Because the World-Honored One does not speak in vain and his words are true, he was able to grant us our predictions a second and a third time;
therefore, we know that the Vaipulya [sūtras] extend up to after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*."
The divination slip (No. 27) states that "after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*" refers to the bestowal of predictions at Rājagṛha being identical to those in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*;
that "the record of Śrāvastī" refers to the *Vaipulya* sūtras following the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. In the latter part of that sūtra, it says:
"When Śāriputra heard that Mañjuśrī had received his prediction, he asked Mañjuśrī, 'What do you think? Mañjuśrī said to Śāriputra..."
"What do you think? Can flowers grow again on a withered tree? (and so forth). Śāriputra said, "No.
Mañjuśrī said, "If it cannot be found, why do you ask whether I have received a prediction of enlightenment and feel joy?
A prediction is formless, signless, selfless, and beyond speech; it has no past, future, or present. It is just like [the aforementioned]..."
One who contemplates the wild horse in this manner is said to have received the prediction. This passage describes the signs by which Mañjuśrī refuted Śāriputra’s attainment of the prediction.
Regarding the phrases (4), (5), and 7 concerning those who have received the prediction and those who have not (and so forth).
The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra of the Mahāyāna (Volume Six, Chapter on Transformations, Case Four). At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, for what reason does the Tathāgata bestow upon the Arhats the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? (and so forth). The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively, and I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati, it is because I [act] for those who have no remainder..."
Because it is the realm of *nirvāṇa*, [the Buddha] secretly exhorts them to cultivate the bodhisattva practices.

This is because there are bodhisattvas in this realm and other lands whose minds delight in seeking the *nirvāṇa* of the śrāvakas; to cause them to abandon such a mind and advance in the great practices, he makes this statement.

Furthermore, it is the transformation-buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) who grants the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) to the transformed śrāvakas, not the Dharma-nature buddha (*dharmatā-buddha*). Mahāmati, it is not that the [Dharma-nature] buddha grants the prediction to the śrāvakas.

The statement that [the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*] records [the prediction for Śrāvakas] is a secret teaching. *Fuxing* (Vol. 6, Part 3): Question: If it is said that in the Vaipulya [sūtras] the two vehicles are not recorded as receiving predictions, why does the second chapter, the "Transformation" (*nirmāṇa*) chapter, of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, record Mahāmati asking the Buddha:
"For what reason, World-Honored One, do you grant predictions to the Śrāvakas? and the Buddha replying: "Because of three intentions"?
1. The bestowing of a prediction upon one who has entered the realm of nirvana without remainder is a secret exhortation to cultivate the bodhisattva practice. 2.
This is for the sake of those bodhisattvas in this world or other lands who delight in seeking the nirvana of śrāvakas, so as to exhort them to abandon such a mind and cultivate the great practice.
3. It is a transformation Buddha who bestows the prediction upon a śrāvaka, not a Dharma-nature Buddha; Mahāmati, this is a secret teaching.
The judgment states: Now we hear that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is an explicit prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), which differs from the implicit predictions found in the *Vaipulya* [sūtras].
If one follows this principle, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* should both contain such predictions; why then would it be unique to the *Laṅkāvatāra*? Thus, the *Vaipulya* says:
"In the second and third [assemblies], we were granted predictions. The first meaning is for those who have already entered parinirvāṇa; the second meaning is merely for...
Regarding the disparagement of bodhisattvas of dull faculties, what does the prediction made for them have to do with the two vehicles?

This third judgment—that it is not the Buddha of the Dharma-nature—is to separate the provisional from the real; it is not like the *Lotus Sūtra*, which reveals that the original [Buddha] from afar has never destroyed his own land, yet the multitudes see it as burning.
If even the Buddha of the Dharma-nature does not grant predictions to bodhisattvas, how much less so to śrāvakas?
Thus we know that these three meanings are all distinct from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. One should understand that Mahāmati initiated this esoteric teaching;

therefore, because he asked questions concerning the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), it is known that the meaning of that sūtra belongs to the Vaipulya class and differs from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

This is evident as it repeatedly refutes and supersedes the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Consequently, within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the three cycles of bestowing predictions are spoken specifically for the sake of the *śrāvakas*.

This is stated in order to manifest what is not taught in other sūtras; therefore, there are textual passages throughout [the canon] concerning the detailed bestowal of the names of kalpas and lands and the conferring of predictions upon bodhisattvas.

Consequently, one may rely on such general statements as "he shall become a Buddha," or even the specific claim from the *Honmon* (Original Gate) that "a person of such-and-such a birth shall attain the *Lotus Sūtra* and be called 'Wondrous'."
*Miaole* (3) (26): Just as the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-realm contains nothing that it does not encompass, [the Buddha] rendered those śrāvakas deaf and mute.

Although there are records of their future attainment in the latter part [of the scriptures], these differ from what was first heard at the Deer Park, where they were exclusively of the Small Vehicle.

Even with the Vaipulya [sutras], they were still obscure regarding the Prajñā; thus, although the *Laṅkāvatāra* and Vaipulya sutras contain words recording the [attainment of] the Small, the *Laṅkāvatāra* is actually a secret response.
The Vaipulya teachings of the Bodhisattvas are intended to supersede those of the Śrāvakas; thus, throughout the entire corpus of the Buddha’s teachings, this alone is most manifest.
In the *Vaipulya Dhāraṇī Prophecy Chapter* (Volume Two, Box Fu), the Buddha addressed the assembly of five hundred great disciples:
"You all shall likewise each become Buddhas, all sharing the same title: Tathāgata Ratnacandrarāja, Arhat."

"Regarding the phrase 'The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha' (and so forth), the Master of the Record states that the *Laṅkāvatāra* is a secret teaching for Bodhisattvas within the Vaipulya sūtras, intended to refute and supersede the Śrāvakas;
this points to the purport of both the *Laṅkāvatāra* and the *Vaipulya-dhāraṇī* sūtras. The *Laṅkāvatāra* secretly records the [limitations of] the Hīnayāna."
The passage concerning the dialogue between Śāriputra and Mañjuśrī, which follows the Buddha’s exposition of the *Vaipulya-dhāraṇī-sūtra* for the Bodhisattvas,
is a refutation and rejection [of the former].
*The Ten Practices:
A Horizontal Study of the Profound Mystery*, (10), (24): "The Separate Teaching further has four [stages]... (*et cetera*).

*The Commentary on the Profound Meaning*, (10), (27): "'The Separate Teaching further has four' means that in the Separate Teaching, the ten abodes cultivate the birthless nature of birth, and the ten practices..."

Because one cultivates the Ten Dedications of the Immeasurables and cultivates non-action (*anabhisamskāra*), attaining the stages (*bhūmi*) and realizing non-action, it is said that there are four [sets of four].
Furthermore, within the Ten Practices (*daśapratipatti*), one studies all Buddha-dharmas and fulfills them through sixteen gates; these are also called the four [sets of four]. Question:

Since one has already practiced the eight [gates] while abiding [in the Ten Abidings], why does one practice sixteen more during the Ten Practices? Answer: The former refers to self-cultivation, wherein one follows a single gate according to its application; the latter...
Because one practices for the sake of transforming others, one further cultivates the first eight within the middle [set]; therefore, all sixteen must be extensively practiced.
(Xuan, 4, 8) The Path and Cessation are identical to Suffering and Origination; Suffering and Origination are identical to the Path and Cessation.

Divination Stick (5) (3): Regarding the statement that "suffering and its accumulation are themselves the path and cessation," who among those who have resolved their minds [for enlightenment] has not severed afflictions and birth-and-death, extensively gathered the Buddha-dharma, and sought the unsurpassed path?
However, the intent of this teaching is that one realizes the essence of the path and cessation *within* birth-and-death and the afflictions;
therefore, it says, "seek this within the mental activities of sentient beings. This is the true knowledge of genuine severance and the wondrous principle of cultivation.

Because they have attained realization, their practice proceeds vertically through the stages of dwelling and proceeding, yet they remain deluded regarding the dedication [of merit]; they possess a slight knowledge and a minor realization of the first stage—this is precisely the meaning [intended here].

*Jian* (5.1): Although these four sets of Four Noble Truths are all included within the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), since they are categorized vertically according to the four aspects such as arising-and-ceasing, the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching employ this very practice of self-cultivation to transform others; therefore, they are explained horizontally within the ten practices (*shixing*).
These four [teachings] are entirely for the sake of benefiting sentient beings; therefore, the four marks each attach to their respective teachings to form their specific characteristics.
*Fuxing* (Vol. 6, Part 2): One should know that herein, if the text were not fully inclusive, how could the original intent be understood? Regarding the sequence:
at the stage of emerging into the provisional (*jia*), one is immediately able to bestow upon others the four gates of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

In the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*), fascicle 6, part 4: "Regarding the 'lower roots' mentioned in the context of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), their emergence into the provisional (*chujia*) is equal in merit to the stage of the Ten Dedications (*shixiang*).

This refers to the stage of emerging into the provisional through the semblance (*xiangsi*) of the perfect fusion of the three truths (*sandi*), which differs from the sequential [attainment of] the provisional."

*Fuxing* (Vol. 6, Part 2, Section 5): "The common and specific [entrances] into emptiness merely illuminate the six realms; the provisional entry into the two teachings differs in its duration, yet neither is yet able to transcend the provisional nature of the Buddha-realm.
How then could they perceive the Middle within the nine realms? Even if these [realms] are accompanied by emptiness, they are still the provisional nature of the ten realms;
since there is no dharma-nature, they are not yet perfectly interfused (*yuanrong*)."
The Master Beifeng said: "It is precisely because the provisional teachings (biejiao) involve a heavy delusion that one cannot suddenly cultivate the contemplation of the Middle Way.

Consequently, the Tathāgata preached this teaching, which proceeds through a sequence from beginning to end, situated at the periphery between the internal and external, wherein the opportunity to realize the One by destroying the nine is received;
yet, though one initiates practice based on this teaching, within the stage of the Ten Practices (shixing), one is still personally unable to achieve perfection."

Cultivating tranquility enables one to provide others with a complete exposition; yet, even while abiding in these stages, one may still be deluded regarding one’s own practice. Both self-cultivation and the transformation of others require the severing of the nine grades of afflictions.

Examining the textual principles, this refers solely to the "Middle Way" (but-mid). Thus, the *Zapien* states: "The ten stages of dedication (daśabhūmi) involve cultivation according to the ultimate path;

the ten practices (daśapāramitā) are truly non-conceptual (anabhisamskāra), yet they provisionally accord with the expedient means. This is because the stage within cultivation has already deepened and emerged."
Since the provisional position is still shallow while the ultimate position is deep, we know that his past transformation of others was nothing other than wondrous practice;

since the provisional position is shallow, we know that his future self-cultivation will likewise be merely the "Middle" (but-mid). One should not use the real to challenge the provisional, nor allow the benefit of others to obstruct one's own path.

Tiantai Śramaṇa Fǎzhào.
Regarding the two characters "wénjù" (文句), the private commentary divides them into four parts; first, the text [itself],
followed by the explanation of the names below.
2. This also [explains] the underlying intention of what follows;
3. From "Anciently" onwards, the differences are distinguished;
4. From "Now, together" onwards, it is concluded and returned to the core.

The Six Difficulties of the Sublime Sūtra (1): It is rare for the Buddhas to appear in the world; even rarer is to encounter them when they have appeared. Even more difficult is for them to preach this Dharma;
and to hear this Dharma throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas is likewise difficult. Those who are able to listen to this Dharma—such people [are truly rare].

These are likewise difficult: (1) it is difficult for a Buddha to appear in the world; it is difficult for a Buddha to preach the Dharma; it is difficult for this to be transmitted and translated; it is difficult to attain self-awakening; it is difficult to hear a teacher’s exposition;
and it is difficult to memorize it after hearing it even once.
Regarding the note under the title of the *Miaoji* (1), which states "the meaning of the six difficulties" (*yún yún*), [it is as follows]:
Zhiyi praises the difficulty of encountering the Dharma to manifest the necessity of its transmission; thus, Zhanran specifically added this note.

Since it accords with the text of the sutra and the praise for the rarity of the Dharma should properly appear beneath the *Wenju*, yet it was his own personal interpretation, he did not write it in large characters.
In the sutras, "hearing" the Dharma refers to hearing what is shallow while being able to listen to what is profound; this is the intended meaning of the phrasing.

If one were to unify these terms as used in the commentaries (*jìwén*), saying that "hearing" refers to the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa and "listening" refers to the time when the Buddha was in the world, that would be incorrect.
Someone asked: "What is the underlying intent (*zhùyì*) behind the *Típódáduō pǐn* (Devadatta Chapter)? [The Master] replied: "This is where Zhàngān (Zhiyi) opens up the Great [Vehicle]."

The Master provides three exegeses on the "Original and Traces" (*benji*)—namely, by way of causes and conditions, by way of the provisional teaching, and by way of the original and traces—and annotates them so they may be easily understood.
This is because the Great Master first evaluates this chapter before explaining the title, and subsequently translates the names and explains the meanings;

since these meanings contain the three exegeses, he annotates them accordingly. Furthermore, it is asked: regarding the "Contact" (*chu*) among the twenty difficulties within the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections*...

Regarding the difficulty of having no mind when facing circumstances and the difficulty of remaining unmoved when encountering objects: what is the difference between them? It is said that the former refers to adverse conditions, while the latter refers to favorable conditions.
Furthermore, it was asked: what is the difference between the "difficulty of being born in the age of a Buddha" and the "difficulty of meeting a Buddha" among the nine difficulties mentioned below?
It is said that the former is the difficulty of being born in the age of a Buddha, whereas the latter is the difficulty of actually seeing a Buddha after having been born in the age of a Buddha.
He asked again: "What is the difference between first explaining twenty difficulties and later explaining nine difficulties? He replied:
"The former was an expository discourse, while the latter was a dialectical discussion; therefore, they are not the same.
This is able to open up the Buddha-wisdom.
Preface (1): Left as a gift for future sages, we shall together aspire toward the Buddha-wisdom.

Regarding the term "Buddha-wisdom" (2–3): one must clarify the provisional and the real within the fruits of the Three Teachings, and reveal the Great and Small Vehicles of the four flavors and their concurrent application;
thus, there will be a destination for persons, principles, teachings, and practices, and no difference between the stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering.

This is precisely the Buddha-wisdom of the present sutra. [Question: Among the various sutras, what distinguishes this "perfect" (yuan) from others, such that it must be said that only through "opening" (kai) does one attain Buddha-wisdom?
[Answer: The perfect is indeed not different; however, those at the initial stage of the path have not yet had it revealed.

They perceive the perfect as being separated from the provisional (pian), and thus they must hear the revelation of the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena. Once they have entered into reality, they merely discuss further advancement; for those with provisional capacities, [the distinction lies in this].
At this point, one must certainly explain [the term "opening"].

I have privately examined the records and questioned: what is the difference between the "perfect" (*yuan*) in various sutras and this [term], such that it must be said that "only by opening" is it the Buddha-wisdom?
This is because of the single character "open" (*kai*) in the preceding text; thus, by means of "opening," the perfect is distinguished [from other forms].

The statement that "the Perfect [Teaching] has not yet been revealed" does not mean that the Perfect is revealed while the Non-perfect is not; rather, it means that the Non-perfect is revealed while the Perfect remains unrevealed.

In my private commentary on the *Jì* (Record) and the detailed exegesis (*wěishì*), I have divided the text into six sections: first, the individual explanation of the lower [passage], followed by the narration of the general revelation.
1. "The second title" indicates the distinct text below; 2.
"Therefore, only" clarifies that the characteristics are manifest; 3.
"Therefore, one knows" refutes the errors of the ancients.
5. Now, the inquiry below is a warning regarding the propagation of the sutra;
6. "However, universally" below concludes the essential pivot (1).
Three: general and specific [sections] based on practice and categorized by teaching.

In the *Myōraku* (Wondrous Joy), fascicles one and two provide a separate commentary on the title. The *Gen* (Profound) [commentary] states that because the initial name encompasses the three dharmas within the middle, and because the beginning and end of these three dharmas span the entire work, there is nothing within this single work that surpasses them.
Among the provisional traces (*jaku*), the "three-in-one" of the original ground (*honji*) is of the highest merit throughout the entire period; thus, the three within the one are eternally distinct.
The preceding teaching is one part of the three; it is not shared with others. It is the trace that is the fundamental, and the discourse on the span of life is the fundamental that is the trace.

All are fully present in what is now being explained. For instance, within the realm of the trace, the substance is neither cause nor effect; yet, by relying upon it, one distinguishes cause and effect.

Only when cause and effect take up the substance does the substance possess its superior function. Thus, these three dharmas all arise from revelation and clarification; if one does not first understand this...
Since the subtle that can open [the truth] must be clarified by means of what it opens—the coarse—it is necessary to distinguish between the provisional traces and the fundamental principle.

Therefore, the explanation of the title cannot be undertaken hastily; the separate explanation provided under the title is not a matter of ease, for the great meaning of the title has already been fully detailed.
Consequently, regarding the main text of the sūtra, one merely makes a rough division into sections. That the title is called "Wenju" (Phrases and Sentences) is precisely because of this.

Therefore, if one merely divides the text into phrases, the great principle will not be revealed; yet if one speaks only of the profound essence (*xuanzhi*), one will be lost regarding its arising and ceasing.

If one explains by combining both approaches, there is nowhere for either to rest. Consequently, when providing commentaries on major themes, I invariably point to the removal of words to reveal the name, essence, substance, function, the three [aspects], the one, the general, and the specific, relying on practice and the provisional teachings. Thus, we know that those who are entirely deluded regarding the profound [essence] are likewise lost.
To gloss over the general purport of the text while attempting to exhaust its meaning through mere phrasing obscures the underlying principle;
to contemplate the profound and subtle while interpreting the meaning solely through phenomenal characteristics is far from propagating this scripture.

Someone asked: "Why are the three and the one mentioned repeatedly as both general and specific? Is it because this follows the sequence of the preceding texts regarding the Origin (hon) and the Trace (saku)?

Furthermore, it is said that within a single section, nothing surpasses the Origin and the Trace, nor the Ground of the Origin and the Ground of the Trace; these general and specific categories exceed all other doctrines.

Within the Trace, the three and the one are of preeminent merit during a single period. This leads to what is later stated: 'Therefore, when explaining and interpreting, all matters reaching the Great Meaning [are treated thus].'"

In the *Zhixuan wen*, it is stated that because the "three and one" (san-yi) are both general and specific, one knows that the three and one are the "knotting of traces" (*jie-ji*), while the general and specific are the "knotting of the source" (*jie-ben*).

As for the statement that [the text] "relies on practice and is based on the teaching," this means that it relies on the sequence of practice and, based on the taught doctrine—the names and phrases that can express it—provides its analysis and interpretation.

Since it speaks of "name, essence, purpose, and function," it is verified that this is an exposition based on the five chapters concerning practice. Furthermore, there is a passage that says "relying on... [and so forth].
In the chapter "Explaining the Names by Way of Practice," it is stated that there are five chapters on "determining the teachings by way of doctrine.

Furthermore, in the chapter "Determining the Teachings by Way of Practice" (which is part of the section on the *Jiyue xing panjiao zhang*), it is stated that these five chapters on determining the teachings by way of doctrine were formulated by the Master of Records (*Jizhu*) based on the intent of the *Xuanyi*.

Fearing that others might suspect that the section on "distinct interpretations" explains only practice and fails to explain doctrine, he therefore states: "He relies on practice to encompass doctrine."
This consists merely of the five chapters on "Entrusting the Practice" and "Clarifying the Teaching," none of which are taken up here.

Regarding the citation from the *Wenju* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) concerning the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*), the first and third [sections] of the *Piyu-pin* (Parable Chapter) state: "If a person believes what you have said, they have already seen me and have also seen..."
"You and the community of bhikṣus, together with all the bodhisattvas, should know that according to whatever you have heard, you must observe it with a discerning mind;

within this mind of faith, you shall behold the Three Jewels: hearing this teaching is seeing the Jewel of the Dharma, seeing me is seeing the Jewel of the Buddha, and seeing you all is seeing the Jewel of the Saṃgha."
*Miaole* (1) (11). Regarding the contemplation within the mind, first the introduction and next "one should know" below conclude the intent. As for the initial passage:
the discourse on phenomena is simply that Śāriputra’s teaching of the meaning is equivalent to seeing the Buddha;

what you have spoken must have been heard from the Buddha, and one who is able to hear it must necessarily be a śrāvaka or bodhisattva. Therefore, hearing your teaching is itself seeing the Buddha, and so forth.
Next, regarding the "binding of the mind": when one hears this Dharma and is able to contemplate it within the mind, that is precisely what is meant by the meaning of "Buddha.
One should see that the Buddha-mind is identical to the minds of the disciples and others. Thus, within one's own mind, one realizes that the Triple Gem is of one essence;
its principle is perfectly complete, as explained in detail in the passage following the words "having heard the teaching."

Record (1)(15): Furthermore, regarding the text on "Contemplating the Mind," with the exception of the section on "cultivating and gathering the mind" within the "Peaceful Practices" (Anrakugyō), all other parts are established through interpretation (*gishitsu*).
(And so forth. Moreover, regarding the text on "Contemplating the Mind," the Prologue and the Circulation sections follow the main body; logically, they must be established through interpretation.
Within the main body itself, only the principle of the "Peaceful Practices" is definitively required as such, while all else is established through interpretation.

Regarding the passage (1.6), the subsequent text states: "If a person believes what you have said, they shall immediately see me, as well as you and the assembly of bhikṣus, along with all the bodhisattvas.
This is the explicit textual evidence for contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
*Miaole* (1.19): Next, the subsequent passage states that it cites the *Upamāna-parivarta* (The Chapter on Similes) to establish and verify the characteristics of contemplation (*guanxiang*).

I have privately examined the text on the "Contemplation of the Mind" (*guansin*) and find that it only emerges from the *Anle-xing* (Peaceful Conduct); all other chapters are established by way of meaning.

Since the text of the *Upamāna-parivarta* is precisely the meaning of the contemplation of the mind, the Great Master decisively stated that this is the clear exposition of the practice of contemplation.
This also demonstrates that the merit of perceiving the Three Jewels arises from contemplating the mind; thus, it is cited as proof.

Regarding the passage on the Three Jewels (1–3): whenever one hears [the teachings], one should investigate them with a discerning mind, so that within the mind of faith, one may perceive the Three Jewels. (It is said:)
(Miaojì, Vol. 1, Section 11): "The Dharma heard is, within the mind capable of contemplation, precisely what is called the Buddha; this is the principle that one shall see the Buddha-mind.
That which is 'within' is the disciples and so forth. Thus, within one's own mind, one realizes that the Three Jewels are of one essence; the principle is perfectly clear."
Sufficient.
Master Beifeng said: "Regarding the Three Refuges, the patriarchs and predecessors of old all instructed one to take refuge in the Three Jewels as One Body (*ekakāya-triratna*).

The patriarchs' words were concise, yet later generations do not understand them; as soon as they hear 'One Body,' they immediately take refuge in their own minds, [reducing it to] mere words and phrases."

The application of the mind is not at all consistent with this; the analysis is divided into three parts: first, identifying errors; second, the correct explanation; third, the critical examination. First, identifying errors:
if taking refuge is solely in the single essence of the Triple Gem within one's own mind, why does the preliminary liturgy first proclaim:
"I take refuge in the Buddha, the Honored One among the Two-legged; I take refuge in the Dharma, the Honored One free from desire; I take refuge in the Saṃgha, the foremost among assemblies"?
The Venerable concludes the passage with the words: "I only pray that the Three Jewels will take pity upon me, receive me, and look upon me with compassion.

This, however, shows a lack of understanding of the text. As for what is called the "Three Jewels of One Essence" (ik-tae sam-bok), it means that although they are called the Three Jewels, their essence is one;
because the three are not distinct in essence, they are called the "Three Jewels of One Essence. How can it be said that as soon as "one essence" is mentioned, it refers to oneself?
Regarding the statement that the fruit of the mind is thus, one must understand that the Buddha and the Three Jewels are not a single entity; this is what is meant by "not recognizing their names.
The Great Master said: "By means of the wisdom of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), awakening to all phenomena as being neither empty nor existent is called the Buddha Jewel.
The principle of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) awakened to therein, which is fully endowed with the three truths, is the Dharma Jewel. Such awakening-wisdom and..."
The harmonious integration of principle and phenomena is called the Sangha Jewel (*Bie xing xuán wén*). Siming states:
"Although the three [jewels] reside in the fruit, they are of one essence" (*Shí yì jì wén*). These passages precisely clarify that the Three Jewels are of one essence;
why do you not reflect upon this? Furthermore, the *Zhǐyào xiǎn* explicitly states: "The Three Jewels are the ultimate of cultivated virtue. Second, the true essence of taking refuge.
Regarding the Three Jewels, one must know that there are four kinds of Three Jewels: 1. The Three Jewels of Sustenance (*zhu-chi san-bao*): clay, wood, cast metal, silk, and cloth used for sculpting;
painting, embroidery, and coloring represent the Buddha Jewel; paper, ink, calligraphy, printing, characters, and scrolls represent the Dharma Jewel;

shaving the head, dyeing the robes, the shaven crown, and the square-cut cassock represent the Sangha Jewel (however, the *Jingming shuji* refers to these as "conforming to characteristics"). 2. The Three Jewels of Conformity (*xiang-cong*).
The Three Jewels arise from the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma; from the Dharma comes the Sangha.

That these Three Jewels have remained uninterrupted until the present day is entirely due to taking refuge in the Buddha, receiving the Dharma, and forming the Sangha. Thus it is said they "mutually follow one another.

This refers to the Three Jewels of distinct characteristics as elucidated in the teachings of the *Hīnayāna* (specifically in the middle volume of the *Guangming xuanyi ji*, in contrast to the *Āgama* and *Vaipulya* teachings). Regarding the three distinct characteristics: Vairocana is the Buddha.
The immeasurable Four Noble Truths taught by the Buddha constitute the Dharma Jewel; the forty-one stages of sages and saints who receive these teachings constitute the Sangha Jewel.
These Three Jewels are such that the Buddha is the fruit of the Sangha, and the Sangha is the cause of the Buddha. The Dharma is both the cause and the fruit—the practice and the realization.
Because the essences of these Three Jewels are distinct, they are called the "Distinct Characteristics" (biphasa), which is what is elucidated in the provisional teachings of the Mahāyāna.

The Three-in-One Treasures (according to the *Guangming xuanyi ji*, middle fascicle, cited in the *Bao*): The Tathāgata, who names his realization of principle and wisdom as the awakening to all phenomena, is called the Buddha Treasure;
the phenomena thus awakened to are the Dharma Treasure; and this wisdom, in its harmonious union with phenomena and principle, is called the Sangha Treasure.
However, these Three Treasures reach their ultimate limit in the wondrous enlightenment of the Tathāgata.
Because they are ultimately perfected, the *Mahāyāna-śāstra* states that above the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) there is the true Saṅgha.

Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* defines the Saṅgha Jewel as that which governs and leads the great assembly. Is this not because the Response-Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) represents the ultimate in governing the masses according to their capacities?
Even down to ordinary beings on the mundane level, there is none who does not possess [these qualities]; thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

"The mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. Although this applies generally to all six stages of realization (*liujie*), from the perspective of true realization being able to manifest responsive transformations, the Patriarchs often designate the forty-one levels of sages and saints as the Sangha.
These Three Jewels as a single essence are precisely what is taught in the Perfect and Sudden Mahāyāna (as cited in the *Biexing xuanyi* and the *Guangming xuanyiji*). Now, regarding this...

Taking refuge is, in essence, the Three Jewels as a single entity; although this encompasses both cause and fruit, because Bodhisattvas and Buddhas have already awakened while sentient beings remain deluded, one now seeks to turn back from delusion toward awakening and requests their empowerment. Thus, with a causal mind, one takes refuge in the resultant essence of the Buddha.
As the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* says: "I pray that the Three Jewels will take pity on me and accept me. The Dharma Master said: "May all..."
Although the Three Jewels are names for a single essence, the profound refuge must proceed from the fruit (*xingfa shu*, lower fascicle). The Venerable Fazhi said:

"The *Avataṃsaka*’s three refuges take the realization of the Great Way as the Buddha, the deep entry into the treasury of the sūtras as the Dharma, and the unified governance of the great assembly as the Saṃgha;
though these three reside in the fruit, they are a single essence" (*Shiyi*, section 2). Furthermore, as Jing... [text fragment].

In the *Fahua Chanwen* (Repentance Text of the Lotus Sutra), Venerable Xixian explains the three refuges as follows: "One should visualize each of the two locations of the Triple Gem simultaneously with the prostrations;
specifically, one must direct the visualization toward taking refuge in the Triple Gem of the ten directions as well as the Triple Gem within the *Lotus Sutra*.
Therefore, it is said that the 'Triple Gem of the two locations' is known [to exist]. Thus, one must take refuge in the Triple Gem of the One Essence."
If you wish to seek the causal mind through the resultant Buddha, you must simply know where this single essence of the Triple Gem resides and what its fundamental nature is.
The Repentance Master said: "The dwelling place of all Buddhas is called the Constant, Quiescent Light (nitya-prabhāsvara).
It pervades every moment and all phenomena. Thus, one knows that the essence of the Mahāyāna’s single-essence Triple Gem pervades all places and all forms.
The entire substance of the mind and all dharmas is itself the single essence of the Triple Gem. As Maitreya (Aśvaghoṣa) said:
"Equal to the realm of empty space, there is nowhere it does not pervade; the single characteristic of the dharma-realm is the eternally abiding Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.
Once one knows that from its very essence it is equal to the realm of empty space and pervades everywhere, then the Triple Gem of the ten directions is entirely present within a single kṣaṇa.
The world and the Tathāgata are not separate from the mind; the mind and the Buddha are non-dual, mutually pervasive and infinitely layered.

Thus, taking the Dharma-realm—the environment and its inhabitants, the Triple Gem—as that which is taken refuge in, while simultaneously taking this same Dharma-realm environment and inhabitants as the one who takes refuge, the essence of the subject and object is one, and all dualistic opposition is forgotten.
In this way, one takes refuge all day long, yet all day long there is no action. Such is it.
Only then can it be called the Perfect and Sudden definitive meaning of taking refuge in the Triple Gem.
If sentient beings and Buddhas were entirely separate and possessed an absolute barrier between them, this would be the Small Vehicle; how could it be called the Perfect and Sudden?

One must reverently cultivate the visualization that the Triple Gem is within one's own mind, taking refuge with a sincere heart and seeking the fruit of Buddhahood. Regarding the threefold selection, the first question concerns the transmission of the Dharma.

Regarding the statement that the Four Ming Patriarch, the Second Ancestor of the Repentance Master, often spoke of the Three Jewels as being one body within the taking refuge in one's own mind—does this mean that the Four Ming Repentance Master was ignorant of terminology or failed to understand names and meanings? Answer:

This is because the Four Ming Repentance Master had attained the fruit of realization wherein his mind fully encompassed all phenomena. If one points to its essential core, it is simply the mind manifest before one.
The essence of the Three Jewels is what is called the nature and virtue of sentient beings; this is precisely the true body of the Buddha (from *Guangming ji*, fascicle 3). Second question:
Previously, you used the term "the Three Jewels as one essence" (*yiti sanbao*)—referring to the Three Jewels being of one essence—to refute others who do not understand the meaning of the name.
Could it also be applied to the "one essence of delusion and awakening, cause and fruit" as the "Three Jewels as one essence"? Answer: If...
If one attains realization, there is nothing improper in the fact that Buddhas and sentient beings are fundamentally of one essence from the beginning.

Now, we merely refute the failure to recognize that the Three Jewels are of one essence; it is not that as soon as "one essence" is mentioned, one identifies it as the mind while remaining ignorant of the unity of cause and effect.
Third question: The Confession Master [states] that the four bodies of the Buddha constitute the Buddha Jewel, and the eighty thousand dharma-treasuries constitute the Dharma Jewel.

Regarding the statement that "taking refuge in the Three Vehicles as the Jewel of the Sangha," from what text does this originate, and in which teaching is it found? Answer: I have not yet seen where this meaning is explicitly stated;
one might suspect it is a corruption. Nevertheless, since these are the words of the Master of Repentance (Zongmi), I do not dare to lightly critique them.

In the fourth chapter on the "General Characteristics of the Four Refuges" within the *Jinyuan ji* (Anthology of the Golden Garden), concerning the Dharma-gate of Releasing Life and Joyful Salvation, it states: "It exists in both cultivation and nature."
Since there is no distinction between cause and fruit, the present discussion on taking refuge requires that one follow the fruit.
(From *Dujiao Ji*, Scroll 8; *Dujiao Ji*, Scroll 9)
Tiantai Śramaṇa Fazhao’s Commentary on the Text (2): Conclusion and Benefits
Commentary (1): Now, the "Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja" was chanted by the Buddha, while the sections concerning "Ghoṣadatta," "Avalokiteśvara," and so forth, were translated by the scribe;
they were not heard [by the Buddha]. Record (1) (3): As stated in the "Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta": The Buddha told Śrīkūṭarāja: "If there be anyone who hears of this Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja..."
In the "Chapter on the Former Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja," those who are able to rejoice in and praise the virtuous are mentioned;
it further states that the "Chapter on the Former Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva" is entrusted to you by Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, continuing until it says:

"If there are women who uphold this chapter, they shall exhaust their female forms and never again receive a female body. At the end of the "Chapter on Gadgadasvara," the compilers of the sutra state: "Having spoken thus of Gadgadasvara..."
At the end of the "Chapter on Coming and Going," it is said that forty-two thousand devaputras attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

At the end of the "Universal Gate Chapter" (*Samantamukha-parivarta*), the narrator likewise states that when the Buddha preached this chapter, eighty-four thousand sentient beings all resolved to attain the peerless *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is also the case at the end of each subsequent chapter, including the "Chapter on Encouraging Resolve through the King Adorned with Dhāraṇīs"; therefore, it is so stated.

Regarding those passages that the translators did not hear and which are now absent from this sutra—if they lack the words of the compilers (*saṃgītikāra*) or the direct utterances of the Buddha—then they likely belong to the translators themselves.
One should know that since the various chapters (*parivarta*) were already complete within the Sanskrit original, these must have been inserted by the compilers;
it is clear that the translators had no part in them. Therefore, most of the other chapters in the present sutra are the work of the compilers.
They are placed here for the purpose of augmenting the category of "those who have not heard";

therefore, there is no concluding summary at the end of this section. (Text, Vol. 10/19) Bhaiṣajyarāja rides upon the vehicle of ascetic practice; Gadgadasvara rides upon the vehicle of samādhi; Dhāraṇī rides upon the vehicle of total retention;
Suvarṇaprabhāsa rides upon the vehicle of vows; and Samantabhadra [rides upon the vehicle of] spiritual power.
For those who interpret this through the lens of the *tongsheng* (universal vehicle), it is convenient for the purpose of propagating [the teaching] to others.

Regarding the section from "Yao Wang" (Bhaiṣajyarāja) to the "convenience of the meaning of propagation": after the Buddha had finished his entrustment (*parindanā*) and the great task was completed, he taught according to the preferences of sentient beings;
thus, while the vehicles differ, the true suchness (*tathatā*) and the real mark (*lakṣaṇa*) are the single vehicle (*ekayāna*), which is the essence of that which is mounted.
Cause and effect are the matters to be traversed; ascetic practices and the like are the vehicle that traverses them.

Because these are adapted to the capacities of sentient beings, the propagators of the teaching allow them to vary according to conditions; thus, the essence of what is traversed is entirely the wondrous Dharma.
Since cause and effect are established based on the One Reality, and since one traverses the vehicle for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, it is called the "Vehicle of Vehicles."
The Master Beifeng said: "According to the sūtra, across its twenty-eight chapters there are twelve instances where the benefits are summarized.

There are six chapters that summarize the benefits of the sūtra, and another six that do so as well. These consist of the three cycles of the sūtra’s benefits, along with the sections on the detailed entrustment (*parindanā*) and the exhortation to resolve (*samādāpana*).
Therefore, the *Myōki* (Vol. 10, p. 26), in the passage concerning the 'Entrustment and Rejoicing,' states: 'At the conclusion of the three cycles...'"
Each [section] concludes with an expression of joy regarding the lifespan. In the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits," upon hearing that the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable, everyone rejoices.
Now that both the provisional and the ultimate [teachings] are complete, how could one not rejoice? Furthermore, the "Ten" (referring to the *Wenju*) states at the end:

"Hearing the sutra brings benefit; the great assembly rejoices. This refers to the benefit of the chapter. As for the benefit of the subsequent chapters, it refers to the six chapters beginning with the "Medicine King" (*Bhaiṣajyarāja*).
The commentary on the phrases is as previously cited: because the Dharma heard differs, the benefits of the general and specific [sections] vary.
Why is this? Since the three cycles of teaching differ, there are three summaries;
furthermore, as the text spans eight chapters and the "Emergence," "Life Span," and "Past Deeds" differ, another summary is made within the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits."
The concluding summary text, which involves the three grades of Dharma masters and so forth, pertains to the five traces of the *Ryūtsūmon* (Chapter on the Dissemination).
How could it be entirely without benefit? This is because one first heard the *Shōshū* (Main Teaching) and now hears the *Ryūtsū*; only through this does one attain awakening.

Furthermore, the four [virtues] such as sympathetic joy (*anumodana*) are likewise not without benefit; for it is by first hearing the *Honji* (Original Ground), the *Shōshū*, and the *Ryūtsū* that one finally attains awakening.
In all cases, these merits do not belong to their respective sections; therefore, they are collectively included within the "Entrustment" (Zhūlèi) as a general conclusion.

The various sections of the Prologue differ increasingly from one another, and the "Correct Teaching" (Zhèngzōng) that follows it likewise does not belong to its own specific section; thus, there is no separate conclusion for them.

However, because the final joyful event is perfect in both principle and phenomena, it serves as a comprehensive conclusion for the entire sutra. These six [conclusions] all proceed from the major divisions.
This is called "benefit for the sūtra" (*jing-yi*). From the "Medicine King" chapter downward, those who propagate the sūtra vary according to the inclinations of sentient beings;

the vehicles they ride differ, what they hear varies, and the benefits accorded in each respective chapter are distinct. Therefore, it is necessary to conclude them separately—this is called "benefit for the chapter" (*pin-yi*).

If this is so, it is not that the twenty-two chapters lack a fundamental or provisional aspect (*ben-ji*); rather, while there is a general conclusion of benefit, because such merit does not pertain specifically to the individual chapter, it is so stated.

The "Wu wen pin" (Chapter on No Hearing) concludes with "The benefit of the ears is subtle and refined. The "Jie pin" (Chapter on Binding) concludes with "One who prefers [seclusion] benefits the thatched hut.
The "Hu xi pin" (Chapter on Tiger Creek) concludes with "Following each section, there is a conclusion; following each chapter, there is a conclusion; and a general conclusion at the end.
As for those not yet concluded elsewhere, they are all concluded in the "Quan fa pin" (Chapter on Exhortation). Question: The "Ti po da duo pin" (Chapter on Devadatta) states, "In the future..."

If there are men or women in the world who hear the "Devadatta Chapter" of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and believe with a pure heart, and as it further says that immeasurable sentient beings hear the Dharma and attain realization, why is it said that there is no benefit for those who do not hear it? The answer is:
the Sūtra itself states that in future ages, they will hear [the Dharma] when the Dragon Girl preaches the Dharma in the South.
Furthermore, it is not that one gains benefit merely by hearing this chapter; rather, observe the scripture’s topical outline:
first, Devadatta mastered the sutra when Śākyamuni attained Buddhahood; second, Mañjuśrī mastered the sutra when the Dragon Girl attained Buddhahood.
Supplementary Notes (4) (2): Dharma Master Dao’an was a native of Fuliu in Changshan and belonged to the Wei clan, a family of distinguished scholars for generations.
At that time, the Ruler of Qin commanded a monk to lecture on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. The lecturer read the text in a flat monotone, without any division of sections.
The Lord of Qin said, "I have heard that the Buddha-dharma is profound and subtle, and its scriptural texts are deep and intricate.

In the dialogues between host and guest, or teacher and disciple, there must be a definite sequence; how can you explain them directly without any formal divisions or structural analysis? The monks had no reply.
Consequently, this report spread in all four directions. At that time, Master An was in Xiangyang, and upon hearing it, he sighed, saying, "How [is this]?"
Because we and our peers shared this same sense of shame, we proceeded to divide all Buddhist scriptures—regardless of whether their length was extensive or concise—into three parts.
Although Master Dao’an had made this three-part classification of the sutras, the great assembly still did not yet believe it.

It was only when the Bodhisattva Bandhuprabha of the Western Regions composed the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* that the treatise, in its commentary on the sutra, indeed divided it into three sections. (Thus it is said.)
It is said: "This is no different from the introductory, main, and concluding sections.

The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* (translated by Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty, Volume Sheng, Case Zi) consists of three parts: first, the Section on the Causes and Conditions for the Arising of the Teaching; second, the Section on What is Taught in the Holy Teachings;
and third, the Section on Practicing in Accordance with the Teachings.

*Miaole* (1, 4): Since ancient times, many commentators have failed to divide the text into sections. It was not until the time of Master Dao’an that the sūtras, regardless of their length, were first divided into three parts.

*Wenju* (1, 2): Tiantai Zhiyi divided the text into three sections: the first chapter constitutes the introduction (*nidāna*), and the section ending with the "Expedient Means" (*upāya*) chapter constitutes the second part.

The nineteen verses on distinct merits comprise fifteen chapters and a half, titled the "Correct" (zhèng) section; from the end of these verses until the conclusion of the sutra, there are eleven chapters and a half, titled the "Circulation" (liútōng) section.

Furthermore, when divided according to time, there are two parts: from the Preface to the "Peaceful Conduct" (Ānle xíng), comprising fourteen chapters, which—based on the provisional traces (*yì*)—reveals the provisional to manifest the real;
from the "Emergence from the Earth" (*Yǒngchū dìxià*) to the end of the sutra, comprising fourteen chapters, which—based on the fundamental source (*běn*)—reveals the provisional.

The revelation of the reality of the original and the manifested [bodies] is divided into three sections: the Introduction, the Main Body, and the Dissemination. The first chapter constitutes the Introduction;

the section from the end of the "Chapter on Expedient Means" up to the "Chapter on Bestowing Predictions upon Learners and Those Beyond Learning" constitutes the Main Body; and the section from the end of the "Chapter on the Dharma Master" through the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices" constitutes the Dissemination.

Following the "Chapter on the Emergence," Maitreya has already asked about this matter, and the Buddha now provides the answer. The half-chapter beginning with "The Buddha addressed Ajita" and ending with the division [of the text] is named the Introduction.
The verses of the "Chapter on Distinctive Merits" constitute the *nītārtha* (definitive meaning) of this scripture; from here until the end of the sutra is the *pratyekārtha* (circulation).

Now, I shall explain the text according to these three preceding sections. Question: How can a single sutra have two prefaces? Answer: In the *Avataṃsaka*, assemblies are gathered at various places; in the *Āgamas*, such is the case for every chapter;
and in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, the entrustment occurs both before and after. Since it is not contradictory for a single work to have two prefaces, what harm is there in this case?

Regarding the five meanings of "insecurity" (*an-āśvāsa*), it is because the Fundamental Gate (*honmon*) is not the primary [sequence]. As for the Trace Gate (*jimon*), its being solely for the sake of circulation means that the preaching of the Dharma has not yet been concluded.

In the *Shūki* (Commentary), it says: "Now, although both [interpretations] are preserved, we provisionally adopt the former meaning; therefore, it is said, 'following the previous question regarding the One.'"
The Sūtra asks, "What are they? Since this question already implies two interpretations, what prevents [the inclusion of both] after the question?

The reason why one does not exclusively adopt the latter interpretation among the two is that the original text establishes the *zheng* (correct) [section] first and then sets forth the *liutong* (circulation). This is merely a provisional approach for the time being.

In the response, it says, "The *Huayan* gathers assemblies in various places," etc.; the details regarding these locations and assemblies are as cited in the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning), with each assembly being treated accordingly.
In all chapters, the introductory section precedes the main body (and so forth). As for the Trace Gate (*jimen*), it contains only the section on the dissemination of the teaching (*liutong*).

This is because, when viewed from the perspective of the Trace in relation to the Origin (*ben*), the Origin serves as the model for the Trace; and while the Origin Gate is not the beginning and thus has its own separate introduction, the Trace Gate is not the end and thus contains only the dissemination.

Consequently, there is only the exhortation to uphold the teaching (*quanchi*) and no entrustment (*zhulei*). Therefore, from the "Dharma Master" chapter to the "Peaceful Practices" (*anle xing*) chapter, there are five chapters in total.

The profound merit of elucidating and circulating the sutra is used here to encourage its dissemination. If, within the "Original Gate" (Honmon), one first takes the extinction [of the Buddha] as the starting point and proceeds through the latter five grades—excluding three and a half grades—to encourage the upholding and circulation [of the teaching], there are eight grades from the "Supernatural Power" (Jinriki) onward that clarify the entrustment and circulation.
Since the sutra has not yet reached its conclusion following the "Trace Gate" (Jikimon), it is not yet the proper occasion for circulation, nor is it necessary to issue an entrustment at this stage.
Section (1) (3): First, the characteristics of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) are demonstrated by means of three stages.

Commentary (1) (11): Regarding the demonstration of characteristics, it is shown solely through this present sutra via four kinds of characteristics. Although these begin with "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) and end with "departed" (*prakrāntaḥ*), all employ the four meanings;
however, the manner in which the textual momentum arises and concludes differs from that used in the explanation of the General Preface (*sūtra-pūrva-mīmāṃsā*).
Thus, every sentence must be understood through fourfold penetration, encompassing both the *zhengzong* (the main body of the teaching) and the *liutong* (the dissemination).

If one explains the *zhengzong*, each of the "original" (*ben*) and "traced" (*ji*) aspects possesses three meanings that penetrate these four modes. If one explains the *liutong*, it likewise requires the fourfold penetration to fully include the *zhengzong*.

Furthermore, since the "traced" gate within the *zhengzong* lacks the "long-distant original" aspect of the original-traced relationship, the categories of essence-function (*ti-yong*) original-traced are borrowed; thus, there are four.
The title is not relevant here. Furthermore, in the preface, regarding the classification of teachings (*jiao*), one must examine the textual flow:
sometimes the teachings are included within the five periods; sometimes they are distinguished by means of the various teachings, using the periods to judge the "Middle" [teachings];

when classifying the teachings according to the "Proper" [text], it exclusively clarifies the opening of the original [truth]; and when classifying the teachings according to the "Original," it does not judge by means of the teachings, but merely points to the distant origin and the distant wondrousness.

If one understands this text, then the intent of the entire scripture will be as clear as looking at one's own palm; there will be no need for further deliberation regarding the four meanings and their subtle shifts.

Therefore, for now, I shall provisionally rely on three major sections of the text to demonstrate their general characteristics. Once these have been understood, one may then apply this same principle in detail to analyze each section individually.

Commentary (1)(13): This is provisionally treated as a single threefold section; since the distinction between the "original" (*hon*) and the "traced" (*soku*) is yet to be made below, two types of threefold sections have not been divided here.

[Textual variants] (3)(7); Commentary (3)(18). Question: Since we have reached this point, it is still too early to refute [the opponent]; why then do you provide a general introduction by explaining the original and the traced?
Answer: The general introduction (tongxu) applies to both the fundamental and the provisional (benji), whereas the specific introduction (biexu) pertains only to the provisional gate (jimen).

Therefore, when explaining the general introduction, one may apply it broadly to the fundamental gate; however, this does not mean that within the general introduction the "Life Span" chapter is extensively expounded.

Furthermore, although the specific introduction contains references to the fundamental and the provisional, at times it merely employs the fundamental and provisional aspects as essence and function (*tiyong*). (As stated above... Nevertheless, since the general introduction serves as the preface, it may be treated with some flexibility, whereas the specific introduction must follow its own distinct requirements.
Relying on the differences [of the various versions], there is no connection to the distant original.

From this chapter downward, ending with the nineteenth verse of the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merit" (*Guǎnzhòng gōngdé pǐn*), or extending through the prose following the verse until the end of the text concerning the four types of faithful disciples in the present age, is designated as the "Section of the Correct Teaching" (*Zhèngshuō fēn*). If divided into two parts, it constitutes the "Correct Teaching."
From this point downward, up to the "Chapter on Bestowing Predictions upon Those in Training and Those Beyond Training," is the formal exposition of the Trace Gate (jìmén).
For now, following the immediate context, we shall further divide this formal exposition of the Trace Gate into two parts (and so forth).

The eight (or seven) sections of the first three cycles constitute the formal exposition of the Trace Gate, concluding with the realization and bestowal of predictions; the five chapters below this constitute the circulation of the Trace Gate.
[Sections] (9) and (10): From here below is the second major section, which reveals the proximate traces of the Master’s school and manifests the remote origin of the Buddha-ground.
This text consists of three parts: first, from here below until "you yourselves shall, by means of this, hear it," which constitutes the introductory section;
second, from "At that time, Śākyamuni addressed Maitreya" down to the end of the *Vibhāga-guṇa-parivarta* (Chapter on the Distinction of Merits), where Maitreya speaks.
The nineteen verses constitute the section of the formal exposition. Following the verses, the remaining eleven chapters and a half constitute the section on the dissemination of the teaching.
(10) (5) Now, according to the Southern tradition, these eleven chapters and a half following the verses are divided into two parts:

first, from here down to the "Chapter on Never-Despising" (*Anupali*), which clarifies the profound merit of propagating the sutra and strongly exhorts its dissemination; second, from the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" (*Rddhy-abhisaṃskāra*).
The final eight chapters constitute the entrustment and circulation.
Now, these three divisions are the great structural framework of this single scripture. Without the general division, one would not perceive the consistent unity from beginning to end;
without the specific division, one would not perceive the two gates of the fundamental and the phenomenal. It is necessary that the general and the specific be employed in mutual interdependence.

Once the lecturer has clarified the general and specific divisions to distinguish the topical sections (*ji-mu*), and upon entering the "Introductory Chapter" (*Xùpǐn*), they should first employ the general division to outline the structure.
Having finished lecturing on the Introductory Chapter, they should then conclude the section, stating: "This constitutes the Introductory Division.

Next, when lecturing on the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (*Fāngbiàn pǐn*), one may set aside the general division and instead employ the specific division to outline the structure; here, the introductory section of the Trace Gate (*jìmén*) refers back to the general introduction.
When the lecture on the "Propagation of the Trace Gate" (Ji-zheng-tong) is concluded, the formal session is adjourned with the words: "This is the Trace Gate; next is the Origin Gate.

When the lecture on the "Origin Gate" reaches the conclusion of the "Correct Teaching" (Zheng-zong), the formal session is adjourned with the words: "This is the Correct Teaching; next is the Propagation," which refers in advance to the general propagation (*sō-ryūtsū*).
After lecturing on the verses of the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits" (*Fen-bie-gong-de-pin*), one may set aside the specific divisions and revert to using the general [propagation].

The division into sections for circulation is likewise; thus, the two gates of the fundamental (hon) and the manifested (jaku), from the beginning to the end of this single sutra, are clearly visible as distinct general and specific divisions.

Although various masters have taught that the general and specific must be mutually dependent, none fail to conclude that within the orthodox teaching (shōjū), the fundamental and manifested are each opened out into three parts.
Thus, the introductory section (jōbun) of the manifested gate and the [introductory section] of the fundamental...

The various gates of transmission all explain this by opening it out from within the orthodox teaching; yet none of these can avoid the fault of abandoning the general for the particular or abandoning the particular for the general.
This is the essential nature of the Dharma as it has been heard.
"Phrase (1) (end of 4)": "Thus" (*evam*) refers to the essential substance (*dharmatā*) of the Dharma as it was heard.

"Recorded (1) (beginning of 15)": Regarding the statement that the essential substance of the Dharma as heard is explained in four ways below, although these refer generally to the entire work, they specifically pertain to the Main Body (*śarīra*) and the Dissemination (*parivarta*).
They may also encompass the Introductory Section (*nidāna*), including the "Questioning with Doubt" and the "Immeasurable" [sections].
Since the meaning extends to both "name" (nāman) and "hearing" (śruta), the falling of flowers and the shaking of the earth are explained according to what they represent;

Regarding their sequential production, this is for the time being based on a general overview; however, if one considers the phrase "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) and the fact that the Teacher of Transformation occupies the initial position, it can also be applied universally.

Yitang said: "Regarding the three—teaching, practice, and principle—as the essential substance (*tattva*): during the Buddha's lifetime, the golden vocal activity of the Tathāgata served as the essential substance;
after his parinirvāṇa and before the formal compilation (*saṃgīti*), the mental recitation of Ānanda served as the essential substance;
and after the compilation, the *palm-leaf* manuscripts of that land and the yellow scrolls of this land served as the essential substance. Now, I ask:"

Regarding the similarities and differences between the essence of the Dharma as heard (*śruta-dharmatā*), the essence of the teaching (*deśanā-dharmatā*), the essence of the sūtra (*sūtra-dharmatā*), the essence of the vehicle (*yāna-dharmatā*), the essence of the carriage (*ratha-dharmatā*), the essence of practice (*caryā-dharmatā*), and the essence of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-dharmatā*): it is said that the essence of the Dharma as heard is the totality, while these other essences are its particulars. Why?

Because the essence of the Dharma as heard encompasses the three aspects of teaching, practice, and principle; thus, it constitutes the essence of all things. This is because all essences do not transcend the teaching.
Because it is the principle of practice, furthermore, since the essence of the Dharma that is heard is both teaching and practice, the principle encompasses both the signifier and the signified.

The essence of the teaching is merely the signifier, while the essence of the sūtra is merely the signified. Since the essence of the vehicle consists of the three tracks, the essence of practice is none other than the four practices.
The essence of the vehicle is precisely true nature; the essence of contemplation does not transcend the three truths. All [are thus encompassed].

Some say that the "proper essence" (*dangti*) consists of the verbal teachings from the golden mouth of the Tathāgata, while the "reliant essence" (*suyiti*) is the true principle of the Middle Way within those teachings.

[The author] critiques this, saying: If one takes the teaching alone as the proper essence, why does [Zhiyi] state in the *Miaole* (The Wonderful Pleasure) that both "that which is transmitted" and "that which is expressed" constitute the essence of what is heard?
Alternatively, some say that the "teaching-text" (*jiaojing*) takes the teaching itself as the proper essence, while the "principle" (*li*) is the reliant essence.

Regarding the "substantiality as the basis" (*āśraya-bhāva*), the *Principle Sūtra* takes principle as the substantiality that constitutes its own essence, while the *Teaching Sūtra* takes the teaching as the substantiality that constitutes its basis.
The critique states: If one grasps only the substantiality that constitutes the essence within the substance of the heard Dharma, one fails to perceive the substantiality that constitutes its basis.

Alternatively, it is said that among the three—teaching, practice, and principle—the sūtras all take the substantiality that constitutes their own essence, while Ānanda’s conceptualization and conduct constitute the substantiality of their basis. This is the evaluation.
It is said that "taking the substance as such" (*dangti keyi*) is appropriate, while "that upon which it relies" (*suoyi*) is too restrictive.

Others say that Ānanda’s conceptualization and activity constitute the substance, and that the substance, teaching, practice, and principle constitute the threefold basis. A critique states: "If one only attains the capacity to hear but does not perceive that which is heard, how can this be called a perversion?"

Moreover, because there was no timetable for attaining Buddhahood, why should one doubt that Ānanda will become a Buddha? It is said that he doubted because his body had been consumed by fire and his wisdom severed;

he doubted the World-Honored One’s re-emergence because there was no mention of other Buddhas, and he doubted the arrival of a Buddha from another direction because there was no timetable for attaining Buddhahood.

Therefore, regarding the statement that Ānanda had three doubts when he was about to attain Buddhahood at the grass hut, there is the meaning of "three doubts" but no actual occurrence of "three doubts.
Some say these were provisional doubts, while others say they were doubts held by those in the realms of humans and devas; yet neither view is correct.

At that time, Mahākāśyapa, together with a thousand followers, arrived at Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha and addressed King Ajātaśatru:

The *Miaoxuan* (10.32) states: Those who compiled the various sūtras consider what was spoken by Bodhisattvas to be the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and what was spoken by Śrāvakas to be the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.

Nāgārjuna, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, also says that Mahākāśyapa and Ānanda compiled the Tripiṭaka at Mount Gandhamādana as the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, while Mañjuśrī and Ānanda [compiled the other].
The Mahāyāna sūtras are collected as the Bodhisattvapiṭaka (and so forth). Now, regarding these two piṭakas, they are distinguished according to their intended purpose and their subject matter.

Within the Śrāvakapiṭaka, there are bodhisattvas who serve as supporting figures; however, since they are not the intended audience, the sūtras cannot be designated as Mahāyāna simply by the name "Bodhisattva.
Likewise, within the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, there are also śrāvakas; yet, because they are not the primary focus of the teaching, it is not the central tenet.
Because it teaches the Dharma for śrāvakas, it cannot be called the "Lesser Vehicle" (Hīnayāna);
however, since the persons addressed and the fixed teachings differ from one another, they are summarized and condensed into only two categories.

Regarding the first and seventh sections of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it states: "When Ānanda compiled the Dharma, he himself said, 'When the Buddha first turned the wheel of the Dharma, I did not see it at that time.

*Miaole* (7) (21): However, the term "council" (*saṃgīti*) generally applies to three occasions: namely, the first council of one thousand [monks], the second of seven hundred, and the third of one thousand.

five hundred years after [the Buddha’s passing], due to King Kaniṣka’s invitation for the Saṃgha to receive offerings, there arose differences in their doctrinal discussions. Consequently, these five hundred [monks] went to Rājagṛha to reconvene the Tripiṭaka.
