Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that when the Dharma-piṭaka was compiled, Upāli and the others each ascended a high seat and all proclaimed, "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*).
This must certainly refer to Ānanda. When asked, "Did Ānanda compile only the Hīnayāna, or did he also compile the Mahāyāna?
the answers given by various commentators differ. Some say that he compiled only the Hīnayāna, while the Mahāyāna sūtras were collectively compiled by Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, and others.
Others say that Ānanda also compiled the Mahāyāna sūtras that are taught in common with the two vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha).
Therefore, just as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* was entrusted to Ānanda, so it is with this sūtra; what makes it unique is that it was compiled by the great Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, it is said that Ānanda also compiled [this] uniquely for those beyond the two vehicles (the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas), as in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* (and so forth).
How could he not have fully upheld the teachings of a single Buddha?
*The Sūtra on the Transmission of the Dharma-treasury* (Volume 1, in the Fei-zi case). At that time, the bhikṣus asked Mahākāśyapa, "What dharma did you first collect?
Kāśyapa replied, "First, the Sūtras. They asked again, "Who did you have collect the Sūtras?
Mahākāśyapa said, "The bhikṣu Ānanda" (and so forth). Then, Kāśyapa asked the bhikṣus, "Was what Ānanda said not erroneous?"

They all replied, "It is no different from what the World-Honored One has taught. Thereupon, Kāśyapa commanded Upāli to compile the Vinaya Piṭaka, while Kāśyapa himself compiled the Abhidharma Piṭaka.

The *Huayan He lun* (Compendium of the Avatamsaka), based on the *Bodhisattva Womb-Sutra* (*Putixin jing*) and the *Four-Part Vinaya* (*Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*), states that seven days after the Tathāgata first entered nirvana,
Mahākāśyapa, together with five hundred arhats, compiled the Tripiṭaka. Furthermore, within the *Nanshan Jitan jing* (Nanshan Ordination Platform Sutra),
there is an account of the circumstances of the compilation during the periods of the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Although various traditions differ regarding the sequence— some placing the five hundred first, some the one thousand, and others the seven hundred—
and though other schools cite different orders with the five hundred at the beginning, one should take the explanation of Jingxi as authoritative.

The Text on the Contemplation of the King of Mind and its Objects (1–11): "King" refers to the king of mind; "house" refers to the house of the five aggregates (*skandha*). The king of mind constructs this house.

If one analyzes the house of the five aggregates until it becomes empty and empty, this constitutes the city of *nirvāṇa*. Since this contemplation is shallow—like seeing mere earth and wood—if one instead realizes the essence...
The house of the aggregates (skandhas) is itself emptiness; this emptiness constitutes the city of Nirvana—this is the Shared Teaching (pāṭha-sāmānya).

If one contemplates the house of the five aggregates through their cessation, one attains the eternal form (rūpa); feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so. These four virtues of eternity are the dwelling place where all Buddhas roam.
If one contemplates the five aggregates as the Dharma-nature (dharmatā), that Dharma-nature is devoid of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
All sentient beings are themselves nirvāṇa; they cannot be extinguished further, for they are ultimately empty and quiescent.
This dwelling of nirvāṇa is the true substance of *tathatā*.

(1) (27) First, regarding the establishment of the object of contemplation: it is said that the "mind-king" constructs the dwelling; this means that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) acts as the king and constructs karma.

All minds are necessarily accompanied by mental factors (*caitta*). Now, in order to analyze the "king" (the mind), we shall first take the wholesome and unwholesome minds as kings to contrast them with the neutral state of indifference (*avyākṛta*);
thus it is said, "The king acts. If one analyzes the following four [categories] below, this demonstrates that the method of contemplation differs from other sutras;

this should be understood as being consistent with the ten vehicles and ten objects (*daśayāna-daśaviṣaya*) of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Contemplation) throughout the subsequent sections.
Regarding the ten wholesome factors (*daśa-kuśala-dharma*): these are faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, joy, tranquility, equanimity, awakening, and morality (*śīla*).
Furthermore, there are the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) which arise together with the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), pervading all states whether wholesome or unwholesome;

these are perception (*saṃjñā*), desire (*chanda*), contact (*sparśa*), wisdom (*prajñā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), volition (*cetanā*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), recollection (*dhāraṇā*), concentration (*samādhi*), and feeling (*vedanā*).

(2) (18) By means of twenty mental factors (*caitasika*) that collectively assist the sovereign mind (*cittarāja*) as it takes a wholesome object—just as when first initiating contemplation one does not depart from the sovereign—the number of factors is comprehensive;
being thus pervasive, they extend even to the realm of the wholesome.

(5) (21) The phrase "the mind-king and mental factors race together" means that they swiftly take objects as their conditions, racing and competing as they traverse all the aggregates, bases, and elements.

Regarding the sixteenth and seventeenth [notes] on the "Mind-King" (*citta-rāja*) and so forth: when first cultivating contemplation, there is no beginning of the practice that does not take the sixth consciousness as the starting point for generating the contemplation.

Even if the objects of contemplation become perfectly integrated and non-dual, since coarse afflictions have not yet been eliminated, it remains the case that these belong to the category of the sixth consciousness-king.
This continues until the six sense-faculties are purified; as long as one has not yet transcended them, one does not leave the realm of the consciousness-kings.
This is because it is the numerical [designation] for the kings of the realms of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi* and *saṃskāra*).
Regarding this mountain city, the *Guangming ji* (Commentary on the Light), fascicle 12, states that this is an "interpretation based on phenomena" (*sūtra-artha-ālambana-vipaśyanā*).

Just as Rājagṛha (the King’s House) takes the sense of "covering" to symbolize the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), it takes the sense of "sovereignty" to symbolize the kings of good and evil; thus, the *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) says: "By means of the good..."
One should know that when the "evil king" faces the "neutral house," the neutral nature pervades all eight consciousnesses;

the "good and evil kings" refer exclusively to the sixth consciousness, because this sixth consciousness permeates the three natures—namely, the nature of goodness, the nature of evil, and the nature of neutrality.

This neutral nature, together with the other four aggregates, constitutes the object of observation (*ālambana*), while taking the natures of good and evil as the observing subject (*ālambaka*); this is the initial stage of contemplation.

There is no cultivation of contemplation that does not rely upon this sixth mind. This is because it is by means of this mind that one can give rise to the discrimination of joy and aversion, and establish the causes for good and evil.
That which is called "good" is so designated in contrast to evil; it is not ultimate goodness.

Since these mental factors (caitasikas) are fundamentally formed by the perfuming of views and craving, those who have merely perfected the names and words have not yet been able to subdue them, even though they may possess them in their entirety.
If one gives rise to wholesome thoughts without being free from views and attachments, then the ten realms of the mind are all termed demonic obstacles.
To speak of "inconceivable contemplation" while merely using this [deluded] mind to contemplate the principle of true reality is like attempting to suspend Mount Sumeru with a lotus fiber;
it only increases conceptual discrimination, and there is no way to sever thought. If one realizes that this mind is inherently evil (*xing-è*), then inherent evil is interfused and harmonized.

Since there is no dharma that does not tend toward the spontaneous inclusion of the seventh, eighth, and ninth consciousnesses as a single wondrous contemplation, it is called "the object is itself the contemplation.
When subject and object have both vanished, conceptual thought is forgotten; thus, this wondrous and perfect contemplation can be cultivated by those at the initial stage of the path.
Therefore, Miaole said: "If one has not yet even heard the name of 'inherent evil,' how could one believe in the practice of inherent virtue?"

One must hear that nature is evil; because one knows that nature is evil, one realizes that the evil of cultivation is fundamentally empty. Thus, the three contemplations and ten vehicles have no delusion to be destroyed and no principle to be revealed.
Since the merit attained through cultivation is quiescent, it is the practice of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*); therefore, this practice is designated by the name of "nature-virtue.
If this meaning is obscure, then to merely speak of the mind-king as the subject of contemplation will ultimately not constitute the perfect contemplation (*pariniṣpanna-vipaśyanā*). How could it be?
Are the three preceding teachings not for those who can contemplate as kings of both good and evil?

According to the *Jiaoxinglu* (The Record of Teaching and Practice: On the Three Uses for Subduing and Eliminating), if the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuantun jiao*) explicates inherent evil (*xing'e*), then the afflictions of view-delusion and thought-delusion (*jiansi wangshu*) are precisely the poisons of the nature itself.
Since the poisons are identical to the nature, one uses these very poisons as the means of subduing and eliminating them; thus, taking poison as the remedy—
If it can be extinguished, then it must be severed in its own place; who then says there is a "destroyer" and a "thing destroyed"? What is there to be grasped as a subject or an object?
Poison strikes right where it is applied. All phenomena tend toward poison; when the mutual exclusion [of subject and object] is blocked, words and thoughts are inexhaustible. Thus, Jingxi said:
"It is not only that the unenlightened ignorance (*avidyā*) and the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*)—the observed—are non-dual in their essence; the observing wisdom is itself unenlightened ignorance."

Since one can contemplate [the truth] within the very poison of irrationality, the three contemplations in a single mind and the ten stages of the Perfect and Sudden (yuan-dun) path do not require separate cultivation;
rather, they are all subjugated through the realization of principle.
Siming takes the natures of good and evil as the contemplating subject, for "contemplation" refers to cultivation being identical to nature. This is a supplementary explanation.
In explaining the scriptural text, one must not regard the fixed object as an obstacle.

Tiantai Śramaṇa Fazhao’s Commentary on the Words and Phrases (3):
Śrāvakas

The Master Beifeng said: "The fourth point in the *Yuanjue jing dashu yichao lun* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra) concerns those who, due to definitive overweening pride, regress from the Great [Vehicle] and transform [into practitioners of] the Small.
In our school, there are five types: first, those who have long practiced the Small; second, those with distinct roots of goodness in the Small; third, those who abide in the fruits [of the Small];

fourth, those who set out to study the Small; and fifth, those of the Buddha-way. If Jingxi says, "Those who originally abide in the Small are precisely those who have set out to study the Small," it is simply for this reason.

When discussing the four [categories], they are subsumed as follows: long-term practice in the Small Vehicle constitutes "fixed nature"; distinct roots of goodness constitute "retrogression from the Great.

Abiding in the fruit includes both the "fixed" and the "retrogression from Bodhi. Although their initial departure was fundamentally small and only the cause and fruit appear different, and the dharma and parable seem distinct for a moment, they all belong to retrogression from the Great, as they are both attained within the latter two weeks.

The *Jiqian* (Notes on the Record) states: "Those who have gained benefit through the two cycles—the Dharma and the Parable—are none other than those with whom [the Buddha] established karmic connections in the past.

Regarding the Buddha-way, the Great Master, following the meaning of the sutras, added the *Lun* (Treatise) to clarify that which was not yet opened; now that it has been opened, there is only one [path].
Someone may ask: "If the original [vehicle] is small and merely subsumes those who regress from the Great, why does the text of the *Ji* say 'contained within this'?"

Regarding the statement that those who have regressed from the Mahāyāna—whether they were originally destined for transformation (*nirmāṇa*) or were originally abiding in the Hīnayāna—and the further claim that "those who have regressed from the Mahāyāna" may also include those who were originally of dull faculties: since it uses the term "and" (*ji*) to conjoin them and then distinguishes between sharp and dull faculties, how can these be considered one class of person? I reply: It is indeed as you have asked. Upon careful examination of the intent of the *Shuji* (Commentary), it appears that after the Prince of Great Pervasion (*Dàtōng Wángzǐ*) established the conditions for connection (*yuan*), he attained two kinds [of realization]. First, there are those who, having been originally of dull faculties, subsequently encounter a Buddha and attain the fruit; second, there are those who, having already attained the fruit, subsequently regress. These two categories are distinct. Therefore, the former refers to those who were originally of dull faculties, while the latter refers to those who were originally of sharp faculties. Because the text speaks of both types, it employs the conjunction "and. Thus, there is no contradiction. This is the meaning of the *Shuji*. Furthermore, the *Jingtu Lunshu* (Commentary on the Treatise on the Pure Land) states: "Those who have regressed from the Mahāyāna are of two kinds: first, those who were originally of sharp faculties but subsequently regress; second, those who were originally of dull faculties and subsequently encounter a Buddha and attain the fruit. Regarding the names: if, after having resolved upon the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), one maintains it during the intermediate stage but then begins to regress, this is called "regressing from the Great.
If, after resolving upon the Great, one immediately ceases to practice it and instead studies the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), this is called "originally belonging to the Lesser.

Thus, among these three types of encounters with the Dharma, the first category achieves accomplishment in the intermediate stage and does not regress; the second category is that which regresses from the Great. The third...

The "three" refers to the original three [vehicles], which are divided into two categories according to their respective degrees of sharpness or dullness. First, regarding those who have already attained awakening in the interim but whose stages vary in being initial or subsequent:
the *Sūtra Commentary* states that they constantly encounter the Mahāyāna and achieve realization in the interim, yet do not reach the present stage.
The *Record* states: "If one is for the sake of Bodhi, one must have already entered the stage of non-retrogression; otherwise, it need not necessarily be so for those at the initial stage."
The first category consists of those who have completely regressed; the second consists of those whose sharp faculties lie in the interim while their dull faculties manifest today;

the *Śū* (Commentary) states: "In the interim they have not yet reached the end, for they now hear the Mahāyāna. The third consists of those whose sharp faculties manifest today while their dull faculties remain after their parinirvāṇa;

the *Śū* states: "In the interim they have not yet been delivered, and even now they have not yet reached the end. Thus we know that those originally of the Small Vehicle belong to this third category today.

Regarding those who enter [the Mahāyāna]: among the two aforementioned classes, those who hear the Great [Vehicle] in the interim but did not hear it at the beginning, and thus first study the Small [Vehicle], are called "originally abiding in the Small.

Since they enter the Great [Vehicle] through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they possess the seeds of the Great from the past; they belong to the category of those who have regressed from the Great and are subsumed under the "extinction" (nirodha).

As for those who enter later, they are subsumed under the category of those with fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*). As Jingxi stated: "Those who regress from the Great are of sharp faculties, while those originally in the Small are of dull faculties."
This is primarily based on the point of the sharpness or dullness of their root-nature (*indriya*).

Master Xiànwén, relying on the teachings expounded in the latter two *zhōu* (turns) of the present text, clarifies that those who have regressed from the Great Matter are called "regressed great persons" (*tàidàrén*). Since the teachings expounded in the first two *zhōu* of the present text clarify that they originally received only the Small Matter, they are called "original small persons" (*yuánxiǎorén*).
Therefore, while it is said at first glance that they were led to the "City of Illusion" (*huàchéng*), the true intent is to show their regression from the Great [Vehicle].
Taking the two superior [categories] among the "lesser persons" (hīna-pudgala) as the starting point for study:

if one discusses their root-nature (gotra) according to the second [category], those who have regressed from the Great [Vehicle] are sharp and correspond to the first two cycles; those who are originally small [in capacity] are dull and should belong to the third.
Thus, the three categories are divided according to their sharpness or dullness. Among these, the former two are peripheral cases of those who have regressed from the Great [Vehicle].

Regarding the "auxiliary" (páng) sections that follow the main discourse: those who sit together to hear the Dharma consider these to be auxiliary precisely because they lie outside the primary subject;

there is no need for further elaboration on this. As for the auxiliary sections of the main text, such as the account of the three occasions of tying the jewel, the parable of tying the jewel at the Bodhi tree, and the account of tying the jewel under twenty-two thousand billion Buddhas—these are merely cited according to the extant text. Furthermore:

Question: The predecessors cited the passage on being "burned by the suffering of extinction" as proof that one was originally in the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), and the passage on the "long road ahead" as proof of falling back from the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna).
They further claimed that those who were originally established in the Small Vehicle received their name at the Deer Park.

Why is this so? Answer: The Master of the *Commentary* followed the literal text and, for the time being, treated them as corresponding pairs. Upon investigating their fundamental capacities (*gotra*), it should be understood that they attained [their status] from the past. Even for those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*), although they...
Those who study the *Hīnayāna* in the interim do not receive the censure (*codanā*) regarding the *Vaipulya* sūtras; therefore, they do not reach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

For this reason, they are specifically designated by the name "those of fixed nature" (*niyata-gotra*). Furthermore, it is asked: "If those who have regressed from the Mahāyāna possess the superior faculties of the two [types of] attainment, why are they not called 'originally small' (*mūla-hīna*)?
And since those who are 'originally small' possess dull faculties and are situated in the third [stage], why are they not called 'regressed from the Mahāyāna'? It is said: This is based on...
Although the "Hearing the Dharma" (śruta-dharma) designation occurs during the first two weeks, it refers to hearing the causes and conditions in brief;
although the third week involves hearing the parable, it is designated as "Dharma" based on the actual teaching. Thus, the three weeks do not overlap in their designations.

*Myōki* (1) (28): According to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, for eight reasons, the Śrāvakas are listed first: (1) to manifest that they heard [the teaching] directly from the Buddha so that they would not later slander it;
(2) to include those of indeterminate nature who turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna; (3) to eliminate pride regarding noble status, as [their realization] is not ultimate;
(4) because they constantly follow the Buddha; (5) because their physical appearance and deportment are identical [to his]; (6) to cause the inner retinue...
It is for the sake of abandoning desire (1), for the sake of causing the bodhisattvas to revere [the teaching] (2), and for the sake of causing sentient beings to have faith (3).

However, among the eight meanings in the treatise, only the second half of the second point alone belongs to this sutra; this is because those of indeterminate nature attain it in this land, yet they still lack the other half.
This is because those of determinate nature attain it in that land, and because they will attain it in the future.

*Miaoji* (1) (29): Having already received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), he is identical to a bodhisattva; how could he then be praised as a śrāvaka? Is this not a case where the compilers have either erred or suppressed his virtue?
Therefore, we know that during the period of the four flavors (*catur-rasa*), the sūtra was modified according to the flavor of the time.

Because the compiler followed the original [status], he listed him among the śrāvakas; thus, based on the original, he praised him. If one did not follow the original, how would one know that there were śrāvakas [who possessed such qualities]?
The provisional has reality; that which is real attains the prediction [of enlightenment] because one knows there is a source from which the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* was heard.

At the time of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there is a distinction between the Great and the Small Vehicles. (24) Question: Since the compilers of the sutras were already established after the "Original Chapter" (*Faben pin*), why does it still refer to them as "śrāvakas"?
Answer: This refers to the period of Mañjuśrī’s questions and answers, at which time they were still śrāvakas. If this were so, why would the title at the beginning of the sutra still not name them?
The Śrāvakas are listed from antiquity as detailed in the introduction and commentary.
Regarding the twelve phrases [of the *Lotus Sūtra*], the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (*Fahua lun*) speaks of four types of Śrāvakas; here, those who abide in the fruit are divided into two:

those who abide in the fruit by means of analytical dharma (*pravicaya-dharma*) are Śrāvakas of the Tripiṭaka teaching, while those who abide in the fruit by means of the essence of dharma (*dharmatā*) are Śrāvakas of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-śāsana*). Those who are manifested through transformation (*nirmāṇa-nairmāṇika*) are further distinguished.

There are two types of śrāvakas who have ascended to the stages through transformation: those of the Separate Teaching (pratyekabuddha-yāna) who have ascended to the dwellings (vihāra) through transformation, and those of the Perfect Teaching (bodhisattva-yāna) who open the way to Buddhahood for śrāvakas.
These śrāvakas are also divided into two: those who cause others to hear the Buddha-way sequentially, which refers to śrāvakas of the Separate Teaching;
and those who cause others to hear the Buddha-way non-sequentially, which refers to śrāvakas of the Perfect Teaching.

Commentary (1) (30): The *Fahua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sūtra) clarifies that those who are to be opened [to the truth] possess both the provisional (*upāya*) and the real (*bhūtārtha*). Before being opened, they possessed four [aspirations], but after being opened, there is only one.

Now, the path of the Buddha is added based on those newly entered. Regarding the four types mentioned in the treatise—namely, those with certainty, those of superior capacity, those who would regress from the Great Vehicle, and those who are transformational beings—the commentary itself explains:
"The latter two are granted predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), while the former two are not, because their faculties are dull and they have not yet matured."
Furthermore, regarding this assembly, it is as stated in the sutra: "Those who conceive the thought of their own parinirvāṇa possess a determinate nature.

If they were able to hear [this], how could Vasubandhu—who has not yet spoken in the treatise—possibly be confused about the meaning of the sutra? The sutra says that they shall hear this sutra in that land;
for now, the treatise relies merely on what is currently manifest. Therefore, the Master here simply removes their overweening pride; thus, there are five [points].

Regarding the "thousand who rose and departed," although they left their seats, they are nonetheless categorized within *nirvāṇa* because they were able to hear [the teaching] at the conclusion of the Four Reliances (*catur-apāśraya*).
Furthermore, those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) are not without hearing; for what was heard previously has been briefly opened up and occurs subsequently.

However, one cannot say that this assembly obtained its prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), for the three stages of the seeds ripening, maturing, and liberation proceed from beginning to end without interruption. Thus, according to the present text, the distant and the near correspond to one another.

Regarding the four types [of practitioners], they all attain the fruit of abiding (*phala-sthita*). Here, "abiding in the fruit" (*phala-sthiti*) is further distinguished by whether it is combined with certainty or with the regression from bodhi;

thus, the teachings are divided into two. For this reason, these two types are collectively established as "abiding in the fruit. Furthermore, as for the "Buddha-way" (*buddha-mārga*), it is established according to the meaning of the sūtras. If that is so, one might ask:

are there distinct differences between the Buddha-way of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the transformation-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), or between the provisional and the perfect? Answer: What is the distinction between the response-body, the transformation-body, and the Buddha-way?

Regarding the "Responsive Transformation" (nirmāṇa-kāya), it refers entirely to the manifestation of traces; regarding the "Buddha Path," it refers to the path of benefiting others according to the ancient sages, while the new commentators refer to it as the path arising from speech.

Furthermore, the Responsive Transformation follows from the Buddha of Body, whereas the Buddha Path follows from the Buddha of Speech. Since there is the verbal expression that causes others [to understand], it is termed "benefiting others.

Since the Responsive Transformation carries the sense of "initiation," it is termed "manifesting traces. Given that one is designated by the name "Śrāvaka" (Voice-hearer) from of old, there would have been no "Responsive" aspect in the past.
The designation "Buddha-path of transformation" does not exist in the present; nor is there a name for the "certainty of abiding in the fruit.
Among those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), how could there not be the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) through shared activity (*samānārthatā*)? How could this be excluded?

Furthermore, in the treatise, it is stated that those with overweening pride are "undetermined," and it is likewise said that they are "not yet matured" and thus unfit for overweening pride—is this not because their faculties are ruined? Others say "not yet" means "no"; as in the case of a sick person who is "not yet" [recovered].

Death is called "non-death," and that which has not yet been produced from the sowing of seeds is called "unborn"; thus, both can give rise to the arrogance of superiority. This is the meaning of "determination.

Furthermore, the citation from the treatise here appears to explain the "original" (ben) and the "traces" (ji) in terms of the manifested transformation (shènghuà): the "original" refers to the fundamental [Buddha], while the remaining three are the "traces.
The transformation manifests as the remaining three; there is no difference in their paths.

*Fuxing* (Vol. 5, Part 1, Section 17): The *Dharmapada-śāstra* states that there are four kinds of śrāvakas: those abiding in the fruit, those who are transformation bodies, those who have regressed from bodhicitta, and those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

The present text says that "the Buddha-way" refers specifically to the transformation bodies; as for the inclusion of the [other] eight types under overweening pride, it is because the two vehicles properly correspond to those abiding in the fruit.
*Miaoxuan* (10) (22): If we consider the manifest stage, even Śrāvakas who have not yet entered the [Bodhisattva] position attain accord according to their respective circumstances;

for example, this refers to the three hundred bhikṣus who received predictions in the *Prajñāpāramitā*. If Śrāvakas abiding in the fruits [of the path] resolutely proceed toward the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they are made to attain accord through the strengthening of their faith;

however, those abiding in the fruits who do not so accord are the five thousand [who departed], who were excluded because they possessed overweening pride (*adhimāna*) and had not yet entered the [true] position.
The assembly rises and proceeds toward *nirvāṇa*, where they finally attain reintegration.

(Fascicle 10 / 25) First, regarding the meaning of "attaining entry at any stage prior to entering the position": this refers to those who do not exclusively rely on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, yet it does not mean they never reach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* at all.
Next, it clarifies that those abiding in the fruit do not transcend the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Third... [untranslated].
In the section following "Entering the Stage" (*rùwèi*), it clarifies that those of overweening pride (*abhimāna*) within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* come next to the *Nirvāṇa*.

In the subsequent text, the phrase "those who possess sincere faith" refers to those who have entered the stage; even if they reach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, should they be unwilling to accord with it, this is precisely the passage concerning "earnest exhortation.
The text states: "If there were one who had truly attained the fruit of Arhatship and yet did not believe in this Dharma, such a thing is impossible. It should be understood thus.
To know that one does not accord [with the Dharma] is precisely to lack faith; because one lacks faith, it is called "attaining what is unreal.

Therefore, it is said that such non-conformity constitutes overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Those who possess overweening pride truly cannot enter [the path], whereas those who do enter are not characterized by overweening pride.
Regarding the third passage which says "five thousand rose up and departed," it means that they will only attain entry into the wondrous [Dharma] at the assembly for *nirvāṇa*.
*Jù* (1) (12): Regarding the meaning of *śrāvaka*, Hao Ran asks, "How can one realize nirvāṇa? and provides a judgment [thereon] (*et cetera*). *Jì* (1) (31):

Regarding the meaning of *śrāvaka*, Hao Ran criticizes others for not being able to discuss it; however, those who employ the teachings say that Mahāyāna *śrāvakas* have not yet attained full understanding.

Now, it is said that these are *nirmāṇakāya* [manifestations]; from the perspective of the fundamental [truth], they are explained according to the assembly, which is entirely within the Small Vehicle.

Regarding the "Middle Vehicle," that which is called "magnificent" (*āha-raṇa*) refers to the eight gates of concealment and penetration; within each gate there are four types, and each gate possesses its own Buddha-way of response and transformation.

The traces [of these teachings] appear before us, and their doctrinal principles are again the same as those previously mentioned. According to the fundamental [classification], they should also be categorized by the stages of the grounds (*bhūmi*), the dwellings (*vihāra*), the practices (*caryā*), and the directions (*pratipatti*).

Furthermore, regarding the confusion caused by pride on the grounds and above, the enumeration is again the same as before. As for others, there is no [distinction of] teaching according to time—whether ancient or modern, fundamental or trace, or provisional.
In the actual explanations regarding opening and closing, etc., it is simply stated that abiding in the fruit and the means, etc., are [the causes]; therefore, the critique says:
"As for those who claim to have realized nirvāṇa," and so forth, which is fully as explained above.

Someone asked: "Regarding the statement that those of fixed nature do not reach the Vaipulya [Mahāyāna], why does this text say there are eight gates for the *zàng* and *tōng* [Hīnayāna] teachings, each with four types?
Since it mentions the *tōng* teaching, does this not imply that those of fixed nature do reach the Vaipulya? The reply was:

"The so-called 'four types' refer to the four fixed natures of those who are responsive manifestations of the Buddha’s path, those with overweening pride (*abhimāna*), and those abiding in the fruits [of the śrāvaka stages]."
[He] was not involved in it.
(1) (14) Originally, these were the traces (*pada*) of twelve thousand bodhisattvas, which became the twelve thousand śrāvakas.
(1) (33) Question: Generally speaking, that which is called a "trace" must have a prior "basis" (*mūla*); how could all twelve thousand [traces] originally be...?
If it is as you say regarding Great Power (Mahāprabhāva), then there would be only that which induces (ākṣepaka) and no that which is induced (ākṣipta). The principle is indeed thus;
however, because one wishes to apply the four meanings equally, it is said that all possess them. Yet, fundamentally they are not the same and must be distinguished.

If one has already entered the stage of perfection (pariniṣpanna-bhūmi), the person who induces becomes the initiator (janaka) and the two assemblies of influence (anubhāva); it is evident that such a person is originally a Bodhisattva who has descended [to this world].

Apart from these, those who have previously awakened the great mind are also called bodhisattvas; those who originally resided in the small [vehicle] are likewise called bodhisattvas even if they have not yet awakened the mind.

Within this, there are those who temporarily regressed from the Great [Vehicle] as skillful means, as well as those who originally resided in the small [vehicle], those who regressed from the Great [Vehicle], and those who resided in the small [vehicle].
After receiving their predictions, they are all capable of being among the assembly of listeners who ask questions during the three weeks of bestowing predictions. Is this not so?
Many were not present at the assembly and were thus commissioned to propagate this teaching; furthermore, these individuals are not limited to the circle of those who heard [the Dharma] directly.

Why, then, does it say "twelve thousand" here? Although the actual number during the three turnings of the wheel was small—such as when Śāriputra received his prediction—the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings were already included therein.
Thus, within the three turnings, there were both those who were manifested through transformation (*nirmāṇa*) and those who were real.

Because practitioners receive their predictions (vyākaraṇa) simultaneously, the Treatise states that there are two types—those who regress from the Mahāyāna and those who are transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya)—who are granted predictions; this is precisely its meaning.

Regarding the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* (Treatise on Stopping and Contemplation, Vols. 5–6), it asks: "How can one who has not yet resolved for enlightenment be called a Bodhisattva? This refers to the persons within the first nine stages of the objective realm as well.
Generally speaking, they are called "bodhisattva persons. If one considers them in relation to the two vehicles, there are four types:
the śrāvaka of overweening pride, who encompasses those who have attained the lower eight stages; and the śrāvaka of the Buddha-way, who encompasses bodhisattva persons.

Within this, there are those who have regressed from the Great [Vehicle] and were originally transformed beings, as well as those who originally resided in the Small [Vehicle] and subsequently regressed from the Great. Regarding the "transformed beings," if one explains it according to their original basis (*mūla*), they can be called "originally [bodhisattvas]. However, how can those who were originally people of the Small [Vehicle] be called "originally bodhisattvas"? For this reason, the Master of the Record specifically brought forth the passage from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* concerning bodhisattvas who have not yet generated the aspiration for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*). Furthermore, he cited [the following]: "How much more so for those who have already generated the aspiration! This is because, although they were originally people of the Small [Vehicle], they later generated the aspiration for the Great [Vehicle]. Thus, by virtue of that subsequent generation of the aspiration, they are designated as "originally bodhisattvas. The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states: "The 'bodhisattva of rational nature' refers precisely to this as the fundamental basis."

[Section Thirteen] (32): Among those in the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, the "definitive śrāvakas" are those who have long practiced distinct roots of goodness with small minds and narrow capacities, thereby accomplishing a small nature.
Being single-mindedly devoted to the Small Vehicle, the Buddha teaches them the Small Vehicle, and they ultimately realize it;

they are unable to proceed toward the Great Vehicle. As for those śrāvakas who are said to have "regressed from the bodhicitta," these individuals once [encountered] former Buddhas and various Bodhisattvas...
When those who have generated the bodhicitta forget their original resolve through the passage of births and deaths, they give rise to a limited mind and aspire toward a Lesser Buddha;
for them, he preaches the Lesser Vehicle until they are finally led toward the Great Vehicle.

However, as for the śrāvakas who are determined to abide solely in the Lesser Vehicle and have regressed from the bodhicitta, although there are cases where they may later proceed to the Great Vehicle, they are considered to have received the Lesser Vehicle once and for all.
Therefore, what was spoken by these two individuals constitutes the Śrāvaka-piṭaka. Someone may ask:

"Why does the *Bieyi shangen wenju* (Text on the Distinct Good Roots) speak of 'retrogression from the Great and Sublime Profundity,' while the *Dingxing lun* (Treatise on Fixed Nature) speaks of 'fixed nature'? The answer is:

While the meaning of "good roots" (*kuśalamūla*) is common to both, there are differences in their underlying natures (*prakṛti*). The *Miaoxuan lun* (Sublime Profundity Treatise) refers specifically to those who cling to inferior good roots; therefore, it is categorized accordingly.

The textual passage concerning "fixed nature" (niyata-gotra) pertains to those who have regressed from the great roots of goodness but have not lost them; thus, it belongs to the category of those who have regressed from the Great [Vehicle].

Regarding the four types of śrāvakas in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-śāstra*: first, the determined; second, the conceited; third, those who have regressed from the Great; and fourth, those who are emanations. Of these, the former two are immature and are not given the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*);

the latter two are given the prediction. According to the present sutra, there should also be [the following]: [Note: The original text contains a parenthetical numbering "(四)(二)" which appears to be a scribal or editorial marker.]

Those who have long practiced the Small Vehicle and whose paths have now matured in this life, having heard the teachings of the Small Vehicle and realized its fruits, are as described in the treatises: these are definitively Śrāvakas.
Furthermore, there are those who were originally Bodhisattvas; having accumulated the path for many kalpas, they grew weary of saṃsāra midway and regressed from the Great Vehicle to adopt the Small.

For these, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* refers to them as "those with distinct roots of goodness. The Buddha, for the time being, brings their small paths to fruition and teaches them the Small Vehicle, harmonizing his instruction with their capacity.
1. Those who have severed their fetters and attained the fruit, having recently regressed from the Great Vehicle and long practiced the Small Vehicle, should logically find it easy to awaken;

as stated in the treatise, these are the Śrāvakas who have regressed from Bodhi. 2. Because of these two reasons, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas internally conceal [their true nature] while externally manifesting [themselves], accomplishing the means to guide and lead them into the Great Vehicle;
as stated in the treatise, these are the Nirmāṇakāya Śrāvakas. 3. If one perceives both the provisional and the ultimate...
Able to transcend birth and death, they take joy in *nirvāṇa* and cultivate the precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom;

possessing a slight degree of contemplative insight, though not yet having entered the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-bhūmi*), they have meager attainments which they claim to be the realization of the fruit. This is called "claiming what has not been attained as attained" and "claiming what has not been realized as realized.
As stated in the treatise, these are the śrāvakas of overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Fifth, there are the Mahāyāna śrāvakas, who, by means of the sound of the Buddha-way, cause all...

If one hears that there are two types of śrāvakas who regress from their resolve for bodhi, this is because, according to the principle of the Mahāyāna, there is no such thing as a final extinction (nirvāṇa) like ashes;

those who seek to dwell in the "transformed city" (the *parīttabuddha* stage) ultimately return to the "jeweled destination" (the *mahāparinirvāṇa*). Since the reality is thus, there is no provisional [vehicle], and therefore no śrāvaka.

Furthermore, as for those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), since they have not yet entered the [bodhisattva] stages, they are not real; and since they are not [true] emanations (*nirmāṇa*), they are not [śrāvakas].
If you, Master Quan, grasp this meaning, the existence or non-existence [of such beings] will become clear and cool; why then need one struggle so hard in debate?

Furthermore, regarding the existence or non-existence of Mahāyāna śrāvakas, if we consider them as provisional manifestations who externally display the traces of the Lesser Vehicle while internally concealing their great virtues, then one would say there are no Mahāyāna śrāvakas.
However, if we follow their own practice (*svacaryā*)—whereby they reveal their origins and manifest their true nature—then one says that Mahāyāna śrāvakas do exist.
Now, the primary intent of opening up the three vehicles to reveal the one is to ensure that those great śrāvakas who are certain to regress are led to achieve the Mahāyāna;
once their own practice is established, they are immediately able to transform others who respond as śrāvakas. If one grasps this intent, one will penetrate both existence and non-existence.

Notes (4) (22): From now on, regarding the formal text that opens the three lower [stages], the underlying intent is that it must be for two types of persons; for those who have regressed from the Great [Vehicle], this does not differ from the *Śāstra*.
Now, taking the definitive intent, it appears slightly different from the *Śāstra*: according to the *Śāstra*, the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) is obtained by those present in the assembly;

whereas according to the current [text], it is opened up for the general public. Thus, even those not present in the assembly may hear it through successive transmission, or even those outside the boundary (*sīmā*) may hear it.

Alternatively, regarding the accounts after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa that urge one to believe this sutra, some records state directly that they were granted predictions, while other treatises claim they "retreated from the Great Vehicle.
For now, let us follow one perspective: among those śrāvakas prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, who would have known they were retreating from the Great?

At assemblies such as these, all were said to have their lineage extinguished. According to the intent of the present sutra, since both parties heard the sutra, both must have been granted predictions. I.
After its opening, there is nothing that remains unaddressed; yet, one must distinguish between the two meanings of "having turned back" and "not having turned back.
One should know that this treatise involves an incomplete exposition and cannot be equated with the thunderous intent of the sūtras.

Regarding the four (or eight) types of "arrogance of claiming what has not been attained" (*aprāpta-pratijñā-māna*): it refers to those who have not yet attained the [first] three fruits and have not realized the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), and so forth.
It is said that "this assembly has no further branches or leaves"; branches and leaves are mere trifles unfit for practical use. These individuals cling to the expedient means of expedient means.
[Commentary] (4) (31) Regarding "branches, leaves, and fine fragments": if one has truly attained the fruit, it is like a great piece of timber from the root that can be used for any vessel;

yet, if one calculates only the branches and leaves, claiming they are sufficient while disparaging the root as being merely equal or inferior, this is called the "conceit of overestimation" (*adhimāna*).

As for those who cling to the "expedient of expedients": the four fruits of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) are themselves already expedients; furthermore, regarding the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*)...
One should know that regarding what is merely superior as being the ultimate truth is overweening pride (*adhimāna*); it is not a case of having no qualities at all.
Rather, when one considers oneself superior based on a shallow stage and becomes proud toward others, this is called overweening pride.

Someone asked: The *Myōryaku* states that those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) among the five thousand [who left] lacked even the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-jñāna*), let alone the wisdoms of reflection (*cintā*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Why, then, does the current text further state: "One should know that those with overweening pride are not entirely devoid of the Dharma; it is simply that, from their shallow stage, they consider themselves superior and are arrogant toward others, saying 'the Great is non-existent' while asserting 'the Small exists. Section Seven (Twenty-two): The Threefold Exposition of the Dharma. First, it clarifies the common formation of karmic conditions in the past; second, it clarifies their mutual encounters during the intermediate period;
third, it clarifies that they have now returned to hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (and so forth). There are three types of such encounters:
those who, upon meeting, constantly receive the Mahāyāna—such individuals had already achieved accomplishment during the intermediate period and did not need to wait until the present.

If they encounter one another, and those who had encountered the Great Vehicle fall away from it, they are instead received by the Small Vehicle; such individuals among this group have still not been fully exhausted.

Now that they are able to once again hear the teaching of the Great Vehicle—provided we speak only of encountering the Small and not of encountering the Great—then those who were not yet saved in the interim and remain incomplete even now, only then begin to receive the Great Vehicle, continuing until after my parinirvāṇa when they attain the Way.

How could there be such [attainment] without contemplative cultivation? This refers generally to the six sense faculties; specifically, it refers to the lineage of those who have emerged from the five grades [of the Five Hundred].
*Nirvāṇa*, fascicle twenty-nine (part nine). Next, the analogy of extracting ghee from clarified butter illustrates the entrustment of the treasure following the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

Because their nature is designated as that of a Buddha, it is said that eight thousand śrāvakas received the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and beheld the Tathāgata-nature;
like the harvest in autumn and the storage in winter, they have nothing further to do and have thus reached the ultimate.

The Text on the Mirror-Substance of Non-Arising (1–17). Regarding the Threefold Canon (Tripitaka Teaching): the analogy of the blind person represents the wisdom of non-arising; the analogy of the mirror represents the realm of non-arising, namely the aggregates, bases, and elements (*skandha-āyatana-dhātu*).
The six parts, such as the head, represent the present causes; the image represents the future fruit. If one opens the eyes...
Because one grasps at the form of the mirror as being produced in opposition to the object, delusion arises and is not severed. If one closes the eyes, like a blind person, there is nothing seen;
thus, the non-arising of the six parts is the non-arising of the cause, and the non-seeing of the mirror-image is the non-arising of the effect.
Commentary (1)(38): Because those who follow the Tripitaka teachings do not understand that images are empty, the *Āgamas* employ the analogy of the blind man.
First, the analogy is established generally regarding the objects and cognition; next, from the section on the head downward, it illustrates the causes and effects of the objects.

Just as the body is composed of the six elements, so too is karma composed through combination. Just as karma relies upon parents, so does the image arise in relation to a form; yet the image must necessarily be unreal.
Because it is considered real, it causes the subsequent aggregates (*skandha*) to arise. It is like the "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpāda-jñāna*), which does not see; it is like not grasping.

Third, if the eyes are opened, light arises; if they do not arise therein, it is first because of grasping the cause that the fruit arises, and next, if the eyes are closed, it is a metaphor for how the fruit does not arise because of the non-grasping of the cause.
The mirror is the auxiliary cause for obtaining the fruit, which further depends on the mind’s apprehension as its object.
This method assists the cause to produce the fruit.
Master Jingxi divided the Great Master’s text into three sections: first, the general establishment of the analogy of the object and the wisdom, which refers to the "blind" passage below;
second, the analogy of the object and its cause-and-effect, which refers to the "head" passage below; and third, the clarification of production.

"Non-arising is like opening the eyes" refers to the subsequent text. Since the initial passage states that the mirror is a metaphor for the non-arising realm (*viṣaya*), it is then explained as the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*);
thus, we know it is certain that the Master took the aggregates, bases, and elements as the substance of the mirror.
Therefore, Jingxi did not add further commentary, but simply categorized it directly. The subsequent text says: "The head and so forth, the six parts."
This is like the present cause. The commentary states: "Just as the six parts combine to form a body" explains the phrase that uses the head and other parts as analogies;
"just as karma is formed by combining [factors]" explains the phrase that uses the present cause as an analogy.
Because one part of the breath at the moment of entering the womb is induced by the cause of present karma, it is called the future fruit. Thus it says:
Karma relies upon the parents; this is explained through an analogy that accords with the principle [of reflection]. It says: "Karma is like the form, and relying on the parents is like the image.
Therefore, it is said that [the self] arises in response to the form as it faces the image.

If one fails to understand this passage, they will take the reliance on the parents to be the substance of the mirror, leading to a proliferation of divergent theories. I have no leisure to debate them; please consult the *Jìwén* (Recorded Texts), section three.
The character "zhè" (this/that) is a dharma-illustration for seeing for oneself.
Regarding the phrase "half the head, heavenly eye" (1) (34): Aniruddha practiced diligence for seven days and seven nights without closing his eyelids in sleep.
If the eyes do not sleep for seven days, the pupils will perish and the physical eyes will be lost. The Buddha then instructed him to seek the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

By fixing his mindfulness upon the object, a pure material form (*rūpa*) derived from the four great elements arose within half his head; it penetrated all obstructions so that he could see clearly both inside and outside, through light and darkness alike.
He addressed the Brahma King, saying: "I see Śākyamuni’s great trichiliocosm as if looking at a fruit in the palm of my hand. The *Ekottarika Āgama* says: "I..."
Within the Buddha-dharma, the bhikṣu Aniruddha is foremost among those who possess the divine eye of clear vision.
Since Aniruddha had lost his physical eyesight, the Buddha and the bhikṣus would constantly sew for him.

While the Buddha was at the Kausāmbī Cave in Śrāvastī, he gathered eight hundred bhikṣus to prepare three robes (trīcīvara) for Aniruddha; the Buddha himself stretched them out while the bhikṣus [sewed them].
A tailor or a seamstress could complete it in a single day.
*The Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, Volume One (15): Aniruddha addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness.
Why is this? I recall that in the past, while I was walking in meditation at a certain place, there was a Brahmā King named..."
[He] purified [the assembly] (and so forth). Bowing his head in prostration, he asked me: "To what extent, Āniruddha, is the range of your divine eye?
I immediately replied: "Virtuous one, I see this Sahā world-system of Śākyamuni Buddha—the trichiliocosm—as clearly as if looking at an āmalaka fruit in the palm of my hand."
*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*, Fascicle 5 (13): [Aniruddha], a son of King Śuklodana of the Kṣatriya caste;

sometimes called Aniruddha, which differs from the former only in dialect, like the "Chu" and "Xia" pronunciations. This is translated as "Wish-Fulfilling" (*Yìrúì*) or "Free from Poverty. (etc. He was a paternal cousin of the Buddha.
When he first entered the Path, he suffered from excessive sleepiness and was rebuked by others. Consequently, he ceased sleeping altogether, which ultimately led to his loss [of sight].
It is explained (as follows): one should cultivate the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) in order to perceive worldly affairs.

By means of this cultivation of dhyāna, one attains the pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) of the four great elements over half the head, and thereby perceives the three thousandfold world system as clearly as a fruit in the palm of one's hand.

While the Buddha’s divine eye—possessing the full extent of the head—is all-pervasive and unimpeded, [the disciple] does not equal the Buddha; nevertheless, among the śrāvakas, he is the foremost. (As follows)... However, in the world...
The Lord of the Realm governs the trichiliocosm, and having attained the divine eye as a karmic reward, he likewise perceives the trichiliocosm (and so forth).

Desiring to know the relative superiority or inferiority [of their powers], he has come to inquire (and so forth). As for the divine eyes obtained by other śrāvakas, none are capable of seeing the trichiliocosm;
therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The divine eye of a great arhat sees only the small chiliocosm, while that of a great pratyekabuddha..."

While the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, can see all Buddha-lands within hundreds of world-systems, and Nanda the Elder alone can see the great trichiliocosm—this being because he specialized in the cultivation of mental attention (*manasikāra*) and counting—he is nonetheless considered the foremost among the Śrāvakas in terms of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). For the time being, his vision is similar to that seen by the Brahmā King (and so forth). Question: If this is so, what is the difference? Answer: The Brahmā King’s vision is obtained through retribution (*vipākaja*), whereas [Nanda’s] is obtained through cultivation (*bhāvanāja*).

Furthermore, the Brahmā King’s vision is limited to his own realm, while Nanda’s extends to the entire great trichiliocosm. Moreover, the Brahmā King’s vision is obstructed by mountains, walls, and forests, whereas Nanda’s is unobstructed. Finally, the Brahmā King’s vision is subject to retrogression, while Nanda’s is not. Thus, there are many differences.

While remaining in his own dwelling, he sees the great trichiliocosm; he does not see other directions, for Ānanda has cultivated the five kinds of fundamental dhyānas and the eightfold purity of form to produce the true divine eye.
Wherever this eye reaches, it sees the three thousandfold world-system as clearly as one observes a fruit in the palm of one's hand.
Although the Arhats do not see the great trichiliocosm, whatever they do see follows their perception like a shadow follows a form. Furthermore:

The Brahma King perceives through general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), and thus his vision is not distinct; Aniruddha perceives through specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), and thus his vision is distinct (and so forth).
Furthermore, the Brahma King’s divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) possesses penetration but lacks clarity, whereas the Arhat’s divine eye possesses both penetration and clarity.

*Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* (5/15): What is meant by this? The Three Piṭakas analyze emptiness (*śūnyatā-vibhāga*) and do not perceive the Middle Way; upon entering meditative contemplation (*samādhi*), they are identical to non-existence.
If one emerges from contemplation with the view of non-existence, it is the same as having the view of existence regarding conditioned phenomena.

(From the "Brief Record," Part 2, Section 13): If, according to Nanda, one loses their eyesight upon emerging from contemplation, they would simply be like ordinary people whose sense organs have been impaired and thus do not see.
*Ekottarika Āgama* (Volume 31): At that time, Aniruddha was sewing old garments. His physical eyes were failing, yet he had attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) which was free from all blemish.
When the Venerable One attempted to sew the garments using his ordinary human methods, he was unable to pass the thread through the eye of the needle. Thereupon, Aniruddha thought to himself:
"May all the Arhats who have attained the Way in the world thread needles for me.
This is because, according to the *Mahānidāna-sūtra* (in thirty fascicles), Āniruddha, by means of his divine eye, can clearly perceive everything within the trichiliocosm,
including even those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), without any obstruction.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Volume 20, end of the "Shou" section) states: "The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not an object of the eye. The commentary explains:

"One who possesses the divine eye acquired at birth does not see the form of a being in the intermediate state. Why is this? Because that form is visible only to the eye of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā-cakṣus*), and not to the divine eye acquired at birth."
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā* (unverified) states that the divine eye obtained as karmic retribution cannot perceive the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) because it lacks form.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* (5.14) cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which clarifies that the divine eye born of retribution exists within the physical eye;
because the divine eye opens up, the physical eye perceives forms, and thus one sees the great trichiliocosm.

The *Fajie Cidi Zhong* (Middle Section), Part Seven, states: "Regarding the cultivation of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*): if, within deep meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one produces the pure derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) of the four great elements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) which abides within the eye faculty (*cakṣurindriya*)."
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (unverified): Question: Regarding the size of the physical form of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), what is it?

Answer: It is the measure of a young child. *Myōki* (10.18): In the initial section on the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), it is not yet discussed that the true divine eye is produced through cultivation;

rather, it is stated that the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) produced by one's parents is able to see the great trichiliocosm. However, if one discusses its actual function, it already surpasses the conditioned (*sāsrava*) divine eye.
The divine eye looks downward and cannot see upward; though what Brahmā King sees pervades the great trichiliocosm, it is blocked at its limit by the wind-wheel.
Shenwu said: "Aligning the brows, the upper half is as transparent and clear as lapis lazuli; now we shall use this to join the head."
Regarding the phrase "divided into six equal parts," Ci Bian further explained: "It is not that the top half of the head is called 'half-head';

rather, it is precisely from the front and back of the head that the whole and the half are distinguished. Since the upper part of the eyes is named the 'head' and the lower part is named the 'face,' and because the front half of the head sees forms while the back half does not, it is said [the eye] is 'from the upper half of the head. Someone asked Naluo (Nalakalāpin):"
Having already attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), why did he ask another person to sew his clothes?

According to the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-ṭīkā*, if one considers that Nanda lost his eyes while emerging from meditative absorption, he would simply be like an ordinary person whose eyes were destroyed and who could not see.
Others say that according to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, because it was a matter of ordinary daily life, he asked another to sew them. As for Nanda’s intermediate state (*antarābhava*)...

Regarding the observation that the perception of forms cannot be hindered by what is obtained through retribution, some have claimed that the doctrine of "clarity before and darkness after" applies to the attainment of compassionate eloquence.
Let us now examine this: the former statement concerns the meritorious function of the eye-faculty itself;

thus we know that the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* contains the phrase "clarity before and darkness after" at the beginning, while it contains the phrase "clarity after and lack of clarity before" later on—these two are distinct.
The phrasing differs while the intent remains the same; how could this be like the "half-head" of the divine eye?
Reading the *Jiaoji* (Records of Teaching), Fascicle Ten; Reading the *Jiaoji*, Fascicle Eleven.
Tiantai Śramaṇa Fǎzhào’s Commentary on the Text (4): The Transmission of the Robe.
[Section] (1) (21): In the village of Vaṃśa, he encountered the Buddha and offered him a precious robe; the Buddha bestowed upon him the *pāṃsukūla* (rag-robe). [As it is said...
therefore it is called "receiving the great [robe]" [and so forth]. Kāśyapa was able to shoulder the burden of the Buddha-dharma, ensuring its long endurance until the coming of the future Buddha.
Having completed the entrustment of the Dharma and the transmission of the robe, he subsequently entered parinirvāṇa; therefore, it is called "the Great Holder of the Dharma."

From the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions), compiled by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty (in thirteen fascicles); and the *Xiyu zhuan* (Biographies of the Western Regions), compiled by Yancong of the Sui Dynasty (in ten fascicles; Fascicle Nine, Volume Yi):

When the Tathāgata’s period of transformative activity was nearing its end and he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he addressed Kāśyapa, saying: [as follows]... "I am now about to enter Great Parinirvāṇa and entrust the treasury of all dharmas to you.
You must maintain and proclaim them so that they do not fall into decline or be lost. As for my maternal aunt..."
Presenting the Gold-Threaded Kāṣāya: Maitreya’s Attainment of Buddhahood and Its Entrustment.
*Inspirational Essentials* (Part II). The World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī, saying: "When I first left the city to renounce the world and entered the mountains to study the Way...
[as previously described] "...the tree deity manifested her body, holding a saṃghāṭī robe in her hand, and addressed me, saying... [as previously described] "...Siddhārtha!"*
"Son, you shall now certainly attain perfect enlightenment through your practice of meditation. In the past, when the Buddha Kāśyapa entered parinirvāṇa,
he entrusted this saṃghāṭī robe to me, commanding me to guard it well until the appearance of a worthy one,
so that I might deliver it to Siddhārtha."
The *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) was first bestowed upon Kāśyapa for him to receive; the golden-threaded *kāṣāya* was subsequently transmitted and held until the time of Maitreya.
Someone may ask: "If Śākyamuni Buddha bestowed his robe upon Kāśyapa to be passed on to Maitreya, why was the robe bestowed by Kāśyapa Buddha transmitted to a tree deity?
One might say: "It is likely because this occurred before the turning of the Wheel of Dharma."

Before the Jewel of the Sangha had yet appeared, there was a tree spirit who manifested. Some rely on the *Āgama* scriptures, claiming that when Kāśyapa emerged from the Piṇḍola Cave and proceeded to the site of the cremation, the Buddha manifested his two feet from within the golden coffin;

it is said that after Kāśyapa had prostrated, this was the time of the entrustment of the robe. This is incorrect. [Question: When Maitreya descends to be born, his body will be one thousand cubits tall, as it is said...
Regarding the entrustment of the robe sixteen feet in length: since it is said that "the Way of every Buddha is the same," why is there this distinction of the "gold-threaded cotton robe"?

Furthermore, how can one single Kāśyapa simultaneously entrust the Dharma, compile the Dharma-treasury, uphold the Vinaya for twenty years as its preserver, and yet remain guarding the robe on Mount Kukkuṭapāda? How could he possibly manage these four matters at once?
Separate Teaching:

The Textual Exegesis on the Nakṣatra Revatī (1) (34) Kapphiṇa is translated here as "Revatī" (pronounced yún-yún-xiù). This bhikṣu had recently left the household life and had not yet seen the Buddha.
When he first set out for the Buddha’s location, he encountered rain at night and took shelter in a potter’s workshop, using grass as [bedding].
Late that evening, another bhikṣu also came along to seek lodging. The first bhikṣu immediately pushed some straw aside for him, and he sat upon the ground.
At midnight, they asked one another where they intended to go. The latter replied, "I am seeking the Buddha. Thereupon, the former bhikṣu preached the Dharma for him (as described at length).
Suddenly, he attained the Way. The latter bhikṣu was none other than the Buddha himself; thus it was that he shared a room with the Buddha.

(From *Yinsu*): Regarding the teaching of attaining the vision of the Dharma-body: The meaning of the Tripiṭaka is that one analyzes and breaks down the house of the sense bases (*āyatana*) and sense objects (*viṣaya*), thereby dwelling together with the Buddha in the chamber of the True Truth (*satyadharma*).

The meaning of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*) is that one realizes that the sense bases and sense objects are identical to those of the Tathāgata, and thus dwells together with the Tathāgata in the chamber of the True Truth.

The meaning of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*) is that by discerning the houses of the sense bases and sense objects across the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*), one attains the vision of the Buddha in all of them.
To see all dwellings within a single sense-faculty, object, or house, and to see all Buddhas therein, is the intended meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
(2) (10) Within the "Exposition of Teachings" (Yuejiao), it is stated that those who "dwell" (*xi*) do so by relying upon the place realized by the Tathāgata; thus, this explains the term "abode.
Accordingly, the specific limits and distinctions of the Buddha as revealed in each teaching differ.
Master Ji said: "Distinguishing the Buddhas is the same as 'dwelling together' (tong su). According to conventional truth (sūdati), the conventional is not uniform;

if one can distinguish each one individually, then it is because one sees each Buddha dwelling together. Therefore, it is said that by distinguishing the faculties (indriya) and objects (viṣaya), one attains the vision of all Buddhas.
This does not mean that the faculties and objects are themselves the Buddhas."
The Master Beifeng said: "Why do the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings speak of 'staying overnight together,' while the *Yuan* (Distinct) teaching speaks of 'seeing the Buddha'?

This is because within the causal explanation (*yinyuan shi*), there is both the meaning of 'staying overnight together' and the meaning of 'seeing the Buddha'; it is simply stated here according to the convenience of the context."

Section Two: The Textual Passages on the Threefold Buddha-Dhātu (2). (2) The Analysis of the Ten Dharma-Dhātus. It is with a distinct intention that [the text] states that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all not "already possessed" [by the Buddha].
(2) (11) Regarding the establishment of the Buddha-dhātu within the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*), there are three intentions: first, by means of the principle of nature (*li-xing*);...

Regarding the "Buddha-realm," there are two [interpretations]: first, taking the *phala-kāya* (the fruit-stage) as the Buddha-realm; second, taking the stage of the first *bhūmi* and beyond as the Buddha-realm.
What is now stated—that all ten realms are not one's own—refers specifically to the Buddha-realm from the first *bhūmi* onward.
If it were referring to the *phala-kāya*, one should have said that the nine realms are not one's own.
Regarding the "fruit-stage" (phala-koṭi) of the Separate Teaching (pratyeka-yāna), it refers to the originally existent Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Since the Dharma-body of the Buddha-realm is already inherently present, one knows that the nine realms are not yet possessed by oneself. Master Beifeng said:

"Since the wondrous enlightenment (*samyagbodhi*) is taken as the fruit-stage, and from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward it is partially termed the 'Buddha-realm,' one should know that this applies from the time one has never heard the teaching until the stage of faith (*śraddhā*)."

The stages of abiding, practice, and advancement are collectively termed the Buddha-realm of the rational nature (*li-xing*). As for what is meant by "rational nature," it refers simply to the Middle Way. Someone may ask:
"How should the three kinds of Buddha-realms be subsumed within the three bodies? The answer is: all three are the Dharma-body.

Some say that when discussed vertically, the rational nature belongs to the Dharma-body, the ultimate fruit (*guo-ting*) belongs to the Reward-body, and partial realization (*fen-zheng*) belongs to the Response-body; this is incorrect.
The Lord of the Three Realms is wondrous and profound; the Universal Monarch exercises sovereignty over the four continents, the Śakra King exercises sovereignty over the Heaven of the Thirty-three,
and the Great Brahmā exercises sovereignty over the three realms.
Commentary (2)(20): Now, although the sutra mentions both Brahmā-rāja and Śikhin as if they were two distinct individuals, according to the *Vyākhyā* (Śāstra), it is correctly Śikhin who is the king.
In this sutra, the title [of king] is used to manifest the name; it likely refers to a single person.

Abiding in the intermediate dhyāna, internally possessing vitarka and vicāra and externally possessing speech, one who attains leadership is a king; those who practice dhyāna alone are Brahma-ministers.
The Four Immeasurable Minds are added as the kings.
*Bie xing shu* (Lower), Part 13: "Brahmā" refers to the Lord of the Realm of Form, whose name is Śikhin; this is translated as "Crest-Ornament.

This clarifies that each of the four dhyānas has its own king. The term "Brahmā" used here likely refers to the King of the First Dhyāna, for even at its summit there is still vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), which constitute speech.
The Dharma-attainer (Dharmottara) becomes the lord of a thousand worlds.
*Miaoji* (2) (25): "Brahmā is the lord of form and also the lord of the three realms; Māra is the lord of desire. *Jingming shu* (2) (13):
"The Brahmā King is the lord of the Sahā world; he dwells in the intermediate stage of the first dhyāna" (*Abhidharma*).
It is said that from the second dhyāna upward, because there is no dharma of speech, the *rājendra-vaipulya-dhyāna* (the king’s ornamental dhyāna) is not established.

While each dhyāna has its Brahmā king, it is here maintained that one becomes a king merely by the superior retribution of cultivating the immeasurable minds (*apramāṇacitta*), and not through the exercise of sovereign command.
In the first dhyāna, however, because there is vitarka and vicāra as well as speech, there is a presiding leader; therefore, one acts as a lord of the world.
*Jingming shu* (5) (13): "Only the lord of the world governs the trichiliocosm. *Buxing* (1a) (26):
"The Great Brahmā Deva King is the sovereign of the three realms; all others are his subjects."
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* (Yuzi-han, Vol. 50) states: "For example, when a great cloud pours down heavy rain upon the entire trichiliocosm, no sentient being is able to know its measure;
were one to attempt to calculate it, it would only cause them to go mad.
Only Maheśvara, the Lord of the Great Trichiliocosm, by the power of the roots of goodness cultivated in the past, can perceive every single drop without exception."
End of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* (1) (24). Next, Mahādeva—that is, Maheśvara—resides at the summit of the Rūpadhātu and presides over the trichiliocosm;
he appears therein as a trace of a Bodhisattva of the Ten Stages. As for his inclusion among the world-rulers in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
Regarding the meaning of "Brahmā-rāja," what is intended? If one says it refers to the Lord of the Sahā World, this is precisely Maheśvara (Śiva).
If one speaks of Mahābrahmā Śikhin and others, these are cited as representatives of the second dhyāna, thereby encompassing the Brahma-kings of the third and fourth dhyānas.

Furthermore, it is said that if one calls him the Lord of the World, in reality he governs only a small chiliocosm; yet, according to the *Jingjia* (Sutra on the Householder), he is praised [as greater].
For this reason, it is said that the Lord of the World privately refers to this as being the master of a great trichiliocosm; one who has descended [into the world] cannot be anything less than this.
*The Sūtra of Auspicious Responses* (Volume 1, Section on Words): "Kapilavastu is [the center of] three thousand suns and moons, and twelve thousand heavens and earths."

It is at the center of this world-system; because the Buddha possesses supreme and most venerable majestic power, he cannot be born in a peripheral region where the earth would tilt, and therefore he dwells in its center to transform the ten directions. All Buddhas of antiquity who arose likewise emerged from here.

Master Beifeng said: "The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* is precisely Master Ding’s commentary on the scripture; it is titled after its most eminent author. As for the questions and answers therein, they are erroneous views that have not been critiqued.
How do we know this is so? Because within the *Śāstra*, it is clearly stated, and it further says: 'It is verified to be the teaching of another.
Considering the word 'if' (*ruo*) mentioned above, there is no doubt that these are the words of another person. Personally, I maintain that the two characters 'private' (*si*) refer to Jingxi."
This is stated during the second period of teaching.
In the *Wuliangyi jing miaoxuan* (6–8),
it is explained that the *Wuliangyi jing* clarifies how the coarse and the subtle arise from a single principle to accommodate the infinite capacities for the coarse and the subtle.

It should be understood that taking a single principle as the "wondrous" and producing the immeasurable as the "coarse" constitutes a separation where the coarse has emerged from the wondrous and they have not yet merged.
In this present sutra, the immeasurable returns to the one; this constitutes the opening of the provisional to reveal the real, wherein the coarse is itself the wondrous (and so forth).
Section Seven (Twenty-five): Three Citations from Sūtras and Treatises. The *Dharmapada-śāstra* enumerates seventeen names, the first being the *Amitārtha-sūtra* (and so forth).

Stanza (8) (15): Next, the *Jiejing* (Exegesis) states: "The remaining names are not explained. Now, to explain the intent of my argument: because the Buddha directly spoke this title and entered this samādhi, it serves as the introduction [to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*] (and so forth).
