thus, attaining immeasurable dharmas and entering into one referential object serves as the introduction. It is like a mathematician who...

One calculation eliminates all subsequent calculations, and all calculations return to the single calculation; because they are eliminated from below, the elimination of the lower serves as the sequence of elimination.
From one, all branches are derived; all are gathered back into one; opening leads to the sequence of synthesis—this is likewise so.
Interpreting it in this manner does not contradict those [other] sūtras and śāstras, and it is also consistent with this sūtra (and so forth).
Commentary (2) (41): Next, regarding the *Dharmapada-sūtra-śāstra*, the current text explains it as follows:

Since the *Śāstra* states that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is an alternative name for the *Anantārtha-sūtra*, we know that the *Anantārtha-sūtra* is likewise an alternative name for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Therefore, there is no logical fault in establishing this title within the introduction.
Having already explained that the *Anantārtha-sūtra* serves as the introduction to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one now proceeds further according to the intent of the *Śāstra*.

This means that one first preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* under its alternative names and then returns to the wondrous samādhi of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. If this is so, one might ask: since it was already explained previously, why is it stated again now? The answer is:
what was previously explained in the sūtra clearly constitutes the introduction (*nidāna*); by restating its name here, the meaning also encompasses the main body (*maula*).

Thus, when the treatise cites this [passage], it serves as an alternative name; in this way, both name and meaning are encompassed, and both the introduction and the main body are attained. (And so forth.)

Now, following the sutra, I shall re-explain the names of the "Innumerable Meanings" (*Anantārtha*) to corroborate the Prologue. First, the sutra text is set forth to clarify the present intent (and so forth).
In the initial passage, that which gives rise [to the teaching] is first presented; next, from the words "That is to say" (*yad uta*), that which is produced is presented (and so forth).

Finally, these [produced elements] are further summarized to demonstrate the producer, namely the specific name of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as the locus of the meaning of the producer, while [the preceding] constitutes that which is produced.
Because the "Infinite" serves as the introduction to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the single name within the introduction carries meaning in both directions.
However, one should know that while the Infinite emerges from the One, although the capacity for emergence is mentioned, it generally belongs to the introduction;

whereas when the Infinite enters the One, although it involves that which is produced, it generally belongs to the main teaching. Thus, while the principle resides in a single dharma, it also constitutes two directions. The principle of emergence belongs to—

The meaning of the "sequence of gathering" (*krama-saṃgraha*) belongs to the section on the "correct" [teaching]. Specifically, from the phrase "from the single principle" (*ekārtha*) downward, the two lines of text represent these two meanings.
Therefore, when the Buddha enters the realm of meaning (*artha-gocara*), his significance encompasses both paths. As for the analogies: the sequence is like [the process] from one producing many;

the correct [teaching] is like [the process] from many returning to one. Thus, we know that the former teachings were adapted to the capacities of beings to benefit them, just as using coins to purchase goods.
Yet none of them know its great number. From one downward, these combined metaphors serve to conclude the preceding [section] regarding the capacity to produce, which establishes two interpretations:

that the producer does not contradict the treatise (*śāstra*), and that the produced does not contradict the sūtra. Relying solely on these two interpretations, the principles of both sūtra and treatise are preserved;
since the exegesis is thus established, what is gained by understanding the meaning? It is simply that the "produced" becomes the "producer," which is merely a different name.

That which is able to produce is the producer, and that which is produced is the produced; this constitutes the sequence. If one were to focus exclusively on the producer, how would it differ from [the views of] those who prioritize "production" and so forth, or from the single perfect teaching of the past?
If one were to discuss exclusively the produced, how would it differ from the commentators or the three teachings of the past? Therefore, to preserve each separately results in a dual failure.
Thus, in our present school, the producer and the produced follow one another, and both meanings are established together. If one were to focus exclusively on the sequence, then the Dharma...
In the previous sections, we have not only discussed how many teachings converge into one, but we have also never stated that one gives rise to many;
therefore, the "Unlimited Meanings" (*Ananta-artha*) is found only in the introduction to this present sutra.

(28) Regarding the phrase "the teaching of the Dharma for bodhisattvas": it is within the locus of unlimited meanings (*ananta-artha-sthāna*) that the bodhisattvas are taught. This is the locus of meaning.
This refers to the principle of the Truth (*tattva*). As stated in the subsequent text: "I shall cause all sentient beings everywhere to likewise attain this Way," and further:
"If I encounter sentient beings, I shall teach them all the Buddha-way"—this is precisely that meaning.

(2) Record (1): The Teaching of the Bodhisattva Dharma, clarifying the basis upon which those who follow this path rely. This section continues by using alternative names for explanation; therefore, "at every stage" (*chùchù*) is added as one of the factors that can give rise [to realization].
This single factor is precisely the ultimate characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Thus, it is called the "truth-principle" (*tīlǐ*).

This truth-principle is no different from that of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; hence, when the Buddha Dīpaṃkara praised the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he also said: [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the omission of the specific quote from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.*
Because it is the teaching for bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas, the passage beginning with "it leads downward and causes all to be equal" is taken as the proof;

this constitutes the locus where the meaning is demonstrated. This is why the title of the sutra appears only in the introduction as "The Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings," but because it encompasses both the provisional and the ultimate, the phrase "teaching for bodhisattvas" is added to the locus [of the proof].
By taking the subsequent samādhi and explaining it comprehensively, the meanings of these two loci are unified.
The *Qijùxù* (Sequence of Simultaneous Alignment) states: "The 'Correct and Auspicious' [section] contains two meanings: first, the true mark (*dharmatā*) is called 'immeasurable' (*apramāṇa*);

second, that which is produced from the true mark is called 'immeasurable. Now, while the name 'immeasurable' may indeed apply to that which is produced, the designation 'true mark' ought to be extended to that which produces it.
Although one may establish both the producer and the produced as being 'immeasurable,' this is ultimately not yet permissible."
If it were the case that the "Dharma capable of producing" (the generative cause) is designated by the name "true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), then that might be acceptable.
However, to simply explain the meaning of the introduction in that manner is entirely incorrect. The Sūtra itself explains: "The Immeasurable Meanings arise from a single Dharma.
Here, "that which is produced" is the single Dharma, and "that which produces" is true reality. How could the ancient masters have justified explaining it as "that which produces"?
Therefore, the Treatise says: "This is when the Tathāgata intends to preach the Dharma. Since it says "intends to preach," it is not yet identical [to the actual preaching].
If it were entirely identical, it would mean the Dharma has already been preached; thus, the Treatise preserves the introduction by stating "intends to preach.

This intention encompasses both the preliminary and the main body, serving as a different name for the same thing. The Treatise possesses these two paths; our current explanation follows them and also accords with the samādhi mentioned in the subsequent text.
To praise this samādhi, its names are listed solely according to what it produces; thus, one should simply say "immeasurable.
From this, we know that while the title of the sutra refers to what is produced, its meaning also encompasses the ability to emerge from the samādhi that was entered;

therefore, both aspects must be contained. This is why the preceding commentary states: "Desiring to expound this sutra, he first enters this concentration. Now, following the perspective indicated by the sutra, [the following] is further [discussed].
The praise based on the *Anantamukhanirhāradhāraṇī* (the Place of Infinite Meanings), as well as the citations of scriptural evidence, are found entirely in this sutra.
[Section] 28: "That which is protected by the Buddha's mindfulness" refers to the *Anantamukha*, which is what the Buddha himself has realized;
therefore, it is that which the Tathāgata protects and keeps in mind. As the subsequent passage states: "The Buddha himself abides in the Mahāyāna. Although he wishes to reveal and teach it...

Because the faculties of sentient beings are dull, he has long remained silent on this essential point, not seeking to speak of it hastily; thus he says, "Having protected the Buddha’s teaching, he entered the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings.
This indicates that wisdom and meditative concentration mutually complete one another: there is no wisdom without dhyāna, and one must first enter dhyāna; yet there is no dhyāna without wisdom.
Therefore, he first expounded the Dharma—this is wisdom within dhyāna—and then entered samādhi—this is dhyāna within wisdom. Thus, they emerge and enter in alternating succession.
Regarding those who harbor doubts because there is no obstruction [to this], one might ask: "If he had not yet expounded the *Immeasurable Meanings*, he could have entered this samādhi;
now that he has finished preaching this sutra, for what reason does he enter samādhi? To explain: it is possible that he first entered this samādhi and subsequently preached this sutra;

or it may be that after finishing the explanation of this sutra, he enters once more—this is merely an introduction to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Why? Because if he did not first open [the way] beforehand, then later...

The phrase "having no prior conjunction" refers to entering the opening concentration (*āyatanasamādhi*) as the preliminary to the concentration of conjunction (*saṃyogasamādhi*); this is what is called a "portentous sign" (*nimitta*), and it is precisely this meaning [that is intended].

[Commentary] (3) (1) Regarding "the Buddha’s protective mindfulness": since that which is protected by the person who has attained the fruit is the source from which immeasurable meanings arise, and furthermore, it is that which the Buddha himself has realized, how could that which the Buddha has realized not be the true reality (*dharmatā*)? Therefore, he cites his own abiding [in that state] as proof.

In the past, because it had not yet been preached, it was termed "protected" (*rakṣita*); this is because, both in terms of the Dharma and the capacity of the audience, it was being guarded and kept in mind.

From the phrase "although he wished" (*yady api... tathāpi*) below, the intention behind this protection is clarified: the Buddha’s original intent was solely to preach that which can give rise [to awakening].

However, because the capacities of the assembly had not yet been awakened, he concealed it and did not preach it; thus it is called "protected. Therefore, following the term "Immeasurable Meanings" (*Anantārthasūtra*), the single word "protected" (*rakṣita*) is also applied.
This establishes two directions. Although that sutra text says "from one, many emerge," it does not yet say "from many, they return to one";
this is still a concealed aspect termed "protective mindfulness. Were it otherwise, since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* had already been preached, how could this be called the "Introduction"?

It is because [the main teaching] has not yet been preached; thus it says, "desiring to reveal and show," and so forth. Because it has not yet been preached, and because protection has not yet been fully expressed.
Reflecting thus: "Those who have long remained silent—from antiquity until now—this essential meaning can be understood through reflection.

If it were merely that which arises from [the Buddha's] birth, it would not be exclusively protected by the Buddha; for in the past, it was universally taught that there has never been a time when this was not so. Therefore, the *Fahua lun* states: "The lotus has two meanings:
first, emerging from the water; second, blooming. That [previous teaching] is like emerging from the water; this [present teaching] is like blooming. Regarding the object [of the teaching]:

Because they continue to be called "lotuses," there is only a distinction between those that have not yet opened and those that are about to open (and so forth). Next, regarding the establishment of the "doubt":

following the sequence, one asks—since all ritual manifestations (*nirmāṇa*) invariably first establish [the principle] and then explain it, why is it here that the explanation comes first and the establishment later?

In the response, first the question is answered in accordance with the inquiry, which is the Buddha’s regular practice; next, the intent of the establishment is presented, desiring to clarify that [the principle] is definitively fixed.
The meaning is divided into two paths; the following section explains the intent of the introduction. Why, at this time, is the subsequent meditative absorption (samādhi) explained first?

According to the established convention, once the teaching has been concluded, the assembly should disperse; yet here, one enters this absorption again to solemnize the present assembly so that it does not disperse, thereby serving as the introduction for the present occasion.
What then is the primary intent of the following section? It is because within a single meditative absorption, the meaning encompasses both intents.

Although the assembly at that time saw only the *Anantārtha* (Infinite Meaning) Sūtra, they subsequently entered a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and did not know what kind of concentration they had entered, nor what dharma he would preach after emerging from it.
Therefore, the compilers, in accordance with the Buddha’s intent, recorded the sūtras he preached simply as the *Anantārtha*;
however, regarding the concentration he entered, they added the specific name of that state—whether it was from the perspective of its meaning or its locus.

By bringing forth the immeasurable, the intent of the introduction is clearly established; yet, by subsuming the immeasurable within the scope of the meaning, the true doctrine is secretly perfected, such that even when the assembly is joined with this scope of meaning, none can perceive it.
Furthermore, when the immeasurable meaning is being expounded, the capacity for the Mahāyāna is awakened. How is this known? Because it is immeasurable.
Within the meaning [of this teaching], it is clarified that seven kinds of expedient means—immeasurable and gradual or sudden—arise from a single dharma. Having heard this explanation, one reflects:
"The three baskets and the three vehicles of the past all arise from this single dharma; thus, these three vehicles should likewise enter into the One.

When one contemplates in this way, the mind gradually becomes unobstructed and expansive, and the great resolve is immediately awakened; therefore, it is said that "one accomplishes the great aspiration."
Commentary (7) (20): Next, regarding the aspect of immeasurable meanings, the time following the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is extremely brief.

Since one has already heard that many meanings arise from the One, one must now gather the many back into the One; this is because it marks the conclusion of the four flavors. Thus it is called "gradual" (*zhan*).
Because there is no longer any distinction or disparity among capacities, it is called "universal" (*tongtai*). Because its manifestation occurs in an instant, it is termed "immediate" (*ji*).
Section Six (31): Therefore, within the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, it was previously collected that he first taught the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination;
next, he taught the twelve divisions of the Vaipulya sūtras; and finally, he taught the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Avataṃsaka*, and the emptiness of the ocean.
This is the universal collection of all sūtras, harmonizing the gradual and sudden teachings to bring them into union; for this reason, it is called the "Assembly of the King."

Furthermore, regarding the record (7) [and] (21), concerning that which was previously collected from among the *Anantārtha* (Infinite Meanings): although it is said that "from one, many arise," there is a subtle doubt as to whether the many all belong to the one;
therefore, it is called "collected. Moreover, it is only by first explaining that "one arises from many" that [the meaning] can then be established.

Because the entry into meditative concentration involves gathering the many back into the one, we know that prior to this, while benefiting sentient beings according to their capacities, although he practiced the three [vehicles] within the one gift, the three obscured the one;
wishing now to speak of the inclusion, he first discussed the opening [of the three].

Thus, below, he cites the *Anantārthika-sūtra* (*Wuliangyi jing*) to demonstrate how it is known that all the various sūtras are collected therein. Since that sūtra states: "The various sūtras are immeasurable, and all..."
Because they emerge from one, the preceding sutras are designated as "immeasurable.

[The characters] "now" (jīn), "already" (yǐ), and "when" (dāng) refer respectively to the various gradual and sudden teachings in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and above; "now" refers to the present assembly, namely the *Anantaparyāya-sūtra*;
"when" refers to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. Thus, the gradual and sudden teachings in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and others are all...
It was easy to gain faith through the provisional means that led to the manifestation of the immeasurable from the one; likewise, it was easy to believe that the immeasurable returns to the one.
However, when the *Lotus Sūtra* discusses the Dharma, it shows how all distinctions are integrated and unified within the One Dharma.

When discussing people, it reveals that both teacher and disciple, as well as their original and manifested forms, have been remote for a long time. Since these two aspects are entirely contrary to what came before, they are difficult to believe and difficult to understand.
The *Fēngnán* (Difficulties of the Peak) states that once the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has been taught, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* follows and is thus easy to believe.
Now, the *Anantamukha-sūtra* (*Wúliàngyì jīng*) is essentially the "produced" [text] that serves as the introduction;

however, because the teaching has not yet harmonized, the capacities of beings remain partial, and the characteristics [of reality] are still obscured, it constitutes a distinct entity. If one follows what the Buddha’s intention expresses, it encompasses both the provisional and the ultimate.
This is capable of generating the single, true *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as its alternative name; it does not refer to the *Anantaparyāya-sūtra*. Simply examine the commentary:

when the "Opening" is divided into the "Introductory Sequence," the "Explanation of the Buddha’s Entry into Meaning," and the "Teaching of the Dharma for Bodhisattvas Protected by the Buddha"—these three sections—it never fails to distinguish between the "capable" (the subject) and the "object.
Once the capable and the object are thus distinguished, one may then silently contemplate the underlying intent.
That which is produced is precisely that which produces; this is merely a different name for what is produced within the family of the producer.
Such being the case, the sequence is established. Thus, the occasion for the *Ananta-artha* (Infinite Meanings) has still not yet arisen; the distinctness of their essences is clearly evident.

4. Hidden Objections (*vighāta*). (Regarding "hidden objections": Mañjuśrī conceives objections within his mind and refuses to answer immediately, remaining in a state of concealed doubt. The text says: Maitreya successively formulates doubts, and Mañjuśrī repeatedly provides resolutions.
Textual Commentary (3) (5).
Disciple of the Buddha, Mañjuśrī, we pray that you resolve the doubts of the assembly.

First, he addresses the objection: "The assembly has doubts, yet the assembly has never doubted before; if they were in doubt, they should have asked. Since the assembly does not doubt, what is there for me to resolve? He explains:
"The fourfold assembly looks up to you with joy, gazing upon both you and me. World-Honored One, for what reason do you emit this radiance?"

Second, regarding the subduing of objections: when the assembly has doubts that are not easily answered, one waits for the Buddha to emerge from meditative concentration before resolving those doubts.
The commentary states: "If the Son of the Buddha were to answer and resolve doubts at that time, causing them to rejoice, what benefit would there be in manifesting this radiance?"
"Śāriputra said, 'It is difficult for the three of us—the two of you and I—to dwell together on the stage of training and attempt to fathom the subtle intent of the Buddha by deliberating together;
it would be unreasonable for me alone to provide the answer.
He explained: 'The wondrous Dharma attained by the Buddha while sitting at the site of enlightenment—does he wish to preach this now, or is he about to bestow a prediction of enlightenment?'"
Fourth, regarding the hidden objection: if it were as you say, that this itself resolves the doubt, why trouble yourself to provide an answer?
The commentary states: "To manifest all Buddha-lands as adorned and purified with various jewels, and to cause one to see all Buddhas—this is no small matter."
Section Three (Fourteen): Because Mañjuśrī extensively cites that previous Buddhas had already preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, Maitreya harbors latent doubts and wishes to inquire.

the present signs are like those of the original auspicious omens; these are the skillful means (*upāya*) of all Buddhas. Now, the Buddha emits light to assist in the manifestation of the reality.
Regarding the meaning of the marks (this section severs doubts concerning the essence of the body):
Third, suppressing doubts as to who can realize the true mark that is markless. [The text] states:
"All people should now know; with palms joined and single-minded, wait for the Buddha, who shall rain down the Dharma-rain to satisfy all seekers."
The Way (this refers to severing the doubts raised by the interlocutor).
The four latent doubts are such that when the Buddha rains down the rain of Dharma, it thoroughly saturates both the Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles.
It is said: "If there are those among the seekers of the Three Vehicles who harbor doubts or regrets, the Buddha shall eliminate and sever them until they are entirely gone."
There are others who, in order to sever their doubts, pose questions [as follows]:

[Commentary on Section One, Question Twenty-five] At the outset, Maitreya suppressed his doubts by posing hidden challenges to Mañjuśrī; consequently, Mañjuśrī secretly resolved those hidden challenges and doubts, saying:
"The fourfold assembly looks up to you with joy and admiration. Why, O World-Honored One, have you emitted this radiance? Mañjuśrī...
The commentary states, "This refers to my own views and so forth.
By employing two instances of the character "qian" (latent/subtle), it highlights the ingenious artistry found beyond the surface of the two layers of text.

The Title and Textual Phrases of the "Expedient Means" Chapter (3) (14): "Fang" (方) means the Dharma; "bian" (便) means function. The Dharma has its square and round aspects, and function has its divergences and convergences.
The three provisional [means] are the square and the ruler; the one reality is the compass and the circle. If wisdom reaches the ruler, then it is skillful function.

When employing partial teachings (*prādeśika-dharma*) to guide sentient beings, if one’s wisdom reaches the specific rules, one skillfully uses the complete teaching (*pariniṣpanna-dharma*) to guide them.
For example, pointing a finger at a partial location is called "pointing"; this refers to using partial teachings to illustrate specific matters.

When using these to explain what is provisional, it is like using a finger to point toward a partial place. However, when generally pointing a finger at a complete location, one should employ the secret [teachings] to provide the explanation.

Fangmiao interprets "expedient" (*upāya*) as "convenience. He explains that citing partial dharmas to illustrate expedients merely accords with the desires of sentient beings and does not represent the Buddha’s original intent;
rather, as the sutra states, it is intended to cause them to leave behind all attachments and emerge from the suffering of the triple world. Therefore, the Tathāgata earnestly extols expedients.
This interpretation may apply to other sutras, but it is not the meaning of this present chapter. Furthermore, "expedient" refers to a "gate"; a gate is so named because it is capable of—
All the skillful means (*upāya*) and expedient strategies (*kauśalya*) that serve as conduits are merely introductory inducements toward the manifestation of the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*).
The merit of the ultimate reality becoming manifest depends upon these skillful means; because it is named after that which makes it manifest, "gate" (*mukha*) is used to explain "skillful means.

As the sutra says: "Opening the gate of skillful means to reveal the aspect of ultimate reality. This interpretation may apply to other sutras, but it is not the intended meaning of this chapter. Furthermore, as for the term "direction" (*fang*):
"Secret" (*guhya*) means "subtle" (*miao*); to subtly penetrate the directions is precisely true secrecy.
The priceless jewel within one's inner garment is no different from the single jewel atop the King’s head; they are non-dual and without distinction.
Pointing to a hired laborer and saying he is the son of the elder is likewise non-dual and without distinction. Such words are secret and subtle, as the Sūtra says: "Only I know [this]."
This mark is likewise true for the Buddhas of the ten directions. "Cease, cease! There is no need to speak, for my Dharma is subtle and inconceivable.

Because the explanation through "secrecy" (*guhya*) leads precisely to the explanation through "subtlety" (*sūkṣma*), this is the intended meaning of the present chapter; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (*Upāya-parivarta*).

*Miaoji* (3) (29): The title of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* refers to the "Chapter on Skillful Means" (*śubha-upāya-varga*), and throughout the commentary on the text, it consistently uses "skillful means" (*śubha-upāya*) [to explain it].

One should know that Dharmarakṣa also explained "means" (*upāya*) by means of "skillful means" (*śubha-upāya*); "skillful" (*śubha*) is simply another name for "expedient" (*kauśalya*). (And so forth. The text itself is divided into three parts:
the first follows the etymological definition of the characters, while the latter two follow the meaning and significance. Furthermore, the first...

Regarding the two [aspects] derived from the ancient teachings and the one belonging to the present sutra, although there are three interpretations, all take the three vehicles as the means (*upāya*).
There are three interpretations because of the differences between that which is capable of penetrating and that which is not, and between identity and non-identity;

however, one must briefly discuss the general principles of these three types before one can analyze the text. Among these three, the first concerns the three vehicles in terms of their functional capacity.

The name "Dharma" refers to that which is employed (the object), while "function" refers to that which employs it (the subject). Although both the Dharma and its function pertain to all four teachings, they differ in their degree of squareness or roundness and in their specific modes of convergence;

thus, the designation "expedient means" (*upāya*) is established based on the provisional. Since the provisional is not identical to the ultimate reality, when contrasted with the past [teachings], it is distinguished as being external to the essence.
However, this is not the intended meaning of the present chapter. Within the text, the presentation of the "round" [teaching] belongs directly to the true reality.
Since these are established in relation to one another, we know that in the past, the "provisional" (*upāya*) should not be explained as the "secret and wondrous.

Rather, it is precisely because [the Buddha] kept it secret and did not preach it that it was termed "provisional. Furthermore, the "perfect" (*pariniṣpanna*) in the past was merely a "concurrent" perfect [teaching].

Therefore, neither the partial nor the perfect [of that era] accords with our present intention. Next, in the second explanation, the provisional belongs to the capacity for penetration; thus, even the three teachings may be called "directional" (*diś*).

This is indeed so; however, because the "ability" (neng) does not immediately serve as the remote designation (*yuan-quan*) for the "perfection" (yuan), the "perfection" designated by it also carries the "ability" as its provisional means.

Therefore, know that neither of these interpretations accords with the intent of this chapter. The previous explanation did not state that the three are the "ability," because the provisional and the real meet and harmonize, each reaching its ultimate limit;
thus, their methods differ, and it is only upon reaching the third explanation that [the meaning is fully realized].

The three provisional [teachings] are identical to the one reality; it is precisely these provisional means that point toward reality which are designated as the "expedient means" (*upāya*) of this present sutra (and so forth).
If, regarding the Tathāgata’s expedient means, they were fundamentally one, this intent would not yet have been proclaimed, and thus they would belong to the teachings of the past.

Although these are expedient means external to the essence, they are nonetheless not non-essential in terms of principle; however, because sentient beings do not yet know them, they are described according to the Buddha’s intention as being "in accordance with" [the truth].
The praise of the provisional means (*upāya*) is not the intent of this present chapter because they have not yet been opened. Second, regarding the designators (*vācaka*):

if one compares principle (*li*) and teaching (*jiao*), each of the four teachings discusses them as being none other than designators. Now, by comparing three to one—wherein the three constitute the one reality and act as the designator—the three are termed "designators.
Thus, within the preceding three teachings, both the teaching, the practitioner, and the principle are all considered designators.

[The commentary] says: Regarding the third interpretation, this is the intended meaning of the present chapter. However, as for the previous two interpretations, they were merely called "the Gate of Universal Names" (遍名門) in the past and were kept secret and not explained.
Now, that partial gate is opened, which is precisely the locus of the Perfect (圓). Therefore, it is called "Secret and Wondrous" (祕妙);
because it is now revealed and manifest, it is called "True Secret" (真祕). [Thus it is said: "In the past it was established as secret; that secret is now opened up in the present."

Regarding the phrase "achieving the subtle and successively reaching the subtle" (*chengmiao cimi dao*), which explains the function (*yòng*) [of the teaching]: "reaching" (*da*) is precisely "opening" (*kai*). This opening serves as the means (*biàn*) for the subtle;
because there is no dharma outside of the opening of the secret and subtle [teaching], it is said that they are "identical" (*jishi*).
(3) (32) If, prior to that, bodhisattvas of sharp faculties regarding the two tastes and three teachings had already attained the two vehicles through the manifest [teachings],
or attained them solely through the secret [teachings], they were called "gates" because they had thereby gained entry.
Section (Three) (Twenty-two): The preceding section clarifies that the Tathāgata is able to know skillful means (*upāya*) and is able to employ skillful means;
this present section explains how the practitioner can accord with and employ skillful means (and so forth).

Of the two aforementioned meanings, employing skillful means and arising from skillful means—this single meaning is that skillful means is itself reality (*tattva*), and reality is itself the perfect cause (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*); the perfect cause is itself one’s own practice.

Regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*), the first section [of the four/five final parts] and so forth clarifies, within the initial discussion of methods, that the Tathāgata is both able to know and able to employ expedient dharmas;
this "ability to know" is his knowledge and this "ability to employ" is his application. Sentient beings do not know these are the Buddha’s expedient means; now, all of these are...
Opening this [text] so that sentient beings may know this one round of clarity means enabling sentient beings to follow the expedient means;

this is because following the gate leads toward the ultimate reality (*bhūta-artha*). Yet, they do not yet realize that the expedient means are themselves the reality being followed. Now, this is further opened up.

Furthermore, while the preceding two chapters both contain the dual significance of the capacity (*tathatā*) and the response (*pratyaya*), the former primarily spoke from the perspective of the response; therefore, for the time being...

It is said that because the Tathāgata subsequently taught much according to the capacities [of sentient beings], he spoke of "practitioners" (xingzhe); thus, the words of earnest praise all derive from the Buddha (and so forth).
Regarding the explanation of distinctions: although they are identical in terms of the five flavors (*pañcarasa*), the objects they correspond to are different.

Although within each flavor there is both "immediacy" (*ji*) and "non-immediacy," the Buddha is eternally immediate, whereas sentient beings are themselves separate [from that immediacy]. Furthermore, the general explanation of the five flavors only captures [one aspect].
Regarding the "Determination of Names" (*nāma-viniścaya*): if it were already established, this present chapter would require further opening.

Although this follows the previous three meanings, in explaining the chapter, the first two meanings have already been opened up by the fifth flavor. Although the third belongs to the "opening," it now also applies generally to what preceded;
thus, the preceding four are also said not to be used here, as they constitute the "coarse and round" that is depended upon and the "square" into which one enters.

Although this subsequent explanation of the "Ultimate Reality" (Zhenshi) further addresses the five periods [of the Buddha’s teaching], one should know that within it—whether as an opening or a judgment—all things without exception are contained, for there is nothing in the *amṛta* (the finest essence) that is not profound and wondrous.

(Question 8–14): Are the provisional means (*upāya*) themselves the gate, or is it because they lead to the realization of the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) that they constitute a gate? [Private Answer]: They possess both qualities. The provisional means are themselves the gate; furthermore, because they lead to the realization of the true reality, they function as a gate. Thus, they are complete in both aspects.

Regarding the two meanings (and so forth): each of these two gates has its own opening and closing. Previously, because it was not said that "three" is the provisional means (*upāya*), that gate was closed;
now, because it is said that "three" is the provisional means, that gate is opened. Previously, because it was not said that "one" is the ultimate reality (*tattva*), the gate of reality was closed;
now, because it is said that "one" is the ultimate reality, the gate of reality is opened. Furthermore, this provisional means also penetrates the ultimate reality.
Because they are characterized [by the same reality], the skillful means of the three vehicles constitute the gateway to the One Vehicle.

Regarding the initial statement "it should be understood according to its essence" (v. 8), this refers to what has not yet been fully integrated; it is spoken in terms of that which lies outside the essence.

For the time being, it is called a "gateway" (*mukha*) because one can enter through the teachings of this specific doctrine. If it is said to be the "gateway to the true nature" (*dharmatā*), it is so designated in reference to the ability to penetrate through to the true nature.
(As stated above) These two gates each have their opening and closing. Although they are able to provide access, the essence of the dharma-body itself does not differ;

this is because they are explained according to the perspectives of the past and the present. What was closed in the past is opened in the present, and the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) is likewise so.

(As stated above) Within the first [gate], that which constitutes the essence itself is also called a "gate," yet it remains closed with respect to the ultimate reality; therefore, its opening must be clarified. However, while the three [gates] are taught as skillful means (*upāya*), one must ultimately speak of the One.
This is because they serve as true relative counterparts. Second, the following explains the "ability to penetrate" (*nengtong*), which constitutes the gate of actualizing reality.
According to the Buddha's original intent, both are capable of penetrating; however, based on the capacities and conditions of sentient beings, there are two ways of understanding it.

Even those bodhisattvas of dull faculties possess the ability to know the "ability to penetrate" of the three teachings, yet before the *Lotus Sūtra*, their capacities had not yet converged with them. Therefore, this was so in the past.
Since both were closed previously and are now opened simultaneously, they are likewise distinguished in contrast to the ultimate reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
How could it be that while the provisional means (*upāya*) remain closed when the ultimate reality is opened, the provisional means would still be closed while the ultimate reality is opened?
*Miaoxuan* (9, 11): Regarding the teachings prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, if one has already entered the profound through either the gate or the principle, what further is there to be opened?
*Jingming shu* (3, 14): First, to briefly explain the name: it refers to the partial dharmas that are the destination of wisdom; it is precisely the skillful application of expedient means (*upāya*).
Because these various dharmas are skillfully applied according to the capacities of beings to benefit them, they are called "expedient means."

*Jilji* (Vol. 1, Part 2) (14). Regarding the brief explanation of *upāya* (expedient means), and so forth: in the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), three types of explanations are established in order to reveal the reality (*tattva*), namely:
the application of the Dharma (*dharmaprayoga*), the gate (*mukha*), and the secret marvel (*guhyamandala*). Herein, two of these are discarded and only the application of the Dharma is adopted.

This is because the "gate" concerns the entry [into the path], while the "secret marvel" involves the disclosure of the provisional (*prajñapti*)—a disclosure that has not yet occurred here; therefore, the latter two explanations are omitted and not taken up.

The gate is that which the Bodhisattva may enter; the Two Vehicles lack this, as they are deficient in relation to the Bodhisattva path. Furthermore, within the context of their respective stages (*svabhāga*), the "entrance by transmission" is set aside;

thus, it is not mentioned here. According to principle, one should also employ the single meaning of "gate," because entering according to one's own stage is identical to the application of the Dharma (*dharmaprayoga*);
therefore, we shall employ only the single sense of "application of the Dharma."

Master Beifeng said: Regarding the fact that the text of the "Expedient Means" chapter speaks of the ultimate reality while the title designates it as "Expedient Means," there are three underlying intentions:

first, to demonstrate that the opening of the provisional is itself the ultimate reality; second, to contrast the internal realization of ultimate wisdom with its external application as the provisional;
and third, to indicate that the provisional possesses the function of revealing the ultimate. Why is this? The merit of the *Lotus Sūtra* lies precisely in its opening of the provisional.

Because it is the actual reality (*tattva*), it is specifically designated so that the meaning may be made manifest: that reality is not separate from the provisional (*upāya*). As the Commentary (*śāstra*) states:
"To skillfully penetrate the directions is itself the true secret function," which serves as proof for the first point.

This is because, by virtue of the Tathāgata’s internal realization of the substantial reality (*vastu-svabhāva*), he is able to exercise external functions with infinite mastery; thus, in contrast to the internal realization of true wisdom (*prajñā-jñāna*), all his transformations...

All such applications are termed "expedient means" (*upāya*). As recorded in [the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*] (III.37), because the internal three virtues are fully endowed with the three bodies (*trikāya*), they cause external manifestations—whether horizontal or vertical, manifest or secret—to be perfected.

Regarding the intent of this sutra’s refutation and establishment in contrast to the former [teachings], it is necessary to employ the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) as a general outline. This is explained in correspondence with the realization of one's own true wisdom;

therefore: [The text continues: ...therefore... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* or a related Tiantai/Tendai doctrinal work, likely discussing the relationship between the provisional and the ultimate, and the specific pedagogical methods used to transition from prior teachings to the present sutra.)

It must be said that the third half-verse is used to corroborate the second meaning. Although both the provisional and the real exist within the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāya-paṛivarta*), the real does not manifest of itself;
rather, it is manifested through the provisional, for the provisional possesses the function of manifesting the real.
Therefore, the title of the chapter is established accordingly, as the *Commentary* (San) states: "Thus, in the ten pairs below, each pair fully possesses both the provisional and the real."
The names [of these chapters] all take the provisional as being identical to the real to serve as the "Expedient Means" chapter (text), thereby proving the third meaning.
Someone may ask: how are the three kinds of expedient means reconciled with the three metaphors of the lotus? I reply:

since the three metaphors of the lotus illustrate the intent behind the dispensation of the teachings throughout the entire lifetime [of the Buddha], the identity of the real and the provisional, and the identity of the provisional and the real, correspond precisely [to those three meanings].
The secret and wondrous skillful means have only now been revealed; it is not that the Buddha’s intent has not been revealed, nor that the secret and wondrous [truth] itself has not been revealed.

Rather, what was revealed were the dharmas clung to by the capacities of sentient beings; this very act of revealing the functional application of the Dharma enables one to penetrate and thereby realize the secret and wondrous.
One must know that among those capable of penetrating from the partial to the perfect, there were none who had entered in the past, though there are now those who have entered.

Having already entered the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there are differences in degree regarding whether it is true or semblance, shallow or deep. If one has already entered the true stage (*bhūmi*), then no opening [of the gates] is required.

However, for those who have entered the semblance stage or have not yet entered it, an opening must indeed be made. Since those who have entered the semblance stage require the opening through hearing, the *Miaole* states:
"The beginner of the Perfect person (*yuanren*) must hear the opening, etc. As for those who have not yet entered, they are exclusively...
"It must be opened. Yitang said:
"What are the characteristics of the three kinds of expedient means? It is said: If one practices the three without knowing the Perfect [Truth], this is the application of the Dharma.
If one practices the three while knowing the Perfect, then one abandons the three to enter the Perfect; this is 'being able to penetrate,' which is to practice while being identical with the three."

"Round" (*yuan*) signifies the secret and wondrous. Furthermore, it was asked: "Now, this sutra opens the three teachings; how does this 'function of the Dharma' (*fayong*) differ from the 'ability to penetrate' (*nengtong*)?
He replied: "Both open the three teachings. As for the function of the Dharma, its skillful means (*fangbian*), human capacity, principle, teaching, and practice all open [the three].
As for the ability to penetrate, although persons have already entered the Round (*yuan*), they merely open the three teachings as the gateway through which that penetration occurs."

[The Sutra on the Essential Characteristics of the Five Turbidities (5)] Prose Explanation, Chapter on Śākyamuni: Śāriputra, all Buddhas appear in the world of the five turbidities and evil ages, namely:

The kalpa-turbidity (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), the affliction-turbidity (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), the sentient-being-turbidity (*sattva-kaṣāya*), the view-turbidity (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), and the life-span-turbidity (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*).
Regarding the textual passage (4.17): the kalpa-turbidity has no separate substantial entity. A "kalpa" is a long duration, while a "kṣaṇa" is a short duration;

this conventional designation is established solely in reference to the four turbidities. The text states, "The kalpa-turbidity is a time of chaos," which is precisely this meaning. The sentient-being-turbidity is likewise...

There is no separate substantial entity; this conventional designation is established based on the retribution of views and pride. As the text states, "the defilements of sentient beings are heavy," which refers precisely to this meaning.

The *kleśa-kaṣāya* (defilement-turbidity) takes the five dull afflictions (*pañca-moha-nīvaraṇa*) as its essence; the *dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya* (view-turbidity) takes the five sharp afflictions (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*) as its essence;

and the *āyuḥ-kaṣāya* (life-span turbidity) takes the continuity of matter and mind (*rūpa-citta*) as its essence, and so forth. As for their characteristics, these four turbidities intensify and converge in this [age].
At that time, as hatred increases, weapons arise; as greed increases, famine arises; and as delusion increases, pestilence arises.
Because these three calamities arise, afflictions descend doubly, while various views blaze fiercely. Coarse and debased form and mind, evil reputations, and foul appellations prevail;
years are diminished, lifespans shortened, and the various turbidities converge like waters rushing toward a dark abyss, where wind and waves surge and fish and dragons struggle.

Agitated and distracted, there is not a single moment of reliance; it is caused by such conditions. It is like when, at the beginning of the kalpa, beings from the Ābhāsvara Heaven fell to earth, and the earth caused them to possess desire.

Or like when the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven enter the Rough and Harsh Garden (Rūkṣavana), and the garden gives rise to thoughts of conflict. This is called the characteristic of the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

As for the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*): the ocean of greed receives all streams yet is never satisfied; hatred is like a venomous snake that drinks poison and agitates the entire world; and ignorance...
Dark, stubborn, and dull-witted beyond lacquer or ink; arrogant and haughty, looking down upon others with boundless contempt;
ensnared by a web of doubt and lacking integrity, such that one cannot be told the truth—this is the characteristic of the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kāṣāya*).

As for the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*), it consists of the sixteen types of knowledge-views, the sixty-two [wrong] views, and so forth, which are like a net or a dense forest that entangles and binds.

Being bent and twisted, unable to emerge—this is the mark of the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). As for the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*): they grasp at form and mind to establish a single sovereign master.
Like sticky glue to which nothing does not adhere, they drift through the six realms of existence, taking birth everywhere.

Whether called poor or short, named long or rich—this is the mark of the turbidity of sentient beings. As for the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*): one is born in the morning and perishes by evening; by day...
The sun rises at evening and sets at dawn; waves roll and smoke swirls, never remaining still for even an instant—this is the characteristic of the turbidity of life (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*), and so forth.

Regarding the sequence: afflictions and views constitute the root. From these two turbidities, the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*) is formed. From sentient beings, there arises the maintenance of life (*jīvitendriya*).
The duration of these four is called the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).
Section One (Commentary on the Thirty-two *Lokadhātus*): At the beginning of the kalpa, when the great waters were blown together by the wind, they formed the world.

The beings from the Ābhāsvara Heaven, their life-span having ended, were born by transformation as human bodies; they possessed light and traveled by flying, taking joy as their food, and there were no distinctions of male or female or high and low.
Among those born together, they were called "sentient beings" (*sattva*). Then, the "taste of the earth" (*pṛthivī-rasa*) appeared naturally, its flavor like clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
The appearance of the food was like fresh butter and its sweetness like honey. Those who ate much lost their radiance and became haggard, unable to fly; those who ate little retained their luster.

Thus, there arose competition and mutual disparagement, leading to the loss of the taste of the earth. They then ate the natural skin of the earth, but through their increasing mutual contempt, they lost even that skin.
They then ate the natural bark of the earth, which gave rise to various evils. They lost the bark and then ate the natural non-glutinous rice.
When rice was produced, male and female sexual organs appeared, and they subsequently became husband and wife. Out of shame, they built houses and stored up large quantities of rice;

however, after the rice grew husks and chaff, it no longer sprouted from the harvested stalks, which withered away. As people began to steal from one another, they established a capable and impartial person as the Lord of the Fields to adjudicate disputes;
this was the origin of the "Lord of Men" (Rājan).

In the *Miaole* (Commentary on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*), fascicle 5 and 9, the characteristics of the kalpas are explained as follows: regarding the four turbidities (*caturkaṣāya*) and so forth, while there are the three turbidities of emptiness, formation, and destruction, there is no "turbidity of the kalpa" (*kalpakaṣāya*).

Within the abiding kalpa (*sthitikāla*), according to the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, from eighty thousand years down to thirty thousand years, there is still no turbidity; it is only when the lifespan reaches twenty thousand years that the five turbidities (*pañcakaṣāya*) begin.
*The Long Āgama* (Volume 22 of the Li-zi box): "The people of the world originally had a lifespan of eighty thousand years...
Subsequently, the human lifespan gradually diminished until it reached ten years. At that time, girls were married at five months of age...
The five grains did not grow; there were only weeds and tares... Brocades, silks, and fine fabrics were all gone, and nothing remained but..."
[They wear] coarse woven garments of grass (and so forth). The seven treasures, pearls, and jade naturally sink into the earth.
In the *Maitreya-buddha-sūtra* (Qi-zi-xuan), the human lifespan is eighty-four thousand years, with no premature deaths;
the height of every person’s body is sixteen zhang (and so forth). Women do not marry until they are five hundred years of age.
[It is said: "Precious things rain from the sky" (and so forth). When the multitude saw this, their minds felt no greed or attachment;

they cast them upon the ground as if they were shards of pottery, stones, grass, wood, or clods of earth. Those who saw it at that time felt a sense of weary detachment in their hearts and said to one another:
"As the Buddha has taught, in the past sentient beings mutually harmed and destroyed one another for the sake of these treasures."
Passage (4) (26): The *Sūtra on the Aggregate of Feeling and the Body* states that for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) receiving a body, during the first seven days there is no transformation;
in the second week, the characteristic of arising appears like thin curd; in the third week, it is like thick curd; in the fourth week, it is like congealed curd;
in the fifth week, it is like a lump of flesh; in the sixth week, it is like a mass of flesh; and in the seventh week, five protrusions—namely the head, hands, and feet—arise from that mass of flesh.
Eight, seven, and again five blisters form on one head and two shoulders; two wrists, nine, seven, and twenty-four blisters arise in succession.
Four blisters form as the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue; twenty blisters become the twenty fingers.

Seventeen transformations manifest the appearance of the abdomen, and gradually the skin and bones separate, producing various distinct forms: seven hundred sinews and seven thousand vessels appear according to their required characteristics.
It is dyed by one wind; if it is to be white, it is dyed by the white wind, and so on for the other winds as well.
Because of the fragrant wind, it is secure and upright; because of the foul-smelling wind, it is insecure and thus ugly, crooked, and deformed.

After emerging from the womb, when it eats the five grains, eighty thousand families of worms are produced. (From the *Zhiguan*, fascicle 4; according to the *Garbha-avakrānti-sūtra*, there are thirty-eight periods of seven days in total; the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* enumerates five stages.)
(One must examine this). Alas!
Those in the five turbidities neither know the substance of the five turbidities nor know their characteristics;
it will be difficult indeed for them to escape the five turbidities.
*Reading Notes on the Teachings*, Scroll Eleven;
*Reading Notes on the Teachings*, Scroll Twelve.
By the Tiantai Śramaṇa Fazhao.
Section Five (5):
The Single Verse on the Chapter Concerning Future Buddhas from the *Dharmāḥ sadā niḥsvabhāvā iti sūtra*.

Section 4 (29): Regarding the knowledge that all phenomena are eternally without self-nature—this means that the true mark is eternally abiding and lacks self-nature, up to and including the absence of a nature of causelessness;
even this "absence of nature" is itself without nature. This is called "the absence of nature."
Commentary (5) (22): The Twofold Emptiness of Nature and Characteristics within the Single Ultimate Reality (*ekārtha-tattva*) (*et cetera*).
My own topical outline divides this into five parts: first, the single ultimate reality; second, the exegesis of the main text;

third, the clarification of the essence of contemplation as exemplified below; fourth, the establishment of the thesis and the refutation of errors; fifth, the explicit demonstration of the characteristics of contemplation.
The fifth question clarifies the selection [of the meaning] by explaining both parts regarding the "Buddha-nature arising from conditions.
Regarding the phrase "Buddha-nature arises from conditions": the Middle Way of non-substantiality (*niḥsvabhāva*) is itself the Buddha-nature (and so forth). *Commentary*:

[The text says: "Commentary on the 'Buddha-lineage' (buddhagotra) section below, divided into two parts: first, refuting ancient [interpretations]; second, the correct explanation thereof. Within the first [part], refuting ancient [interpretations], there are two sections:

first, refuting [the view that] the Buddha-lineage [is eternal]; second, [the section beginning with] 'However, it should be... which refutes [the view regarding] dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). First, refuting [the view that] the Buddha-lineage..."

Furthermore, there are two parts. First, because the two ancient [views] are refuted, the meaning is demonstrated below in two sections. Second, the refutation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) also has two parts.

First, the demonstration of the meaning. Second, the refutation of the ancient views, beginning with "Others say... and so forth. Within this, the formal explanation has two parts. First, establishing that original non-nature (*anādikālika-prakṛti-nihsvabhāvatā*) is itself the Buddha-seed (*tathāgatagotra*).
Second, from "Deluded regarding this... onwards, both defiled and pure types of dependent origination are explained together. This is divided into three sections; first, the heading for the defiled.

Purifying the two defilements (middle section); explaining defilement and purification (third section). Regarding "If it is... and below, there is a re-discussion of defilement and purification. This explanation is divided into two parts:
first, explaining the nature of the seeds of the defiled dependent origination; second, explaining the categories of the seeds of the pure dependent origination.

This is further divided into two: first, explaining the pure dependent origination; second, regarding "Desiring to arise... and below, explaining the conclusion that the pure dependent origination accords with the scriptures.

The first commentary, explaining the section on the mutual establishment of the result-vehicle, is divided into four parts: 1. "First, 'cultivation and nature' below" indicates the nature; 2. "'Fully clarifying' below" points to the extensive [explanation];
3. "'Therefore, one knows' below" concerns self and others; 4. "'In this way' below" relies on principle. Within this, there are again four sections concerning self and others:
1. A general heading; 2. "'First, inferring' below" is the specific explanation; 3. "'If one infers' below" is the departure from conceptualization.
Fourth, the conclusion is shown by means of the nature [of the request].

Regarding the phrases on "requesting the vehicle" (4): those who aspire to seek the Buddha-way are precisely requesting the Great [Vehicle], not seeking the small fruit. There are three types of such requests.

The mind constitutes one "great occasion" (*mahā-avasarana*) in the sense that it possesses the capacity to evoke a fruit; within this occasion, there is the seeking [of the Dharma], and within the two emotions, there is the secret quest.
To inquire whether [the goal] is attained or not is precisely this third aspect of the mind. To speak and seek is itself the earnest triple entreaty (*tri-yācanā*).

Although the two types of seeking already existed within the teachings of the past, they did not yet involve verbal expression; until this day, these three modes of seeking are fully present. Thus, the inquiry regarding the past is brought forth.
Regarding the "seeking the three": as for the seeker, the text says, "As previously promised, this is seeking the three; what does it have to do with seeking the one?

The answer is that because one does not see [the one] outside [the three], there must be a different path; thus, using the former promise of the three to seek a different meaning is indeed also a way of seeking the one.

Regarding the three meanings of the "two cords" (in the fifth section, thirty-third): since the two cords are said to reside in the "mechanism" (*ji*) and in "sentiment" (*qing*), the mechanism is simply described as having the sense of being "responsive" (*yougan*) to the fruit;
whereas sentiment is simply described as "secretly seeking. Therefore, while the former two pertain to the past, the expression regarding speech pertains only to the present.

Although these terms generally apply to all four periods of the teachings (*sīwèi*), here they specifically refer to the two *sūtra* periods (the *Prajñāpāramitā* and *Nirvāṇa*) when one simultaneously hears the Mahāyāna. For this reason...
Regarding the statement "there are two kinds of 'two strands' (dvisūtra)," there are both general and specific senses. In the general sense, both [the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*] are included;

that is, while the two flavors [of teaching] are implicitly present within the internal disposition, and the internal emotion is stirred from within, the two flavors are thus consistent, which is why it is called "general.

In the specific sense, the two strands correspond separately to the two flavors; specifically, within the Vaipulya (*fangdeng*) period, although one hears of the inconceivable [Buddha-nature], it is still disparaged as being incorrect.
In the profound depths there is great benefit; though one is rejected, not slandering the meaning is appropriate for seeking it.

Thus we know that the principle of non-slander lies in having a request and in being mature. At the time of the clarified butter (*ghṛta*), there was great enticement; although there was no desire to take [it], the intention to transmit the teaching was intimate.

Even if one does not speak openly to seek it, the meaning gradually becomes pressing. Although these two cases differ, the capacity is remote while the sentiment is near. As for "attaining" or "not attaining," this refers exclusively to the Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the progress and retreat within the mentalities of the Śrāvakas, one should seek this out; thus, their mentalities are imbued with a "trigger" (*ki*) that is somewhat more acute than in the past.

Consequently, upon reaching the *Prajñāpāramitā*, they are specifically designated by the name "mentalities. When it comes to the time of realization and understanding, because the attainment reveals the loss, it is said:
"I wish to ask the World-Honored One: is this a loss, or is it not lost? Although this seeking occurs only within the present teaching, when it arrives...

The capacity for expression (*vāk-karaṇa*) and the underlying intention (*citta*) must both be present; while the former is primarily associated with the mouth, the latter—though distinct—is likewise essential.

In the past, these [intentions] lay dormant within the heart, but now they assist in manifesting through speech. When the three inquiries are all addressed to the Most Holy One, the responses are naturally distinguished as explicit or esoteric.
When the time is ripe, the internal causes are fully assembled; because one hears this brief exposition, the external conditions are fulfilled. Thus, the causal conditions are complete.

Regarding the statement that "because [the conditions] are complete, he speaks here," and the reference to "leaving the house" and so forth, this cites the *Upamāna-parivarta* (The Chapter on Parables) to clarify the present context. Therein it says:

"The sons approached their father and requested, 'Please grant us three kinds of precious chariots. Why, then, can it now be said that they "sought the reality"? The intended meaning of the answer is this:
while they had not yet left the house, they heard the promise; but once they had left, they did not see the chariots for which they were promised, seeing only the person who had granted the promise.

Therefore, when one asks others for what was previously promised, if that which was promised is not given, there must be some underlying reason. Thus, when asking for what was promised in the past, one is fundamentally seeking the fulfillment of a different intention.
[The questioner asks: "When you spoke at the Deer Park and left the household, you only maintained the goal of the Lesser Fruit; why did you ever ask for the vehicle? [The answer is:

"If it were according to the Dharma-exposition, by the time we reached the Deer Park, the meaning would have been 'leaving the household. Furthermore, having passed through the two flavors, the two requests remained in our hearts."

The short parable contains the long meaning because it extends to the beginning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Thus, the intermediate parable of the sons approaching their father and requesting vehicles—whereupon he grants them and bestows upon them the great [vehicles]—contains the intent of both [parables].
The parable of the "Belief and Understanding" (*śraddhādhimukti*) contains the long [meaning], as it opens up the essence and the life-force.
Therefore, the text and meaning of the Parable Chapter contain the three types of requests.
The Record (5) (25): Just as the parable contrasts the three carts with the single cart, so too do the teachings contrast the provisional and the real, the partial and the perfect.
If it were not so, what would there be to open? Originally, the three carts were promised but not given; yet when the teaching was finally proclaimed, they were all equally granted the great carts.
One should know that these carts originally did not consist of three; they were established as one as a skillful means for the sake of sentient beings.
Provisionally establishing three names, one leaves the house; discarding the provisional, one shatters the three to reach the One.
(5) [Section Fifteen: The Gate of the Two Houses and the Gate of the Chariot. "House" refers to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). "Gate" refers to the essential path for exiting [it];
this is the definitive expression of the provisional teachings. "Chariot" refers to the Mahāyāna Dharma. "Gate" refers to the definitive expression of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*).
Furthermore, if the gate of the house were the same as the gate of the chariot, then the three chariots that rescued the children would also have to be granted equally;
yet since the gate exited from is not the gate entered through, it is proven that the chariot and the house are different.

Commentary (6) (8): Fifth, if one raises an objection based on the contrast between the present and the past, it is as follows: the house is the place from which one departs, while the carriage is that into which one enters;
the gate of the house is the path by which one exits, whereas the gate of the carriage is the path by which one enters.
Since these two paths are not the same and their functions of exit and entry differ, the gate of the house is not the gate of the carriage. Therefore, the present objection states: "If..."

Regarding the gate of the house for the great chariot: for what reason has he left the house but still not obtained the chariot? If it were a matter of absolute transcendence (*atyantāpekṣā*), one should now challenge him thus:
"If the gate of the great chariot is not the gate of the house, then when seeking [the chariot], there should likewise be a separate exit;

why then does he seek the great chariot from the very same place he departed? Furthermore, the Great Elder merely gave the great [chariot] right here. Again, having already obtained the gate of the house, he has still not obtained [the chariot].
Question: Where do the gates of the chariots reside? Answer: Because the great and the small follow different paths, they are said to be distinct.

If the small is identical to the great, how can they be different? Now I shall explain this: if one excludes them, the chariot and the house are eternally distinct; if one opens them, the two gates are not different.

Since the house and the chariot are one, how can the two gates be different? Therefore, the three vehicles possess both meanings: they emerge from the house by way of the teaching, yet [the vehicle and the house remain as one].
Seeing that within the small carriage the two flavors had already been harmonized and matured, he then requested from his father the carriage previously promised.

Since it was requested, it had to be granted; thus, opening that small door represents the principle that beneath the Great Teaching there are only minor details, for in the end there is no separate path, no divergent principles, and the essence of the coarse and the subtle is one.
*Ghoṣa* (5) (22): "Seeking" (*ghoṣa*) is another name for requesting. When it resides in the mind, it is called "seeking" (*mārgaṇa*); when it resides in speech, it is called "requesting" (*yācanā*);
when it resides in the body, it is called "begging" (*arthana*). It is like a blind person seeking knowledge, a hungry person requesting food, or a lost person asking the way.
For one dwelling in a place of ignorance, how could there not be a reason to seek? Because of seeking, there is granting; because of granting, there is fulfillment.
Therefore, in this present text, the Dharma of the Request and the Dharma of Rejoicing are fully contained.
Among the two thousand people, Śāriputra was the leader; among the assembly of Bodhisattvas, Maitreya was the leader.

These sons born from the Buddha’s own mouth, numbering eighty thousand in total, joined their palms with a heart of reverence, desiring to hear the parable that illustrates the complete Path. At the beginning, Śāriputra...
This is the request made by those of medium capacity; furthermore, it serves as a general request for the fourfold assembly and an indirect request for those of inferior capacity, the text stating:
"Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly... (and so forth).

[Commentary] (6) (18): "Seeking" (*paryeṣaṇā*) means to request or to pursue; it is called "seeking" because it refers back to the three preceding types of action, all of which contain the term "seeking.

There are three meanings of "seeking," and the textual evidence is cited in full, detailing the beginning and end [of the argument]. Since there is seeking, there must be permission (*anujñā*); since there is permission, there must be granting (*dāna*).
As there is a scriptural passage regarding granting, how could there not be seeking?

Section Five (Twenty-three): A Separate Refutation of One [Point]. It is said that the Tripitaka Master of Qi clarified four propositions regarding the Bodhisattva’s non-interruption of afflictions based on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:

namely, the movement of the great capacity when obstacles have been removed; the movement of the great capacity when obstacles have not yet been removed; and knowing that one seeks [the path] when there is movement of the capacity.

Regarding the sixteenth [section] of the Record, concerning the statement that there are four propositions based on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: this means that, according to the present sutra, one must employ four propositions to encompass all capacities (*indriya*) so as to be exhaustive.
If these four propositions were absent, one might fear that people would think the arousal of capacity occurs only in those who are free from obstructions.

Therefore, the second proposition refers to the bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka; for if it referred only to the two vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas), how could it be said that their obstructions have not yet been removed? (Since they have indeed been removed).

(5) (26) However, merely relying on the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*) which encompass both cause and fruit to sever the delusions of views and thought is entirely the causal vehicle (*hetu-yāna*).

The knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) that exhausts [delusion] is all termed the resultant vehicle (*phala-yāna*). This is because one must first rely on the causal vehicle to sever and exhaust all delusions before attaining the resultant vehicle’s knowledge of non-arising.
Therefore, it is said that "the carriage is outside the gate" refers only to the primary cause, while the secondary aspects are treated in terms of the result.
It is said that the carriage is outside the gate.

(5) [Section] Twenty-six: Now, regarding the "seeking through words," in the past one relied on the teachings, believing that by exhausting the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*), one could enter the realm of Nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
However, within the Vaipulya sūtras, one sees the inconceivable nature of the Bodhisattvas; having heard Vimalakīrti’s censure, one realizes that if what I previously held were true...
If one has attained this reality, one should not be discouraged; if I am not truly a Buddha, I should not speak of the truth.
Thus, it is said that he was "bewildered and did not know what to say. Upon reaching the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he comprehended the Great Dharma;

hearing this, his joy in the Great [Vehicle] arose, and he was just about to advance in the practice of the Mahāyāna when he could not discern whether he had attained it or not. All such instances are merely matters of subjective sentiment.
Having already sought the meaning of the Mahāyāna, Śāriputra understood and resolved his former doubts;

seeing that the various bodhisattvas were receiving predictions of Buddhahood while he was not included in this matter, he sighed in self-reproach, wishing to ask the World-Honored One whether he had failed or not.
This refers to the fact that he had already sought it with his mind during the Vaipulya period; now, adding the verbal seeking, is because he heard the Vaipulya [sūtras].

In the first verse of the "Chapter on Expedients," it is briefly heard that all the Buddha’s teachings were expedient means; yet, because one immediately clings to these present expedients while doubting that the past teachings had not reached the ultimate, it is said:
"I do not now know where this meaning leads. Thus, one stirs long-standing doubts and speaks three times in request, seeking the true intent of what was taught in the past;
the capacity for this lies in the Mahāyāna, as the mind seeks the reality of the past and the mind seeks its realization.
In the *Dacheng kouwen* (Oral Questions on the Mahāyāna), it is stated that in the past, the six perfections were common to the teachings;

this is likewise the case for the *Ji* (Record). Regarding the phrase "in the past" (*xīrì*), since one formerly resided in the Small Vehicle teachings, having been rejected from them, there was still an expectation remaining.

Judging by this intended meaning, the sentiment encompasses both flavors [of the Dharma]. Because the old interpretations were rejected and the mind sought a principle that contradicted them, they are now established [as such].

Regarding the meaning of "seeking through emotion" (*qing-suo*): if one discusses it solely in terms of emotional apprehension, it is spoken of as such because it arises from a stimulus (*ji*). Thus, because emotion is stirred, the stimulus and emotion "seek.

This "seeking" (*suo*) pervades both the Two Vehicles (*su*) and is distinguished by the Two Flavors (*wei*). As for those who seek the ultimate reality, if this were merely a provisional means (*fangbian*), where would the reality have been previously?
Regarding the phrase "the stimulus resides in the *tian-cheng* (celestial vehicle)," etc., this explains the intent of seeking reality up until the point of "seeking with the mouth."

The great capacity has already been aroused, and the longing seeks the former reality; the intent now lies in the present truth. This means that while the capacity and reality are present, the longing is provisional;

furthermore, because the lower level of longing repeatedly reiterates the provisional to strike at the real, the longing and reality are present while the words are provisional. Thus, when the capacity and longing have not yet been manifested in speech, they must be fully present on the day one seeks through speech.

The same applies to the six perfections and the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna). As for what was explained previously regarding the two [aspects]: *Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a commentary on the stages of spiritual development, specifically concerning the relationship between the "capacity" (*indriya*), the "longing" (*chanda*), and the "reality" (*tattva*) as expressed through provisional and ultimate discourse.*

Since the teaching for the two vehicles is thus, we know that it is the same for the bodhisattvas of the two teachings as well. Why? Previously, five hundred and eight thousand [monks] were all rebuked;

their experience of being refined and purified by the *Prajñāpāramitā* was identical. Having seen Śāriputra raise doubts, the Buddha explained the principle, so it stands to reason that they too should have been moistened [by the Dharma].
Yet they remained silent in their seats, waiting for a holy one to clarify the matter for them.

Section Six (Twenty-seven): The Fourth Analogy of Entrusting the Family Estate. This refers proximately to the entrustment [of the sons] from the "Fire-House" chapter and so forth, and distantly to the "Supreme Path" within the "Dharma-Teaching" chapter.
This section is divided into two parts: first, the entrustment, and second, the bestowal. Each of these is further divided into two.
