There is no reason why those who are included within the name "Bodhisattva" could not all be considered Bodhisattvas; however, in relation to the superior [teachings], their meaning would not be established.

Since even those of the Two Vehicles in the two provisional teachings still turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], how could Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching possibly remain fixed in the old [views]?

If one follows the principle of transforming one's perspective, both Bodhisattvas of the Shared and Distinct Teachings must resolve to attain enlightenment; therefore, it is said that they are "instructed to practice and study," and it does not specify them as being distinct.

This is because these five persons are taken as a collective proof. If one were to discuss the number of persons in the stage of *upāya* (expedient means) comprehensively, one should say there are nine:

two in the *śrāvaka* vehicle, three in the distinct [vehicle], and three in the perfect [vehicle]; one cannot simply say "five. However, for the time being, in contrast to the *Hīnayāna*, it is said to be "five.
(7) (29) The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "One who is a *srotāpanna* will reach [Bodhi] after eighty thousand kalpas; reaching [it], they first give rise to Bodhicitta."
This refers to the stage of dull faculties (*mṛdv-indriya*) who practice through effort; they attain eighty thousand or ten thousand meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
If, as in the Tripiṭaka, one attains the four fruits of the path without passing even a short time, how could there be a need for eighty thousand or ten thousand [attainments]? (And so forth.)

[Commentary] (8) (12) In the latter part of the *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra*, the formal judgment concludes only at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*). This refers to those of dull faculties, which has two meanings:

first, among the five [types of practitioners], the first three are of dull faculties because they abide in the fruits; second, these five people have dull Mahāyāna faculties because their teaching is provisional.
Therefore, it is said: "If it were like the Tripiṭaka, how could there be a need for eighty thousand or ten thousand [verses]?"

If one examines the evidence that the teachings of eighty thousand [kalpas] and so forth are provisional (*upāya*), then even those who have not yet reached outside the realm [of saṃsāra] may, in this very life, hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and immediately attain awakening.
How could it be certain that those outside the realm must necessarily wait for such a long duration? This explains why the provisional nature of the teachings must eventually be discarded;

one should know that the long-term stages of the various teachings are mostly the path of instruction (*śāsana-mārga*). How could there be anyone who hears the superior [teaching] only after having exited the realm?
It should be said that one must further pass through eight, six, four, and two [kalpas].

Regarding those who harbor doubts in the *Zabian* (Miscellaneous Compilation), it is said: "If it is permissible for Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas to transcend the realm, how can those in the first three fruits, whose pervasive afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) are not yet exhausted, transcend the realm and give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) after passing through kalpas? This statement regarding Nirvana must incorporate both meanings.
First, those of dull faculties must wait until they reach outside the realm before they can realize their nature.
Second, those of sharp faculties are intended to be made remote from obstacles so that they may immediately give rise to the capacity for awakening. As for those of sharp faculties:

having heard what the Buddha taught, if they remain in their present body and attain only the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), or even merely realize the stage of a *pratyekabuddha* without studying the Mahāyāna, they will still have to pass through eight more [kalpas] in the future.
It would take six equal eons to reach Bodhi; therefore, by turning the mind in this present life, one avoids passing through these kalpas.
Thus, the words "seeking the place of treasure, do not dwell in the conjured city" perfectly capture the essential intent of the Sūtra.
Someone asked: "The text simply states that those five who have severed the pervasive delusions will be reborn in that land;
what was the intention of the Commentator (*Ji-zhu*) in explaining them as being the four fruits [of the śrāvaka] and pratyekabuddhas? I replied:

"Since it is said that they are 'purely' instructed to train in the 'family business' of the Mahāyāna, these words are exhortations and urgings, exactly like the encouragement to arouse the aspiration found in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. As for the five..."
The human life’s skillful means are found only in the Great Sūtra;
thus it is said. *Dujiao Ji*, Scroll 12; *Dujiao Ji*, Scroll 13.
Tiantai Śramaṇa Fazhao’s Commentary on the Words and Phrases (6): A Comprehensive Exploration of the *Zhengfa Nianchu Jing* (Sutra on the Contemplation of the Correct Dharma) Part Six.
The Lotus Sutra (2): Chapter on Faith and Understanding.
Textual Commentary (6) (14). The Parables are divided into five parts: 1. From "Having abandoned his father and fled" onwards is titled "The Parable of the Father and Son Losing Sight of Each Other.

This serves as a proximate summary of the general parable of the Burning House and a remote summary of the brief verses on the Expedient Means. 2. From "The impoverished son working for hire" onwards is titled... [text continues]
The meeting of father and son is analogous to the near guidance from within the burning house; seeing the fire and the distant guidance through skillful means (*upāya*).

When I observe with my Buddha-eye, I see the three [kinds of] followers and immediately dispatch attendants to urgently pursue and bring them back—this is called the analogy of "pursuing and inducing.

The near guidance from within the burning house involves abandoning the small bench and employing the carts; this is the distant guidance through skillful means. This includes the bestowing of the great upon the great and the small upon the small. Following these, there is the aspect of the mind.
The passage from "He embodies trust" (*tǐ xìn*) down to "entrusting him with the family estate" (*fù jiā yè*) is analogous to this:

it does not refer to the immediate and distant [teachings] above, but rather follows up on the intent of the *Vaipulya* (fangděng) and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* (dàpǐn), which involve censure and the turning of the teaching. The section from "After a short while had passed, the father knew his son's intention" down to "entrusting him with the family estate" is analogous to the immediate leading out from the burning house by bestowing the one great vehicle (*mahāyāna*), and the distant leading [to the realization] of the "Direct Teaching" (*dharmadeśanā*) which abandons expedient means for the sake of the straight path.
Furthermore, the fourth and fifth [sections] are combined into one summary, which is explained below to clarify their meaning.

Regarding the "Summary of the Burning House Parable" (Section 7.3): having understood the parable upon hearing it, one must necessarily understand the Dharma; how could there be confusion regarding what was previously realized after having attained awakening?
Therefore, both the Dharma and the parable must be summarized together (etc.). The text of the parable consists of five parts, beginning from...

The section on "losing one another" concludes the stage of forming a karmic connection; thereafter, the passage ending with "ultimately reaching equal bestowal" corresponds to the analogy of "hearing [the Dharma]. This consists of approximately four or five sections, yet effectively forms four parts.

Since these do not pertain to the realm of those who have already formed a karmic connection, it says: "having long dwelt in another land," and so forth. The first analogy is as follows: [Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a commentary or structural analysis of a Buddhist scripture, likely concerning the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* or a similar text dealing with the stages of spiritual development.]

The analogy of a person leading twenty children illustrates that the stages and practices of the Bodhisattva position for those of the Two Vehicles are difficult to know; for now, they are merely equalized by being led [by the Buddha].

Regarding the phrase "not yet having established the conditions" (*fei jieyuan yiji*) and so forth: originally, one established the great vow with the Land of Peaceful Light (*Jiguang*) as the realm and the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) realized through the aspiration of the mind as the objective capacity (*tāyin*).

Since the time of retreating from the Great Vehicle, both the objective capacity and the realm have been entirely lost. Now, flowing through the five paths of existence, one looks back toward the original state.

If even those who possess skillful means and remain in the state of *śaikṣa* (those with training remaining) have not yet reached their own realm, how much less so for those who wander through the five destinies?
(and so forth). The first simile concerns the one who perceives the ear; the third sutra’s initial passage describes the perception that does not reach the mind, which is the point here.

Among the ten realms and the seven wholesome factors—whether advancing or retreating—the Bodhisattva faces the greatest difficulty because they must simultaneously fulfill three roles; therefore, the Bodhisattva is mentioned separately.
Even so, the fruit of Buddhahood is forever severed.
(Verse 6) (23) "Wishing to entice and lead" refers to the secret dispatching of two persons to entice them; this constitutes two parts:

first, teaching them all at once to take the three vehicles as their immediate refuge while rescuing the sons; second, leading them to distant Vārāṇasī to bestow skillful means. Next, furthermore, by means of others...

Drawing upon the essential meaning from "Under the Sun," one realizes that the Dharma-body has long been manifest; expedient means have been illuminating for a duration prior to the Bodhi tree, and it is only now that one understands their application.

Having early on discerned the difficulties faced by sentient beings, the Honored One intimately associated with them even while clad in soiled robes; thus, he retrospectively realized his former state to establish his present understanding. Question:
For what reason were the four great disciples able to know that the Dharma-body had long been manifest? Answer: By inferring the distant through the near; if it were only at the beginning...
Under the Tree of Enlightenment, he realized that there were no beings with great spiritual capacity; thus, it was not appropriate for him to descend from Tuṣita.

With perfect wisdom, he entrusted himself to a womb, even manifesting the possession of afflictions by taking a consort and fathering a son. Following the thirty-four moments of mind, his final body severed all fetters.

It was verified that he had already long since cast off the subtle and wondrous jeweled necklaces of the marks and signs of a Great Man, donning instead the coarse, shabby robes of a six-foot-tall being stained with impurities.
Record (7) (14): Furthermore, on another occasion, regarding the passage that takes the meaning from below to encompass the stage of the Dharma-body, it is stated therein:

"It is before the Bodhi tree. This intention refers collectively to the period prior to both the gradual and sudden teachings, as it mentions reaching the difficulty of the *zuntè* (special/extraordinary).

Thus, we know this extends back to the period preceding the sudden teaching. As for the question concerning the four great disciples, the meaning within the answer is that once they have heard the parable, they fully comprehend it.

Because entering the Great [Vehicle] twice is not in vain, he reflects for himself, saying, "If it were as you say," and so forth. Since his reception of the Dharma was profound, he must certainly possess this knowledge;
this is explained according to the ritual of conversion, which proceeds with deliberate ease and retreat. Thus, he first aligns himself and subsequently probes further.
How could it be that he has only recently attained the Small [Vehicle], being but fifty years old, yet has fully beheld the inconceivable realms of the Bodhisattvas and universally heard all dharmas?

Although it is not entirely unknown that [the teachings] are harmoniously integrated, one has not yet fathomed their ultimate source. Upon reflecting on oneself, one realizes one’s own limitations; now, through the analogy of the Dharma, one discerns that the defiled and the perfect-permanent are distinct.
By inferring this, one understands that the Tathāgata’s illumination was already present in the past; therefore, the Buddha below praises this as being most rare.
Thus, by examining what is perceived through the two flavors, one verifies that what was previously seen was not the truth (and so forth).

Regarding the record (7) [and] (12): "He immediately dispatched his attendants and others" means that from this point onward, he led the recipients of the gift through both sudden and gradual transformation;
thus we know that prior to this, whether great or small, was illustrated by the metaphors for the sudden and gradual [teachings].
Section Six (Twenty-two): Regarding those whom he first intends to attract—once the great transformation has ceased, he cannot allow them to be left isolated;

thus, wishing to establish skillful means, he says, "he intends to secretly dispatch two persons. This refers to the four great disciples, who, being at the level of the Śrāvakas, each lead their own group and do not involve themselves with the Bodhisattvas;
hence the term "two persons" (and so forth). To this extent, they lead the Dharma according to the intended meaning within the parable; the text concludes from here.

Furthermore, on another day, the second [point] follows the intent: the guiding spiritual wisdom first illuminates that he had long since established skillful means and followed him through difficult circumstances;
it was not only under the tree that he first perceived the causal conditions, as has already been explained above.

[Commentary] (7) (15) "Ending here" refers to the sections on the "Reception of the Dharma" and the "Parable. When reaching the conclusion of the text for these two locations—namely, the "Great Bestowal" (*mahādāna*) and the "Small Bestowal" (*kṣudradāna*)—the preceding sections have already concluded.

From this point onward, in the "Dharma-exposition" (*dharmadeśanā*), there is only the revelation of the provisional (*upāya*), while in the "Parable-exposition" (*dṛṣṭāntadeśanā*), there is only the equal bestowal;
both lack the two intermediate flavors (*rasa*). Even if one considers the reception of the Dharma and the parable, although these two locations do not [explicitly] contain them...

The main text merely points to the eye that can see—both the Dharma and the parable—which is the Dharmakāya; thus, "attaining through the Equal Teaching" (齊教領) refers for now to attaining the initial stage of the gradual teaching.
Because what was received is of a small capacity, it is termed the "Equal Teaching"; since there is a separate attainment through further inquiry, the text says, "and furthermore."

Section Six (Twenty-four): Regarding the intent to grasp the ground of the Dharma-body and long knowing the capacities of the Great and Small Vehicles, the Buddha’s teaching was reiterated through the application of the three vehicles;

thus, this chapter is titled "Again" (*yòu*). As for "another day," it refers to the two vehicles considering their own provisional means as their own and the non-two-vehicle Dharma as belonging to others—this is precisely what corresponds to the Dharma-body. "Day" (*rì*) means time, and it also... [text fragment].
Regarding wisdom (*jñāna*), when it functions in accordance with the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), it is said that "on other days" [it acts] because wisdom illuminates the capacities of beings.
According to this principle, true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*) illuminating reality is for oneself, while provisional wisdom (*upāyajñāna*) illuminating skillful means is for others.

In terms of the teachings, the activities of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) are taken as "one's own days," whereas the non-activities of the transformation body are taken as "others' days. This is based on the distinction between the provisional and the real within the Tathāgata’s own practice.
All wisdom is termed "self," while the Tathāgata’s transformative illumination of the provisional and the real for others is termed "other.
From the perspective of the Tathāgata’s own illumination of the provisional and the real, that which illuminates the real is the "self," and that which illuminates the provisional is the "other.

When one probes and grasps this function of the Dharma-body, the provisional wisdom that transforms others illuminates the provisional capacities of beings—whether they exist or do not exist—as the provisional application of its illuminating activity.

Whether it be "self" or "other," both are illuminated by expedient wisdom; therefore, it is said that on another day, based on this principle, one harmonizes the teachings and understands the expedient matters of transforming others—thus the Two Vehicles refer to their own affairs as "others.

Because these expedients are not the affairs of the Two Vehicles themselves, they are termed "other. Although there are these two meanings, both are established on another day; for now, we rely on the second.
Furthermore, following the phrasing of "subsequently" (*tad-anu*) in the text, one should investigate how the Dharma-body, which is being received, illuminates the capacities [of sentient beings].

In the first section of the commentary (7.16), the term "other" (*para*) is explained in two parts: first, the explanation; second, the judgment. Regarding the explanation: it refers to those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayāyānika*), who view the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) as "other" in comparison to the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
Regarding the judgment: although the preceding section took the Two Vehicles as the point of reference, it was not yet known that even within the Great Vehicle there exists a sense of "other."
Regarding what body this Great Original [Buddha] employs, it is now determined to be the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Next, to explain "the Sun":

within the stage of the Dharma-body, there is the employment of both the provisional and the real; since the wisdom of the Dharma-body does not exist within the two vehicles of the provisional and the self, they are termed "other.
If judged from below, even when the provisional wisdom is employed from the perspective of the Dharma-body, it is still in relation to those of the two vehicles.
The term "other" (*tad*) here must refer to the Buddha’s provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). Next, regarding the explanation by combining the characters, there are three interpretations therein;
these follow the three categories from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*—namely, "speaking according to others," and so forth, including "transforming others"—as the formal method.

Furthermore, by aligning them with the teachings, one extracts and understands the texts of the two periods [the first and second turnings] as threefold: first, the explanation of the three characteristics; next, the judgment of their current affiliation starting from "if one follows," and so on.

Third, now based on the subsequent application, the intention of the present [text] concludes the first section, which is further divided into two parts. First, regarding the transformation of others, this refers to the "Teaching of Equality" (*zhìjiào*);
second, regarding self-cultivation as well as both self and others, this refers to the "Exploration and Comprehension" (*tàn lǐng*).

As for the "Teaching of Equality," it refers to the two texts of the Dharma and the Parable, which extend only to the Deer Park because they rely solely on what exists according to that teaching; thus it is called the "Teaching of Equality. As for "exploration" (*tàn*), it means to explore beyond [the Deer Park].
Inquiring into the stage prior to the tranquil site of the Bodhi tree, those who first align with the teachings belong to the initial meaning;
thus, the alignment with the teachings refers only to receiving [the teaching] from the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), which is not yet the time of the *nirmāṇakāya* itself for the sake of others.
Next, following the phrase "if one proceeds," there are two parts: first, the explicit clarification of the two meanings; second, the conclusion below that [section]. This is the first passage.

Although this refers to the Dharma-body, since it is established by contrasting one’s own practice with that of others, both the provisional and the real aspects of transforming others are categorized as "other.

Therefore, even the Two Vehicles of the past could not fathom its purport. Within this context, the term "one's own practice" (svayam-caryā) appears to involve both self and other, because when contrasted with the self, the other possesses both the provisional and the real;
thus, both are mentioned together. Next, regarding self and other within the context of self and other...

Regarding the provisional and ultimate aspects of each single term, according to principle they should be paired. Here, the terminology appears to refer to "self-practice" in contrast to "transforming others," thereby establishing both self and other.
Thus, "self-practice" also points to transforming others as the "other," and "self and other" likewise points to transforming others as the "other.

Therefore, one knows that throughout [the text], when referring to the Dharmakāya, both the provisional and the two vehicles are included; even though the two vehicles received the minor teachings from him, they are encompassed therein.
The two vehicles do not understand the provisional [expedient means] that is of the same substance as the Buddha;
when both [the Buddha and the two vehicles] point to the Dharma-body of the same substance, although the provisional has two meanings, they will all eventually become [enlightened].

Next, regarding the concluding phrase "whether there is or whether there is not," this concludes that the provisional wisdom of the Dharma-body illuminates whether there is a capacity [for enlightenment] or no capacity. As for the terms "approval" and "disapproval," these clarify the Dharma-body.
Using wisdom to accommodate beings means affirming when the capacity is met and denying when it is not; affirming when the time has arrived and denying when it must wait.

Although there are instances of affirmation and denial, existence and non-existence, these are all provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) and provisional capacities. Regarding the subsequent classification of names, the *Zhongpan* (Middle Classification) states:

"If one follows [the equality]," etc. This classifies the aforementioned simultaneous investigation; as for "investigating and receiving both self and other," "self" refers to the second stage, that of one's own practice.
"Other" (*tad*) is the third [category]; one should emphasize "self" (*ātman*) in order to clarify the meaning of the third.

Both are considered "other" in relation to the *dharmakāya*, and thus they do not pertain to the vehicles of the two [śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha]. Although there are these two perspectives, both equally explore the middle way, as both possess the sense of "other";

therefore, it is said that both are established. Regarding the exploration of the middle, the *dharmakāya* illuminating sentient beings is taken as "other," thereby encompassing both meanings within the middle.
Thus, within the Tathāgata’s own practice, all that is provisionally designated as "for others" (parārtha) is precisely what is utilized by the two vehicles (dvayayāna).
Although there are two distinct intentions—namely, that which is utilized by the two vehicles and that which is not utilized by the two vehicles—both receive the designation "for others.

Now, according to the meaning of the subsequent correlating text, we rely on what is realized by the two vehicles; this refers to their realization as it accords with the teachings. Furthermore, it follows from the term "for others."

The "One Day" [Sūtra] and the "Probing" [Sūtra] both reach the two instances of "otherness"; thus, after the Two Vehicles have received [the teaching], they further expect to receive it from the Buddha.
As for the Tathāgata’s use of the words of another to probe and receive [the teaching], one should also say that the "Equal Teaching" is merely an abbreviation in the text.
Therefore, both instances of receiving refer to the capacity of the sentient beings as grasped by the Dharmakāya; however, according to their distinct meanings, the two types of "otherness" differ.

Section Six (28): Furthermore, within the previous allegory of the enticement, there was a sequential teaching that led from the beginning at the Bodhi Tree to the end at the departure from the house;

there was also a probing lead-in from the Dharmakāya to the end where contemplation is exhausted. Now, this lead-in likewise has two parts: first, the probing lead-in of compassion and the four flavors to bring them to maturity;
second, the final lead-in of entrusting the wealth, which is the ultimate single flavor. Thus, the distant and near, the beginning and the end, are unified.
The treatise asks, "Regarding the five flavors, which one is that which dispatches the bystanders and others? This refers to the first flavor (and so forth).

The four great disciples deeply grasped the Buddha’s intention and thoroughly mastered the sequential order of the teachings on the five flavors throughout the beginning and end of his entire ministry; this text is where that account originates.
Notes (7–8, 10): Furthermore, regarding the previous passage on "inducing" up to the point where it says "until the end of reflection," the term "inducing" refers to secretly dispatching two people.
Regarding the phrase "leaving the house" and so forth, leaving the house and the "end of reflection" share the same meaning of conclusion;
however, the distance between the *dharmakāya* and the Bodhi tree is not equal. Now, in the section on "receiving" and so forth, both [meanings] are combined with the two preceding texts.
Since each beginning and end constitutes a single beginning and end, it is said that "the distant and near beginnings and ends" are thus equal.

Taking the teaching as the "near beginning" and the probing and receiving [of the Dharma] as the "distant beginning," these two ends together form a single perspective. Within the process of "inducing and leading," the end reaches its ultimate limit in the "bestowing of equality";

therefore, it is said that the four flavors constitute the beginning and the entrustment of the treasure constitutes the end. Since the four flavors are established as the beginning, we know through verification that this refers to the probing and receiving.

Regarding the passage "Upon reaching the site of enlightenment," the subsequent section provides an explanation. This explanation constitutes a single beginning-to-end exposition on the mutual identity of the five flavors.

Of the thirty-four characters, the first three lines of verse employ the analogy of the *gūḍha* (the secret/hidden), while the following four and a half lines of verse employ the analogy of the teaching (*śāsana*).

Commentary (7) (23): Regarding the analogy of "hired labor" versus "teaching through direct instruction," "hired labor" refers to the meaning of the text from the time [the Buddha] was at the Bodhi tree, wherein he employed the principle of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) as his labor.
"Teaching through direct instruction" refers to the meaning of the text concerning the attainment of the Great Vehicle;
for in the stage of the Dharmakāya, there is no time when he does not take pity on beings—when has he not taught? How could he wait to be entreated? Therefore...
It is said that this is the teaching on how to act. (7) (1) The Master says: "One should not be partial. The Sūtra speaks of the "well-spoken" [teaching] regarding the Tathāgata’s true merits;

a detailed exposition of his mastery over both the provisional and the ultimate is clearly set forth herein (and so forth). What is stated here is that it comprehensively describes his universal and all-encompassing realization.

Beginning with the karmic connection of innate nature, proceeding through the subsequent inducement, and concluding with the entrustment of the Dharma-treasure—from the subtle to the manifest—these are the immeasurable and boundless virtues of grace (and so forth).
There are two pairs of "Excellent! (sādhu): the first pair describes what is beyond [the capacity of] the recipient; the second pair consists of one "Excellent!
describing the two instances where he received the reality, and another "Excellent! describing the two instances where he received the provisional skillful teaching.
The true merits of the Tathāgata refer to the "true" as describing ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) and the "merits" as describing provisional means (*upāya*).
Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka* is intended to lead one toward the realization of the ultimate; the *Tripiṭaka* guides one by leading through the provisional;

the *Vaipulya* (Madhyama-pratītyasamutpāda) involves embodying faith, while the *Prajñāpāramitā* involves receiving the teaching—both of these lead to both the provisional and the ultimate. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, however, in its entrustment of the Dharma-treasure, discusses exclusively the ultimate. (And so forth.)
Furthermore, from the Tathāgata there is again the following description of that which his comprehension does not reach. What is it that he does not reach?
It is said that whether advancing or retreating, horizontally or vertically, both horizontal and vertical, or neither horizontal nor vertical—none of these are reached (and so forth).

The meaning of "not reaching" is not a total and sudden negation; rather, it is simply called "inexhaustible" because the initial mind, when compared to the subsequent mind, has not yet reached the ultimate ground.

The Master’s statement refers to [the teaching of] Nanyue. Although the Three Vehicles each lead their own respective realms, since it is said that they "well explain" [the truth], this means they have fully grasped the provisional and the real throughout the entire dispensation of the Buddha's life. Now, the Buddha has related in full detail what they have grasped (and so forth).
Regarding the phrase "beginning with Tianxing" (Heavenly Nature): "Tianxing" refers to the time of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Buddha (and so forth); "Tianxing" is still [a stage of] commonality.

"Forming a karmic connection from a different perspective" (and so forth). Regarding the phrase "narrating both places together," the two places refer to the stage of skillful means and the burning house.
Since [the text] summarizes both places within the section on faith and understanding (*adhimukti*), it now likewise narrates both places that were summarized there.

If this were not the case, what benefit would there be in this narration? In the following section on "Excellently Explained," its comprehensive summary is presented; however, the explanation based solely on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) is limited.
... (and so forth). Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka* says: "To go everywhere and fully recount what one has received" refers precisely to the teaching (*yàojiào*). (And so forth).

Next, regarding the section below which clarifies the Buddha’s intention for reproaching [the śrāvakas] for their inadequacy: when the two vehicles first hear [the Dharma], they initially enter the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) and merely describe for themselves the dharma they have entered.
The Buddha wishes to detail those things they have not yet received; such dharmas are still numerous, and if the two vehicles were to hear them...
It also establishes the comprehensive reception [of the teaching] as previously explained.
Verses (7–12): "You, Kāśyapa... and so forth, which restate the thesis and provide a descriptive citation in order to resolve doubts.

Those who hear of the Buddha’s immeasurable merits might wonder whether it is necessarily the case that all four disciples equally received and understood the teaching; therefore, the Buddha provides this descriptive citation. Although...
Before reaching the stage of Buddhahood, the teachings are uniform and not in vain.

Regarding the seventh section (36), "Next, Restoring the Thesis and Resolving Doubts": Although it has not yet been said that they are permitted as equals, once they have received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), they immediately become true Buddhas.
From the Deer Park, they have fully mastered both the provisional and the real; by the time of the *tī-mo* (the final stage of the five flavors), they have fully realized their karma.
One should know that this was not in vain; the previous praise of Śākyamuni was intended to extol what Mahākāśyapa leads.

To resolve doubts, [the Buddha] feared that if the assembly at that time heard the Buddha describe what he himself led, they might fail to understand the Buddha’s intent and claim that what Mahākāśyapa leads is improper.
Therefore, he described his own provisional and ultimate teachings to praise Mahākāśyapa’s ability to understand the Tathāgata’s preaching according to suitability.
Question: Although the Dharma is personally realized by the Buddha himself and encompasses all things, why does he not resolve the doubts of those who inquire? Answer:

Because within the *zhèi jiào* (the teaching of the equal stage), the manifest reality and its nature are easily distinguished, the Buddha has provisionally concluded the *zhèi jiào* and uttered words of praise. Question: If that is so, then the *tàn yì* (exploring the ultimate) is even more worthy of doubt;

why then is it only the *zhèi jiào* that is praised? Answer: Although difficult, it is easy [to understand] because when the assembly hears this discourse, they perceive through the Tathāgata’s two types of wisdom that the Buddha possesses the Dharma-body.

I have constantly reflected that there is some apprehension that the understanding of the teachings may not be entirely perfect; therefore, the Buddha, through the two teachings and the two wisdoms, described how these parallel teachings are without error.

Furthermore, since even the understanding of the parallel teachings is already verified as not being in vain, one can know that the exploration and understanding [of the ultimate] must likewise not be erroneous.
(Section Four, Thirty-three): Knowing that the Buddha abides in the stage of the Dharma-body, he uses the Buddha-eye of eternal quiescence to universally illumine all capacities.
If their faculties are sharp and their afflictions light, he teaches the One Vehicle Dharma through the form of Vairocana.

If their faculties are dull and their afflictions heavy, he removes his jeweled necklace and appears in the form of an old bhikṣu to startle them into entering the burning house, employing skillful means to open the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. This is so.
Because [the Buddha] discerns capacities at that moment, he says, "I see with the Buddha-eye. If he were observing material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), he would employ the divine eye;
if he were analyzing capacities and faculties, he would employ the Dharma-eye. Why, then, does he say he sees with the Buddha-eye? The Buddha-eye is all-pervasive and comprehensive;
it subsumes the superior while encompassing the inferior. Furthermore, when the four eyes enter the Buddha-eye, they are all designated as the Buddha-eye.
*Miaoxuan* (1, 8): "Great Power and Fierce Majesty, Benefiting Beings Throughout the Three Times," is explained in full detail as stated in the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding.

*Jiqian* (1, 24): Therefore, he further cites the passage from the "Emergence" chapter to assist in clarifying the provisional traces (*jì*), hence the statement "Great Power and Fierce Majesty," and so forth.
Next, regarding the reference to the "Faith and Understanding" chapter, it refers to what is said therein: "Furthermore, on another day, at the window..."

"Middle" here refers to the stage of the Dharmakāya, which has long since reflected upon the capacities of sentient beings; thus, this single phrase simultaneously encompasses the aspect of benefiting beings throughout the three periods of time.
Furthermore, when one understands and accepts the five flavors of a single lifetime, one knows that the five flavors of the three periods of time are likewise so.
Now, the meaning of "investigating" (*tàn*) does not exceed two principles: first, that those who lead [the investigation] are persons of the Two Vehicles;

second, that what is led is the Dharma of the provisional and the real. Why is this? Since the four great disciples had already attained the First Stage (*prathamabhūmi*) and realized the One Reality, they were at the beginning of the stage where the teaching is completed;
yet they further investigated the provisional matters of the *nirmāṇakāya* at the Deer Park.

When one first attains [the realization of] the Dharma-body, it transcends the provisional stage prior to the site of enlightenment (Śrāvastī). Once the distinctions between the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the Dharma-body, as well as between skillful means (*upāya*) and reality, have been established, there arises the difference between "attaining the beginning" and "probing the beginning. Thus, the *Wenju* states: "Attaining through the 'Equal Teaching' refers to attaining the provisional acts of transforming others; probing through the 'Equal Teaching' refers to attaining the provisional powers of both self and others.

Regarding this "attaining through the Equal": *Note: This passage discusses the progression from the provisional teachings of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings toward the Perfect Teaching of the Lotus Sūtra, specifically focusing on the attainment of the Buddha’s provisional powers of transformation and self-realization.*

The middle passage states, "Equalizing one's own realm and equalizing the teaching. Here, "self" refers to oneself; "realm" refers to the boundaries of one's sphere; and "teaching" refers to the Dharma-methods.
This refers to how the four great disciples received the teaching of equalizing their own realms, beginning at the Bodhi tree and ending with the departure from the palace.
Therefore, Jingxi said: "Equalizing the teaching means receiving only the initial stage of the gradual [vehicle]; because what they received was small, it is termed 'equalizing the teaching'."

Furthermore, regarding the statement "the teaching is uniform" (*qi jiao*), this refers to the two passages consisting of the Dharma and the Parable [in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*], which concern all that was taught uniformly at the Deer Park.
Again, it is said that the meaning of the "uniform teaching" passage is that from the time of the Bodhi Tree onward, those with inferior capacities were taken as "hired laborers.

Furthermore, it is said that although the followers of the Two Vehicles had realized their own respective realms, these four passages represent the teaching that they all equally realized them. These are the words extracted from the section on "realization."

Regarding the phrase "taking the meaning to comprehend the stage of the Dharma-body" (*dharmakāya-bhūmi*): this refers to taking up the intent of self-attainment and probing to comprehend the Buddha’s intention, beginning from the Dharma-body and culminating in the exhaustion of thought.
Thus, Jingxi said: "Within the words, it is said 'prior to the Bodhi tree'; in terms of the underlying meaning, both refer to the period prior to the gradual and sudden teachings. He further stated:
"Therefore, one knows that probing and comprehending extends back to the site of the tranquil terrace (*śītavana*)," and he also said: "One knows..."
"The Buddha's Dharma-body constantly contemplates both the great and the small"—these three passages represent the doctrine of "probing and receiving" (*tantou*).

Now, within the section on "receiving and entrusting," the text first cites the preceding passage on "inducing and leading," stating: "In accordance with the teaching, it begins at the Bodhi tree and ends with the departure from the palace;

probing and receiving begins with the Dharma-body and ends with the contemplation of the exhaustion [of phenomena]. Next, the formal explanation of the receiving and entrusting states: "The present receiving is also twofold," meaning "in accordance with."

The "exploration" (*tàn*) refers to the initial exploration that induces [the disciples]; thus, because the word "also" (*zhì*) is attached, it is said that the initial exploration leads to the four flavors of compassion and maturation.

The final exploration leads to the entrustment of the treasure, which is the ultimate single flavor. When the distant and near, the beginning and the end, are discussed together, they constitute the five flavors.

Thus, one knows that by combining the two instances of "beginning and end" from the preceding "inducing exploration," they form a single instance of "beginning and end" to discuss the five flavors in detail.

Looking at Jingxi’s commentary, it says: "Regarding 'leaving the house' and so forth," the two ends of "leaving the house" and "the exhaustion of thought" share the same meaning, whereas the distance between the *dharmakāya* and the Bodhi tree is not equal.
This section of the record and commentary restates the two ends of the beginning and conclusion from the preceding introductory passage;
from "Now, receiving [it] also has two... onwards, he himself explains the union of the distant and near beginnings and conclusions within the entrustment.
The treatise consists of only two lines concerning the five flavors; thus it says, "In view of the 'inducement' and so forth.

Furthermore, the later text states, "Revealing and explaining them together as one beginning and end. If this is so, why does the section on "receiving and entrusting" not say "equal" (*chi*) but rather "probe" (*tan*)?
The Great Master said, "It should be combined with the treatise. Moreover, how do we know they are combined? Because we find the terms "probe" and "receive."

The meaning of "equalizing" (*zhèi*) is already contained within this teaching. Now, although the text regarding that which exceeds one's own comprehension is indeed about equalizing oneself, how can it be so?

The Buddha’s concluding statement says, "He has well expounded the Tathāgata’s true merits," and the Buddha’s summary of praise says, "He is able to know the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate.
Both passages speak of the "Tathāgata. Jingxi [Zhiyi] says, "Regarding 'well expounded'... [and so forth].
In describing his full mastery of the provisional and ultimate teachings, he further states: "I only fear that the 'Equal' teaching may not be entirely perfect.

Thus, the Buddha, through the two teachings and two wisdoms, describes this "Equal" teaching; if one examines the sutras, commentaries (*shu*), and records (*ji*) closely, this is the World-Honored One’s praise of the Equal teaching to demonstrate the intent of its universal mastery.
Simply by looking at the single character "universal" (*bian*), it is identical to "mastery" (*ling*).

Although the textual divisions differ from what [the Master] did not reach, even within the *Ji jiao* (Comprehensive Teaching), one is still able to comprehend them exhaustively; how much more so for one who probes and comprehends them?

Master Beifeng’s *Xun nan* (Discourse on Difficulties) sets forth four points: first, he asks why the *Shu* (Commentary) clearly explains that the five sections of sūtra text concerning father and son losing each other and father and son meeting again all refer to "near comprehension" (*jin ling*) and "far comprehension" (*yuan ling*), and whether these are the Comprehensive Teaching or the Probing Teaching.

If one speaks of "seeking and receiving" (*qiantan*), the *Shupanjie* (Exposition of the Judgments) clarifies that the two categories of "enticement" (*yuke*) must be distinct; it says that the obstruction of the "equal seeking" (*qitantan*) is likewise the same [as the obstruction of the two receptions].
Does this mean there must be a separate reception apart from the two receptions? Second, regarding the scriptural passage on "equal seeking," there are four points:

first, the small-scale suitability; second, knowing their prior intentions; third, praising the three vehicles; and fourth, fulfilling their wishes. All of these pertain to the Small Vehicle (*xiǎo*). Why is this so?

Therefore, the Commentary (Shu) explains the word "also" (*yu*) by stating: "On the ground of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), having long known the capacities of those of Great and Small Vehicles, one bestows transformation through the 'one' and 'three'.

The third question probes what the Dharma-body is and where that Dharma-body resides. The fourth question concerns the integration of the distant and the near, the beginning and the end, and the discussion of the five flavors as four;
does this accord with the *Sūtra* itself, or does it accord with the Tiantai Commentary?
To explain the first point: according to the *Huxi* [Record], "Qi" (齊) refers to one’s own sphere and is also called "Qi-jiao" (齊教);
"ling" (領) is also called "jiao-ling" (教領). The character "Qi" signifies one's own portion and also one's own realm; it refers to the person who is capable of receiving [the teaching].

The character "Jiao" (教) signifies the words of the teaching received and the Dharma that is mastered. Thus, we know that "Qi" encompasses both one's own portion and one's own realm. It does not [refer to]... [The text continues with a negation of a specific interpretation].
This can be divided into two types. Regarding those who receive the teaching: the Deer Park is the beginning of receiving the teaching, while the Lotus Sūtra is the end of receiving the teaching.

Even for those prior to the Deer Park who had not yet received the teaching by the time of the Great Universal Wisdom (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū), they had already attained benefit and possessed the capacity as recipients; therefore, among the twenty sons, they are also said to have received the teaching simultaneously. However—

Regarding "receiving according to the faculty" (ling-gen-xing): this refers to receiving [the teaching] in accordance with one's own spiritual capacity, rather than receiving the teaching as it was originally imparted; thus, it can only be called "receiving in unison" (qi-ling) and cannot be called "receiving the teaching" (jiao-ling).

Next, regarding "exploring and receiving" (tan-ling): "exploring" (tan) means to look back retrospectively—that is, looking back before the Deer Park and the site of enlightenment (Ji-chang) to the stage of the Dharmakāya, where one presciently discerns whether the five periods of teaching are suited for the Great or the Small Vehicle; it does not begin with the seven weeks of contemplation under the Bodhi tree.
Furthermore, one must be careful not to mistake the phrase "seeking beyond" for the passage concerning father and son losing and finding each other;
one should know that "seeking" (探) refers to grasping the underlying meaning within the context of "receiving" (領). This is why it is said that by inferring the near, one knows the distant.
If one were to determine this based on its general meaning, there are six broad categories of meaning: first, regarding oneself and others; second... [text truncated].

Regarding the transformation of the body through the three periods of past, present, and future; the internal and external of the four lands; the five reflections on the capacities of beings for preaching the Dharma;

and the near and far of the initial [manifestation]: if these were restricted and determined separately, they would merely lead to the name "Dharmakāya" being received, while the name "Nirmāṇakāya" would be received equally.
Beipeng raised a doubt, saying: "The thirteen verses of the *Wenju* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) refer only to the Equal Teaching (*Samatā-śāsana*)."
In the *Enshō Shitenkō Ketsuen-ki* (Record of the Encompassing Grace and the Initial Innate Disposition for the Formation of Karmic Bonds), it states:

"The 'innate disposition' refers to that which was established at the stage of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Buddha. Regarding the designation "Teaching of Equality" (*Saijō*), the commentary notes that this term is applied restrictively to the Deer Park period.

It explains that the name "Teaching of Equality" must refer to those who have received the teaching; thus, the commentary further clarifies: "Furthermore, one accepts the initial stage of the gradual teaching; because the teaching received is designated as the 'Teaching of Equality,' its application is fixed and restricted [to that specific stage]."

At the Deer Park, they had been lost to one another until they met again; the four great disciples, according to the Dharma and through analogies, understood the matters of their innate natures and the conditions of their karmic connections.
This is also a case of "teaching in parallel," wherein the later clarifies the former. Regarding the second point, the Tiger Brook (Huxi):
when distinguishing between the Great and Small Vehicles, the provisional and the real, it does not go beyond two meanings. First, both [leaders] are present.

Regarding the passage on "the provisional and the small" (*quan xiao*): first, it states that the teaching of the three vehicles to save the sons is a provisional means for the near term, while the bestowal at Vārāṇasī is the provisional means for the distant term;

furthermore, it says that on another day, the intent was taken to lead [beings] to the stage of the Dharma-body, where expedient means have long been illuminated—both of these explore the provisional and the small.

Second, regarding the two types of "leading" (*ling*) which penetrate both the great and the small, the provisional and the real, the text says: "The four great... (referring to the four great elements).
The disciple has deeply grasped the Buddha’s intention, fathoming and leading forth the profound teachings of the five periods of transformation.

The *Xuánwén* states: "The meaning of such passages as these all pertains to the stage of the Dharmakāya, which is quiescent yet eternally luminous; it is not something first realized at the Bodhi tree. Whether for the Great Vehicle or the Small Vehicle, the Buddha’s wisdom has long ago discerned the capacities of beings.
This fathoming and leading forth thus encompasses both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Furthermore, it says: "The *Avataṃsaka* was intended for those who were suitable [for its teaching]."

"Leading the Real" (shōjitsu) refers to the guidance of the Tripiṭaka; "leading the Expedient" (shōgon) refers to the guidance of the Provisional. This [text] aligns the leadings of both the Great and Small Vehicles regarding the provisional and the real.

One should know that the two leadings—both being provisional and both belonging to the Small Vehicle—accord with the section on "Guiding through Secret Inducement," where both the beginning and the end are short in meaning.

The two leadings that encompass both the Great and Small Vehicles regarding the provisional and the real accord with the section on "The Entrustment of the Leadings," where both the beginning and the end are long in meaning. (Northern School)

Feng said: "When the four great disciples received their understanding, they fully knew that the Dharma-body has long been illuminating both the Great and the Small, as well as the intermediate stages;

yet they had regressed from the Great to take up the Small. Today, at the Lotus Assembly, the Great is set aside and the Small is bestowed, so that all who return from the Small to the Great are entirely encompassed within the breast of the Tathāgata.
How could it be that they receive only the Small and not the Great, or receive only the provisional and not the real? This is why..."

The Patriarch sometimes said that he only received the Small [Vehicle], and sometimes that he received both the Small and the Great; these were merely differences according to the intent of the specific teaching.

Regarding the third point, Huxi said: "To 'probe and receive' the Dharma-body—in terms of the four lands—since it is said that one has long discerned both the small and the great, one must point to the mirror-like essence of the *sukhāvatī* (Jigaku) Dharma-body. Beifeng raised a doubt, saying: "This..."

If one asks: "Before he has yet begun his transformative activity, while he is precisely dwelling in a single city as a land of skillful means (*upāya-bhūmi*), why would it be improper to name this 'Victorious Response' (*vairocana*) as the *dharmakāya*?

One must understand that the three bodies and four lands of the Tathāgata—the body which is the support and the land which is the supported—are in essence eternally identical and have never for a moment been separated.
When we speak of the *dharmakāya*, it is at every moment reflecting upon the capacities of sentient beings.

To speak of the *saṃbhogakāya*, it benefits sentient beings from time to time; however, if one discusses the period prior to the manifestation of transformation, its discernment of capacities (*jñāna*) is precisely the *dharmakāya* abiding in the Constantly Quiescent Light (*nitya-śānta-prabhā*).
Therefore, when the Great Master explained "I observe with the Buddha-eye" as the *dharmakāya* of constant quiescence discerning capacities, he was referring to this.
If one discusses the period prior to the manifestation of transformation, its observation of capacities is precisely the cessation of provisional means (*upāya*).

This is the reason why, within the Great Master’s commentary on the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, he designates one city as the "expedient land" (*upāya-kṣetra*) and explains its four [aspects] as follows:

first, the four great disciples’ realization at the Deer Park; second, the two inducements, which extensively open up and thoroughly investigate the beginnings and ends of both [the *Āgamas* and the *Vaipulya*];
third, the section on the entrustment, from which the two *Vaipulya* sūtras and the two *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras no longer appear.
The *Lotus Sūtra* then combines the preceding two inducements, unifying the beginnings and ends of these two into one.

Since the beginnings and ends of the five flavors are thus aligned, the beginnings and ends of both the distant and the near are explored and unified into a single beginning and end; this is what is referred to as "the beginning and end of the distant and the near.
The *Shuji* (Commentary) explains: "Together they form a single beginning and end, which is identical to the five flavors. Thus, we know this refers to the entrustment (*parindanā*).

The "classification" (he) here does not refer to the combination of the prose commentary itself; rather, it is the combination of the sūtra text and the treatise (*śāstra*) regarding the four great disciples.

The reason for this combination is that if the four great disciples did not receive two successive rounds of instruction through the two inducements, the simultaneous investigation of the two sets of five flavors would not be revealed.
Furthermore, if they did not receive one combined round of instruction through the equal bestowal, the two sets of five [flavors] would likewise not be revealed.

[Question: When leading [the disciples] to the site of the tranquil field (Śītavana), why was it established that they did not collectively receive the *Avataṃsaka*? [Answer:

The two inducements are correctly termed "Deer Park" when speaking according to the intent of the classification; however, if one follows the chronological sequence, it also encompasses the *Avataṃsaka*.
This is because the Bodhi Tree is likewise called a "field," and thus it is but a single location that receives two names according to its relative scale—referring to the small [scale].
Regarding what is seen by those of great capacity: they attain the Way beneath this tree, and after twenty-one days, they go to the Deer Park to preach the Dharma.

As for what is seen by those of small capacity: they likewise attain the Way beneath this tree and realize the principle of quiescent extinction, whereby it is named the "Site of Quiescence" (Jichang).
Because they do not require twenty-one days to preach the Great Dharma, it is said that from beginning to end there is no change in what is seen by the great, while the small see only the conclusion.

Staying for twenty-one days signifies that the "Equal" (Qi) stage encompasses the beginning at the Bodhi Tree; following the intent of the classification by time period, this refers to the site of tranquility (Jichang), which includes the *Avataṃsaka* as well.
Furthermore, one might doubt that if the "Equal" stage encompasses both the beginning and the end, it would be too brief, whereas if it were to encompass the entire sequence, it would be too long.
How then can it be said that the meanings of the two "ends" are identical? Moreover, these two ends are simply unified as one, which is termed "Equal."
The first "reception" (*ling*) refers to the five periods of today; this is the stage of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), capable of mirroring the Dharma-body.

Although that which is mirrored is distant, what is mirrored in the five periods of today is not distant. "Subtle and refined" refers to the reception at Vārāṇasī, while the "provisional name" refers to the entrustment of the treasury (*dhanadāna*).
These two receptions differ from the two categories of "enticement. The entrustment of the treasury and the reception at Vārāṇasī are, by means of today’s five [periods]...
At that time, both were called "Equal Bestowal" (Qiyu), yet only [Zhiyi’s] Deer Park was distinct from [Tanyan’s] "Exploring the Extraordinary" (Tanyi).

Later, [Tanyan’s] "Hanging Mirror of the Five Periods" (Xuanying Wushi) and [Zhiyi’s] "Categorization of the Two Bestowals" (Eryu Ke) both encompassed today’s [Huayan teachings]. The *Huayan* also belongs to "Exploring the Extraordinary. Master Caotang said:

"The 'Equal Bestowal' leads one to understand the affairs of today; 'Exploring the Extraordinary' leads one to understand the long-illuminating affairs of today. Although these are called two types of "leading," both lead to the understanding of the five periods.

At that time, Yitang said: "The 'receiving' (ling) mentioned here refers to the four great disciples who, upon hearing the Dharma, were enlightened and attained understanding through the revelation [of the Buddha's intent].
Regarding the 'exploring and receiving' (tanting): they too were granted enlightenment through the revelation [of the Buddha's intent] later on.

As for the 'exploring and receiving' of the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya, it refers to the distant observation from the stage of the *bhūmi* of the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya of how he today, at the Deer Park, bestows the Lesser Vehicle in response to the capacities of his audience."

This refers to the function of receiving the Dharma-body; one must know that since the "Simultaneous Exploration" (*sahajñāna*) occurs within the section on "Inducing and Guiding," it cannot receive the Great [Vehicle] when contrasted with the Deer Park—both receptions therein are of the Small [Vehicle].

Although the Great Master spoke of the "One and Three" as the bestowing of transformation, this was merely said from the perspective of the Buddha’s intention being perceived. Within the section on "Receiving and Entrusting," both the Simultaneous and the Gradual are included.
To encompass both the Great and Small Vehicles within the scope of "comprehensive mastery" (齊領), one must understand two meanings: first, the teachings mastered and expounded;

second, the dharmas mastered and entered. Regarding the teachings expounded, this refers to the comprehensive mastery of the Great and Small Vehicles—the provisional and real teachings of the single transformation.
It is termed "comprehensive mastery" (齊領) because it brings together the present stage in contrast to the preceding stages of sudden and gradual [teachings].
Jianji states that today’s single transformation is all equally named "Equal Reception" (*qí lǐng*). The *Shū* (Commentary) says:

"Beginning with the four flavors and ending with the entrustment of the Dharma-treasure—these two [stages] represent the dharma-reach of those who enter. Thus, the Two Vehicles receive for themselves what they have traversed throughout all the flavors; the results obtained also encompass both the Great and Small Vehicles.

However, because they only receive what they have attained for themselves, it is called 'Equal Reception within their own realm. One must not say it is 'Equal Reception for oneself' [in the universal sense]."

Regarding the "Mirror Hermitage" (Jing’an): as for "pervasive and limited," this refers to tracing back the causes and conditions by which one gains benefit. In terms of the text, it is fully contained within the two inducements (*yòu*), encompassing the beginning and end of receiving transformation.

In terms of the meaning, it pervades the four categories (*sīkē*). Nevertheless, although it pervades the four [categories], when one probes the concise [teaching] of another day, it is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) that has long been reflected in the five periods (*wǔshí*).
When one uniformly delimits the teaching of today’s responsive body (*nirmāṇakāya*) manifesting transformation, it is the five periods.

The Fivefold Bonds of the Higher and Lower Realms (7) (17). The five higher fetters (*pañcordhvabhāgīya*) are restlessness (*auddhatya*), conceit (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga*), and attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*).

The five lower fetters (*pañcādharabhāgīya*) are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), and ill-will (*vyāpāda*). Among the five higher fetters, [the last two are] attachment to the realm of form and attachment to the formless realm.
The three factors—restlessness, pride, and so forth—are exclusively upper-tier; although they extend downward, they cannot pull one down, and are therefore called "upper-tier" (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*).
As for those called "lower-tier" (*avarabhāgīya*): although craving extends upward, it is not exclusively upper-tier; hatred is exclusively lower-tier and does not extend upward;
and the remaining three encompass all delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). Although these latter three extend upward, they are able to pull one down, and are thus named "lower-tier."

Therefore, according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, one does not transcend the desire realm by means of two [attainments], but returns to the lower realms by means of three; even if one has severed craving up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one may still return to the desire realm due to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and other afflictions, as explained at length in the *Abhidharmakośa*.

Divination Stick (5) (18): The *Abhidharmakośa* states that one does not transcend the desire realm due to two [fetters], namely greed and hatred; and one returns to the lower realms due to three, namely the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Jiantang said: Someone asked, "The afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) obstruct the principle, while the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) draw one toward rebirth.

Why is it that even when one has severed greed and other [afflictions] up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one still returns to the desire realm due to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth? Does this not imply that the afflictions of view also draw one toward rebirth?

He replied: "The afflictions of view are fundamentally obstructions to the principle. Because one has not yet seen the principle, even if one is able to sever the afflictions of thought, one has not yet escaped from existence (*bhava*)."
Because they are outflows (*āsrava*), the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) also draw forth rebirth.
This is from the "Chapter on Contemplating Sentient Beings" in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*.
Commentary (8) (18); Bestowing Abundant Benefit (9) (24); *Miaoxuan* (8) (7); *Zhiguan* (8) (1). Classified Compilation of the *Fahua Jing*: Section on the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs.

When the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, it is of a single characteristic and a single flavor—namely, the characteristic of liberation, the characteristic of detachment, and the characteristic of cessation, ultimately reaching the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Section (7) (9): The so-called "lower" section provides a dual explanation of the single characteristic and single flavor. The nature of the sentient being’s mind is itself the nature-endowment (*prakṛti-guṇa*) of liberation, which is characterized by three aspects:
remoteness (*viveka*), tranquility (*śānti*), and cessation (*nirodha*). When the Tathāgata speaks these three dharmas with a single voice, they constitute the three flavors.
These three aspects serve as the objective realm for the practice of the Middle Way arising from conditions; ultimately, they become one.
Because it is the fruit of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), it is said that one ultimately reaches all-aspect knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) (and so forth).

As for the characteristic of liberation, there is no characteristic of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); as for the characteristic of detachment, there is no characteristic of nirvana; as for the characteristic of cessation, there is neither characteristic nor non-characteristic, but only the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, it is called the "one characteristic. This one characteristic is the foundation of non-abiding from which all dharmas are established; it is non-abiding and without [intrinsic] nature.

The characteristics are themselves without distinction; yet the establishment of all dharmas involves distinction. This distinction is like that of various plants and trees, while their lack of distinction is like the single earth.
Although the earth has no distinction, it can produce the differences of peaches, plums, and various plants and trees.

Although the peaches, plums, and plants differ from one another, they are equally of the same single characteristic of solidity. If one knows that the earth possesses both peaches and plums, [then one understands this].
To know that within the provisional understanding there is no differentiation is itself differentiation;
if one knows the solid nature of peaches and plums, then knowing that within the provisional there is the real understanding of differentiation is itself non-differentiation.

*Śikṣānanda’s Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Samādhi*, Fascicle 8 (29), *Fǔxíng Tǒngjì*, Fascicle 8b (9): Now we clarify that in the Perfect Teaching (*yánjiào*), the substance of the stages (*dìtǐ*) and the nature of their arising (*shēngxìng*) are entirely complete.

Commentary (7) [33]: Regarding what is called the "initial double explanation," the first part presents the principle and the teaching through a pair.

Next, regarding the section on the "assembly" and so forth, it first explains the characteristics of the nature (*prakṛti*) in relation to the principle and its virtues. First, it generally cites liberation; next, it lists and concludes this nature.

Although these three virtues of the nature possess three aspects, they are in fact only one aspect. Regarding the section on the "Tathāgata" and so forth, it explains the single flavor (*ekarasa*); because it is spoken by the Buddha, this nature...

By practicing in reliance upon this instruction, one is then said to cultivate the three [aspects]. (And so forth). Regarding these three aspects below, the three natures are again pointed out as the objects of cultivation.

Because the conditions for arising are presented below, the characteristics of cultivation are further raised; thus they are called "practice" (*caryā*). Practice is the cause. Finally, below... [the result] is raised.

Because the three sets of three wisdoms are perfected at the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*), they are designated by way of wisdom; that is, the three aspects of wisdom, the three aspects of practice, and the three aspects of nature.

The variations in their opening and closing, and their relative extent, can be understood by analogy. (As stated above. First, regarding the explanation of the characteristics within the nature of virtue:
the "characteristics of the path of liberation" refer to the quality of liberation within the path of karma; the "separation from characteristics" refers to [liberation] within the afflictions.

This mark of quiescence (*śānta-lakṣaṇa*) which is the virtue of *prajñā* is precisely the virtue of the *dharmakāya* within the path of suffering; it is free from birth-and-death and the like, and is established through cultivation.

Because there is only the concluding summary below, it says: "The true mark is a single mark. Below, this further explains that the single mark is the basis of non-abiding upon which all phenomena are established.
In principle, this is the nature-virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*); in fact, it is the practice-virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa*). The three causes are delusion... [text ends]

Since this "root of non-abiding" has already been explained in detail in the seventh fascicle of the *Shiqian*, both ignorance and true reality are termed "non-abiding.
Now, when "formlessness" is contrasted with "differentiation," it specifically refers to true reality as the "root of non-abiding."
Non-abiding is its original name; "the basis of non-abiding" refers to the principle that it accords with conditions while remaining unchanging—this is the underlying meaning.
The two gates of the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* can be understood by analogy with this principle. The two categories of defilement and purity are fully contained within these ten gates.

if one establishes all dharmas by taking ignorance as the root, then it begins with the Three Paths and ends with the Three Virtues.

One must understand that the fundamental principle of non-abiding (*an-ālaya*) is fully expounded through four aspects: the general discourse and the specific analysis.

It is said that this "basis of non-abiding" is as already explained in the seventh fascicle of the *Śuqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning), specifically in the passage stating, "That which is ignorance is itself the Dharma-nature. One should rely on this text to explain the basis of non-abiding;

is it not the case that both ignorance and Dharma-nature lack any nature of firm abiding, and both lack a nature of fixed identity? Yet, in order to establish one's own doctrine, you have instead changed the name.
If the nature [of things] does not abide determinately, what harm is there in this skillful exposition regarding the meaning? The commentary states:
