However, since the faculties and objects must necessarily correspond, it follows that...

Because greed, hatred, and delusion arise therein, giving rise to the three actions of body and the four of speech, they are called the three types of action—body, speech, and mind—consisting of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, which are produced by one's own karma and serve as the habitual causes. Now, let us briefly illustrate how the ten non-virtuous acts arise from a single atom;
since the substance of these ten non-virtuous karmas arises based on atoms, they likewise do not depart from the twelve directions and worlds. By means of these ten...
Because one universally creates evil karma, it is called "karmic existence" (*karmabhava*). Since these ten evils and so forth exist in the preceding thought-moment, they are called the "past.
Because the ten evils and so forth thus intermingle and overlap with one another, there are ten within each;
therefore, they total one hundred and twenty. This subsequent increase in number constitutes the second layer. In reality, however, there are only ten.
The evil [elements] are simply summoned according to direction and time to total one hundred and twenty;
one should know that within the first layer, only the four directions and three times are discussed, thus forming twelve.

This is because each single direction, when traversing the three times, constitutes only one set of four directions; since every age consists of the four directions, they form twelve. Thus far for the directions.
Since the world is thus, now based on the directions and the world, the ten unwholesome acts (*daśākuśala*) are also not merely ten;

rather, by pervading the directions and the world, they become one hundred and twenty. This is analogous to how our own school [the Tendai] takes only one thousand [dharmas] and, by applying them to the real dharma-realm and provisional names, establishes three thousand. If the three [realms] of the eye-faculty and so forth are applied, they likewise become eighty.
Although these ten unwholesome acts may be complete without deficiency, it is simply because the world upon which they depend originally lacks one part.
Next, when these ten unwholesome acts are performed with fervor, they are necessarily mutually adorned;
within them, taking one evil as that which is adorned, the remaining nine must serve as the adorners. For example, how could one who wishes to kill do so without being possessed of hatred?
Because ignorance involves theft, sexual misconduct, and so forth, one commits killing; thus, it is known that nine can adorn one.

The remaining nine mutually adorning one another may be understood by analogy. In reality, there are only ten evil acts, but because they mutually adorn one another, there are ten within each one, thereby forming a hundred.
This is also illustrated by our school’s principle of discussing the mutual inclusion of the single ten realms.

Thus, one hundred realms are established. Now, since these are mutually adorned to form one hundred, it should be understood that within each of the aforementioned twelve realms of the ten directions, there are again one hundred;
thus, they total one thousand two hundred, forming the third layer of increased numbers as the third stratum.
The same principle applies to the three faculties, such as the eye, which likewise result in eight hundred.
The preceding may be understood; however, these three sections are as follows: first, the basis upon which the ten unwholesome actions depend;
second, the actual discussion of how the ten unwholesome actions arise, which—by being applied universally across twelve categories—results in one hundred and twenty items;

third, the clarification of how the ten unwholesome actions mutually reinforce one another. Although there are three layers resulting in one thousand two hundred items, they do not transcend the ten unwholesome actions themselves. This is so.
The general intent of the scripture is merely to clarify that the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) and the three types of action (*tri-karma*) constitute the root of afflictions (*kleśa*).
However, because what is produced by these organs and their objects (*viṣaya*) must necessarily rely upon spatial dimensions, they further require mutual refinement;

thus, they form three layers, increasing to a maximum number of one thousand two hundred. This is simply the nature of the Dharma-principle; how could it be due to mental elaboration? Nevertheless, as for those organs...
That each faculty possesses twelve hundred [qualities] is a summary of the beginning and end, spoken in terms of the six faculties' shared capacity for discernment.
For although the eyes and other faculties experience light in front and darkness behind during their engagement with objects—
thus appearing to have increase and decrease— in reality, the nature of their discernment still possesses the virtue of being able to look in all four directions.
Since it penetrates the four directions, it totals one thousand two hundred; the body and the nose are likewise so. Thus the Sūtra says:
"What you see and hear originally have no different natures; though various objects are separated and distinct, they easily give rise to [cognition].

Within the nature, they know one another; in their function, they oppose one another. Guishan’s commentary states: "'Originally there is no difference in nature' means that the mind which discriminates is one and only."
As for the "separation by various dusts," it is because the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) are distinct;
yet, the reason why the ten evils committed through the six faculties are all called "merit" is that the substance of these ten evils is entirely the Dharma-gate of inherent evil (*prakṛti-pāpa*).

Thus, the Tathāgata wishes to cause sentient beings with appropriate capacities to attain liberation in their very place, such that the entire body becomes perfectly penetrating. Since there is resonance within words, one speaks of "merit."
Because of this virtue and clarity, I encourage you below to carefully select [the path]. The Sūtra says: "I have now fully revealed the six kinds of profound stillness and perfect luminosity;
the original measure of these merits is as follows. According to what you have carefully selected as being suitable for entry, I shall illuminate it for you so that you may progress.
It further says: "The root of the bonds of birth and death is none other than your own six sense faculties; there is no other substance."
The "delightful, wondrous, and eternal" also refers to the six sense faculties and nothing else. As for the "twelvefold interplay of three and four, four and three":
when the three periods of time intersect with the four directions, there are twelve; likewise, when the four directions intersect with the three periods of time, there are also twelve.

According to the sutra, "three times four and four times three, winding and turning twelve, flowing and transforming in three layers, one, ten, hundred, and thousand" means that when the three periods of time intersect with the four directions, there are twelve;
and when the four directions intersect with the three periods of time, there are likewise twelve. Thus it is called "winding and turning.
Indeed, as soon as a single thought-moment moves, it immediately falls into the categories of direction and time, forming these twelve numbers; this is precisely what is meant.
The twelve each transform into ten, forming one hundred and twenty; furthermore, each of these one hundred and twenty transforms into ten, forming one thousand two hundred.
By applying the world to the directions and the directions to the world, the analogy can be understood.
Thus, transforming one into ten is the first layer of transformation; transforming ten into a hundred is the second layer; transforming a hundred into... [one thousand].
A thousand is the third stage; thus it is called the three stages of flux and transformation: ten, hundred, and thousand.
Therefore, the efficacy of a single thought-moment has not yet reached the third stage, yet its momentum cannot be halted; once the third stage is reached, it can no longer be increased.
Although there are differences across immeasurable eons, they do not transcend these three stages; and although there are boundless directions, they likewise do not exceed them.
How could these inequalities exceed four? Now, while twelve hundred merits may be manifested in a single thought, good has its power and evil likewise has its power;
it is like water that can carry a boat and yet can also overturn it.
Should one not be cautious?

Beifeng asked: "The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* both state that the eyes, nose, and body possess eight hundred merits, while the ears, tongue, and mind possess twelve hundred merits.
Since the number of faculties is the same in both, are their textual meanings identical?

He replied: "There are two points of difference: first, the difference between delusion and awakening; second, the difference in the numerical methods employed. Regarding the first point, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* clarifies..."

The root of afflictions arises from the delusions of ordinary beings; because the functions of the six sense organs vary in their superiority and inferiority—being inferior by eight hundred [units] and superior by one thousand two hundred—the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies that through upholding this scripture, one attains awakening and gives rise to the function of a semblance-saint (*sādharmya-ārya*).
Regarding the merit of the mutual functioning of the six sense organs, they can expand and contract: contracting by eight hundred and expanding by one thousand two hundred.

Regarding the meaning of "one hundred": in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, based on the twelve directions (the three periods of time and the four cardinal points), each possesses ten evils, thus forming one hundred and twenty;
furthermore, based on the mutual inclusion of these ten evils, each being endowed with ten, they form one thousand two hundred.
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, based on the single mind being endowed with the ten dharma-realms, and each realm possessing the ten suchnesses (*yathābhūta*), they likewise form one hundred.

If one faculty universally apprehends the six objects, there are six hundred; when combined with the two adornments of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), this constitutes one thousand two hundred.
Since each and every faculty is adorned by both concentration and wisdom, there are likewise one thousand two hundred.
Furthermore, regarding the "valley-echo" [analogy], the Jin translation of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, chapter thirty-five, states: "Bodhisattvas possess ten kinds of eyes, namely: the fleshly eye..."

The eye, the celestial eye, the wisdom-eye, the Dharma-eye, the Buddha-eye, the knowledge-eye, the clarity-eye, the eye that transcends birth and death, the unimpeded eye, and the universal eye—the same applies to the other faculties.

How does this differ from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*? Answer: In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, each of the six faculties possesses five [aspects], which corresponds to the stage of semblance (*sadr̥śa-bhūmi*).

In the *Avataṃsaka*, each of the six faculties possesses ten [aspects], which corresponds to the true stage (*bhūta-bhūmi*). Although there is a difference in the levels of these stages, [the essential nature remains the same].
The essence of these dharmas is identical; they differ only in their combination and separation. That is to say, the Dharma-eye is separated from the Wisdom-eye and the Prajna-eye;
the Eye of Liberation from Birth and Death is separated from the Buddha-eye; and the Eye of Illumination is separated from the Unobstructed-eye and the Universal-eye.
The *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) on the *Wuliangyi Jing* (Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings), Fascicle Seven: Chapter on Wondrous Sound (*Miaoyin Pin*).
Textual Exegesis (10) [22]. Question: If Mañjuśrī’s rank were lower, his words would not have sought an audience; yet if Mañjuśrī’s rank...
Gaosanglai asked, "Nahan, why do you suddenly not recognize me? Nahan replied, "Although we occupy the same rank, there is a beginning, middle, and end.

You have failed to understand this single matter; thus, you do not disgrace your high position. Furthermore, seeing an auspicious sign among the assembly, I did not know its origin or purpose, so I questioned the Buddha."
[Commentary (10) (35)] Regarding the passage "If [Mañjuśrī] were at a lower station," etc.: when he spoke with such wondrous tones to that Buddha, he said, "I have also seen Mañjuśrī.
How could it be that he has come from afar seeking to see one of a lower station? Since Mañjuśrī’s station is high, his seeing the flower should be understood accordingly.

Why, then, did he ask the Buddha about the causes and conditions, etc.? In the response, two meanings are presented: either [the interlocutor] is of a higher station than Mañjuśrī, or they are both equally *pūrvayoga* (previously associated).
Within a single position, there are divisions of beginning, middle, and end; if they were all equally ancient Buddhas, there would be no distinction of high or low.

When occupying a position at the beginning before [the others] have retired, one who is unaware of their status might feel humiliated—how could it be that not knowing a single thing constitutes a disgrace?
Furthermore, among the great assembly, none dared to ask; although Mañjuśrī was of high standing, he manifested himself as being unaware in order to inspire [the others].
*Bie xing xuan* (Part One) (8): The lower grade does not know the upper grade regarding the two benefits of the hidden and the manifest, as in the text.

Furthermore, it fails to realize that Miaoyin’s record (*Ji*) (Part One) (23) states that even those at the highest level cannot fathom the highest, as this also applies to those of the Perfect Teaching; thus, it cites Miaode’s ignorance of the Subtle.
[Section on] Sound. *Bie xing shu* (Lower), Part 11. As for the "True Buddha," this refers to Vairocana at the ultimate stage of the wondrously enlightened Dharma-body;
he alone is named the True Buddha. The True Buddha is profound and remote, beyond description or demonstration; how could he be understood? It is like [the case of] Miaoyin.
If even the author of this work does not understand this, how much less could an ordinary person of the lower realms recognize the True Body when it manifests?

(Part II, 11) Question: According to the record, when Mañjuśrī saw eighty-four thousand precious lotus flowers appear before him as the Wondrous Sound Bodhisattva arrived from the east, he questioned the Buddha about them.
Based on this, [the author] also fails to recognize the manifested form (*nirmāṇakāya*); why then do you cite this as scriptural evidence? I do not understand.
The True Body answers this by saying that one sees only the traces but does not recognize their source; this is precisely what it means to not know the True Body.
Therefore, the following question asks: "What roots of goodness did these bodhisattvas plant? What merits and virtues did they cultivate? What samādhi did they practice? Samādhi is the true Dharma.
According to the two texts, the *Shuji* (Commentary on the Record), it is stated that Mañjuśrī himself is a person of high rank;
this does not mean that Mañjuśrī is superior to Miao-yin (Ghoṣila). See the fourteenth fascicle of the *Du Jiaoji* (Record of Reading the Teachings).
Reading the *Jiaoji* (Record of Teachings), Volume Fifteen.
Tiantai Śramaṇa Fǎzhào’s Preface to the *Zhiguan Xuannu* (Profound Introduction to the *Zhi-guan*).

The *Tingang Yuandun Zhiguan* (The Outline of Sudden and Perfect Calm Abiding and Insight) is the Dharma-gate practiced within my own heart, as taught by our Patriarch. It is vast and immense, dispersed throughout the great void;

it illuminates the masses of darkness with its solitary brilliance—is this not the book that saves the world and clarifies the Way? Sentient beings have, from time immemorial, turned their backs on awakening.

The six realms of existence, joined with sensory objects, revolve in a cycle of nothing but delusion and distraction; the Buddha, the World-Honored One, took pity on them and brought them to their ultimate end by opening the Six Sublime Gates.
According to how one awakens and enters them, the sublime *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) emerge between them.

As the distance from the Buddha grew ever greater, those who practiced a "dark" meditation (*andha-dhyāna*) based on both emptiness and existence were mostly full of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), while those who relied on words attributed all merit to the Sage. Thus, [the teaching of] the Perfect...

If sudden *zhiguan* (calming and contemplation) remains obscure and lacks clarity, it cannot escape the criticism of being merely calculative; it has not yet exhausted the principle of "immediately possessing" [the truth].
Only our Master Zhiyi attained sudden enlightenment through the *Lotus Sūtra*, merging the myriad realms within the single mind and purifying the spiritual essence to its profoundest depths.

Transcending discursive thought and allowing no room for conjecture, those of like voice naturally respond to one another, and those of like breath naturally seek one another out. Thus ends this chapter.
An said: "Cessation and contemplation, luminous and still—a teaching unheard of in previous generations—this is because this wondrous Dharma of cessation and contemplation is beyond being named.
Cessation is the counterpart to distraction; contemplation is the counterpart to dullness. When there is cessation, there is contemplation; one is never dull, and one is never distracted.
Because they are established through mutual dependence, they transcend dependence to illuminate the source. It is like the *agada* medicine."

When one is compelled to employ them, once the illness has departed, the medicine is discarded, and even the physician no longer stands; how then can one speak of "stopping" (*śamatha*) and "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) as being either luminous or still?

As for stopping and contemplation: for those of lofty character they are lofty, and for those of inferior capacity they are inferior. They encompass both the ordinary and the sage, and pervade all time from antiquity to the present.
When the dust of the passions is cleansed, the sun shines brightly across the vast sky; when the eye of wisdom is clear, the moon sinks into the cold void.
My Buddha transmitted this to Kāśyapa; it was passed down twenty-three times in the Western Heavens until it reached the Venerable Siṃha.
Subsequently, as it was transmitted to the East and reached Zhendan (China), it finally came to rest with me at Tiantai.

That one’s own radiance emerges and universally illumines the great trichiliocosm—who else but one who has returned from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa could participate in this? Yet, sages and worthies appear from time to time.
"To transmit mind by means of mind—who is it that transmits, and what is this mind? Alas! Is the Way of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* something that cannot be transmitted?
If it truly cannot be transmitted, why is it said that you received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) from Dīpaṃkara?

If *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* can indeed be transmitted, why do you say, 'I practice without a teacher or protector'? Whether it is transmitted or not, I cannot know; let each person [decide for themselves]."
Try to settle [the mind] and observe.

Regarding the state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the essential doctrine of the Guo family (the Chan/Zen school) must first be examined in detail through the texts on understanding and practice (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*). If understanding and practice are detailed, then...
The clarity of the object and the contemplation is evident; the essential point of this single volume on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* lies in understanding and practice.
Understanding refers to the perfect realization that all phenomena are fundamentally true; practice refers to establishing conduct within a settled state through the application of contemplation.

The fifth section of the text states: "The previous six stages relied upon the *sūtras* to open up sublime understanding; now, relying on this sublime understanding, we establish sublime practice. This is the distinction between understanding and practice.

I have previously concluded that one opens up wondrous understanding before the state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and employs wondrous contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) after the state of concentration;

thus, we know that the application of contemplation within the state of concentration is entirely contained within the section on "establishing practice" (*li xing*), and does not at all intersect with the section on "opening up understanding" (*kai jie*).
This is largely the same for both the *Jingxi Yili* and the *Ten Gates of Non-duality*, both of which first open up understanding and subsequently establish practice.

Regarding the practice of cultivation, there are two stages: first, establishing the object, and second, applying contemplation. What is meant by "establishing the object"? It is the establishment of the *skandhas* (aggregates).

If the *skandhas* were not established, from where would the wondrous contemplation be applied? From where would the wondrous object be manifested? Therefore, the *Shi yi shu* (Ten Meanings Book) by Siming states:

"Establishing the object and cultivating contemplation constitute the structural framework of the entire treatise on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and are the essential core for advancing along the Path. They serve as an aid.

The textual passage concerning practicing within the realms of the aggregates (*skandha*) is divided into two sections: first, it reiterates the realms of the aggregates, specifically selecting only the consciousness-mind from among the three categories (the *triskandha*), which is the text that "leaves the foot to reach the inch";
second, it clarifies the cultivation of contemplation, which is the text on "the ten dharmas constituting the vehicle.
The errors of the Shanwai school can thus be understood. Recently, there have been those who claim that one should employ sublime understanding only after the state of meditative concentration.

If one does not investigate this text concerning interpretation and practice according to its explanation, it would follow that the state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) comes first and the opening of understanding (*prajñā*) comes later.

Furthermore, there are those who claim that first using inconceivable contemplation (*acintya-vipaśyanā*) to contemplate the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*) constitutes the first level of subject and object;
subsequently, merging the inconceivable realm and inconceivable contemplation to contemplate the aggregates (*skandha*) constitutes the second level of subject and object. Indeed, this is the case.

Furthermore, the text concerning the investigation of the meditative object (*ālambana*) and the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) does not state that the cultivation of contemplation comes first and the meditative object follows;
such an inversion and error is hardly worth critiquing. What I am now critiquing is merely the "selection of the object.

The selection of the object refers to the deluded mind within the aggregates (*skandha*). To select the present momentary thought of the deluded aggregate and observe its inherent threefold nature—this is what is meant here.

The three thousand realms are precisely one thought-moment, and one thought-moment is precisely the three thousand realms; they are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither before nor after, like the eight qualities of water.
At this time, the realm of the five aggregates (*skandhas*) is transformed into the inconceivable realm. In the inconceivable realm, the object is itself the contemplation;
these two layers of subject and object are distinct and clear, like the ten realms and the ten vehicles, or the opening and closing of form and mind.

The four categories of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) and their various doctrinal positions regarding similarities and differences are fully contained within the original text; here, they shall be briefly concluded. Regarding *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, it is said:
"All aggregates (*skandha*) and bases (*āyatana*), both within and outside the realms, are created by the mind.

The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "One dharma encompasses all dharmas, namely, the mind. A treatise states: "Within all worlds, there are only name (*nāman*) and form (*rūpa*). If one wishes to be as [it is],...
In actual contemplation, one should contemplate only name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); the mind is the root of delusion, and its meaning is thus.

If one wishes to investigate this, it is like felling a tree by reaching its roots, or treating a disease by finding the correct acupuncture point. Now, one should set aside the four aggregates of form and so forth, and contemplate only the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*);
that which is the aggregate of consciousness is the mind. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) categorizes this as "Now, one should... [and so on].

The passage beginning with "Discarding the *zhàng* (丈) and adopting the *chǐ* (尺)" serves as a precise demonstration of the substance of the object (*ālambana*). Having finished explaining this text, he then analyzes it by posing a question: "Question:

Among the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), the five mental consciousnesses (*pañca-manovijñāna*), and the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*), all of which are capable of producing the three types of mind such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, which specific consciousness and which of the produced three minds constitute the object of observation in the present context? Answer: "The five sensory consciousnesses and the five mental consciousnesses are certainly the objects of the present context."
Because that which has not yet become associated with afflictions (*kleśa*) is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), among the six [consciousnesses], one must still take that which can summon retribution;

only when it has actually been produced does it belong to the sphere of afflictions. As for the remaining types of discrimination, they constitute the present object. However, regarding this analytical selection (*vicāra*), the explanations are not uniform:
some say it refers to the realms (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*); some say the name "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) applies universally; and some say it refers to the "kings" (*rāja*) of the two schools.

Regarding the enumeration of similarities and differences, some say that [the categories] generally apply to both the objects of the aggregates (*skandha*) and the objects of the afflictions (*kleśa*), but here we exclude both;

one should know that when sitting upright to contemplate the aggregates, there are naturally three sections: first, the specific indication of the essential nature of the object, which refers to the current passage on "discerning the object"; second, the sequential application of the same principle to the remaining [aggregates], minds, and so forth;

and third, the application of this model to the remaining aggregates and bases (*āyatana*), which appears at the end of the section on "breaking through universality" in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary). Since the *Fuxing* states "specifically," it refers to the first section.
In the *Four Clarifications on the Ten Meanings*, it is pointed out that this refers to the "total ignorance-mind" (*sammūḍha-citta*).
One should contemplate the words "essence" (*tǐ*) and "total" (*zǒng*). I have once said: "This aspect must be discerned; this essence must be observed.

Because the master of the record [Zhiyi] held that the essence of consciousness contains many implications, he carefully discerned it until there was nothing left to discern. This is crucial for determining the objective realm (*viṣaya*). This is the main pillar [of the argument].
The text concerning the "objects" (*viṣaya*) contrasts them with the remaining single minds and the objects of affliction (*kleśa-viṣaya*).

Later, in the section on the remaining single minds, the text again distinguishes these objects from the objects of affliction. Now, in explaining the text that performs this discrimination, the question is asked:

among the five sensory consciousnesses, the five mental consciousnesses, and the sixth consciousness, all of which are capable of producing the three types of mind beginning with feeling (*vedanā*), which consciousnesses and...

The three minds that arise are the objects of the present contemplation; the character "guan" (觀) is pronounced in the level tone (*píngshēng*). This question concerns the characteristics of consciousness (*vijñāna-lakṣaṇa*). The answer states:

"The five sensory consciousnesses and the fifth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are certainly the objects of the present. Since it no longer mentions the "three minds that arise," the answer refers to the substance of consciousness (*vijñāna-svabhāva*).
These do not yet belong to the afflictions (*kleśa*); they are the objects of the afflictions, not the afflictions themselves, because they are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

The retributive latent dispositions (*vipāka-anuśaya*) are neutral (*avyākṛta*). These five consciousnesses and the fifth mental consciousness are distinguished from active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*);
since the present object does not yet belong to active afflictions, it is not differentiated from the objects of innate, heavy afflictions.

Furthermore, it is said that among the sixth [consciousness], only those [objects] capable of attracting retribution—which must be innate—belong to the category of afflictive objects; the rest do not.
This distinction belongs specifically to the present context. Here, in contrast to the objects of affliction (*kleśa*), the present context is being identified.

Since we are taking that which can summon retribution and must have already arisen as the object of affliction, then the active afflictions that summon retribution belong to the category of "passing through" (*yili*) within one mind.
However, this single passage inherently possesses two meanings; thus, the *Siming Zhijue Zhiyao Chao* states regarding the *Fuxing*: [text follows].
Furthermore, one must distinguish between the mind that attracts retribution and the mind that brings about attainment;

the term "lower object" (*adhobhūmi-viṣaya*) is used because it applies across all other single moments of mind as well as to objects associated with afflictions, both of which belong to the lower [realms].

Modern masters all take the passage concerning its being "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) as a general explanation, distinguishing the objects of the aggregates (*skandha*) from the objects of afflictions within the context of the sixth consciousness.
The passage beginning with "taking that which can summon retribution" and extending down to "the remaining distinctions" specifically indicates the present object of observation;

this interrogative text constitutes the question regarding the present object of observation, while the responsive text first distinguishes and indicates the present object by means of the five sensory consciousnesses and the fifth mental consciousness,

and subsequently distinguishes and indicates the present object within the sixth mental consciousness— thus, throughout the question and answer, there are three instances where the "present object" is mentioned.

If one points to the essence of the mind, how could there be such a contradiction between high and low? This is an explanation for the sake of discerning the objective realm (*ālambana*). Next is the application of contemplation:
when the World-Honored One rose from his samādhi with serene composure, and the Master [Zhiyi] realized the diligence of Bhaiṣajyarāja, those on Vulture Peak had not yet [perceived it].
If it were not for Nan Yue, who would have known this wondrous realm? This realm cannot be understood through discursive thought or conceptual discrimination;
our Patriarch Zhiyi had no choice but to provisionally name it "the single contemplation of the mind" as the inconceivable realm.
With these three words alone, the five aggregates and the deluded mind are shattered; with these three words alone, subject and object are forgotten. Forgotten!

Because it involves the subject and the object, it receives its name from the object (*viṣaya*). In contrast to the aggregates (*skandha*) that are to be refuted, it is called the "contemplating subject" (*nirūpaka*); in contrast to inconceivable contemplation, it is called the "inconceivable object";

and in contrast to the realization of the Middle Way through the destruction of delusions, it is called the "principle revealed. Although there are these three names, there is only one reality: the True Aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Jingxi said:
"The specific designation of the wondrous object originates from the *Lotus Sūtra*, namely, the 'True Aspect of all dharmas' (*sarvadharmāṇāṃ bhūtalakṣaṇam*). This is the True Aspect.

All phenomena necessarily consist of all phenomena; all phenomena necessarily consist of the ten suchnesses; the ten suchnesses necessarily consist of the ten realms; the ten realms necessarily consist of the body and the land.
Furthermore, based on the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, the three worlds are established; these constitute the three thousand [worlds], which are the three truths.

What are the characteristics of one who cultivates this contemplation? It is simply that within a single thought-moment, the ten realms, the hundred realms, and the thousand suchnesses—including the dependent retribution—are fully present.
Provisional names are likewise thus; therefore it is said that with the slightest stirring of thought, the three thousand realms are fully present.

Just as when the eight phases of transformation move through objects, the objects are not moved by being in front of the phases, nor are the phases moved by being in front of the objects—it is simply that when discussing objects, one speaks of the movement of the phases, and when discussing the phases, one speaks of the movement of the objects.
It is like a wish-fulfilling jewel raining down treasures in abundance, or like the three poisons manifesting in every moment of mind.

The marks are universally distributed like the events of a dream; when the dream-objects appear vividly, they are but one mind. All minds are one mind, all phenomena are one phenomenon. Within every single atom there are all lands, within every single land there are all atoms, and within every single body and land it is no different. Therefore, for the observer, there is no distinction; they are mutually identical, mutually complete, mutually extinguished, and mutually fused. As it is said: "As for the nature of the mind, it is neither born nor extinguished. It is like the reflection of the moon in water: the moon does not enter the water, yet its image appears therein. Thus, the three realms are but the mind, and the ten directions are but consciousness. This is called the Dharma-gate of the Non-duality of Mind and Matter. Furthermore, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata’s wisdom-body is immeasurable and boundless; it is the essence of all dharmas, and it is the realm of the Tathāgata’s own realization. This is called the Dharma-gate of the Non-duality of Principle and Phenomena. Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* states: "If one can contemplate the nature of the mind as being like empty space, then one will see that the nature of all dharmas is also like empty space. This is called the Dharma-gate of the Non-duality of Mind and Dharmas. Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The nature of the mind is originally pure, and the nature of all dharmas is also originally pure. The nature of the mind is originally tranquil, and the nature of all dharmas is also originally tranquil. This is called the Dharma-gate of the Non-duality of Mind and Dharmas. Furthermore, the *Mahāyāna-abhidharma-samuccaya* states: "The nature of the mind is originally non-arising, and the nature of all dharmas is also originally non-arising. The nature of the mind is originally non-ceasing, and the nature of all dharmas is also originally non-ceasing. This is called the Dharma-gate of the Non-duality of Mind and Dharmas. Furthermore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The nature of the mind is originally unconditioned, and the nature of all dharmas is also originally unconditioned. The nature of the mind is originally free from conceptual proliferation, and the nature of all dharmas is also originally free from conceptual proliferation. This is called the Dharma-gate of the Non-duality of Mind and Dharmas. Furthermore, the *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra* states: "The nature of the mind is originally luminous, and the nature of all dharmas is also originally luminous. The nature of the mind is originally immutable, and the nature of all dharmas is also originally immutable. This is called the Dharma-gate of the Non-duality of Mind and Dharmas. Furthermore, the *Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The nature of the mind is originally equal, and the nature of all dharmas is also originally equal. The nature of the mind is originally undifferentiated, and the nature of all dharmas is also originally undifferentiated. This is called the Dharma-gate of the Non-duality of Mind and Dharmas. Furthermore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The nature of the mind is originally eternal, and the nature of all dharmas is also originally eternal. The nature of the mind is originally blissful, and the nature of all dharmas is also originally blissful. The nature of the mind is originally self, and the nature of all dharmas is also originally self. The nature of the mind is originally pure, and the nature of all dharmas is also originally pure. When one contemplates in this way, it is called "right contemplation" and it is called "the equipment for contemplation. This equipment is provisional; the provisional is emptiness.

When one is empty, all are empty—there is neither the provisional nor the middle that is not empty; the three thousand realms are all empty. When one is provisional, all are provisional—there is neither emptiness nor the middle that is not provisional;

the three thousand realms are all provisional. When one is the middle, all are the middle—there is neither emptiness nor the provisional... [that is not the middle]. The three thousand realms are all the middle.
There is nothing provisional that is not the Mean; the three thousand [realms] are all the Mean. The *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) says:

"Now, when one wishes to cultivate contemplation, one contemplates only the inherent reality (*liju*), wherein both the delusions to be destroyed and the virtues to be established are simultaneously the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

As for the three paths and the three virtues, the ten kinds of triple dharmas, and even the hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of triple dharmas—how could these ever exceed this? They penetrate from cause to fruit, encompass both self and others, and include all."

Correctly encompassing the basis, the phenomena, and the principle constitutes the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*). However, what is called "contemplating the mind" (*guanxin*) is not a separate mind;
it is precisely that aforementioned object of concentration, namely the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). This mind has no mind apart from itself.
This inconceivable realm is the axe for felling the tree, the fire for cauterizing the ailment, and the method for dismantling the roof-beam.

As for the strategic methods of the thief, the three contemplations (*trividha-avalokana*) are broad, while the ten vehicles (*daśa-yāna*) are but one; these ten vehicles encompass all three faculties (*trividha-indriya*).

For those of superior faculty, a single contemplation enters directly into the essence of the object, wherein the ten vehicles are fully contained. For those of middling faculty, they apply preparatory practices (*prayoga*), feeling acute pain regarding themselves and others;

whether two, three, or up to seven stages, they pass through these positions with patient endurance, remaining free from attachment to phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*). As for those of inferior faculty, there are obstructions.
Furthermore, one must advance in the cultivation of the "hidden" (yin) realms. Since all these realms are analogous, both the fivefold summary and the tenfold expansion are inconceivable.

Nevertheless, because the characteristics of these realms cannot be fully unfolded all at once through words, there is a distinction between the three realms of the rational nature (*li-xing*), cultivated virtue (*xiu-de*), and transformation for others (*hua-ta*).

To summarize: the illumination of the single principle of mind as it is inherently complete is called "nature" (*xing*); contemplating that this inherent completeness lacks [independent] substantiality is called "cultivation" (*xiu*).
To cultivate and explain the absence of intrinsic nature is what is called the spontaneous principle of transforming others; it is neither a matter of mutual production nor mutual containment.

Therefore, within daily life—whether burning incense, prostrating, snapping fingers, scattering flowers, expounding the Dharma, sitting in meditation, dressing, or eating—all are the complete manifestation of the inconceivable realm.
Some may claim that the realm of inherent virtue does not extend to cultivation, or...

This means that when one cultivates the realm of inherent virtue, one examines the four natures as belonging to phenomena; or, when one considers the realm of cultivated virtue, it corresponds to principle, while the other two correspond to phenomena.
These points are fully contained within the topical sections (*zhānmén*) and cannot be exhausted here. Do you all understand? Cultivation is identical to inherent nature;
at the early dawn on the path of Tiantai, inherent nature and cultivation are both forgotten. Wearing brocade robes, one returns to one’s native village.
Cessation and Contemplation (1):

The Patriarchal Lineage of Cessation and Contemplation (1). (1) If a practitioner hears of the *Dharmaguptaka-śāstra* (The Treasury of the Transmission of the Dharma), they will recognize the fundamental source [of the teaching]... [and so forth]. The persons who transmitted the Dharma.
Beginning with Kāśyapa and ending with Siṃha, there are twenty-three persons; if Maitreya and Śaṇakavāsin are included together, there are twenty-four.
All these masters were recorded by the golden mouth [of the Buddha] and were all noble ones capable of bringing great benefit (and so forth).
Such is the merit of the essentials for hearing the Dharma. It was for this benefit that the Buddha entrusted the Dharma-piṭaka.
*Fuxing* (Vol. 1, Part 5): "If one does not first point to the Tathāgata, the Great Sage, there would be no basis for enumerating the twenty-three patriarchs;
if the twenty-three patriarchs were not enumerated, there would be no basis for pointing to the thirteenth master;

if the thirteenth master were not pointed out, there would be no basis for placing faith in [the teachings of] Heng, Ya, Tai, and Yue, and so forth. The Tathāgata established [the lineage] according to principle while adapting to capacities."
In this age of names and forms, the four reliances are used to propagate the Buddha’s transformation; those who receive this transformation and study its teachings must investigate their source.

If one is confused about the source, one will increase the confusion between the provisional and the true realization. If the fragrance of the Dharma loses its thread, then heterodox views will mingle with the Mahāyāna.
From this we know that the Tiantai, Sanlun, and Huiwen traditions take Nāgārjuna as their root, and twenty-three sages have followed in his footsteps with steadfastness.
Lin’s arguments are indeed well-founded and highly credible.

In the *Fuxing* (Vol. 1, Part 12), it says: "The 'Golden Mouth' refers to what was recorded by the Tathāgata’s golden-colored body and oral karma. Question: To what stage of practice do these various venerable ones belong? Answer:

According to the stages of the Four Reliances (*catur-pratisaraṇa*), they belong to the first reliance, which is still within the realm of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and has not yet attained [the supramundane].

Since the *Śrī-māla-alaṃkāra-śāstra* (or relevant authoritative tradition) does not definitively determine their specific stages, but states that they are all "sages," they are mostly considered persons of the fourth reliance (*caturtha-pratisaraṇa*); yet this may also extend to the third and second [reliances] (and so forth).

Since hearing the Dharma brings such profound benefit, the Buddha entrusted the teaching so that it might reach future generations and be heard in succession, thereby ensuring that after Nāgārjuna, the sublime...
Observing this, it depends fundamentally upon this [text].

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-śāstra* (translated by Jñānagupta and Tanyao during the Northern Wei dynasty, contained in the sixth volume of the Fei manuscript): now, following this sūtra briefly, I shall present the diagrams for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, which are identical to those cited in the *Fuxingchuan* (Commentary on the Mohe Zhiguan).
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "After my parinirvāṇa, twenty-four venerable ones shall appear in the world to propagate my Dharma.

The bhikṣuṇī acted as a great refuge no different from myself; Kāśyapa transmitted it to Ānanda, Ānanda transmitted it to Madhyāntika, Madhyāntika transmitted it to Śāṇakavāsin, and Śāṇakavāsin transmitted it to Upagupta.
In the *Āgama Sūtras*, it is stated that during the hundred years following my parinirvāṇa, the elder Madhyantika will appear in the world.
(Nirvāṇa Commentary, Part 5, Section 19): Although the Buddha is a "Right Person" (*samyak-pudgala*), because he has passed away, one does not fashion images of the Tathāgata [for him].

As for those who have attained the four fruits [of the śrāvaka], they are "Non-Right Persons"; since they are true fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) and the path of conversion is easily practiced through them, it is appropriate to fashion such images for them.

(As stated above) Now, taking one perspective, these four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*) constitute the images of the four fruits (of the śrāvaka path). (As stated above) The ancient [exegesis] clarifies that the stages of the four reliances differ.

(As stated above) Now, from the perspective of the stage prior to the [first] bhūmi, where distinct afflictions have not yet been severed, this is the first reliance; from the stage of the bhūmis onward, where distinct afflictions are severed, there are three reliances—this is the specific meaning.
From the perspective of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), this is the first reliance; from the thirty minds (*triṃśat-citta*) through the ten bhūmis, distinct afflictions are severed.
Regarding the delusions acting as the three bases, this refers to the meaning of the Perfect [Teaching]. Within the meaning of the Perfect, there are further general and specific applications.

The general application is that the forty minds collectively constitute the four bases. The specific application is as follows: the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) are the first basis; from the first abode (*vihāra*) to the sixth abode is the second basis;
from the seventh abode to the ninth abode is the third basis; and the tenth abode is the fourth basis.
The *Zhiguī chāo* (7) [26]: Because it greatly disparages the Lesser Vehicle, it says "it is not the orthodox," since this occurs after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa (*etc.*).
If one were to manifest in the form of a Buddha, it would then be confused with the appearance of a Buddha in the world.

*The Profound Meaning*, Part 11 (5): The five grades and the six faculties constitute the first reliance; the ten abidings constitute the second reliance; the ten practices and the ten transferences constitute the third reliance;

*Dharmatrāta-saṃgīti-sūtra* (Tuzi-han; translated by Buddhavarman of the Eastern Jin Dynasty).

The Venerable Ratnamitra and other upholders of the Dharma transmitted this lamp of wisdom in succession.

As for those who harbor doubts, asking why Zhiyan clarifies the lineage of patriarchal succession within the *Mohe Zhiguan*, the answer is: the profound passages of the commentaries explain the sutras and establish contemplation based upon them, thereby providing clear evidence for faith.
If the *Zhiguan* were merely expounding what he himself had realized and transmitting it to those with the capacity [to receive it], [the lineage would not be necessary].
Because it prevents the dark realization of those who deviate into heterodox views, clarity is required; the text of the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) makes this very clear.

Furthermore, one may wonder: "If this treatise inherits the Great Dharma of the Perfect and Sudden from its patriarchs, why is it that masters such as Kukkuta attained only the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle?
The answer is: according to the meaning of Jingxi’s discernment, in the "Longevity" chapter of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Kāśyapa...
The Bodhisattva questioned the Buddha, who answered with the "Chapter on the Four Reliances" (*catvāri pratiśaraṇāni*), clearly enumerating the four fruits as the four reliances.
The fourth reliance refers to the person named Arhat, who dwells in the tenth stage (*daśamī bhūmi*).

Since the four reliances in this sutra refer precisely to those who propagated the Dharma after the Buddha—namely, the twenty-four patriarchs—it is clear that the stages are determined by means of these four reliances. Thus one knows [this].
The various masters of the Golden Mouth all refute [the claim that one can attain] the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle through the destruction of ignorance;

those of the Great Vehicle’s Perfect Teaching (yuanren) say they "realize" the four fruits, taking the four reliances (catur-niśraya) as the four fruits. The Commentary states: "The four reliances are the four fruits in form. (5/19) Guishan says:

"Listing the various patriarchs who have already received the Buddha’s prediction, their status lies within the four reliances; while internally they accord with the Great Vehicle, externally they manifest the forms of the Lesser Vehicle. 4.
Because the fruit is indeed the true field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), twenty-four patriarchs frequently spoke of "realizing the fruit. Furthermore,
there is doubt as to whether the Chan lineage should include Vṛṣabha, Śīlabhadra, Prajñātāra, and Bodhidharma to constitute twenty-eight patriarchs,
as recorded in Daoxuan’s *Chuan deng lu*, Zhiju’s *Bao lin zhuan*, and Songshan’s *Zheng zong ji*.
In the record, they jointly praised him; furthermore, the Preface to the Chart of the Fixed Patriarchs states:
"To begin with, Bodhidharma was indeed the twenty-eighth patriarch of the Buddha’s lineage, and like Mahākāśyapa, he was one who received the direct transmission from Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
Our Buddha took the essentials of the True Dharma as the core of this Great Teaching and transmitted it secretly."

To designate [Bodhidharma] as the patriarch of a single great teaching and even its originator—to cause confusion regarding our ancestral lineage—is nothing like the *Fu fazang zhuan* (The Transmission of the Dharma-treasury) for deluding scholars throughout the world.
To rectify the ancestral lineages and sever the disputes of ten thousand generations—nothing is better than the *Chan jing* (Sutra on Meditation).
The emergence of the *Chan jing* predates that of the *Fu fazang zhuan* by sixty-two years.
The record of the beginning and end, detailing the twenty-eight patriarchs, was already visible during the Jin dynasty.

As for the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Fu fazang zhuan), it was compiled after the suppression of the teachings under Emperor Zhenjun; it mentions only twenty-four patriarchs, noting that the lineage reached the Wei period at that point.

Furthermore, prior to the various patriarchs in the *Chuan deng lu*, there is the succession of the Seven Buddhas, including the verses of entrustment (*dharmakṣepa-gāthā*) and the account of Śākyamuni.
Regarding the accounts of the "Plucking of the Flower" and Kāśyapa’s smile, which seem to contradict the present [teachings], how can this be explained? It is said:
"To claim that one has realized the mind and attained thorough awakening, and that there are those who establish patriarchs and judge the scriptures—of this I dare not speak.

Guifeng once said: "Chan is the Buddha’s mind; the Teachings (Dharma) are the Buddha’s mouth. How could the nature of mind and mouth be fundamentally contradictory? However, the lineage of the school lacks true realization.
This group of people recklessly criticized the *Fu fazang zhuan* (The Record of the Transmission of the Dharma-treasury), deeming it erroneous and fallacious.
From this, it is clearly evident that the account of the twenty-eight patriarchs in India was not composed by Guifeng.

Now, I shall evaluate Daoxuan’s various theories based on four points: first, the establishment of the patriarchal lineage lacks any basis, as if [the lineage were derived from] the *Fu fazang zhuan*.
The tradition establishing twenty-four patriarchs is recorded by sages and worthies of the Western Land and has undergone three translations;
this is our current authority. As for the twenty-eight patriarchs of the Chan school, what evidence is there for them?

If Master Song says that the *Chan jing* (Dhyāna-sūtra) contains a complete record of the twenty-eight patriarchs from beginning to end, we have now examined the *Chan jing* and find that it mentions only nine patriarchs. Why is this so?
To recklessly enumerate many instances where names are not entirely identical and differ between earlier and later sources—how can these be used for cross-referencing?

Furthermore, these two accounts fail to investigate the historical periods; some claim that Bodhidharma was a man from the Western Regions who came here and personally preached, while Hui'an seeks separate evidence elsewhere.

Moreover, they do not rely on the *Chuan deng lu* (Transmission of the Lamp) or the *Bao lin zhuan* (Precious Forest Record), but instead exclusively rely on the *Chan jing* (Dhyāna Sūtra) to provide a superficial and misleading connection to Bodhidharma.
Tara was later transformed into Bodhidharma, who is said to be the twenty-eighth patriarch of the Western Land.
This claim originates from the *Chan jing* (Dhyāna Sūtra), which was translated during the reign of Yao Qin, specifically in the Long’an era of the Eastern Jin.

From that time, several generations passed through the Song and Qi dynasties until the eighth year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty, when Bodhidharma finally arrived in the Northern Wei during the reign of Emperor Xiaowen.
On the fifth day of the tenth month in the nineteenth year of the Taihe era, he entered nirvana after living for over one hundred years.

How could it be that he manifested his passing at the end of the Wei dynasty while the scriptures translated during the Jin dynasty earlier on state that Bodhidharma lived a long life and had not yet entered nirvana?
Since he had not yet entered nirvana, he should not have been established as the Patriarch; even if his lifespan were long, it should not have approached two [hundred years].

Regarding the "Three Slanderous Verses on the Seven Buddhas" from the *Bai-nian jing* (The Scripture of a Hundred Years), the frequent elucidation of the Seven Buddhas therein is intended to facilitate easy understanding and inspire confidence.
It is not that one Buddha personally hands over the Dharma to another; rather, each Buddha transmits the Dharma according to the specific capacities and conditions of his disciples.

This being the case, these Seven Buddhas span vast temporal intervals: the first three Buddhas belong to the period prior to the *kalpa* of emptiness (*śūnyakalpa*), while the latter four Buddhas belong to the period following the *kalpa* of formation (*vivartakalpa*). Thus, the distance between their respective eras is immense.
When have they ever met and transmitted the Dharma? How could Śākyamuni have ever personally seen Maitreya? Even assuming there is a teaching regarding a prediction, it was received from Dīpaṃkara;
furthermore, he did not receive a prediction from Kāśyapa Buddha. Moreover, from which sutra or śāstra do these "Verses on the Transmission of the Dharma by the Seven Buddhas" originate?
This is the fourth false claim regarding the "Plucking of the Flower. Furthermore, as for Śākyamuni plucking the flower: [The text continues with a critique of this tradition.]
Kāśyapa smiled, and as for the verse of entrusting the Dharma, since no such text has appeared, it is merely a groundless fabrication that has produced a superfluous growth.
*Nirvāṇa* (1)(17):
All the Buddhas’ worlds and all the great Bodhisattvas gathered together, as well as Jambudvīpa...
The entire great assembly was also gathered there, with the sole exception of the two groups: the Venerable Mahākāśyapa and Ānanda. (Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra, Part 1, Section 21).

Regarding the selection of these two groups, there are both factual reasons and implied meanings. As for the facts: Mahākāśyapa did not come because he was sustained by the power of his meditative absorption (*samādhi*) as he had entered *nirvāṇa-dhyāna*;
Ānanda did not come because he was ensnared by Māra. These are the factual reasons. There are also implied meanings.
Kāśyapa, in order to demonstrate that he would not abandon even the minor precepts, was the eldest son of the Buddha who upheld the Buddha’s Dharma;

had the Buddha been on the verge of passing into *parinirvāṇa*, he should have forgiven the minor precepts (and so forth). Furthermore, because the heterodox teachers mocked him, saying, "The precepts established by the Teacher will all be abandoned after his death," Kāśyapa thought, "If he were to come now, how could I maintain what is correct? Ānanda, however, acted thus to manifest that he was the Buddha’s final attendant.

[The text] praises and entrusts [the teaching] (as detailed above). Question: Why did Kāśyapa not permit the Buddha’s instruction to relinquish the minor precepts, such that master and disciple were at odds?

Answer: It is not so. The Buddha acted for those of sharp faculties according to what was beneficial for them, whereas Kāśyapa acted for those of dull faculties by returning them to their former state;
therefore, it was not a case of defiance or opposition.

From the *Xiyu ji* (Volume 9, Yi-zi-han): When the World-Honored One Maitreya appears in the world and has finished preaching the Dharma at the three assemblies, there will remain immeasurable sentient beings of prideful arrogance.

They shall ascend this mountain to the abode of Kāśyapa; then, upon Maitreya’s snapping his fingers, the mountain peaks will open of their own accord. Once those sentient beings behold Kāśyapa, they will immediately abandon their arrogance. At that time, Mahākāśyapa...
After Śāriputra had finished delivering his farewell address and paying his respects, he ascended into the void and displayed various supernatural transformations.
He then consumed his body by fire and entered parinirvāṇa.
*The Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Volume 3 (1): "If the Dharma-treasure is entrusted to Ānanda and the bhikṣus, they shall not remain for long."
Why is this? Because all śrāvakas, including Mahākāśyapa, are subject to impermanence, just as that old man who received a deposit from another;

therefore, the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma should be entrusted to the bodhisattvas, for it is they who are well able to inquire about and answer concerning such treasures of the Dharma, so that they may endure for a long time.
Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra (Part 3, Section 22): The Buddha responds to the request. He states that all the True Dharma (saddharma) now existing has been entrusted to Kāśyapa.

Because the Tathāgata’s conditions for remaining have expired, he departs; because Kāśyapa’s capacity has arisen, the Dharma is entrusted to him. Internally, [the Dharma] is identical to the Buddha’s own virtue;

externally, it is committed to a great minister who upholds the teachings of the True Dharma. This refers to the "perfect" and "I" [Sanskrit characters] as the basis of reliance, responding thus to the request made therein. Regarding this matter:
Because those who study the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* (New Yi) are for that reason said to have the Dharma entrusted to Kāśyapa;

whereas for those who do not study the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, it is said that Kāśyapa is impermanent and incapable of receiving the entrustment, each being a condition according to their respective circumstances.
*Zhiguī chāo*, Scroll 5 (12). Regarding "each acting as a condition": this praises [the teaching] and subsequently critiques it, as each serves as a specific opportunity for a particular capacity.

Although Mahākāśyapa’s great practice remained unchanged from beginning to end, the reason he is criticized for impermanence is that this is a case of employing a lofty teaching to command those of partial understanding to abandon their bias and enter the Perfect [Teaching].
The transmission of the Dharma entrusted by the Patriarchs took place precisely at the moment when the *Lotus Sūtra* was revealed and Kāśyapa attained realization;
thus, Kāśyapa’s narrative states: "Now the great jewel of the Dharma King has arrived spontaneously; all that a son of the Buddha ought to obtain has already been obtained.
This is fully detailed in the descriptive passage of the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter. Furthermore, the second fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"All the unsurpassed True Dharma that I possess, I have now entirely entrusted to Mahākāśyapa; once he has seen it, [the matter] is settled.

From this single word "seen," it is clear that [the entrustment] took place within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Some may claim that the entrustment of the Dharma occurred at the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, but since Kāśyapa was not present at that assembly, what would there have been to entrust?

If that were the case, then regarding the statement in the *Fofa chuan* (The Transmission of the Dharma) that [Kāśyapa’s] "conditions for transformation" [had ended], how could he have received the entrustment?
As he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he addressed his great disciple Mahākāśyapa: "Just as I am now about to pass into parinirvāṇa, I entrust this profound Dharma to you.
You must, in the future, respectfully follow my intention and widely proclaim and disseminate it, so that it shall not be severed.
Kāśyapa replied, "Excellent! I accept your instruction. [The Buddha] asked, "Why is this? [Kāśyapa said: "Because..."
This is merely a detailed account of the events from beginning to end within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* compiled by those who wrote the biographies after his passing.

Regarding the first and second [sections] on *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*: Master Zhizhe served Nanyue (and so forth). Nanyue served Chan Master Huiwen (and so forth). Master Wen applied his mind strictly in accordance with the *Śāstra*;
that *Śāstra* was expounded by Nāgārjuna and is the thirteenth master in the *Dharmatara-paramparā* (The Lineage of the Transmission of the Dharma).

Regarding the *Fùxíng* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), Volume One, Part One (13): "The oral transmission from the Golden Mouth [the Buddha] proceeds from the past toward the future; whereas the present Master’s patriarchal succession proceeds from the future back toward the past, as this serves to point to the text.

According to what the Wise One (Zhiyi) pointed out, one should take Mount Nanyue as the father-teacher, Huiven as the ancestral teacher, and Nāgārjuna as the great-great-ancestral teacher (and so forth).
Thus, from the perspective of Zhang’an, Nāgārjuna is merely the great-great-grandfather.
The present school likewise takes Nāgārjuna as the beginning; for this reason, the Wise One designated him as the great-great-ancestral teacher.
Master Beifeng said: "When our Buddha appeared in the world, he universally transformed all sentient beings, benefiting them according to their capacities;
he taught extensively to those of great capacity and briefly to those of small capacity, guiding them step by step with skillful means to bring them to maturity so that all might attain Buddhahood.
He did not allow even a single person to attain extinction alone. Why, then, does the Chan school only deliver those of one kind—those of great capacity—while neglecting those of small capacity?"
If the fruit of salvation were not universal in this way, for what purpose would the Buddha have preached the various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras?

Since the Buddha taught both the Great and Small Dharma because he intended to universally save those with the appropriate capacities, if you, in transmitting and propagating the Buddha-dharma, only receive those with Mahāyāna capacities, how could you fully realize the Buddha’s intent?

Now, Tiantai has revealed the Buddha’s intention for his transformation of beings: first, he universally benefited beings according to their individual capacities; subsequently, [he led them all] to...
The Buddha-vehicle is unified and the secret treasury is at peace; there are no longer the distinctions of the Small Vehicle’s two or three vehicles.

Since the Tathāgata’s conditions for transformation have ceased and the Dharma has been entrusted to the Patriarchs, once it has been revealed and clarified, all realize the Mahāyāna and cultivate the Perfect and Sudden path together.

Yet, without the aid of auxiliary practices, the primary practice is difficult to accomplish; therefore, the primary and auxiliary must support one another, benefiting both self and others, and encompassing both the Great and Small Vehicles.

The transmission is complete without any remaining dharma; thus the Great Master said: "From the Deer Park in the beginning, to Vulture Peak in the middle, and finally to the Śāla Grove at the end—the Dharma was entrusted to Mahākāśyapa.
The Record-keeper remarked: "Since the attainment of the Way has already been accomplished, the teaching must necessarily rely upon a place.

Therefore, these three stages—beginning, middle, and end—are briefly cited to verify the Dharma through its locations and to manifest the Dharma through those places; this is precisely the Dharma that has been transmitted.
This precisely refers to this point. Furthermore, the *Yili* (Exemplification of Meaning) states: "Although all rely on the *Lotus Sūtra*, they all return to the Single Reality (*ekayāna*).
Yet, in the Final Age, when faculties are dull, if there is no assistance, the correct practice will collapse. Only when the correct and the auxiliary are combined can one travel far.

Even the Buddha’s transformation [of beings] took the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* as its life-span; how much more so for those practicing in the Final Age, who cannot advance without assistance? Therefore, one must support the Vinaya."

(Text) Furthermore, although those in the Buddha’s era encountered the Sage and yet remained in the Lesser Vehicle, each adhering to a single gate, how much more so in this final age when the capacities of sentient beings are never of just one kind?

Since the Patriarchs knew that the *Lotus Sūtra* reveals and clarifies [the truth], and that even the biased practices of worldly wisdom are none other than causes for Buddhahood, they propagated and expounded [the teaching] according to the capacities [of beings]; it is appropriate to preach the Great when addressing the Great.
It is appropriate to explain the minor [teachings] in accordance with their respective cultivation and realization, pointing out each point as being none other than the true mark (*dharmatā*).

Although they differ according to the faculties and applications of beings, once it is known that the true mark is entirely a matter of the perfect capacity (*pariniṣpanna-yogya*), they are not termed "partial" or "minor.

Thus, the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*—whether gradual, sudden, or indeterminate—converge upon the precepts, meditative concentration, the untainted (*anāsrava*) state, and compassionate response.

This samādhi encompasses both the settled and the distracted, as well as the partial and the small; it does not abandon a single dharma, for all are Mahāyāna and none are not the true mark (*dharmatā*).
All lead to the fruit of Buddhahood. Thus one knows that the teachings are fully equipped to gather in all capacities of beings.
Therefore, the Master of Mount Tiantai praised the legacy of Nāgārjuna and followed the wondrous interpretations of Mount Huo, employing the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* to complete this work.
The causes and conditions of phenomena encompass all dharmas within the single mind, opening the ten vehicles across the eight teachings.

The discourse on precepts, concentration, and wisdom, along with the contemplations of emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle Way, are laid out clearly and plainly, ready to be put into practice.

Thus, there are no teachings left untaught, no dharmas abandoned, no persons neglected, and no minds that do not attain realization; through these practices, there is realization, and through realization, there is [liberation].

The reason this school’s great master’s teachings have flourished is that, from the transmission of the Dharma by Zhiyi through five generations until the present Master Zhannan, he has revived the Way;
he spoke of this to me in such a manner, and thus I have recorded it here to conclude this section.
As for other divergent theories and heterodox doctrines, they may be omitted.
*Heleixing Fuxing* (1a–8): As for "Helei" (Crane Forest), it refers to the place by the Ajiravatī River in the city of Kuśinagara. There were four pairs of trees;

alternatively, they are called "double trees" (*yishu*) because there were two pairs in each of the four directions. Furthermore, it is said that their roots branched out below while their trunks joined above.
Therefore, it is named "The Pair" (Yugandhara). When the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa within this grove, the forest turned white like a white crane;
for this reason, it is called the Crane Forest (Hakurin) [and so forth].

*Fuxing* (Vol. 7, Part 1, Section 11): "In every direction, some were entirely withered and others entirely flourishing. Flourishing symbolizes permanence and so forth; withering symbolizes impermanence and so forth.

Having entered nirvāṇa, the two pairs in the east and west merged into a single tree, and the two pairs in the south and north likewise merged into a single tree."

Therefore, one should believe that this is precisely what has been transmitted. Thus, he left a final instruction stating: "The *zhiguan* need not be transmitted; it is my private record which you shall teach to others.

This "private record" refers specifically to the ten fascicles recorded by Zhizhe (Zhang'an). The intent of the instruction was to emphasize that the true meaning must be conveyed through direct personal transmission.
For the most part, this private record is not exhaustive;

The essential core of our school’s transmission of the mind can be set forth by no one other than Zhizhe (Zhanran), and its true meaning can be elucidated by no one other than Jingxi (Zhiyi).

Regarding those [other vehicles], they are common to the three teachings; people practice them as causes, whereas here we speak only of what is practiced by those of the Perfect Teaching—thus the difference lies in the cause.

Regarding those [other vehicles], they commonly lead to the realization of small fruits, such as when Subhadra heard of the eternal and realized a small fruit; whereas here we speak only of realizing the great fruit—thus the difference lies in the result. Therefore, the divisions are not the same.

This is precisely the non-duality of calming and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), wherein object and wisdom are darkly unified (and so forth). Within the Middle Way elucidated by the teachings of our own mountain school, there are only two meanings:
first, the departure from annihilationism and eternalism, which belongs to the former two teachings; second, Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), which belongs to the latter two teachings.

Within the teaching on Buddha-nature, because it is divided into provisional and real, there are both the aspects of identity and separation; here, we follow the meaning of identity, and thus it is said:

For now, let us evaluate this through ten points so that one will not be confused regarding the principle; the rest may be understood by analogy (and so forth).
From the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (Volume 37 of the Shuai Character Case), Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said:

The world is like space, O son of good family. Because space is non-existent, it is neither internal nor external;
because the Buddha-nature is eternal, it is neither internal nor external. Therefore, it is said that the Buddha-nature is like space.
Son of good family, just as in the world that which is unobstructed is called space, so too has the Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

regarding the principle of Buddha-nature, there are both progression and exclusion. To speak in terms of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the three Buddhas are all pervasive and the three causes are likewise pervasive.
Yet, if explained according to the provisional, the three Buddhas are all limited and the three causes are likewise limited. This is when one still retains the provisional.
Regarding the passage on "explaining the real," it states that when explaining the real teaching, it refers to the true cause (*dharmakāya*);

whereas when explaining the provisional in contrast to the real, it means that the conditions and the completion (*pratyaya* and *niṣpatti*) of the provisional teaching are not universal. Thus, we know that the single term "Buddha-nature" in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* constitutes the true cause of the real teaching for the Buddha, yet constitutes the conditions and completion of the provisional teaching for Kāśyapa. Therefore, Zhiyi (Zhang’an) categorized the "Buddha-nature of sentient beings."

The statement that "the Buddha-nature is like space" is based on the meaning of the Buddha-nature being identical to space; the statement that "the Tathāgata’s Buddha-nature and *nirvāṇa* exist" is based on the meaning of the Buddha-nature being different from space.

The masters of the Qingliang school only knew that the essence of the Tathāgata’s *dharmakāya* is all-pervasive, but they did not know that the essence of the sentient beings’ primary cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) is also all-pervasive.
Consequently, they remained deluded regarding the principle of the cause while preoccupied with the phenomena of the results of affliction.
This is to be deluded by the name while failing to understand its meaning.

Is this not the case of one’s own practice giving rise to the teaching? These four points are the subtle [teachings] of Ming.
Whenever one grasps the meaning beyond the literal text, one immediately brings forth that intent;
whether it be the names, positions, stages, the five grades, or the ten levels of faith, when compared to the first stage (*ādikarmika-bhūmi*), they all belong to the initial mind.

Therefore, we know that the teachings of Nanyue, Zhiyi, and Siming—whether integrating the sutras and śāstras, unraveling the knots, emerging from the cage, or penetrating the gradual and sudden teachings—all instances of lecturing and establishing karmic connections are of this nature.

This is the aspect of cultivating the contemplation of the teachings while still within the causal stage. The text on "Tearing the Net" (*lièwǎng*) is consistent with the *Shēngqǐ* (Arising) in its presentation and explanation of the meaning;
however, because the *Shēngqǐ* contains the phrase "untying the knots and exiting the cage," Fazhi remarked:
"Is it not that one's own practice is able to tear the nets of others? Furthermore, the explanatory text contains the phrase "thoroughly penetrating the gradual and sudden teachings."

Therefore, it is said: "Is it not that one's own practice gives rise to the teaching? By examining the characters for "conclusion" (結) and "teaching" (教), one will know that the initial practice being able to "tear the net of others" has the same meaning as "one's own practice giving rise to the teaching"; it is merely a variation of the phrasing.

If one looks toward the eightfold manifestation for the sake of others after attaining the fruit, then both "the initial practice being able to tear the net of others" and "one's own practice giving rise to the teaching" belong to the stage of the first resolve.

In the subsequent section of the *Subcommentary* (*Fuxing*), when distinguishing the realm of transforming others (*huatā jìng*) in relation to the arousal of the teaching (*qǐjiào*), it is stated that there is a difference in meaning between the beginner relying on principle to produce understanding and the [Buddha] manifesting the eight phases of birth in the stage of true retribution (*shíbào*) to benefit sentient beings; this can be understood by analogy.

However, the realm of transforming others involves generating the perfect understanding (*yuánjiě*) for the sake of others through the fourfold preaching; this arousal of the teaching (*qǐjiào guān*) is thus universal (*tōng*).
The various teachings of the Sudden and Gradual vehicles are fundamentally unified; it is only that the meanings of the diverse sutras and treatises differ.

Thus we know that if one cannot cultivate the contemplation of one’s own practice and the arousal of the teaching during the causal stage, how could one possibly achieve the function of transforming others and preaching the Dharma after the fruition?
It is truly lamentable that those of pure awakening remain ignorant of this.
