"Dust" (*rajas*) refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), which are the creators, and the four subtle particles (*tanmātra*), which are the created.

It is through the combination of these four subtle particles—form, odor, taste, and touch—that the sense organs are formed. Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "I now observe these floating roots of the four dusts;

they reside only upon my face. Master Zizhong commented: "They are as empty and unreal as floating clouds, obscuring the true nature; hence they are called 'floating dust. Outside of this floating dust..."

Regarding the term "ultimate" (*paramārtha*) applied to the faculties: Master Hongmin’s *Commentary* states that although these ultimate faculties take the eight factors—both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derived matter (*bhautika*)—as their substance, they are invisible and possess resistance (*sapratigha*).

Because they can illuminate objects and give rise to consciousness, they are the domain known by the noble ones (*ārya*); their meaning is profound and far-reaching, unlike the coarse and shallow nature of the sensory objects (*viṣaya*).
This is called "purity" (*viśuddhi*); it refers to purity spoken of within the context of defilement, not the purity of untainted (*anāsrava*) wondrous clarity.
This is the internal faculty (*indriya*) of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). (Cited from *Fanyi Mingyi Ji*, Fascicle 6, Section on the Aggregates, Elements, and Bases, No.

58). *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, Volume 6 (Shengzi Case). Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) [the eighth consciousness]; Equality Wisdom (*samatā-jñāna*) [the seventh consciousness]; Wondrous Discernment Wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*).

The six consciousnesses constitute the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*); the five consciousnesses pertain to the domain of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), while the concentrated mind free from conceptualization pertains to the domain of inference (*anumāna*), and the distracted mind with conceptualization likewise pertains to the domain of inference.

The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (translated by Daotai; fascicle seven of the phonetic transcription section) asks: "What is the dharma of wisdom (*jñāna*)? What is the dharma of consciousness (*vijñāna*)? [and so forth].

It states that consciousness is itself wisdom, and wisdom is itself consciousness. The only difference is one character: *jñāna* is translated into Chinese as "wisdom" (*zhì*), while *vijñāna* is translated as "consciousness" (*shí*).
This single additional character is the syllable *vi*. To eliminate such misconceptions and explain their distinct meanings, [the text] provides this differentiation.
Therefore, wisdom is taught first, followed by consciousness. Furthermore, some say that both are fundamental dharmas:
in the context of the increasing dharmas, consciousness is the foundation; in the context of the dharmas of cessation, wisdom is the foundation.

Others say that both are primary dharmas, just as among the factors of the path (mārga-aṅga), it is asked who is the leader, and the answer is wisdom. [The same applies to] birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
Within the Dharma, who is the sovereign? It is what is called consciousness (*vijñāna*).
In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (composed by Maitreya, translated by Xuanzang; Volume 15, Section "Ting"), direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is of three kinds:

first, that which is not non-manifest; second, that which is neither already thought nor to be thought; and third, that which is not a realm of error. (The commentary is not recorded here. Question: Such direct perception...

To whom does this pramāṇa belong? The answer is: briefly stated, there are four kinds of that which exists: first, sensory direct perception (*indriya-pratyakṣa*); second, mental-cognitive direct perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*); third, worldly direct perception (*loka-pratyakṣa*);

and fourth, pure direct perception (*viśuddha-pratyakṣa*). Regarding sensory direct perception: it refers to the objects within the range of the five physical sense-faculties, as previously described regarding the essential characteristics of direct perception.

Regarding mental-cognitive direct perception: it refers to all... [the objects] of the various... *(Note: The source text appears to be a fragment. The translation provided reflects the available portion accurately according to the technical terminology of Abhidharma and Pramāṇa literature.)*
The objects traversed by the mental faculty (*manas*) are as previously described regarding the essential characteristics of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
"Worldly direct perception" refers to these two types taken together and collectively termed worldly direct perception.
"Pure direct perception" refers to all that is worldly direct perception, which may also be called pure direct perception; however, there is also pure direct perception that is not worldly.

Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that transcends the mundane refers to supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*), which, regarding its objects of engagement, knows existence as existence and non-existence as non-existence;
it knows the presence of the surpassable as surpassable and the presence of the unsurpassable as unsurpassable. Such categories are called "pure direct perception that is not shared with the mundane.
Inferential cognition (*anumāna*) refers to that which is accompanied by analytical investigation (*vicāra*), concerning all objects already investigated or yet to be investigated. Furthermore...

There are five kinds: (1) inference by signs (*liṅga-anumāna*), (2) inference by essence (*svabhāva-anumāna*), (3) inference by activity (*kārya-anumāna*), (4) inference by dharma (*dharma-anumāna*), and (5) inference by cause and effect (*hetu-phala-anumāna*).
Regarding inference by signs: this refers to the estimation of an object by means of its various characteristics, whether through what is presently perceived or what was previously seen.
For example, because one sees a banner, one infers that there is a chariot; because one sees smoke, one infers that there is fire.

Fire is thus: the king is compared to the country, the husband to the wife, and the horn to the ox (and so forth). Inference based on the nature of the thing (*svabhāvānumāna*) refers to inferring an unperceived entity by means of perceiving its own essential nature; or, it refers to inferring other parts by means of perceiving one part of its essential nature, such as inferring the past by means of the present (and so forth). [Inference] based on effect (*kāryānumāna*)... [inference] based on non-perception (*anupalabdhy-anumāna*)... [inference] based on the non-perception of what is perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi-anumāna*)... [inference] based on the perception of what is not perceptible (*adṛśyānupalabdhi-anumāna*)... [inference] based on the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi-anumāna*)... [inference] based on the perception of the cause (*kāraṇopalabdhi-anumāna*)... [inference] based on the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi-anumāna*)... [inference] based on the perception of the pervader (*vyāpakopalabdhi-anumāna*)... [inference] based on the non-perception of the contradictory (*viruddhānupalabdhi-anumāna*)... [inference] based on the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi-anumāna*). These are the nine types of inference. Furthermore, there are three types of inference: inference from cause to effect (*pūrvavat*), inference from effect to cause (*śeṣavat*), and inference from general correlation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*). Inference from cause to effect is, for example, when one sees smoke rising from a mountain and infers that there is fire on the mountain. Inference from effect to cause is, for example, when one hears the sound of a drum being beaten and infers that there is a drum. Inference from general correlation is, for example, when one sees that the sun has moved across the sky during the day and infers that it will rise again tomorrow morning. Furthermore, there are two types of inference: inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) and inference for others (*parārthānumāna*). Inference for oneself is when one, having personally perceived the three marks (*trirūpa*), generates certainty regarding the object of inference. Inference for others is when one, having personally perceived the three marks, explains them to another person using the five members of a syllogism (*pañcāvayava*). What are the five members? First, the proposition (*pratijñā*); second, the reason (*hetu*); third, the example (*udāharaṇa*); fourth, the application (*upanaya*); and fifth, the conclusion (*nigamana*). Among these, the proposition is the statement of the subject of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*). The reason is the statement of the property that establishes the connection (*saṃbandhavacana*). The example is the statement of the locus where the connection is established (*saṃbandhasiddhisthānavacana*). The application is the statement that shows the similarity between the subject and the example (*tulyatādarśanavacana*). The conclusion is the statement that summarizes the meaning of the reason (*hetvarthasaṃgrahavacana*). This is called inference for others. Furthermore, there are two types of reasons: the correct reason (*saddhetu*) and the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). The correct reason is that which possesses the three characteristics of the reason (*trirūpa-hetu*). The fallacious reason is that which lacks one or more of these three characteristics. What are the three characteristics? First, the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*); second, the presence of the reason in similar instances (*sapakṣasattva*); and third, the absolute absence of the reason in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣāsattva*). That which possesses these three characteristics is called the correct reason. That which lacks even one of these is called a fallacious reason. What are the fallacious reasons? There are five types: the contradictory reason (*viruddha*), the uncertain reason (*anaikāntika*), the unestablished reason (*asiddha*), the counter-balanced reason (*prakaraṇasama*), and the mistimed reason (*kālātīta*). The contradictory reason is that which proves the opposite of the intended thesis. The uncertain reason is that which is common to both the similar and dissimilar instances. The unestablished reason is that which is not admitted by either the proponent or the opponent. The counter-balanced reason is that which, though possessing the three characteristics, is refuted by another reason of equal force. The mistimed reason is that which, though possessing the three characteristics, is stated after the time for its proof has passed. These are the five types of fallacious reasons. Furthermore, there are two types of examples: the concordant example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) and the discordant example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). The concordant example is that which possesses the same properties as the subject. The discordant example is that which possesses different properties from the subject. Furthermore, there are two types of application: the application of similarity (*sādharmya-upanaya*) and the application of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-upanaya*). The application of similarity is the statement that shows the subject possesses the same property as the example. The application of dissimilarity is the statement that shows the subject does not possess the property that is absent in the example. Furthermore, there are two types of conclusion: the conclusion of similarity (*sādharmya-nigamana*) and the conclusion of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-nigamana*). The conclusion of similarity is the statement that summarizes the meaning of the concordant example. The conclusion of dissimilarity is the statement that summarizes the meaning of the discordant example. These are the five members of a syllogism. Furthermore, there are two types of debate (*vāda*): the formal debate (*vāda*) and the contentious debate (*jalpa*). Formal debate is when two parties, relying on valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and correct reasoning (*yukti*), seek to establish their respective positions. Contentious debate is when two parties, relying on sophistry (*chala*), quibble (*jāti*), and futile rejoinders (*nigrahasthāna*), seek to defeat each other. Sophistry is the misrepresentation of another’s words. Quibble is the finding of fault through equivocation. Futile rejoinders are the attempts to refute an argument through superficial similarities or differences. These are the various categories of debate. Furthermore, there are two types of refutation (*dūṣaṇa*): the true refutation (*saddūṣaṇa*) and the false refutation (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*). The true refutation is the pointing out of a flaw in the opponent’s argument. The false refutation is the pointing out of a non-existent flaw. These are the various categories of refutation. Furthermore, there are two types of victory (*vijaya*): the victory of truth (*satyavijaya*) and the victory of skill (*kauśalyavijaya*). The victory of truth is when one’s own position is established and the opponent’s position is refuted through valid cognition and correct reasoning. The victory of skill is when one defeats the opponent through sophistry, quibble, and futile rejoinders. These are the various categories of victory. Furthermore, there are two types of defeat (*parājaya*): the defeat of truth (*satyaparājaya*) and the defeat of skill (*kauśalyaparājaya*). The defeat of truth is when one’s own position is not established and the opponent’s position is not refuted through valid cognition and correct reasoning. The defeat of skill is when one is defeated by the opponent through sophistry, quibble, and futile rejoinders. These are the various categories of defeat. Furthermore, there are two types of neutralization (*avyākṛta*): the neutralization of the question (*praśnāvyākṛta*) and the neutralization of the answer (*uttarāvyākṛta*). Neutralization of the question is when a question is not answered because it is irrelevant or leads to confusion. Neutralization of the answer is when an answer is not given because it would lead to further dispute or because the matter is beyond the scope of knowledge. These are the various categories of neutralization. Furthermore, there are two types of skillful means (*upāya*): the skillful means of wisdom (*prajñopāya*) and the skillful means of compassion (*karuṇopāya*). The skillful means of wisdom is the cultivation of insight into emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the lack of self (*anātman*). The skillful means of compassion

Inference (*anumāna*) refers to the cognition of the basis of an action through its already performed activity, such as when one sees an object from afar that does not move, and seeing a bird perched upon it;
by such matters, one infers that it is a pillar. If there is movement and so forth, one infers that it is a person.

If one hears the sound of neighing, one infers that it is a horse (and so on). Inferential cognition regarding phenomena (*dharma-anumāna*) refers to [cognition] based on immediate proximity and connection.
Inference based on dharma (*dharmatā-anumāna*) is the inference of a property based on its relation to other properties that are adjacent or connected to it;

for example, inferring the presence of suffering based on [the observation of] impermanence (and so forth). Inference based on cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇa-anumāna*) refers to the successive comparison of causes and effects.
For instance, seeing that there was movement [to reach] another place, one infers that there was prior movement; or seeing a person eating in an uneven manner, and so forth.
One should know that these categories are collectively termed "inference based on cause and effect" (kāryakāraṇānumāna);
this is what is called inference (*anumāna*). In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Volume 63, Box Fú): [1] The ālayavijñāna; [2] The evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).

The ālayavijñāna is the basis (*āśraya*), and the evolving consciousnesses are that which depend upon it (*āśrita*). These, moreover, are of seven kinds, namely: visual consciousness through to mental consciousness.
For example, it is like waves depending upon a torrential current, or like a reflection depending upon a bright mirror.
Furthermore, all consciousnesses are termed *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna*. However, the *ālayavijñāna* is designated as *citta* in its most preeminent sense. Why?

Because this consciousness is able to gather the seeds of all phenomena (*dharma*). At all times, it takes as its object the appropriated realm (*upātta-viṣaya*) and... [the object]... not... [discontinuous].

It should be understood that a certain class of mind, the *ālayavijñāna*, has as its nature the constant, moment-to-moment cogitation (*manana*) of grasping at "I" and "mine," as well as the conceit of "I am" (*asmimāna*).
Other consciousnesses are termed "cognition" (*vijñāna*), characterized by the discernment of objects.

Thus, in all states where there is mind, these three—the *citta* (storehouse), *manas* (intellect), and *manovijñāna* (mental cognition)—arise simultaneously at all times. This is also the case for visual consciousness.

When the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) do not arise, they are inactive; when they do arise, one should know that they function in conjunction with those [evolving consciousnesses] as co-existent factors (*sahabhū*).
Thus, at times four consciousnesses evolve together, and so on, up to eight consciousnesses evolving together.

Furthermore, a single mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) discriminates within all these intervals—whether regarding one object, two, or many—its own objects as well as the objects of others; therefore, the mental consciousness is said to be inconceivable.

Furthermore, while the ālayavijñāna is not associated with afflictions, the manas is constantly associated with four types of spontaneous afflictions that arise together at all times without interruption—
namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) regarding "I" and "mine," the conceit of "I" (*asmimāna*),
self-love (*ātmasneha*), and the unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*). These afflictions [are associated] with both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
It is associated with neutral consciousness and is not in contradiction with it; its nature is exclusively obscured-neutral (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*) and arises spontaneously.
One should know that all other [consciousnesses] arising from conceptualization evolve according to the power of various conditions and their specific differences (and so forth).
The *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* (compiled by Bodhisattva Sthiramati; translated by Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty), Volume Two, asks: "How is the aggregate of consciousness established?

It refers to the distinctions between mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). 'Mind' refers to the ālayavijñāna, which is perfumed by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the aggregates, elements, and bases, and contains all seeds.
It is also called the 'ripening consciousness' (*vipākavijñāna*) and the 'appropriating consciousness' (*ādānavijñāna*), because it can plant and accumulate all habitual tendencies."
(The foregoing) means that at all times, the manas has the nature of reflecting upon and deliberating regarding the ālayavijñāna as its object, and it is associated with the four afflictions, namely:

self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), self-love (*ātma-sneha*), self-pride (*ātma-māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*). (The foregoing) "consciousness" refers to the six groups of consciousness, from visual consciousness up to mental consciousness, which have the nature of discernment (*vijñapti*).
*Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* (Composed by Vasubandhu Bodhisattva; translated by Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang; Volume One, Case "Xiao") The Three Natures: 1.
The Dependent Nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) 2. The Imagined Nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) 3. The Perfected Nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) The Treatise states:
Because it contains and stores all the seeds of phenomena, it is called the *ālaya*. I, the Victorious One, have revealed this. Furthermore, it says:
The ādāna-vijñāna is extremely subtle; it contains all seeds and is like a violent torrent.
I do not reveal this to the ignorant and the foolish, fearing that they might conceptually grasp it as a self.
This consciousness is also called the ādāna-vijñāna because this consciousness follows and clings to the body.
Therefore, it is also called the *ālayavijñāna*. Why? Because this consciousness, in relation to the body, performs the functions of grasping, concealing, and sharing a common fate.
It is also called "mind" (*citta*). Why? Because by means of this consciousness, form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and so forth are accumulated and nurtured.

From the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* (composed by Vasubandhu, translated by Paramārtha during the Chen dynasty; Volume Three, Case Jie): "Mind" (*citta*) refers to the six consciousnesses; "mental faculty" (*manas*) refers to the *ādāna-vijñāna*;
and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
Mahāyāna-Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra (composed by Vasubandhu, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of the Chen Dynasty; Li-zi box): "In reality, there are no external objects;
consciousness arises appearing as if there were objects, just as a person with cataracts sees hairs, two moons, and so forth."
In the Mahāyāna, it is established that external objects do not exist as real entities. If this is so, how is it that external objects are perceived?

To prove this point, it is said that consciousness arises appearing as an object (*viṣayābhāsa-vijñāna*). Because consciousness manifests in the likeness of an object, sentient beings perceive an object within what is actually objectless.
To clarify the nature of this consciousness, it is compared to one who has an eye disease or a disorder of the visual faculty.
In the absence of any external object, consciousness appears as two moons.

In the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci, a śramaṇa from India under the Wei Dynasty; Zhongzi Box), it is stated that the four dharmas—mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and discernment (*vijñapti*)—are identical in meaning though different in name.
This is explained based on the mind associated with its corresponding [mental factors], and not based on [the mind alone].
Regarding the mind that is dissociated (*viprayukta*), it is said that there are two kinds of mind.

The first is the associated mind (*saṃprayukta-citta*), which refers to all afflictions (*kleśa*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), as well as feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Because these are associated with the mind, it is said that "mind" (*citta*), "intellect" (*manas*), "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), and "discernment" (*vijñapti*) are one in meaning though different in name. The dissociated mind refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is eternally abiding.

The transformation of the intrinsically pure mind is explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (composed by Dharmapālabodhi and translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang; Volume Ze). Although the images transformed by consciousness are of immeasurable kinds, the types of consciousness that perform this transformation are classified into three:
first, the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), which is the eighth consciousness, so called because it is predominantly of a ripened nature.

The second refers to deliberation (*manas*), because the seventh consciousness constantly and thoroughly deliberates; the third refers to the apprehension of objects (*vijñapti*), because the six preceding consciousnesses apprehend objects with coarse characteristics.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* (Volume One, Yan Section) explains: "When the eye-faculty takes external visible forms as its object, eye-consciousness arises; it is simultaneous with the eye-consciousness."

At one time, when there is a common object, a conceptualizing mental consciousness arises. If a single visual consciousness arises, at that time a conceptualizing mental consciousness arises together with that visual consciousness, sharing the same object.

If this visual consciousness arises together with two, three, four, or five [sensory] consciousnesses, at that time there is a single conceptualizing mental consciousness that arises together with the five consciousnesses, taking the object as its cognitive support.

*The Cessation and Contemplation of Mount Nanyue*, Part Two (10). Question: When deluded discrimination occurs within semblance-consciousness (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*), does the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) function as a whole to discriminate all six sense-objects, or do the six consciousnesses each individually discriminate a single object? Answer:

When the five consciousnesses perceive objects, each arises simultaneously with the mental consciousness. For instance, when the visual consciousness perceives a semblance of form, there is immediately a mental consciousness that arises concurrently.
At that time, there is the conceptualization and false attachment [of the sixth consciousness]. The same applies to the other consciousnesses;

therefore, the manas-consciousness (manovijñāna) is generally able to conceptualize and falsely attach to the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), whereas the five sensory consciousnesses can only apprehend the five sense-objects and do not give rise to conceptualization or false attachment. Question:
Is it the five sensory consciousnesses or the sixth consciousness that falsely attach to the five sense-objects as being real? Answer: According to the Mahāyāna...
It is not clearly distinguished whether the five consciousnesses and the sixth are separate; however, all that is capable of discrimination is termed "manovijñāna" (mental consciousness).

The *Fuxing* (Vol. 7, Part 2, p. 29), citing the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, states: "As for the term 'vijñaptimātra' (consciousness-only), it refers to a single consciousness which is further divided into two kinds:
first, the discriminative, and second, the non-discriminative. The discriminative consciousness is called 'vijñāna' (consciousness); the non-discriminative is called..."
All worlds are constituted by consciousness that appears as objects (*viṣayābhāsa-vijñāna*).

Since the three natures and other phenomena of form and mind are fundamentally non-dual, when those [natures] are divided into two types of consciousness, they are likewise divided into two types of form. Question:
How are form and consciousness similar or different? Answer: If form and mind are contrasted, then there is form and there is mind; thus it is discussed.
Its essential nature is such that it is devoid of form when there is no mind, and devoid of mind when there is no form. If form and mind were identical, then where there are two, both would be two;

and where there is one, both would be one. Therefore, those who speak of the "perfect" (pariniṣpanna) should also be able to say "only form," "only sound," "only fragrance," "only taste," or "only touch.
Why can they only say "consciousness-only" (vijñapti-mātra)? If these are discussed collectively, there is nothing that does not fully possess all [of them].
The Footprint of the Dharma Realm. Furthermore, if one speaks from the perspective of the derivative [phenomena], all sentient beings differ in two ways:

those in the upper realms are mostly attached to consciousness (*vijñāna*), while those in the lower realms are mostly attached to form (*rūpa*). If one takes consciousness as the basis for "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*), by gathering the outward-directed [mind] and turning it inward, one contemplates that internal consciousness is all a single consciousness.
Once consciousness is realized as empty, the ten realms are all empty. If consciousness is merely provisional, then the ten realms are likewise [provisional].

If consciousness is the middle way, then the ten realms are all the middle way. By focusing exclusively on the internal mind to contemplate all phenomena, one contemplates the external ten realms and thereby perceives the internal mind.
Therefore, one should know that whether it be consciousness or form, both are merely form; whether it be consciousness or form, both are merely consciousness.
Although one speaks of matter and mind, there are only these two names; yet when discussing their actual substance, they are simply the Dharma.

In the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*), fascicle 5, part 1, section 24, it further states: "There is a school [of thought] that maintains that the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*), the five mental consciousnesses (*pañca-manovijñāna*), and the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*) together are capable of giving rise to the three types of minds, such as feeling (*vedanā*).

However, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there is certainly no principle by which the five sensory consciousnesses could give rise to these three minds; although this point is the same [in our current context],..."

Setting aside for now the present [discussion], let us first examine the various consciousnesses as objects. Regarding the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), there is a school that asserts it is the sovereign mind-king (*citta-rāja*).
How, then, can one distinguish it from the mind-king when practicing meditation? The answer is: this is merely a sectarian tenet; in truth, it is not so.
To simply observe the mind is, in principle, equivalent to observing the sovereign.
*Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (5)(9): Now, all aggregates (*skandha*) and bases (*āyatana*), both within and outside the realms, arise from the mind.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "One dharma encompasses all dharmas; that is to say, the mind. The treatise states: "Within all the world, there are only name (*nāma*) and form (*rūpa*).
If one wishes to contemplate them as they truly are, one should contemplate only name and form. The mind is the root of delusion; its meaning is thus. If...
If you wish to investigate [the nature of phenomena], you must cut their roots, just as one cauterizes a disease by finding its precise point.
Now, one should set aside the four aggregates of form and so forth, and attend only to the aggregate of consciousness; for that which observes the aggregates is the mind itself.

*Fuxing* (Vol. 5, Part 1), Section 25: Now, in order to demonstrate that the mind and consciousness serve as the objects of contemplation within the realms below, one first generally grasps the mind as the source from which [phenomena] arise;

this is precisely what was cited previously from the sūtras and śāstras. "The Buddha said... and so forth, which again cites the *Āgama* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* to prove that the mind creates [all things].
"If one wishes... and so forth, which presents two analogies together: the aggregates (*skandha*) of the mundane and supramundane are like branches and like illnesses.

If one contemplates the mind for a single thought-moment—regarding it as the root, the cavity, or the flower—and if the physician’s medicinal decoctions do not exceed one or two kinds and the moxibustion does not exceed one or two points, then contemplating the mind alone would be sufficient.

Why, then, at the end of the fourth section on "Breaking Through Pervasiveness," is there a further analogy for contemplating the remaining aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*)?
The answer is: it is because one wishes to harmonize all phenomena and demonstrate that the objects of contemplation are universal. Therefore...
The following passage illustrates the remaining *dhātus* and *āyatanas*. If one demonstrates the essence of their objects, it is sufficient to contemplate the mind itself;

for the mind is all-pervasive and subsumes all other phenomena. Furthermore, it is not only that the mind subsumes everything, but everything also subsumes the mind. As the *Catuḥsmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states:
"It is not only consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), but also sound-only, fragrance-and-taste-only," and so forth. Now, we shall proceed from the broad to the narrow.

To demonstrate the nature of the objective sphere (*ālambana*), the three categories of aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) could all serve as its objects; however, because these are so vast and diffuse that they are difficult to indicate, one narrows the focus for brevity.

First, by reducing from the four [aggregates] to the three [aggregates], it is like going from a *zhang* to a *chi*. Second, by reducing from the five aggregates to the four [aggregates], it is like going from a *chi* to an *cun*. Third, by reducing from the consciousness aggregate to the other four, it is like going from an *cun* to a *fen*.

This is because the elements and bases encompass a wider range than the aggregates, and within the aggregates, while there are both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned phenomena, the meaning here includes both mind and matter; therefore, "matter" (*rūpa*) is specifically set aside.

The term "mind" (*citta*) when referring to the "abiding mind" (*citte sthāpayati*) includes both the mind and its mental factors (*caitta*). For now, we shall observe the mind-king (*cittarāja*), setting aside the mental factors;

thus, one first observes consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the subsequent cases follow this pattern. Question: Among the five sensory consciousnesses, the five types of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the sixth consciousness, all of which are capable of producing the three types of minds beginning with feeling (*vedanā*), which specific consciousness and which of the three produced minds constitute the object of observation in this practice? Answer: The five [sensory] consciousnesses.

The five consciousnesses and the five mental consciousnesses definitely take present objects; because these objects have not yet become associated with afflictions and remain in a state of neutrality (*avyākṛta*), they do not belong to the category of afflictions within the sixth consciousness.
Rather, it is that which can attract retribution—only when it has been activated—that belongs to the realm of afflictions; other types of discrimination then belong to the present objects.
Although these five consciousnesses and five mental consciousnesses pertain to present objects, they are still to be examined in detail below in the section on "Examining Conditions."
Clarifying the Object of Contemplation.

*Tenyi Shu* (2): For instance, when in *śamatha-vipaśyanā* one discards the "feet" and "inches" and takes only the "inch," this means that within the process of phenomenal construction (*saṃskṛta*), one discards that which is constructed and takes the constructing agent as the object of contemplation; therefore, it is said, "one cuts down the tree and obtains [the wood]."

When one applies moxibustion to the roots and finds the correct point, it is as if removing a thousand branches and a hundred vessels to take up only a single root and a single point to establish the object of contemplation;
therefore, it is said that "first, the object is again clarified. Thus, the *Fuzong* states: "The object is taken to be the single thought-moment of consciousness (*vijñāna-citta*)."

6. Stopping and Contemplation (37): Regarding the sequential application of the three contemplations to other states of mind—if the general state of ignorance is not necessarily suitable, one should further apply them to other minds.
When minds such as desire, anger, or pride arise, they are immediately empty, immediately provisional, and immediately the Middle, just as was explained in the section on the general case (*etc.*).
What has been discussed thus far concerns contemplating the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) in this manner.

The explanation that the other four aggregates (*skandha*) are likewise, and that the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are likewise, is called the completion of the universal investigation of phenomena through the entry into the contemplation of the aggregates, elements, and bases.

*Fuxing* (6b24): Next, regarding the sequential traversal of the single mind: this refers to traversing [the path] by means of the previously mentioned non-dual single mind, both horizontally and vertically.
All minds—indeed, every single mind—is none other than ignorance; therefore, one first contemplates ignorance in its totality.
Since this total view is not yet sufficient, one must open up the general to reveal the particular, for within the mind of ignorance all other states of mind are contained.

Question: The preceding text spoke only of contemplating the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*); how, then, can there be minds such as desire and the like? Answer: First, all minds do not transcend consciousness.

Second, because it is intended as a counterpoint for those who are expedient, it is necessary to list them together. Question: Since greed and the other [afflictions] are subsumed under the category of defilements (*kleśa*), why are they called the "contemplation of the aggregates" (*skandha-vipaśyanā*)?

Answer: Although these are indeed defilements, they are nonetheless subsumed within the aggregates of the wholesome and unwholesome; moreover, this contemplation concerns only the mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*) such as desire and so forth.
Question: If that is so, what difference is there between this and the objects of the defilements? Answer: These are the defilements themselves, whereas those are not the defilements.

Regarding the object (*viṣaya*), it arises from the observation of that [object] and is produced by past and present habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); because it differs from those belonging to the lower realms, it is included here.

In reality, these afflictions (*kleśa*) are not part of the *vipākaskandha* (the aggregate of retribution). Although they are subsumed under the aggregates (*skandha*), they do not exhaustively comprise them;

therefore, the subsequent passage further cites other aggregates as examples. As for the term "successively" (*krama*), it means to inspect or examine in turn. Because they are considered individually in relation to the whole, they are termed "others."

Because it emerges from ignorance, it is called "one mind. Next, regarding the phrase "the preceding section concludes with examples for the remaining aggregates (*skandha*) and bases (*āyatana*)," a question is raised:

Should this not have been at the end of the seventh fascicle, after the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*) were fully explained? If the remaining aggregates and bases are all practiced through the ten vehicles, why are they exemplified here?

The answer is: For the sake of convenience in the exposition (*arthasaṃvāsa*). From the beginning up to this point, the discussion has focused solely on the consciousness-mind (*vijñānacitta*). From this point onward...
From "departing" up to "separation from craving," it is only by encompassing the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) that the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) are established;

therefore, within the context of penetration and obstruction, since one examines the truths and their conditions, these conditions must necessarily be complete with the five aggregates. Among the factors of the path (*mārga-pakṣya-dharma*), the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛty-upasthāna*) cannot be explained in isolation as being merely a single aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Thus, the "primary" and "auxiliary" practices are simply aids to the factors of the path, while the [remaining] three lower sections merely clarify the successive stages of observing the aggregates.

Since they are equal, one must take this as an example to apply it to the remaining aggregates (*skandha*) and bases (*āyatana*), using those remaining aggregates and bases collectively as the objects of contemplation. Question:
What is the difference between contemplating the remaining single mind and the four aggregates? Answer: There are both similarities and differences, as detailed in the preceding analysis.

Furthermore, when contemplating the remaining single mind, one discusses the general and the particular by contrasting mind with mind; when taking the remaining aggregates as examples, one discusses them by contrasting aggregate with aggregate.

Because the characteristics of coarse and subtle phenomena, as well as those that are karmic retribution and those that are not, are distinct, they must be explained separately. Although they are explained separately, one should know their similarities and differences:

the aggregates (*skandha*) do not transcend the mind, and the mind does not depart from the aggregates. The aggregates arise from that which can conceal, while the mind arises from that which can create;
the former is direct concealment and the latter is indirect concealment, both taking the mind as their object.

Cessation and Contemplation (8) (1) Second, regarding the contemplation of the realm of afflictions: if one does not awaken to the aforementioned aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*), it is not appropriate;

yet, through unceasing observation, the afflictions of greed and hatred are stirred and provoked. At that time, one should abandon the contemplation of the aggregates and sense bases and instead contemplate the afflictions.

One should censure the five desires, recognize their faults and transgressions, and discard the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). This is the abandonment of ordinary contemplation of the aggregates and sense bases.
Regarding the retribution within that [state], one seeks a subtle understanding; now, observing its manifestation and flourishing, one gives rise to intense greed and hatred.

*Fuxing* (Vol. 8, Part 1): "Previously, one contemplates the aggregates (*skandha*) and bases (*āyatana*). Since the retributive aggregates are neutral (*avyākṛta*), one seeks a sublime understanding regarding those aggregates;
therefore, the objects of those aggregates are not yet termed afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore, previously, in the passage concerning the sequential examination of a single moment of mind..."

Although greed and hatred are observed, they are not the "present object" (*pratyutpanna-viṣaya*) intended here; rather, all currently arising wholesome or unwholesome afflictions are subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

Therefore, the afflictions that arise based on the aggregates are all termed "objects of the aggregates. The "present object" must necessarily be that which is triggered by the contemplation of the aggregates—such as when it triggers intense greed and so forth—and only then is it called the "present object.
From this present contemplation onward, one specifically raises the "present object," which is distinct from the aggregates, coverings (*nīvaraṇa*), and so forth.
Therefore it is said that they give rise to intense greed and hatred.
Regarding the phrase "the body is oppressed": this refers to the five consciousnesses; "the mind" refers to the sovereign mind-king, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Although the body is oppressed by the eight kinds of suffering, the mind does not feel weary or distressed.

Regarding the sixth [section], (13): "The five consciousnesses and so forth" refers to proximity (*upavicāra*). Turbidity resides in the five consciousnesses, which is why they are called "proximate. They are termed "pressing" (*upagata*) because they directly afflict the self.

Furthermore, it is because the body simultaneously experiences painful objects together with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); this is not the case during the first moment when there is no yet-discriminated [state].
Moreover, the very essence of these five consciousnesses is the maturation (*vipāka*) of the eight types of suffering. How could proximity exceed this? Therefore...

At this time, how could one become weary of and averse to this? Thus, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) cannot achieve meditative contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) by means of this mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);
they can only engage in discrimination to form the three feelings (*vedanā*). Because the meaning of these three feelings is established, it is said that they are "intimately pressing and extreme.

Because they are intimate, each instance of suffering arises through the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) as they encounter their respective objects, and subsequently reaches the sixth consciousness, where it is further differentiated.
Furthermore, what other cause of suffering could there be that would give rise to revulsion?

The *Sphūṭārthā-Abhidharmakośavyākhyā* (Fǔxíng, Vol. 5, Part 2, Section 17) states: "The *Abhidharmakośa* says: 'That which is the six consciousness-bodies immediately preceding their cessation constitutes the substance of the mind-body (*manas-kāya*);

at the moment they cease without interval, they constitute the substance of the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*). At that time, the five consciousnesses likewise rely upon the mind that has just ceased."

The five sense organs serve as the immediate conditions (*pratyaya*), while their respective objects serve as the remote conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*), thereby giving rise to the five consciousnesses. Immediately following the five consciousnesses, when discernment arises, it is termed the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Regarding the preceding critique of the five desires: these refer to the five consciousnesses arising from the five sense organs in response to the five present sensory objects.

Now, abandoning the five hindrances means that the five consciousnesses transform and enter the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), where they retrospectively trace past objects and prospectively anticipate future phenomena regarding the five sensory realms;
these constitute great obstacles within the mind.

*Fuxing* (Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*), Vol. 4, Part 2, Section 14: Regarding the "desire" previously censured, which arises as consciousness is triggered by sense objects (*viṣaya*), it is not merely the five sensory consciousnesses that receive the name "five desires.

Rather, it is because the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes the five present objects as its conditions, giving rise to the five sensory consciousnesses, which then engage in conceptualization and attachment, producing a mind of longing and necessity;
for this reason, it is called "desire. Now, when these five hindrances (*pañcanīvaraṇa*) are said to "turn and enter the mental stage," this refers to the aforementioned [mental] five [desires].

When one enters meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), even though the sense objects have ceased, the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) remains defiled and can still obscure meditative concentration; therefore, they are called "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*).

Whereas the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) exclusively opposes agreeable sense objects, the hindrances [of ill-will and so forth] apply generally to both disagreeable and agreeable objects, being explained in relation to meditative concentration itself.

*Fuxing* (Vol. 5, Part 1, Section 24): If one relies on the Sautrāntika school’s Mahāyāna theory of the simultaneous arising of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which takes as its objects the five present sensory realms as well as past realms—those portions subsumed under the *dharmāyatana* that belong to matter and those that belong to mind—then for the time being, when observing the mind, the mind is itself consciousness.
Regarding the five aggregates (*skandha*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and eighteen elements (*dhātu*) of form and mind:

when distinguishing objects from the broadest to the narrowest, the "consciousness" within the five aggregates refers to the "mind" within form and mind; thus, it is said that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is precisely the mind.

Zhiyi (Sì-míng) states that this refers to the mind of universal ignorance, while Zhìyǐ (Jīng-xī) states that it specifically indicates the substance of the object. Once the object is established, it is followed by its function.
In this contemplation, he specifically raises up the single character "mind" (*citta*), saying:

"The first contemplation of the mind is the inconceivable realm," rather than saying "the first contemplation of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the inconceivable realm. There is a profound purpose for this.

The superficial sensory organs (*tuccha-mūla-indriya*) cannot confront their objects, like those who are blind, deaf, mute, or paralyzed; that which can confront objects is the ultimate sensory organ (*paramārtha-indriya*).

Because consciousness has not yet arisen, they are called the internal faculties (*indriya*). The five consciousnesses are the cognitions produced by the mutual encounter of the faculties and their objects.

The five mental consciousnesses and the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), though differing in name, are both cognitions that arise subsequent to the initial perception and engage in discrimination and deliberation.
Since both matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) are equally the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), they are referred to as "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).

Since there is no form outside of consciousness, as it is the dharma-realm of consciousness, if one analyzes the term "consciousness-only" (vijñapti-mātra), there are two types: first, conceptualizing consciousness, which refers to the mind;

second, non-conceptualizing consciousness, which refers to form. Since there is nothing distinct from this single consciousness—namely, no form existing apart from it—one knows that whether it be consciousness or form, all are consciousness-only.
This is illustrated by the statement "consciousness-only. If one were to speak of "form-only," the principle would be the same.
Because there is no dharma of consciousness apart from form—that is, the dharma-realm of form—if one discriminates and says that "it is only form," there are two types:
first, non-discriminative form, which refers to matter; second, discriminative form, which refers to the mind.
Since there is nothing distinct from form itself that constitutes consciousness, one knows that whether it be consciousness or form, all are "only form. Jingxi said: "Although it is said..."
Regarding matter and mind, there are merely two names; when their essential nature is discussed, they are simply the dharma-nature (dharmatā).
Now, the mind is the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) that can create all dharmas, and matter is the dharma-realm that can create all dharmas—who could say otherwise?
