This refers to external phenomena.

Regarding the statement that "the sands of dust are all the Master’s teachings," one must know that the sands of dust have no separate essence of delusion; they consist entirely of the medicinal prescriptions for the diseases of *dṛṣṭi* (views) and *saṃjñā* (thoughts).

The Dharma is said to be as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; how is this known? It is because the *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation) teaches that there are three aspects to emerging from the provisional:

knowing the illness, identifying the medicine, and the method of administering the medicine. "Knowing the illness" means knowing the illnesses of view-delusion (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and thought-delusion (*bhāva-kleśa*) of all sentient beings;
it means knowing the root of view- and thought-delusion, and knowing their causes and conditions, their duration, and their frequency. "Identifying the medicine" means... [text continues].
There are mundane medicines, supramundane medicines, and the supreme of the supramundane medicines. Regarding the method for administering these medicines:

one must be able to observe the faculties [of the recipient] and provide medicine according to the illness. First, one must personally understand both the medicine and the illness, and furthermore, master the method of administration;
then, one should prescribe the medicine according to the specific ailment, causing others to take joy in it, so that they may be cured by taking it accordingly.
If one can thoroughly understand and realize the three names—sickness, etc.—this is called "shattering the dust-like sands" (*rajas*). If these three are not understood, they are termed "delusions.
Because the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi* and *saṃjñā*) have both general and specific aspects, the dust-like sand delusions have both internal and external dimensions.

If one can distinguish those that generally pertain to views and generally pertain to thoughts, and administer medicine to treat them, one shatters the dust-like sands within the realm; if one can further distinguish [the specific ones], [one shatters the external dust-like sands].
By separately discerning and separately contemplating, one bestows medicine and provides treatment; this is precisely what breaks through the "dust-sands" (rajas) beyond the boundaries.

Thus, we know that the "dust-sands" have no separate essence as afflictions other than referring to the skillful ability to distinguish between the characteristics of the medicines and diseases of *dṛṣṭi* (views) and *cetanā* (thought).

Such a Bodhisattva is called a "Dust-Sand Breaker. Since he takes benefiting sentient beings as his primary concern, he studies the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to extensively serve the masses.

Regarding the medicine of generating discernment for the disease: although one has not yet broken through ignorance outside the realms, one can still study the fourfold Four Noble Truths and their sixteen aspects.
Upon reaching the stage of abiding on the grounds (*bhūmi*), one breaks through a single grade of ignorance; only then is it called "true benefit.

Thus, the afflictions as numerous as motes of dust belong to the category of others—the diseases of view-delusion and thought-delusion (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *kleśa-vicikitsā*). It is these very view-delusions and thought-delusions [that must be severed].
The causes and conditions for the duration and intensity of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), as well as the medicinal remedies for treating these views and afflictions, are as follows:
the reason one cannot be led into rebirth is that one has already severed one's own views and afflictions long ago;

it is simply that one has not yet discerned how the views and afflictions of others lead to one's own rebirth. Thus, one knows that the delusions existing within one's own domain [are what truly bind].
These [afflictions] consist solely of the two types of ignorance—those of view and thought—which are capable of drawing forth birth within and beyond the realms.

To desire to extinguish these delusions, one cultivates emptiness and the Middle Way to sever these two types of affliction; thus, because the merit of one's own practice is fulfilled, it is said that "one's own practice resides solely in emptiness.

However, regarding the office of a Bodhisattva, which lies in benefiting others, from the very first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), sentient beings are the primary foundation.

Because this fundamental text proclaims the boundless vows to deliver all beings, one must distinguish for others the various layers of the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*), so that all people may develop weary detachment from birth and death and forever emerge from the cycle of saṃsāra.

If one cannot thoroughly penetrate these dharma-gates of views and thoughts, yet remains seated amidst "dust and sand" [of delusions], how can one act as a guide for sentient beings? Therefore, it is called "dust."
Only Master Siming alone has understood that these delusions, which obstruct transformation and guidance, consist of the "dust and sand" of afflictions;
thus it is said that the layers of view-delusions and thought-delusions are like dust and sand.

To interpret it in this way is not only to recognize the essence of these dust-and-sand delusions, but also to perceive the principles elucidated by the Four Teachings, thereby personally entering the Way. Therefore, it is only from the perspective of the True and the Middle [that this is fully realized].
Because one emerges from the provisional to transform sentient beings, the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is integrated;

that is, this very practice for oneself serves as the means to transform others, leading them to cultivate according to these four teachings and two principles. Therefore, the conventional truth pervades all four teachings.

When distinguished within the boundaries of the internal and external, it is called "conventional" when it breaks through the dust-like delusions (*rajas*), and it is called "emptiness" when it breaks through duality.

Because of delusion, one knows that conventional truth lies in the study of the Dharma-gates; for the sake of others, one makes distinctions, heals their illnesses, and breaks through their birth-and-death.
Because others do not know these things are illnesses, they invite immeasurable birth-and-death and undergo immeasurable retributions.
Thus, the *Four Foundations of Mindfulness* says: "Immeasurable grasping at signs brings about immeasurable birth-and-death."
As many as the sands of the Ganges, they summon immeasurable retributions; through immeasurable ignorance, one receives the immeasurable reward-body (*vipāka-kāya*).
If the text says, "If there were no four abidings, the segmented birth would not arise; if there were no ignorance, the provisional means would not arise;
if there were no ignorance, the true reward would not arise," this is the principle of correlating afflictions with their respective lands. (Text) The remainder...
